Aldehydes have one fewer donating alkyl group
electrophiles.why: Alkyl groups are weakly electron-donating and bulky; a ketone has two of them stabilizing and shielding the carbonyl carbon, while an aldehyde's single alkyl group (plus a small hydrogen) leaves it more electrophilic and more accessible to nucleophiles.

electrophiles.q: An aromatic ring undergoing electrophilic aromatic substitution reacts with an electrophile such as Br+ generated from Br2 and a Lewis acid catalyst.
electrophiles.why: In electrophilic aromatic substitution, a Lewis acid (like FeBr3) helps generate a highly electrophilic species (such as Br+) that the electron-rich aromatic ring then attacks as the nucleophile.

electrophiles.q: Which statement correctly relates electrophile strength to reaction rate with a given nucleophile?
options: Stronger electrophiles (more electron-poor, more accessible) generally react faster with a given nucleophile, all else equal
Stronger electrophiles generally react more slowly because they are more stable
Electrophile strength has no bearing on reaction rate
Only nucleophile strength affects reaction rate, never electrophile strength
electrophiles.why: Just as nucleophile strength affects rate, a more electron-deficient and accessible electrophile is attacked more readily and rapidly by a given nucleophile, since there is a greater driving force for electron transfer.

electrophiles.q: In a protonated ketone the plus sign is drawn on oxygen. Which atom does a nucleophile attack?
options: The oxygen, because that is where the charge is drawn
The carbon, because that is the atom short of density
Neither, since a protonated ketone resists nucleophiles
Whichever of the two the nucleophile reaches first
electrophiles.why: A drawn charge is formal bookkeeping, not a measure of electron deficiency. Oxygen with three bonds and a plus still has lone pairs and a full octet; the carbon is the atom that is short, and the minor contributor placing the positive charge on it says so. Hunt for the deficient atom, not the symbol.

electrophiles.q: Why does conjugation of a carbonyl with an adjacent C=C double bond (as in an enone, an alpha,beta-unsaturated ketone) create a second electrophilic site at the beta carbon?
options: Conjugation has no effect on electrophilicity anywhere in the molecule
The beta carbon becomes negatively charged instead
Resonance places partial positive charge on the beta carbon
Only the carbonyl carbon is ever electrophilic in an enone
electrophiles.why: A resonance structure of an enone shows the C=C pi electrons shifting all the way to the very electronegative oxygen, leaving a positive charge on the beta carbon; this explains why nucleophiles can add either directly to the carbonyl carbon or to this more remote beta carbon (conjugate addition).

electrophiles.q: Which of the following best explains why CO2 (carbon dioxide) reacts readily as an electrophile with strong nucleophiles like Grignard reagents?
options: CO2's oxygen atoms are the electrophilic sites, not carbon
CO2 cannot react with any nucleophile
Two oxygens leave its carbon very electron-poor
electrophiles.why: The two electronegative oxygens withdraw significant electron density from the central carbon, making it quite electrophilic; Grignard reagents readily attack this carbon to eventually form a carboxylic acid after workup.

electrophiles.q: Why does protonating a ketone's oxygen make its carbon a far better electrophile?
options: The proton attaches to the carbon and gives it a positive charge
A contributor now places a full positive charge on that carbon
The carbonyl pi bond is destroyed outright by the incoming proton
Protonation turns the oxygen itself into the site of attack
electrophiles.why: A protonated carbonyl has two contributors: one with the plus on oxygen and every octet full, and one with the plus on carbon and only six electrons there. The second is minor but real, and its share of the hybrid is what deepens the carbon's positive character. That is why so many carbonyl reactions are run under acid.

electrophiles.q: A terminal alkyne's acidic proton can be removed by a strong base. In this acid-base reaction, which species is acting as the electrophile?
options: The acidic hydrogen atom on the terminal alkyne carbon
electrophiles.why: The acidic C–H proton is the electrophilic site being attacked by the base's lone pair; the carbon framework itself is not what is directly attacked in this proton-transfer step.

electrophiles.q: What makes sulfonate esters (like tosylates, R-OTs) useful electrophiles in substitution reactions, much like alkyl halides?
options: Sulfonates make carbon into a nucleophile
Sulfonate esters have no leaving group at all
Sulfur is the site that nucleophiles attack, not carbon
electrophiles.why: Like halides, the oxygen in a sulfonate ester polarizes the attached carbon (making it electrophilic), and the resulting sulfonate anion is exceptionally stable (weak base) due to extensive resonance and charge delocalization, making it depart easily as a leaving group.

electrophiles.q: In general, increasing the number of electron-donating alkyl substituents directly on an electrophilic carbon tends to:
options: Increase its electrophilicity by adding more positive character
Have absolutely no effect on electrophilicity under any circumstances
Decrease its electrophilicity by donating density and bulk
Convert the carbon into a full nucleophile
electrophiles.why: Alkyl groups are weak electron donors (by induction/hyperconjugation) and also physically block approach, so more substitution at a potentially electrophilic carbon generally reduces how strongly and how accessibly electrophilic it is (this is part of why more substituted carbonyls are less reactive toward nucleophiles).

electrophiles.q: A tertiary carbocation forms more readily than a primary carbocation.
electrophiles.why: Alkyl groups donate electron density to an adjacent positive charge, so a tertiary cation sits lower in energy than a primary one and the ionization that produces it is easier. Every carbocation remains a strong electrophile once formed; this comparison is about how readily they appear, not how hungry they are.

electrophiles.q: Which best explains why methyl iodide (CH3I) is often used as a model electrophile in SN2 reactions despite iodine being a relatively weak inductive electron-withdrawer compared to fluorine?
options: Iodine makes the carbon extremely electron-rich
Methyl iodide has no electrophilic carbon
Fluorine is always a better leaving group than iodine
Iodide is an excellent, polarizable leaving group
electrophiles.why: Even though the C–I bond is only modestly polarized, the weak, long C–I bond breaks easily and iodide is a very stable, weakly basic leaving group, so the overall reaction is fast even if carbon itself is not the most electron-poor among the halomethanes.

leaving-groups.q: A good leaving group is generally one that is:
options: Stable once it departs with the electron pair (weak base)
Unable to hold a negative charge
leaving-groups.why: Good leaving groups are stable as the departed anion/molecule — i.e., weak bases, since weak bases are comfortable holding the extra electron density.

leaving-groups.q: Which of these is typically the best leaving group?
leaving-groups.why: Iodide is a large, very weak base — very stable once it leaves — making it an excellent leaving group, unlike OH⁻, NH₂⁻, or CH₃⁻ which are strong bases.

leaving-groups.q: An alcohol does not react with NaBr, but the same alcohol with HBr gives the alkyl bromide. What does the acid change?
options: It makes bromide a stronger nucleophile than it was before
It protonates the OH, so the group that leaves is water
It raises the temperature of the reaction mixture
It adds positive charge directly onto the reacting carbon
leaving-groups.why: Nothing was wrong with the nucleophile: bromide is the same species in both flasks. The blocked step was the departure, because hydroxide (pKaH 15.7) will not leave a carbon. Protonation changes the departing species to neutral water (pKaH −1.7), and the reaction goes.

leaving-groups.q: A good leaving group should be the conjugate base of a:
leaving-groups.why: Good leaving groups are stable, weak bases, which are exactly the conjugate bases of strong acids (like HI, HBr, or TsOH); weak bases hold their extra electron pair loosely and leave readily.

leaving-groups.q: Which reagent turns R–OH into a substrate with an excellent leaving group without strong acid?
leaving-groups.why: TsCl with pyridine converts the alcohol to a tosylate under mild, neutral conditions. Sulfuric acid also activates the OH, by protonation, but every acid-sensitive group in the molecule then has to survive it; the other two reagents do nothing useful here at all.

leaving-groups.q: Rank Cl-, Br-, and I- in order of decreasing ability to act as a leaving group.
options: All three are identical leaving groups
leaving-groups.why: Leaving group ability tracks with anion stability (weak basicity); I- is the weakest base of the three halides and the most stable once it leaves, making it the best leaving group, followed by Br- then Cl-.

leaving-groups.q: Why is F- generally a poor leaving group compared to the other halides even though fluorine is the most electronegative halogen?
options: Fluorine cannot form a stable anion
Fluoride is a strong base and holds its charge tightly
The C–F bond is the weakest of all the C–halogen bonds
Fluoride is actually the best leaving group of the halides
leaving-groups.why: F- is a much stronger base than the other halide ions because its small size concentrates negative charge, making the C–F bond strong and fluoride reluctant to depart with the electron pair, unlike the larger, more stable, weaker-base halide ions.

leaving-groups.q: A tosylate group (OTs-, the conjugate base of a strong sulfonic acid) is considered an excellent leaving group for the same general reason that halides are, namely:
options: It is a strong base that holds electrons tightly
It has no negative charge when it leaves
It is a very weak, highly resonance-stabilized base that readily accommodates the departing negative charge
It forms only under basic conditions
leaving-groups.why: The negative charge on a sulfonate leaving group is delocalized over multiple oxygens by resonance (and stabilized further by the electron-withdrawing sulfonyl group), making it a very weak base and thus an excellent, stable leaving group.

leaving-groups.q: Amide ion (NH2-) is generally considered one of the worst common leaving groups in organic chemistry.
leaving-groups.why: NH2- is the conjugate base of ammonia, an extremely weak acid, making amide ion an extremely strong base that holds on tightly to its electrons and essentially never leaves under normal conditions.

leaving-groups.q: Why does protonating the oxygen of an alcohol (forming R-OH2+) convert a poor leaving group into a good one?
options: Protonation removes the leaving group entirely
Protonation has no effect on leaving group ability
Protonation makes oxygen a better nucleophile instead
Protonation gives neutral water, a weak base
leaving-groups.why: Once protonated, the group that leaves is neutral water rather than negatively charged hydroxide; water is a much weaker base (conjugate base of the strong acid H3O+) and leaves far more easily, which is why acid catalysis activates alcohols for substitution/elimination.

leaving-groups.q: Which of the following is generally NOT a good leaving group under typical SN1/SN2 conditions?
leaving-groups.why: A carbanion like CH3- is an extraordinarily strong base (conjugate base of methane, an exceedingly weak acid) and essentially never acts as a leaving group under normal conditions, unlike halides or neutral water.

leaving-groups.q: Resonance stabilization of the departing anion (as in a sulfonate or carboxylate leaving group) generally makes that group a better leaving group.
leaving-groups.why: Delocalizing the negative charge over several atoms lowers the energy of the anion, making it more stable (a weaker base) and thus more willing to depart, which is exactly why sulfonate esters are popular synthetic leaving groups.

leaving-groups.q: In the reaction of an epoxide with a nucleophile under basic conditions, what effectively serves as the leaving group when the ring opens?
options: The ring oxygen, which becomes an alkoxide as the strained C–O bond breaks
leaving-groups.why: As a nucleophile attacks a ring carbon, the strained C–O bond breaks and the oxygen (now bearing the electron pair) becomes an alkoxide leaving group still attached elsewhere in the molecule, relieving ring strain.

leaving-groups.q: Why is it generally true that weaker bases make better leaving groups?
options: Weak bases are more electronegative than strong bases in every case
Weak bases always carry a positive charge
A weak base holds negative charge comfortably, so it departs readily
There is no real relationship between base strength and leaving group ability
leaving-groups.why: Base strength measures how strongly a species wants to grab and hold a proton (or, analogously, electron density); weak bases are inherently stable on their own and 'happy' to leave with the bonding electron pair, which is the core reason leaving group ability and base strength are inversely related.

leaving-groups.q: Which species would you predict to be a better leaving group: the conjugate base of acetic acid (CH3COO-, pKa of acid ≈ 4.8) or the conjugate base of ethanol (CH3CH2O-, pKa of acid ≈ 16)?
options: Ethoxide, because alcohols are weaker acids
They are equally good leaving groups
Neither can ever act as a leaving group
Acetate, because it is the conjugate base of the stronger acid and is therefore a weaker, more stable base
leaving-groups.why: Acetic acid (pKa ≈ 4.8) is a much stronger acid than ethanol (pKa ≈ 16), meaning acetate is a much weaker base than ethoxide and therefore a considerably better leaving group.

leaving-groups.q: A carbocation can be thought of as having 'lost' a leaving group from the original substrate. Which best describes the leaving group's role right before departure?
options: It must be stable once it takes the electron pair
It must remain a strong nucleophile even as it departs
It must become more reactive after leaving
It plays no role in determining the reaction rate
leaving-groups.why: Because the leaving group departs with the bonding electrons, its ability to stabilize that extra electron density (i.e., be a weak, stable base) directly controls how readily ionization occurs and therefore the rate of SN1/E1 reactions.

leaving-groups.q: Converting an alcohol's -OH into a mesylate (OMs) or tosylate (OTs) group before a substitution reaction is a common strategy because:
options: It makes the oxygen a stronger base
It turns a poor leaving group into a sulfonate
Mesylates and tosylates are never good leaving groups
It removes the need for any leaving group at all
leaving-groups.why: Sulfonate esters are prepared under mild, non-acidic conditions and then provide a highly stabilized, weak-base leaving group, giving chemists a practical alternative to strongly acidic activation of alcohols.

leaving-groups.q: A proposed mechanism has a nucleophile attacking a carbon while hydroxide is pushed off that same carbon. What is wrong with it?
options: Nothing is wrong; this is an ordinary substitution step
Hydroxide is a strong base and will not leave unassisted
The nucleophile ought to attack the oxygen instead
Two arrows may not be drawn within one mechanism step
leaving-groups.why: Hydroxide is the conjugate base of water, pKaH 15.7, so it is a strong base and does not depart from carbon on its own. The missing piece is an activation step — protonate the OH, tosylate it, or convert it to a halide — and only then can something leave.

leaving-groups.q: Which leaving group would most likely make an SN2 reaction proceed fastest, all else being equal: Cl-, Br-, or a tosylate (OTs-)?
options: Cl-, because it is the smallest
Br-, because halides are always best
Tosylate, a very weak, stable base
All three give identical reaction rates
leaving-groups.why: Tosylate's negative charge is spread over three oxygens and stabilized further by the adjacent aromatic sulfonyl group, making it one of the best common leaving groups, generally outperforming simple halides.

leaving-groups.q: An amine (R–NH₂) is a poor leaving group, but it can depart once its nitrogen carries a positive charge, as in R–NH₃⁺ or R–NR₃⁺, because what leaves is then a neutral amine.
leaving-groups.why: The amide anion ⁻NH₂ is far too strong a base to leave a carbon. Put a positive charge on the nitrogen first, by protonation or by alkylation to a quaternary ammonium, and the departing species is a neutral amine rather than an anion, which is a much cheaper thing to become.

leaving-groups.q: Why does pKa of the leaving group's conjugate acid serve as a useful predictor of leaving group ability?
options: Higher pKa always means a better leaving group
pKa has no relationship to leaving group ability
pKa only matters for nucleophiles, not leaving groups
Lower pKa means a weaker, more stable base
leaving-groups.why: Since leaving groups are conjugate bases, the pKa of their conjugate acid directly reflects base strength: a low pKa (strong acid) means a weak, stable conjugate base, and therefore a good leaving group.

leaving-groups.q: Which of these would you predict to be the best leaving group based on its conjugate acid's strength: leaving group X whose conjugate acid has pKa 9, or leaving group Y whose conjugate acid has pKa -7?
options: Leaving group Y, the much weaker and more stable base
Leaving group X, because higher pKa means a better leaving group
Both are equally good leaving groups regardless of pKa
pKa values cannot be used to compare leaving groups
leaving-groups.why: A conjugate acid pKa of -7 corresponds to an extremely strong acid (such as HI), meaning its conjugate base is extremely weak and stable — exactly the profile of an excellent leaving group, far better than one with a conjugate acid pKa of 9.

leaving-groups.q: Cyanide ion (CN-) is generally a poor leaving group.
leaving-groups.why: HCN is only a moderately weak acid (pKa around 9), making cyanide a fairly strong base relative to halides or sulfonates, so it does not readily depart as a leaving group under typical substitution conditions.

leaving-groups.q: In a Grignard or organolithium reagent, the carbon bonded to the metal behaves as a strong nucleophile/base. If this carbon were instead asked to act as a leaving group, what would you predict?
options: It would be an excellent leaving group, since strong bases always make excellent leaving groups too
It would be an extremely poor leaving group, since strong bases resist departing
Leaving group ability is unrelated to nucleophilicity or basicity in this case
Carbanions cannot be discussed in terms of leaving group ability at all
leaving-groups.why: Because strong bases/nucleophiles and good leaving groups are generally opposite ends of the same stability spectrum, a reactive carbanion (strong base) is a very poor leaving group — it simply does not want to depart and take the electron pair in an already-stable low-energy form elsewhere.

leaving-groups.q: Which best explains why water (H2O) can act as a leaving group in acid-catalyzed reactions but hydroxide (OH-) generally cannot under the same mild acidic conditions?
options: Water and hydroxide are equally good leaving groups always
Hydroxide has no electron pairs to take with it
Water is a weak base; hydroxide is a much stronger one
Water cannot leave under any circumstances
leaving-groups.why: Protonation shifts the leaving species from hydroxide (conjugate base of water, pKa ≈ 15.7, a fairly strong base) to water itself (conjugate base of H3O+, pKa ≈ -1.7, a very weak base), dramatically improving its willingness to leave.

leaving-groups.q: Which reagent would you supply to convert an alcohol directly into an alkyl bromide in one step?
options: Sodium bromide, which supplies bromide ion
Phosphorus tribromide, which activates and substitutes
Bromine, which adds across a double bond
Sodium hydroxide, which deprotonates the alcohol
leaving-groups.why: Bromide on its own cannot displace hydroxide, and deprotonating the alcohol makes the leaving group worse rather than better. PBr₃ converts the OH into a good leaving group and delivers bromide in the same operation, which is why it is the standard one-step route.

leaving-groups.q: Phosphate groups (such as those in ATP) are biologically important leaving groups. Why are they effective leaving groups despite carrying a full negative charge?
options: Phosphate has no resonance stabilization at all
Phosphate groups are actually poor leaving groups in every biological context
Phosphate always leaves as a neutral, uncharged species
Its charge is delocalized over several oxygens by resonance
leaving-groups.why: Like sulfonates and carboxylates, phosphate leaving groups spread their negative charge over several oxygen atoms via resonance, lowering their basicity and making them effective leaving groups despite the formal negative charge, which is central to many biochemical substitution reactions.

leaving-groups.q: Which of the following best ranks typical leaving group ability from best to worst: I-, OH-, OTs-?
leaving-groups.why: Hydroxide is a strong base and a poor leaving group, so it is clearly last. Tosylate and iodide are both conjugate bases of very strong acids and belong to the same top tier; measured substitution rates put tosylate marginally ahead of iodide, which is the order keyed here. Getting the tiers right matters more than the order inside one.

leaving-groups.q: A trifluoromethanesulfonate group (triflate, OTf-) is considered one of the best leaving groups known, even better than tosylate, largely because of the strongly electron-withdrawing fluorines.
leaving-groups.why: The three highly electronegative fluorine atoms further withdraw electron density and help delocalize/stabilize the negative charge on the departing sulfonate oxygen, making triflate an exceptionally weak base and outstanding leaving group, even better than a simple tosylate.

leaving-groups.q: If a leaving group is a poor one (a strong base) in a proposed SN1 mechanism, what is the most likely consequence for the reaction?
options: The reaction proceeds at the same rate regardless of leaving group quality
Ionization becomes rate-limiting and the reaction is very slow
The reaction mechanism switches automatically to E2
leaving-groups.why: Since SN1 rate depends on how readily the substrate ionizes, a poor leaving group (strong base, high-energy anion) makes that ionization step slow or unfavorable, often requiring the substrate to be activated first (e.g., protonation or conversion to a sulfonate) before substitution can proceed.

electron-rich-poor.q: An electron-rich atom in a mechanism tends to act as a(n):
electron-rich-poor.why: Electron-rich atoms have extra electron density to donate, making them nucleophilic.

electron-rich-poor.q: Why is the carbon of C=O electron-poor while the oxygen is electron-rich?
options: There is no difference — they’re equal
electron-rich-poor.why: The electronegativity difference polarizes the pi bond, making O δ− (electron-rich) and C δ+ (electron-poor).

electron-rich-poor.q: In a C–Mg bond (as in a Grignard reagent), which atom is electron-rich?
electron-rich-poor.why: Carbon is more electronegative than magnesium, so the bonding electrons sit closer to carbon, making it electron-rich (and strongly nucleophilic/basic).

electron-rich-poor.q: An electron-poor atom in a mechanism generally acts as a(n):
electron-rich-poor.why: Electron-poor atoms lack sufficient electron density and therefore seek it out from an electron-rich partner, which is exactly the defining behavior of an electrophile.

electron-rich-poor.q: A carbon bonded directly to a highly electronegative atom like oxygen, nitrogen, or a halogen is generally electron-poor relative to a carbon bonded only to other carbons and hydrogens.
electron-rich-poor.why: Electronegative substituents pull electron density away from the attached carbon through the polar sigma bond (an inductive effect), leaving that carbon partially positive (δ+) relative to one surrounded only by similarly electronegative C and H.

electron-rich-poor.q: In CH₃–CH₂–O–CH₂–CH₂–Cl, which carbon does a nucleophile attack?
options: A carbon next to the oxygen, the most electronegative atom here
The carbon bonded to chlorine, which is δ+ and holds a leaving group
The terminal methyl carbon, the least hindered site in the chain
None of them, since ethers resist attack by any nucleophile
electron-rich-poor.why: Oxygen (3.44) is more electronegative than chlorine (3.16), so the carbons flanking the ether oxygen are polarized at least as strongly as the Cl-bearing one. What decides it is the second condition: only the chlorine-bearing carbon holds a group that will actually depart. Electron-poor makes a carbon a candidate; a leaving group makes it the answer.

electron-rich-poor.q: In an enolate, the negative charge is delocalized between the alpha carbon and the carbonyl oxygen. Which site is more electron-rich in the major resonance contributor?
options: The alpha carbon, since carbon always holds more electron density than oxygen
The oxygen, since it is more electronegative and better able to stabilize the negative charge
Both are equally electron-rich with no distinction possible
Neither site carries any electron density
electron-rich-poor.why: The resonance structure placing the negative charge on oxygen is the larger contributor to the hybrid, since oxygen is far better suited to stabilize a negative charge than carbon is — making the oxygen the more electron-rich site overall.

electron-rich-poor.q: An aromatic ring substituted with an electron-donating group, such as an amine or alkoxy group, becomes more electron-rich overall, making it more reactive toward electrophiles.
electron-rich-poor.why: Electron-donating substituents push additional electron density into the aromatic ring (by resonance and/or induction), increasing the ring's overall nucleophilicity and accelerating electrophilic aromatic substitution.

electron-rich-poor.q: Which atom in a hydrogen halide (H–X, such as H–Cl) is electron-poor and thus reacts as the acidic proton source?
options: Neither atom has any partial charge
electron-rich-poor.why: The halogen is more electronegative than hydrogen, pulling bonding electron density toward itself and leaving hydrogen partially positive (δ+), which is why H–X compounds act as proton (acid) sources.

electron-rich-poor.q: A nitro group (-NO2) attached to an aromatic ring makes the ring more electron-rich due to strong electron donation by resonance.
electron-rich-poor.why: The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing (both by induction and resonance, since nitrogen is positively charged with electronegative oxygens), making an attached ring more electron-poor, not electron-rich.

electron-rich-poor.q: Why does an alkene substituted with several alkyl groups (a more substituted alkene) tend to be more electron-rich and thus a better nucleophile than a less substituted one?
options: Alkyl groups withdraw electron density from the pi bond through induction
Substitution pattern has no effect on an alkene's electron density
More substituted alkenes always have fewer electrons overall
Alkyl groups donate electron density into the pi bond
electron-rich-poor.why: Alkyl groups are weak electron donors (through hyperconjugation with adjacent C–H/C–C bonds and simple induction), so each additional alkyl substituent on a double bond increases the electron density of the pi bond, making the alkene a better nucleophile.

electron-rich-poor.q: Comparing a C–F bond to a C–I bond, which carbon is more electron-poor (more δ+)?
options: The carbon bonded to iodine, because iodine is larger
Both carbons have identical electron density
electron-rich-poor.why: Fluorine's very high electronegativity creates a strongly polarized C–F bond, pulling substantial electron density away from carbon, more so than the much less electronegative iodine does in a C–I bond, even though the C–I bond is actually weaker and breaks more easily.

electron-rich-poor.q: A carbanion is an example of an electron-rich carbon species, while a carbocation is an example of an electron-poor carbon species.
electron-rich-poor.why: A carbanion carries a full negative charge and a lone pair (electron-rich, nucleophilic), while a carbocation has an empty orbital and a full positive charge (electron-poor, electrophilic) — they sit at opposite ends of the electron-density spectrum.

electron-rich-poor.q: In an enol (the tautomer of a ketone with a C=C–OH arrangement), which carbon is electron-rich and acts as the nucleophilic site?
options: The carbon bonded directly to oxygen
The carbon at the far end of the double bond, away from oxygen (the alpha carbon)
Neither carbon has extra electron density
The oxygen atom itself is the only reactive site
electron-rich-poor.why: A resonance structure of the enol places a lone pair from oxygen into the pi system, shifting electron density to the terminal (alpha) carbon and giving it significant nucleophilic, electron-rich character, which is why enols react with electrophiles at that carbon.

electron-rich-poor.q: Why is the nitrogen of an amide less electron-rich (less basic/nucleophilic) than the nitrogen of a simple amine?
options: Amide nitrogen has no lone pair at all
Amide nitrogen is bonded to more hydrogens than amine nitrogen
The amide lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl
There is no difference between amide and amine nitrogen electron density
electron-rich-poor.why: Conjugation of the nitrogen lone pair with the carbonyl pi system pulls electron density away from nitrogen toward the electronegative oxygen, leaving the amide nitrogen considerably less electron-rich than an isolated amine nitrogen.

electron-rich-poor.q: Which of these atoms, all found within a molecule of acetonitrile (CH3-C≡N), is the most electron-rich and would be expected to act as a nucleophile/base site?
options: All atoms have identical electron density
The nitrogen atom, due to its lone pair
electron-rich-poor.why: The nitrogen of a nitrile carries a lone pair in an sp orbital and, despite nitrogen's electronegativity pulling some density toward it within the triple bond, this lone pair is the most electron-rich, available site for interacting with electrophiles or protons.

electron-rich-poor.q: An amino group on a benzene ring makes the ring more reactive toward electrophiles, though nitrogen is more electronegative than carbon. Which effect explains it?
options: Induction, because electronegativity sets the outcome here
Resonance, because the nitrogen lone pair is donated in
Neither, since the effect comes from the size of the group
Both, since the two effects act in the same direction
electron-rich-poor.why: The two effects point opposite ways in this molecule. Induction pulls density out of the ring, because nitrogen is the more electronegative atom, while resonance pushes a whole lone pair in. A relocated pair beats a tilted one, so resonance wins and the ring ends up electron-rich.

electron-rich-poor.q: Between the carbon and the boron atom in a carbon-boron bond (as found in certain organoborane reagents), which atom is electron-rich?
options: Carbon, because boron is less electronegative than carbon
Boron, because it is a metalloid
Neither atom has partial charge in a C–B bond
electron-rich-poor.why: Boron's electronegativity is lower than carbon's, so the shared electrons in a C–B bond sit closer to carbon, making that carbon somewhat electron-rich, similar to the polarization seen in Grignard C–Mg bonds though less pronounced.

electron-rich-poor.q: Inductive electron withdrawal through sigma bonds (as from a nearby halogen) typically has its strongest effect on the immediately adjacent atom and weakens rapidly as you move further away through the chain.
electron-rich-poor.why: Inductive effects act through sigma bonds and fall off quickly with distance, so a halogen's electron-withdrawing influence is strongest on the carbon it's directly attached to and becomes much weaker two or three carbons away.

electron-rich-poor.q: Why does protonation of a carbonyl oxygen (under acid catalysis) make the attached carbonyl carbon even more electron-poor than it already was?
options: Protonation adds extra electron density to the whole system
Protonation leaves oxygen positive, pulling more density
Protonation occurs on carbon, not oxygen, in this mechanism
Protonation has no effect on the carbon's electron density
electron-rich-poor.why: Adding a full positive charge directly onto the already electronegative oxygen dramatically increases its pull on the shared electrons, making the attached carbon even more electron-deficient and far more reactive to nucleophilic attack.

electron-rich-poor.q: Which species is more electron-rich at its reactive carbon: a simple alkene (C=C) or an enolate ion (C=C–O-)?
options: The simple alkene, because it has fewer atoms
The enolate, whose oxygen donates by resonance
Enolates have no electron density on carbon at all
electron-rich-poor.why: The negatively charged oxygen of an enolate strongly donates its extra electron density through resonance into the adjacent carbon, making the enolate's nucleophilic carbon considerably more electron-rich (and thus more reactive) than a simple, unactivated alkene carbon.

electron-rich-poor.q: A sulfur atom in a thiol (R-SH) is generally considered more electron-rich and nucleophilic than the oxygen in a comparable alcohol (R-OH), even though oxygen is more electronegative.
electron-rich-poor.why: Although oxygen holds its own electrons more tightly (higher electronegativity, stronger base), sulfur's larger, more polarizable, more loosely held electron cloud makes it more willing to donate electron density in bond-forming reactions, so it behaves as more nucleophilic/electron-rich in a reactivity sense.

electron-rich-poor.q: In the molecule CH3-CH2-Cl, which carbon carries the greater partial positive charge (is more electron-poor)?
options: The terminal CH3 carbon, farther from chlorine
Both carbons carry identical partial charge
Neither carbon has any partial charge
The CH2 carbon directly bonded to chlorine
electron-rich-poor.why: The carbon directly bonded to the electronegative chlorine experiences the strongest inductive pull of electron density, making it the most electron-poor carbon in the molecule; the effect diminishes sharply at the next carbon over.

electron-rich-poor.q: Why is the oxygen of a carboxylic acid's hydroxyl group (the O–H oxygen, not the carbonyl oxygen) considered relatively electron-poor compared to the oxygen of a simple alcohol?
options: Its lone pairs are delocalized into the carbonyl
It is bonded to more hydrogens than an alcohol oxygen
Carboxylic acid oxygens have no lone pairs
There is no difference between the two oxygens
electron-rich-poor.why: One of the hydroxyl oxygen's lone pairs conjugates with the carbonyl pi system, pulling electron density toward the carbonyl oxygen; this depletion of electron density on the OH oxygen is part of why the O–H bond is more acidic (and the oxygen less basic) than in a simple alcohol.

electron-rich-poor.q: A carbon at the end of a polarized C≡N (nitrile) triple bond is generally electron-poor and can act as an electrophile toward strong nucleophiles like Grignard reagents.
electron-rich-poor.why: Nitrogen's higher electronegativity polarizes the triple bond, leaving the nitrile carbon partially positive and electrophilic, which is why Grignard and organolithium reagents can add to nitriles to eventually form ketones after hydrolysis.

electron-rich-poor.q: Which best explains why the alpha carbon of an alkyl halide (directly bonded to the halogen) is electron-poor, yet the beta carbon (one carbon further away) shows only a weak inductive effect?
options: The beta carbon is always more electron-poor than the alpha carbon
Inductive effects fall off with each bond traversed
Halogens only affect carbons they are not bonded to
Inductive effects have no distance dependence
electron-rich-poor.why: Inductive (sigma-bond) electron withdrawal falls off rapidly with each bond, so while the alpha carbon feels the halogen's pull strongly, the beta carbon experiences only a faint residual effect.

electron-rich-poor.q: Why can an enamine's beta carbon (the carbon two atoms from nitrogen, across the double bond) be considered especially electron-rich and strongly nucleophilic?
options: Nitrogen withdraws electron density from that carbon
Beta carbons are never affected by resonance
The nitrogen lone pair donates into the pi system
Enamines have no nitrogen lone pair available to donate
electron-rich-poor.why: Just as an enolate's oxygen lone pair activates the alpha carbon through resonance, an enamine's nitrogen lone pair conjugates through the C=C pi system to make the beta carbon unusually electron-rich and nucleophilic, a key feature exploited in many carbon-carbon bond-forming reactions.

electron-rich-poor.q: Both inductive and resonance (conjugative) effects can make a given atom more electron-poor or more electron-rich, and in some molecules these two effects can act in opposing directions on the same atom.
electron-rich-poor.why: A classic example is a halogen substituent on an aromatic ring: it withdraws electron density inductively (making the ring somewhat electron-poor overall) while donating electron density by resonance at the ortho/para positions (making those specific positions more electron-rich), so the two effects can genuinely pull in opposite directions.

electron-rich-poor.q: Which contributor of CH₂=CH–CHO puts a positive charge on the beta carbon, and what does it predict?
options: The one moving the C=C electrons toward oxygen; nucleophiles can attack there
The one moving an oxygen lone pair onto carbon; the beta carbon turns rich
The one moving a hydrogen onto the oxygen; the molecule becomes an enol
No contributor does, since the beta carbon is three bonds from the oxygen
electron-rich-poor.why: Push the C=C electrons into the central C–C bond and the carbonyl pi electrons onto oxygen, and the result carries a minus on oxygen and a plus on the far, beta carbon. That contributor is a genuine part of the hybrid, which is why nucleophiles add at the beta position — conjugate addition.

electron-rich-poor.q: A bromonium ion intermediate (formed when Br2 adds to an alkene) carries its formal positive charge on bromine, so it is bromine itself, not either ring carbon, that an incoming nucleophile attacks.
electron-rich-poor.why: Although bromine formally bears the positive charge in the strained three-membered bromonium ring, the nucleophile actually attacks one of the electrophilic ring carbons from the backside, displacing bromine and opening the ring; formal charge location does not always mark the exact site of nucleophilic attack.

naming-parent-chain.q: CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃. What is the name?
naming-parent-chain.why: Count the row: six carbons, and the methyl is a one-carbon branch that cannot extend any path, so the parent is hexane. From the left the methyl is on C3, from the right on C4; 3 beats 4. 3-methylhexane.

naming-parent-chain.q: A student names CH₃CH(CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₃ as 2-ethylbutane. What is the correct name?
naming-parent-chain.why: Trace from the far end of the ethyl through the branch carbon and along the row: two ethyl carbons, the branch carbon, then two more is five. The row was only four. So the parent is pentane, and the carbon left over (the near end of the row) is a methyl on C3. An ethyl on C2 can never be right, because the route through it always beats the row by one.

naming-parent-chain.q: Which of these names cannot be correct as written?
naming-parent-chain.why: An ethyl on the second carbon of a chain always extends it: two ethyl carbons plus C2 plus the rest of the chain is one longer than the chain itself. 2-ethylbutane is really 3-methylpentane. The other three describe a molecule where the row is genuinely the longest path.

naming-parent-chain.q: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH(CH₂CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₃. How many carbons are in the parent chain?
naming-parent-chain.why: Three arms leave the branch carbon: three carbons to the left, three in the propyl, two to the right. A chain joins the two longest arms through that carbon: 3 + 1 + 3 = 7. The two-carbon arm is an ethyl on C4: 4-ethylheptane. Counting every carbon in the molecule (nine) as one chain would need the path to pass through the branch carbon twice.

naming-parent-chain.q: How is the parent chain defined?
options: The chain with the fewest branches
naming-parent-chain.why: The longest unbroken path of carbons, turning as many corners as it needs to. It is very often not the row lying across the page, which is why every end has to be checked.

naming-parent-chain.q: Two seven-carbon paths run through a molecule. One carries a single ethyl group, the other carries two methyls. Which is the parent?
options: Either; a tie means both names are valid
naming-parent-chain.why: A tie on length is broken by the number of substituents, and the chain with more wins. It reads backwards, but a name should put as much of the molecule as possible into numbered prefixes instead of hiding it inside a big branch name.

naming-parent-chain.q: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₃. Which name is right?
naming-parent-chain.why: Two five-carbon chains tie. The one along the row carries a methyl and an ethyl (two substituents); the one through the ethyl carries a single isopropyl. More substituents wins, so the parent is the row with methyl at C2 and ethyl at C3. Then the alphabet orders the words: ethyl before methyl.

naming-parent-chain.q: From one end a chain’s substituents fall at {2, 2, 5}; from the other at {2, 5, 5}. Which numbering is right?
options: {2, 5, 5}: the higher last term breaks the tie
Neither; renumber from a middle carbon
{2, 2, 5}: it wins at the second term
naming-parent-chain.why: Compare term by term and stop at the first difference. Both open with 2; then 2 beats 5. That settles it without looking at the third term.

naming-parent-chain.q: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃. What is the name?
naming-parent-chain.why: Seven carbons in the row and nothing longer through a methyl. From the left the methyls are at {2, 5}; from the right at {3, 6}. 2 beats 3 at the first term. Two methyls take di- and two locants: 2,5-dimethylheptane.

naming-parent-chain.q: A chain of six carbons is drawn with how many bonds between them?
naming-parent-chain.why: Always one fewer bond than carbons. Counting the line segments and calling a hexane a pentane is the standard off-by-one, and it is the same miscount as forgetting the ends of a skeletal structure.

naming-parent-chain.q: A student writes 1-methylpentane. What is wrong with it?
options: Nothing; it is a valid name
A methyl on C1 lengthens the chain: it is hexane
The locant belongs after the word
naming-parent-chain.why: A methyl on the end carbon is one more carbon in a straight line, so the chain is six long, not five. A name with a 1-alkyl locant on an unbranched chain is a sign the parent was chosen wrongly.

naming-parent-chain.q: Which condensed formula is 2,3-dimethylpentane?
naming-parent-chain.why: Pentane is five in a row; put methyls on the second and third. CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₃ is 2,4-dimethylpentane, CH₃C(CH₃)₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ is 2,2-dimethylpentane, and CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃ has six carbons in the row (2,3-dimethylhexane).

naming-parent-chain.q: (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃. What is the name?
naming-parent-chain.why: The longest path runs through one of the two end methyls: six carbons, hexane. The other methyl is the branch, on C2 counting from that end (C5 from the other). Isopropylbutane buries two chain carbons in the branch name.

naming-parent-chain.q: Which condensed formula is 4-ethylheptane?
naming-parent-chain.why: Seven in a row with a two-carbon branch on the fourth. CH₃CH₂CH(CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃ is a hexane (3-ethylhexane), CH₃CH₂CH₂C(CH₃)₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ has two methyls on one carbon, and CH₃CH₂CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃ is 4-methylheptane.

naming-parent-chain.q: CH₃CH₂C(CH₂CH₃)₂CH₂CH₃. A student rejects the name 3,3-diethylpentane, saying the longest chain must run through an ethyl. Who is right?
options: The student; through an ethyl it is heptane
The name; all four arms are two carbons long
naming-parent-chain.why: Four two-carbon arms leave the central carbon, so every route through it is 2 + 1 + 2 = 5. All the candidate chains tie at five with the same two substituents, and the name is 3,3-diethylpentane. The longest-chain rule only changes an answer when an arm is longer than the ones it competes with.

naming-parent-chain.q: CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃. What is the name?
naming-parent-chain.why: Eight in the row. From the left the methyls are at {3, 5}, from the right at {4, 6}; 3 beats 4. The ethyl name has the wrong parent, since an ethyl on C2 would extend the chain.

naming-parent-chain.q: A structure is drawn as a five-carbon row with an ethyl on the middle carbon. What is the parent?
options: Hexane, turning the corner into the ethyl group
Heptane, counting every carbon in the drawing
Pentane; row and corner routes all tie at five
Propane, the shortest path through the middle
naming-parent-chain.why: Three ends: the two row ends and the ethyl end. Row end to row end is five. Ethyl end to either row end is two, plus the middle carbon, plus two: also five. Nothing is longer than the row, so it stays the parent.

naming-parent-chain.q: That same structure, a five-carbon row with an ethyl on the middle carbon, is correctly named what?
naming-parent-chain.why: Pentane parent, two-carbon branch on C3 from either end. The ethyl survives as an ethyl because every route through it ties the row instead of beating it.

naming-parent-chain.q: A molecule is drawn as a Y: three arms of 3, 3 and 2 carbons leave one central carbon. What is the parent?
options: Nonane, every carbon in the molecule
Heptane, through the two longest arms
naming-parent-chain.why: A chain is a path and cannot pass through the same carbon twice, so only two arms can be joined: the two three-carbon arms plus the center is seven. The two-carbon arm is an ethyl on C4: 4-ethylheptane.

naming-parent-chain.q: Why is choosing the parent chain the highest-stakes step in a name?
options: Every later number depends on it
naming-parent-chain.why: Pick the wrong parent and the numbering, the locants and the substituent names that follow are all wrong too. It is the step where a name goes wrong earliest and most completely.

naming-parent-chain.q: Which name shows the modern IUPAC placement of the locant?
naming-parent-chain.why: Current IUPAC puts a locant immediately before the part of the name it refers to. Older texts write 2-butene, so read both; write the first.

naming-parent-chain.q: A molecule has two eight-carbon paths and nothing longer. What decides between them?
naming-parent-chain.why: When chains tie on length, the one carrying more substituents is the parent. If that ties too, the numbering rule decides: the chain whose substituents get the lower locants.

naming-parent-chain.q: A decane’s substituents fall at {2, 7, 8} from one end and {3, 4, 9} from the other. Which numbering is right?
options: {2, 7, 8}: it wins at the first term
{3, 4, 9}: more of its numbers are low
Either; the sets are equally low
naming-parent-chain.why: First point of difference: 2 against 3, decided at once. The totals (17 against 16) point the other way, which is exactly why adding locants up is not the rule.

naming-parent-chain.q: A molecule is drawn as a horizontal five-carbon row with a three-carbon branch on the second carbon. What is the parent?
naming-parent-chain.why: From the branch carbon: one carbon to the left, three in the branch, three to the right. Join the two longest arms through it: 3 + 1 + 3 = 7. The leftover carbon is a methyl: 4-methylheptane.

naming-parent-chain.q: Which condensed formula is 2,2-dimethylbutane?
naming-parent-chain.why: Four in a row with two methyls on the second carbon, which gives a carbon bearing three methyls at one end. The first is 2-methylpentane, the third 2,2-dimethylpentane, the last 2,3-dimethylbutane.

naming-parent-chain.q: CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃. A student writes 3,4-dimethylhexane. Is that right?
naming-parent-chain.why: Six in the row, methyls on the middle two carbons. From either end the set is {3, 4}: the molecule is symmetric, so there is no direction to choose and the name is simply 3,4-dimethylhexane.

naming-parent-chain.q: Which of these is the same compound as 3-methylhexane, under a wrong name?
naming-parent-chain.why: Number the same chain from the other end and the methyl lands on C4. Same structure, wrong direction. The other three are genuinely different molecules.

naming-parent-chain.q: Which of these is a correctly punctuated name?
naming-parent-chain.why: Comma between the two numbers, hyphen between the numbers and the word, and no space anywhere inside the name of a single compound.

naming-parent-chain.q: Two candidate parents are the same length and carry the same number of substituents. What decides?
naming-parent-chain.why: After length and substituent count, the numbering rule is the next tie-break: take the chain whose substituents get the lower set of locants at the first point of difference.

naming-parent-chain.q: Which condensed formula is 3-ethyl-2-methylhexane?
naming-parent-chain.why: Hexane row, methyl on C2, ethyl on C3. Check the parent: from C3 the arms are 2 (left), 2 (ethyl) and 3 (right), so the six-carbon row is the longest and the ethyl is a real branch. CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH(CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₃ is 4-ethyl-2-methylhexane, and CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃ is 2,3-dimethylhexane.

naming-substituents.q: A branch –CH₂CH(CH₃)₂ hangs off a parent chain. Which group is it?
naming-substituents.why: Attached through a CH₂, then a CH carrying two methyls: a three-carbon chain attached at its end with a methyl on its second carbon. That is isobutyl. sec-Butyl attaches through the branch point itself.

naming-substituents.q: Which group attaches through its middle carbon?
naming-substituents.why: Isopropyl, systematically propan-2-yl, attaches at C2 of a three-carbon fragment. Propyl and butyl attach at an end; isobutyl attaches at the end of a branched three-chain.

naming-substituents.q: What is the systematic name of the tert-butyl group, (CH₃)₃C–?
naming-substituents.why: The attached carbon carries three methyls: a propane chain attached through its middle carbon with a methyl on that same carbon, so propan-2-yl with a 2-methyl. Almost nobody says it aloud, but you should be able to decode it.

naming-substituents.q: CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)– attached to the parent through the CH. What is its common name?
naming-substituents.why: Four carbons, attached through the second one: butan-2-yl, called sec-butyl. Isobutyl attaches through a CH₂; tert-butyl through a carbon bearing three methyls.

naming-substituents.q: How is a halogen named in a systematic name?
options: As a prefix in every case
As a suffix when two are present
naming-substituents.why: fluoro, chloro, bromo, iodo. A halogen is a prefix wherever it sits and is not a suffix, but it ranks equally with alkyl groups for numbering, so a chloro can claim the low locant over a methyl on first-point-of-difference terms.

naming-substituents.q: CH₃OCH₂CH₂CH₃. What is the name?
naming-substituents.why: An ether has no suffix; it is an alkoxy prefix on the longer chain. Propane is the parent, and the –OCH₃ is methoxy on C1, numbered from the end nearer it.

naming-substituents.q: CH₃C(CH₃)₂CH₂CH₂CH₃. What is the name?
naming-substituents.why: Two methyls on C2 of a pentane. Each substituent keeps its own locant even when they share a carbon: di- promises two numbers, and the repeated 2 is the only thing saying where the second methyl is.

naming-substituents.q: CH₃CH₂C(CH₃)(CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃. Which name is right?
naming-substituents.why: Six in the longest row; from either end the branch carbon is C3 or C4, and 3 wins. Both substituents sit on C3, and the alphabet orders the words: ethyl before methyl. The numbers being equal does not change the word order.

naming-substituents.q: CH₃CH(Cl)CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃. What is the name?
naming-substituents.why: From the left: chloro 2, methyl 4, so {2, 4}. From the right: methyl 3, chloro 5, so {3, 5}. 2 beats 3, and the halogen and the alkyl are equals in that comparison. Then chloro before methyl alphabetically.

naming-substituents.q: A hexane carries an ethyl on C4 and two methyls on C2. Which is the correct name?
naming-substituents.why: Ignore di- when alphabetizing: you are comparing ethyl with methyl, and e comes before m, so ethyl is cited first despite its higher locant. di- needs two locants, which rules out “4-ethyl-2-dimethylhexane”, and a name cannot run two prefixes together without locants, which rules out “2,2,4-dimethylethylhexane”.

naming-substituents.q: Under which letter does tert-butyl file when substituents are alphabetized?
naming-substituents.why: The italic, hyphenated tert- is ignored, so the name files under b. The typography is the tell: hyphenated italic prefixes are skipped, prefixes joined to the word are counted.

naming-substituents.q: A parent carries a tert-butyl, an isopropyl and two methyls. In what order are they written?
naming-substituents.why: File each name: tert-butyl under b (tert- ignored), isopropyl under i (iso counts), dimethyl under m (di- ignored). b, i, m.

naming-substituents.q: sec-Butyl and ethyl are both substituents on one parent. Which is cited first?
naming-substituents.why: sec- is an italic hyphenated prefix and is ignored, so sec-butyl files under b, ahead of ethyl under e. Locants play no part in the order of the words.

naming-substituents.q: A hexane has methyls on C2 and C4 and an ethyl on C3, numbering already fixed. Write the name.
naming-substituents.why: Collect the two methyls as 2,4-dimethyl, then alphabetize with di- ignored: ethyl before methyl. Identical substituents are always gathered under one multiplying prefix.

naming-substituents.q: Which structure is tert-butyl chloride?
naming-substituents.why: Common halide names are alkyl group plus halide: the chlorine sits on a carbon bearing three methyls. Systematically, 2-chloro-2-methylpropane. The others are isobutyl, sec-butyl and butyl chloride.

naming-substituents.q: An octane carries an ethyl on C3 and a methyl on C6 counting from the left; from the right the methyl is on C3 and the ethyl on C6. What is the name?
naming-substituents.why: Both directions give {3, 6}: a genuine tie, and the one situation where the alphabet touches the numbering. The substituent cited first (ethyl) takes the lower locant. 6-ethyl-3-methyloctane numbers the wrong way.

naming-substituents.q: In what order do the rules apply when naming a substituted alkane?
naming-substituents.why: First number for lowest locants; then, only on an exact tie, give the alphabetically first substituent the lower number; last, write the substituents in alphabetical order whatever their numbers.

naming-substituents.q: Locants are fixed as bromo-4, methyl-2, propyl-5 on an octane. How is the name written?
naming-substituents.why: Alphabetical order sets the order of the words: bromo, methyl, propyl. The numbers travel with their substituents, so they end up out of numerical order, which is normal.

naming-substituents.q: A branch is itself branched. How is its name written?
naming-substituents.why: Parentheses tell the reader that the number inside counts along the branch, from its attaching carbon, and not along the parent chain.

naming-substituents.q: A complex substituent is numbered from where?
naming-substituents.why: The attaching carbon is C1 of the substituent, always. So –CH₂CH(CH₃)₂ is (2-methylpropyl), with the methyl on the branch’s own C2.

naming-substituents.q: A branch –CH₂CH(CH₃)₂ on a parent chain is named, in parentheses, as:
naming-substituents.why: Numbered from the attachment point, the CH₂ is C1 and the CH bearing the methyl is C2; the branch is three carbons long. This group is also called isobutyl.

naming-substituents.q: The same group is called (2-methylpropyl) or isobutyl. Under which letter does each name file?
naming-substituents.why: A complex substituent files under the first letter of its complete name, m. The common name files under i, because iso is joined to the word. Which name you use can change where the group sits in a longer name.

naming-substituents.q: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br is commonly called what?
naming-substituents.why: Alkyl group plus halide: the bromine is on the end carbon of a three-chain, so propyl bromide (1-bromopropane). Isopropyl bromide would put it on the middle carbon.

naming-substituents.q: Which condensed formula is 4-isopropylheptane?
naming-substituents.why: Heptane row, with a three-carbon group attached through its middle carbon on C4. CH₃CH₂CH₂CH(CH₂CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃ is 4-propylheptane, CH₃CH₂CH(CH(CH₃)₂)CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ puts the branch on C3, and (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ is 2-methyloctane.

naming-substituents.q: sec-Butyl attaches through which carbon?
naming-substituents.why: sec-Butyl is butan-2-yl. C1 of a four-chain is butyl; C2 of a three-chain is isopropyl; a carbon bearing three methyls is tert-butyl.

naming-substituents.q: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH₃. What is the name?
naming-substituents.why: Five in the longest row, methyls on C2, C3 and C4 from either end. Three identical substituents take tri- and three locants; they are never split between two prefixes. A methyl on C1 would extend the chain.

naming-substituents.q: BrCH₂CH₂CH₂Cl. What is the name?
naming-substituents.why: From either end the locant set is {1, 3}: a tie, so the alphabetically first substituent takes the lower number. Bromo before chloro, so the bromine gets 1. The words are then written in that same order.

naming-substituents.q: CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH(CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₃. What is the name?
naming-substituents.why: Seven in the longest chain (the route through the ethyl also gives seven, with the same two substituents). From the left: methyl 3, ethyl 5. From the right: ethyl 3, methyl 5. Both {3, 5}, so ethyl, cited first, takes the 3.

naming-substituents.q: Which statement about alphabetizing substituents is correct?
naming-substituents.why: Ignore di-, tri-, tetra- and the italic sec-, tert-. Do not ignore iso, neo or cyclo, which are joined to the word and count as part of it.

naming-substituents.q: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂Cl: systematic name, and common name?
naming-substituents.why: Propane parent with a methyl on C2 and a chlorine on C1, cited alphabetically: chloro before methyl. The group carrying the chlorine is –CH₂CH(CH₃)₂, isobutyl, so the common name is isobutyl chloride.

naming-functional-groups.q: CH₃COCH₂CH₂OH. What is the name?
naming-functional-groups.why: Ketone outranks alcohol, so the suffix is -one and the OH is demoted to hydroxy-. The ketone claims the lower locant: C2 from its end, which puts the OH on C4.

naming-functional-groups.q: Which of these groups has the highest priority?
naming-functional-groups.why: acid > ester > amide > nitrile > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine > alkene/alkyne. The acid and its derivatives are the top block.

naming-functional-groups.q: ClCH₂CH₂CO₂H. What is the name?
naming-functional-groups.why: The acid carbon is C1 by necessity and needs no locant; count from it and the chlorine sits on C3. Halogens are prefixes in every name.

naming-functional-groups.q: An –OH is outranked by a ketone in the same molecule. What prefix does it take?
naming-functional-groups.why: A demoted alcohol becomes hydroxy-. Nothing about the oxygen changed; its rank did. oxo- is a demoted ketone, carboxy- a demoted acid.

naming-functional-groups.q: A ketone is outranked by a carboxylic acid. What prefix does it take?
naming-functional-groups.why: The IUPAC prefix is oxo-, not keto-. A compound chemists call a keto acid has no mention of a ketone in its systematic name.

naming-functional-groups.q: HOCH₂CH₂CHO. What is the name?
naming-functional-groups.why: Aldehyde outranks alcohol: suffix -al, C1 is the CHO and no locant is written for it. The OH is hydroxy- on C3.

naming-functional-groups.q: CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CO₂H. What is the name?
naming-functional-groups.why: The acid wins the suffix and is C1. Counting from it, the OH is on C3. The acid needs no locant; writing -1-oic is redundant.

naming-functional-groups.q: NCCH₂CH₂CH₂OH. What is the name?
naming-functional-groups.why: Nitrile outranks alcohol, so -nitrile is the suffix and the nitrile carbon is C1 (four carbons in the parent, including it). The OH is hydroxy- on C4. Nitrile begins with a consonant, so the e of butane stays.

naming-functional-groups.q: H₂NCH₂CH₂CH₂OH. What is the name?
naming-functional-groups.why: Alcohol outranks amine: suffix -ol, OH on C1. The NH₂ is demoted to amino- on C3.

naming-functional-groups.q: Aldehyde outranks ketone in the priority order. What is the basis of that ranking?
options: The aldehyde carbon is more oxidized
The ketone carbon is more oxidized
Convention; both carbons have two bonds to oxygen
naming-functional-groups.why: An aldehyde carbon and a ketone carbon are at the same oxidation level, two bonds to oxygen each; the aldehyde’s extra C–H is why it can be oxidized further, but it does not make it a higher level. The order within that pair, like the order within the acid-derivative block, is convention.

naming-functional-groups.q: How do the functional carbons of an acid, an ester, an amide and a nitrile compare in oxidation level?
options: They descend from acid to nitrile
They ascend from acid to nitrile
All the same: three bonds to O or N
Only the acid and ester match
naming-functional-groups.why: Each has three bonds from carbon to oxygen or nitrogen (the nitrile’s are all to one nitrogen), so all four sit at the same level. The order within the block is a convention that happens to run with their reactivity.

naming-functional-groups.q: Once a principal characteristic group is present, which feature gets the lowest locant first?
naming-functional-groups.why: The principal group claims the low number before multiple bonds or substituents are considered at all. The old lowest-locants-to-substituents rule was only ever for molecules with nothing to outrank them.

naming-functional-groups.q: A heptane has an OH reachable at C3 from one end and a methyl at C2 from the other. What is the name?
naming-functional-groups.why: The alcohol takes the lower locant first: number from its end, OH at C3. The methyl is then C6, whatever it would have been the other way. Giving the methyl the 2 out of habit is the commonest error here.

naming-functional-groups.q: The longest chain in a molecule does not contain the –OH. What is the parent?
options: The longest chain in the molecule
The longest chain that contains the OH
The shortest chain that contains the OH
naming-functional-groups.why: Priority beats length. The parent must contain the principal characteristic group, so you take the longest chain that does, even when a longer one exists.

naming-functional-groups.q: Why does a carboxylic acid need no locant?
naming-functional-groups.why: The functional carbon is necessarily at the end of a chain, so it is C1 by construction. Butan-1-al is redundant for the same reason.

naming-functional-groups.q: Propane plus the -ol suffix is spelled how?
naming-functional-groups.why: When the suffix begins with a vowel the parent’s final e is dropped. Before a consonant it stays: propanenitrile.

naming-functional-groups.q: HOCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂OH. What is the name?
naming-functional-groups.why: Two alcohols take -diol with two locants, and because di- begins with a consonant the e of butane is kept. Both OH groups are principal, so neither is demoted to hydroxy-.

naming-functional-groups.q: OHC–CH₂–CO–CH₃. What is the name?
naming-functional-groups.why: Aldehyde outranks ketone: suffix -al, the CHO is C1. The ketone is demoted to oxo- on C3. keto- is not an IUPAC prefix.

naming-functional-groups.q: What is the systematic name for acetone?
naming-functional-groups.why: Three carbons with the C=O on the middle one. Acetone is a retained name and cannot be read back into a structure; propan-2-one can.

naming-functional-groups.q: What is the systematic name for acetic acid?
naming-functional-groups.why: Two carbons, including the acid carbon, so eth-. Methanoic acid is formic acid.

naming-functional-groups.q: CH₃CH₂COOCH₃. What is the name?
naming-functional-groups.why: Find the C=O and count its chain: three carbons, so the acid part is propanoate. The carbon on the single-bonded oxygen is the alcohol part: methyl. Two words, alcohol part first.

naming-functional-groups.q: In ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, which fragment is the "ethyl"?
options: The two carbons nearest the C=O
The carbons on the single-bonded O
The carbons of the C=O chain
naming-functional-groups.why: The first word of an ester name is the alcohol’s carbon chain, attached through the single-bonded oxygen. The second word is the acid’s chain, counted from the C=O. Here both happen to be two carbons, which is why the example is worth checking.

naming-functional-groups.q: A cyclohexane ring has a C=O as one ring carbon and a methyl two carbons away from it. What is the name?
naming-functional-groups.why: The ketone takes the suffix and C1; the ring is the parent. Going round the direction that reaches the methyl sooner gives 3 rather than 5.

naming-functional-groups.q: A cyclohexane ring carries a –COOH. What is the name?
naming-functional-groups.why: The acid carbon cannot be part of the ring, so it is not counted in the parent: the ring is cyclohexane and the group is the suffix -carboxylic acid. The e is kept because the suffix begins with a consonant.

naming-functional-groups.q: What does "principal characteristic group" mean?
options: The largest group in the molecule
naming-functional-groups.why: It is chosen by the fixed priority order, not by size, position or interest, and it is the one group named as the suffix.

naming-functional-groups.q: Where do double and triple bonds sit in the priority order?
options: Below the functional groups, above alkane
naming-functional-groups.why: Alkenes and alkynes rank below every group in the list, so a functional group always claims the lower locant over a multiple bond.

naming-functional-groups.q: CH₃OCH₂CH₂NH₂. What is the name?
naming-functional-groups.why: An ether can never be a suffix, so the amine wins by default: -amine on C1 of a two-carbon parent, and methoxy- on C2.

naming-functional-groups.q: CH₂=CHCH₂OH. What is the name?
naming-functional-groups.why: The alcohol outranks the double bond and takes C1. The double bond then starts at C2. Both suffixes appear, the multiple bond first and with its e dropped before -ol.

naming-functional-groups.q: A cyclohexane ring carries a –CHO. What is the name?
naming-functional-groups.why: Like the acid, the aldehyde carbon hangs off the ring and cannot be part of it, so the ring is the parent and the group becomes -carbaldehyde. Formyl- is the prefix for a demoted aldehyde, and nothing outranks it here.

naming-functional-groups.q: Why is the naming priority order worth knowing beyond naming?
naming-functional-groups.why: The top of the list is close to the reactivity ladder of the Carboxylic Acids chapter: an acid or acyl chloride converts to an ester, an ester to an amide. Going back up is not a direct step; an ester or amide is hydrolyzed to the acid first.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₃. What is the name?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: Five carbons, double bond between C2 and C3 counting from the nearer end. Only the lower of the two carbons is cited; the reader infers the bond runs to the next one.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: A cyclohexane ring carries one ethyl group. What is the name?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: The ring has six carbons to the chain’s two, so the ring is the parent. With only one substituent there is nowhere else it could be, and no locant is written.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: How does numbering a ring differ from numbering a chain?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: You choose both the starting carbon and the direction, subject to the same priority rules as a chain: principal group at C1, then lowest locants.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: A three-carbon chain is attached to a cyclohexane ring. Which name is right?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: Six ring carbons beat three chain carbons, so the ring is the parent and the chain is a propyl substituent. One substituent needs no locant.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: A cyclohexane ring is attached to the end of an eight-carbon chain, with no functional groups. What is the parent?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: With no higher-priority group present, the parent is whichever has more carbons. Eight beats six, so the ring becomes a cyclohexyl substituent: 1-cyclohexyloctane.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: A cyclopentane ring is attached to a five-carbon chain, with no functional groups. What is the parent?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: Five against five is a tie, and on a tie the ring is the parent: pentylcyclopentane. Current IUPAC recommendations go further and prefer the ring whatever the chain length, but exams count carbons.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: A benzene ring bonded to the parent directly through one of its ring carbons is called what?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: Phenyl is C₆H₅–, the ring itself. Benzyl is the ring plus a CH₂, attached through the CH₂; confusing the two changes the molecule by a carbon.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: C₆H₅CH₂– as a substituent is called what?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: A benzene ring attached through an extra CH₂ is benzyl. Phenyl is the bare ring, and benzoyl is C₆H₅CO–.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: CH₃C≡CCH₂CH₃. What is the name?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: A triple bond takes -yne and one locant, the lower of the two carbons: from the nearer end the bond runs from C2. Nothing else about the procedure changes.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: CH₂=CHCH₂C≡CH. What is the name?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: From the left the double bond is at 1 and the triple at 4; from the right it is the other way round. The locant sets tie, so the double bond takes the lower number. The suffix order is fixed, en before yne, and the e of ene is dropped before the y.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: CH₂=CHCH₂CH₂CH₃. What is the name?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: Five carbons, double bond starting at C1 from the nearer end. The locant is needed because pent-2-ene is a different compound, and only the first of the two carbons is cited.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: Which carbon number is cited for a double bond?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: By convention the locant is the lower-numbered of the two carbons the bond joins; the reader infers that the bond runs to the next carbon along.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: CH₂=CH–CH=CH–CH₃. What is the name?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: Two double bonds take -diene with two locants, one per bond, from the end that gives the lower set: {1, 3} beats {2, 4}. The a in penta- is kept before the consonant d.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: A six-carbon chain has an OH at C1 and a double bond starting at C5. What is the name?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: The alcohol outranks the double bond and claims the lower locant, even though that gives the double bond a 5 rather than a 1. The e of ene is dropped before the vowel of -ol.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: CH₃CH=CH–C≡CH. What is the name?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: From the left: ene at 2, yne at 4, so {2, 4}. From the right: yne at 1, ene at 3, so {1, 3}. The lower set wins regardless of which bond it favors, so the triple bond gets the 1 here; the double bond only gets preference on an exact tie.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: A name contains both a double bond and an alcohol. Which suffix is written first?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: Both appear, the multiple bond first and the principal group last: hex-5-en-1-ol. The order of suffixes is fixed whatever the locants.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: 1,2-dimethylbenzene is also called what?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: Xylene is the retained name for dimethylbenzene, and adjacent methyls are ortho: o-xylene. Toluene is methylbenzene.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: A benzene ring carries chlorines at positions 1 and 3. What is the name?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: One ring carbon between the two substituents is the 1,3 relationship, meta. The numbers and the word say the same thing, and both are in constant use.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: Two substituents at positions 1 and 4 of a benzene ring are described by which prefix?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: Straight across a six-membered ring is three bonds away, the 1,4 relationship: para. Adjacent is ortho (1,2) and one apart is meta (1,3).

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: CH₂=C(CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃. A student uses the longest chain and writes 3-methylidenehexane. What does the textbook rule say?
options: The parent must contain the C=C: 2-ethylpent-1-ene
The parent must contain the C=C: 3-ethylpent-1-ene
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: The six-carbon chain misses the double bond, so it is not the parent; the longest chain through the C=C is five, starting at the CH₂. The double bond takes C1 and the two carbons left over are an ethyl on C2. The 2013 IUPAC rules relaxed this, but textbooks and exams still apply it.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: Why can the name but-2-ene describe two different compounds?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: The two alkene carbons cannot rotate, so the methyls are fixed either on the same side (cis) or on opposite sides (trans). The name needs a prefix to say which.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃. What is the name?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: The longest chain through the double bond is four carbons, with a methyl on one of the alkene carbons. The double bond is at 2 from either end, a tie; the methyl then takes the lower number, 2 rather than 3.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: A double bond in a ring is numbered so that its two carbons are which?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: The double bond takes the lowest possible pair of locants before substituents are considered; only the direction round the ring is left for them to decide.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: A cyclohexene ring has an OH on the carbon next to one of the alkene carbons. What is the name?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: The alcohol is the principal group and takes C1. Numbering then goes round the way that reaches the double bond soonest, so it starts at C2. The e of ene is dropped before -ol.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: Which condensed formula is 3-methylbut-1-ene?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: Four carbons in the parent, double bond starting at C1, methyl on C3. CH₃CH=C(CH₃)₂ is 2-methylbut-2-ene, CH₂=C(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ is 2-methylbut-1-ene, and CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₃ is pent-2-ene.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: A principal characteristic group sits on a ring, and the ring is attached to a longer chain. What must the parent be?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: The parent must contain the principal characteristic group, and that overrides the more-carbons rule exactly as it overrides the longest-chain rule.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: A cyclohexane ring carries an ethyl and a methyl on adjacent carbons. What is the name?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: Either direction gives {1, 2}: a tie, so the alphabetically first substituent takes C1. Ethyl before methyl. Locants are needed because the two groups could also be 1,3 or 1,4.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: A cyclohexane ring carries three methyls. Numbered one way they fall at {1, 2, 4}; the other way at {1, 3, 4}. Which set is used?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: First point of difference: both start at 1, then 2 beats 3. On a ring you try every starting carbon and both directions, and {1, 2, 4} is the lowest set this arrangement can give.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: A cyclohexane ring carries an OH, with a methyl on the carbon two positions away. What is the name?
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: The alcohol takes the suffix and C1. Going round the direction that reaches the methyl sooner gives 3 rather than 5.

naming-rings-unsaturation.q: What does the prefix in cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane tell you?
options: Whether the methyls are on the same face of the ring
Whether the ring is a chair
naming-rings-unsaturation.why: The locants already say the methyls are adjacent. cis and trans on a ring say whether the two groups are on the same face or opposite faces, which are different compounds; the full treatment is in Stereochemistry.

bronsted.q: A Brønsted-Lowry acid is defined as a species that:
bronsted.why: Brønsted-Lowry acids are proton donors; bases are proton acceptors.

bronsted.q: When an acid donates a proton, what is left behind called?
bronsted.why: After losing H⁺, the acid becomes its conjugate base (one less proton, one more negative/less positive charge).

bronsted.q: A mechanism step shows R–OH₂⁺ handing a proton to a chloride ion. Which assignment of roles is right?
options: Chloride is the acid; the oxygen of R–OH₂⁺ is the base
R–OH₂⁺ is the acid; chloride is the base
R–OH₂⁺ is the base; chloride is the acid
R–OH₂⁺ is the acid; the water it releases is the base
bronsted.why: Follow the proton. It leaves R–OH₂⁺, so that species is the donor, which is the definition of the Brønsted acid. It lands on chloride, so chloride is the acceptor, the Brønsted base. The fact that the acid is a cation rather than a bottled reagent is what makes this look unfamiliar, and it is also why it works so readily: losing the proton neutralizes the positive charge instead of creating a negative one, which is worth about seventeen pKa units. R–OH₂⁺ sits near pKa −2 while the alcohol it came from sits near 16. Chloride is a very weak base (HCl, pKa −7), so this particular transfer is not especially favorable, but it happens constantly in mechanisms because both species are present and proton transfers are fast.

bronsted.q: Which species is the Bronsted base in the reaction NH3 + H2O → NH4+ + OH-?
bronsted.why: NH3 accepts a proton from water to form NH4+, making it the Bronsted base while water acts as the acid.

bronsted.q: The curved arrow that forms the new bond in a proton transfer starts on the acidic hydrogen.
bronsted.why: False, and this is the single most common arrow mistake in the chapter. A curved arrow always starts on the electrons that move, and a proton has none — it is a bare nucleus. The electrons that make the new bond are supplied entirely by the base, so the arrow starts on the base’s lone pair and ends on the hydrogen. The second arrow starts on the old X–H bond and ends on the atom that keeps the pair, which is what leaves the conjugate base with its negative charge. Draw the arrow from the hydrogen and you have said the hydrogen donated electrons it does not have.

bronsted.q: What is formed when a Bronsted base accepts a proton?
bronsted.why: Accepting H+ turns a base into its conjugate acid, which now carries one more proton.

bronsted.q: Which of the following best describes HCl dissolving in water?
options: HCl acts as a Bronsted base
HCl donates a proton to water
