conformational-analysis.why: This systematic approach, summing A-value-based penalties for axial groups in each chair, is the standard method for predicting which conformer of a multiply-substituted cyclohexane will dominate.

conformational-analysis.q: If the two chair conformers of a disubstituted cyclohexane happen to have equal total axial-substituent strain penalties, the predicted equilibrium population is approximately:
options: It cannot be predicted in this case
conformational-analysis.why: When neither conformer has a net strain advantage over the other, there is no free energy difference driving the equilibrium toward one side, giving an approximately equal population.

conformational-analysis.q: For cis-1-ethyl-2-methylcyclohexane, the two interconverting chair conformers place the ethyl and methyl groups in opposite ax/eq roles from each other. Which conformer is more stable?
options: The one with methyl equatorial and ethyl axial
Both conformers are exactly equal in energy
Neither conformer is accessible for this compound
The one with ethyl equatorial and methyl axial
conformational-analysis.why: Since ethyl has a somewhat larger A-value than methyl, putting the bulkier ethyl group equatorial (and accepting methyl axial instead) minimizes the total axial strain, making that conformer more stable.

conformational-analysis.q: Between the two stereoisomers of 1-methyl-4-tert-butylcyclohexane, which one is, at its most stable conformation, lower in overall energy: cis, or trans?
options: Trans, since cis always forces one axial
Cis, because it forces tert-butyl axial
They are equal in energy because both rings have the same formula
Neither isomer can adopt a chair conformation
conformational-analysis.why: The trans isomer enjoys a genuinely diequatorial lowest-energy conformer, avoiding all 1,3-diaxial strain, whereas the cis isomer is stuck with at least one substituent axial no matter which chair it adopts.

conformational-analysis.q: Using approximate A-values (methyl about 1.7 kcal/mol), the energy difference between the diequatorial and diaxial conformers of trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane is roughly:
options: There is no energy difference between them
conformational-analysis.why: The diaxial chair carries two axial methyls: 1.7 + 1.7 = 3.4. The diequatorial chair carries no axial penalty, but its two methyls are on adjacent carbons and therefore gauche to each other, worth 0.9. So the preference is 3.4 − 0.9 = 2.5, against a measured 2.7. Adding A-values alone overstates it, and the gauche correction is what closes the gap.

conformational-analysis.q: Why does cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane show a much smaller energy difference between its two chair conformers than trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane does?
options: Because cis-1,2 substituents cannot exist in a chair at all
Because cis compounds never have an energy difference between conformers
Because both cis conformers are ax,eq and similar in strain
Because the methyl groups are chemically different in the cis isomer
conformational-analysis.why: For cis-1,2, both interconverting chairs are ax,eq combinations of roughly comparable strain, so the energy gap between them is small; for trans-1,2, one chair is diequatorial (very favorable) and the other diaxial (very unfavorable), producing a much larger gap.

conformational-analysis.q: A student concludes that any disubstituted cyclohexane can reach a diequatorial conformation. Where does that go wrong?
options: Nowhere — with enough flipping every ring reaches diequatorial
It is available only when the pattern matches: trans on 1,2 and 1,4, cis on 1,3
It is available only for rings carrying two identical substituent groups
It is unavailable as soon as one substituent is larger than a methyl group
conformational-analysis.why: Whether both groups can be equatorial at once is fixed before any energy is considered: it depends on the two faces and the two positions, and a ring flip cannot change either. cis-1,2, cis-1,4 and trans-1,3 rings have one group axial in both chairs, so the question becomes which group pays rather than whether anything has to.

conformational-analysis.q: Which general rule correctly summarizes when a diequatorial conformation is geometrically available for a disubstituted cyclohexane?
options: Diequatorial placement is possible only for 1,4-disubstitution, regardless of cis or trans
Diequatorial placement is possible for cis-1,2-, cis-1,4-, and trans-1,3-disubstitution patterns
Diequatorial placement is never possible for any disubstituted cyclohexane
Diequatorial placement is possible for trans-1,2-, trans-1,4-, and cis-1,3-disubstitution patterns
conformational-analysis.why: The geometric rule is that trans works for the 1,2 and 1,4 relationships while cis works for the 1,3 relationship; the opposite stereochemistry in each case is always forced into a mixed axial/equatorial arrangement.

conformational-analysis.q: For a 1,4-disubstituted cyclohexane bearing an OH group (small A-value) and a tert-butyl group (very large A-value) in a trans relationship, the predicted dominant conformer places:
options: OH leaves the ring in this conformation
conformational-analysis.why: Because trans-1,4 substitution permits both substituents to be equatorial at once, and both OH and tert-butyl individually prefer equatorial, the diequatorial conformer is strongly favored with no conflict between them.

conformational-analysis.q: For the same OH and tert-butyl substituents but in a cis-1,4 relationship, the predicted dominant conformer places:
conformational-analysis.why: Since cis-1,4 substitution forces one group axial, the molecule 'sacrifices' the position of the substituent with the smaller A-value (OH) to keep the much bulkier, higher-A-value tert-butyl group equatorial.

conformational-analysis.q: In determining the most stable conformer of a polysubstituted cyclohexane, only the single largest substituent matters, and all smaller substituents can be ignored entirely.
conformational-analysis.why: While the bulkiest substituent's A-value often dominates the decision, every substituent contributes some strain energy when axial, so a rigorous analysis sums the contributions of all substituents rather than ignoring the smaller ones.

conformational-analysis.q: What is the structural reason the axial conformer of tert-butylcyclohexane is so strongly disfavored, in terms of the number and severity of steric clashes?
options: An axial tert-butyl group breaks a covalent bond in the ring
Axial tert-butyl changes the hybridization of ring carbons from sp3 to sp2
Its three methyls clash 1,3-diaxially with the axial H's at C3 and C5
There is no real difference in strain between axial and equatorial tert-butyl
conformational-analysis.why: Because tert-butyl presents three methyl groups on one carbon, forcing it axial creates multiple simultaneous 1,3-diaxial clashes rather than just one, which is why its A-value is so much larger than a simple alkyl group's.

conformational-analysis.q: Predicting relative conformer stability using A-values gives only an approximate, not perfectly exact, result because the method does not account for every possible interaction in a given molecule.
conformational-analysis.why: A-values are empirically averaged steric parameters; real molecules can have additional effects (electronic, hydrogen bonding, or unusual geometries) not captured by a simple sum of standard A-values, so predictions are approximate.

radical-halogenation.q: What condition is required for an alkane to react with a halogen?
radical-halogenation.why: Br2 and an alkane in a dark flask do nothing at all. The light or heat is what initiates the chain, which is why bromine water distinguishes an alkene from an alkane.

radical-halogenation.q: How does the halogen bond break in the initiation step?
options: It is not broken at all
Heterolytically, giving a pair of ions
radical-halogenation.why: Homolysis sends one electron to each atom, giving two neutral radicals rather than a cation and an anion.

radical-halogenation.q: What kind of arrow shows the movement of a single electron?
radical-halogenation.why: Two fishhooks are needed to break one bond, one for each electron. Mixing arrow types is the commonest drawing error here.

radical-halogenation.q: How do you tell which stage of a chain a step belongs to?
options: By whether a product appears in the step
By the change in radical count
radical-halogenation.why: Up from zero is initiation, unchanged is propagation, down to zero is termination. The product is not what distinguishes them.

radical-halogenation.q: A step consumes one radical and produces one. Which stage?
radical-halogenation.why: The count is unchanged, so the chain can go round again. This is propagation even when the product appears in this very step.

radical-halogenation.q: Chlorination of propane. Six primary hydrogens, two secondary, and chlorine prefers secondary over primary by about 4 to 1 per hydrogen. What is the product ratio?
options: About 80% of the secondary product, since it is four times more reactive
About 57% of the secondary product and 43% of the primary
About 75% of the primary product, since there are three times as many
Exactly 50:50, since the two effects cancel completely
radical-halogenation.why: Multiply count by rate. Primary: 6 × 1 = 6. Secondary: 2 × 4 = 8. Total 14, so 8/14 ≈ 57% secondary and 6/14 ≈ 43% primary. The four-to-one selectivity nearly cancels against three times as many primary hydrogens, which is why chlorination of propane is a mixture you would have to separate.

radical-halogenation.q: Why is termination rare while the reaction runs?
options: It is actually the commonest step
Radicals are too stable to pair
radical-halogenation.why: Two radicals have to collide, and there are very few in the flask at any moment. A single initiation can turn over thousands of molecules first.

radical-halogenation.q: What is the order of radical stability?
radical-halogenation.why: Radicals follow the same order as carbocations, and for the same reason: hyperconjugation from neighboring C-H bonds into the half-filled orbital.

radical-halogenation.q: Per hydrogen, bromination prefers tertiary over primary by roughly what factor?
radical-halogenation.why: Bromine is highly selective. Chlorine's corresponding figure is only about 5, which is why chlorination gives mixtures.

radical-halogenation.q: 2-Methylpropane has nine primary hydrogens and one tertiary. Chlorine prefers tertiary over primary by about 5 to 1 per hydrogen. Which product dominates?
options: The two are formed in equal amounts
radical-halogenation.why: Primary: 9 × 1 = 9. Tertiary: 1 × 5 = 5. Total 14, so the primary chloride is 9/14 ≈ 64% — the major product comes from the less stable radical. Run the same substrate with bromine (1600 to 1) and the tertiary bromide is about 99%. One molecule, two halogens, opposite answers: that is the whole selectivity story in one calculation.

radical-halogenation.q: Why is the less reactive bromine radical the more selective one?
options: It is larger and more hindered
radical-halogenation.why: Abstraction by bromine is endothermic — a C–H at about 98 kcal/mol is traded for an H–Br at 87.5 — so by the Hammond postulate the transition state resembles the products. The radical is essentially fully formed at the top of the barrier, so every kcal/mol of its stability is already showing up in the rate.

radical-halogenation.q: Bond dissociation energies: a secondary C–H is about 98 kcal/mol, H–Cl is 103 and H–Br is 87.5. What do those numbers say about the two abstraction steps?
options: Both are exothermic, so both transition states come early
Both are endothermic, so both transition states come late
Chlorine's is endothermic by about 5 and bromine's exothermic by about 11
Chlorine's is exothermic by about 5 and bromine's endothermic by about 11
radical-halogenation.why: ΔH is the bond broken minus the bond made. For chlorine, 98 − 103 = −5, downhill. For bromine, 98 − 87.5 = +10.5, uphill. By the Hammond postulate the downhill step has an early, reactant-like transition state where the radical has barely formed, and the uphill one has a late, radical-like transition state where the radical's stability is already priced in — which is exactly the selectivity difference.

radical-halogenation.q: A radical reaction creates a new stereocenter. What is the outcome?
radical-halogenation.why: The carbon radical is essentially planar with its electron in a p orbital, so the halogen arrives on either face equally. No conditions make this enantioselective.

radical-halogenation.q: Propane gives roughly even amounts of two chlorination products. Why?
radical-halogenation.why: Six primary hydrogens at rate 1 against two secondary at about 4 gives 6 to 8 — close to even, because the counts nearly offset the modest selectivity.

radical-halogenation.q: How many different monochlorination products can butane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃, give?
options: Two: substitution at an end carbon or at a middle carbon
Three, since the two middle carbons differ
One, because chlorination always goes to the most substituted carbon
radical-halogenation.why: Count sets of equivalent hydrogens, not carbons. The two end methyls are equivalent to each other and the two middle CH₂ groups are equivalent to each other, so there are two sets and therefore two products: 1-chlorobutane and 2-chlorobutane. Finding the sets first is half the marks in any 'how many products' question.

radical-halogenation.q: Which reagent is used for allylic bromination?
radical-halogenation.why: N-bromosuccinimide releases bromine slowly and keeps its concentration permanently low.

radical-halogenation.q: Why does NBS give substitution rather than addition?
options: It cannot reach a double bond
radical-halogenation.why: Adding Br2 to an alkene is faster than the radical chain, but addition needs a reasonable Br2 concentration and the chain does not. Starve it and substitution wins.

radical-halogenation.q: Why is an allylic hydrogen unusually easy to abstract?
options: Allylic bonds are simply weaker than most
It is more acidic than most
radical-halogenation.why: The unpaired electron is delocalized across the pi system, which makes the abstraction much easier than the substitution pattern alone would suggest.

radical-halogenation.q: Allylic bromination often gives two products. Why?
options: The radical is a resonance hybrid
radical-halogenation.why: Bromine can end up at either end of the delocalized system. Drawing both resonance forms of the radical is how you predict the second product.

radical-halogenation.q: HBr plus peroxides adds to an alkene with which regiochemistry?
radical-halogenation.why: The peroxide starts a radical chain, so a bromine radical adds first rather than a proton.

radical-halogenation.q: Why do peroxides flip HBr addition to anti-Markovnikov?
radical-halogenation.why: The first species to add is no longer a proton seeking the better carbocation, but a bromine radical seeking the more stable carbon radical — which puts Br on the other carbon.

radical-halogenation.q: Which of these steps is NOT a termination step?
radical-halogenation.why: Count radicals across each step. The three terminations go from two radicals to none. The odd one out starts with one radical and ends with one — it consumes a carbon radical and hands back a bromine radical, so the chain carries on. It makes the product, which is exactly why it gets mislabeled; the stage is read off the radical count and never off the product.

radical-halogenation.q: Bromine water is decolorized by a compound with a double bond but not by an alkane. What is the difference?
options: The alkane needs light or heat before it will touch bromine at all
Alkenes are inert to bromine in every condition
The two react at the same rate under all conditions
Alkanes decolorize bromine water noticeably faster
radical-halogenation.why: Radical halogenation of an alkane has to be started, and in a dark flask at room temperature nothing initiates it. A double bond reacts with bromine directly, with no initiation step, which is why the test works. The reaction behind that is taught in the Alkenes & Alkynes chapter — here it matters only as the reason the light in these conditions is not decoration.

radical-halogenation.q: A step in your radical mechanism produces a charged species. What does that mean?
options: It was not a radical step
radical-halogenation.why: Radical steps move single electrons and give neutral species. A charge means a pair of electrons moved, which is a different mechanism.

radical-halogenation.q: Fluorine and iodine are not used for radical halogenation of alkanes. What rules each out?
options: Both are too unreactive to abstract a hydrogen at any temperature
Both react, but the products decompose before they can be isolated
Fluorine's abstraction is far too exothermic; iodine's is uphill
Neither forms radicals under UV light, their bonds being too strong
radical-halogenation.why: It is the same ΔH arithmetic. H–F is 136 kcal/mol, so abstraction by F• is downhill by nearly 40 — unselective to the point of uselessness and often explosive. H–I is only 71, so abstraction by I• is uphill by about 27, a barrier too high to cross at any workable temperature. Chlorine and bromine sit in the narrow window between the two.

radical-halogenation.q: You need to install a bromine at the single tertiary position of 2-methylpropane, cleanly. Which conditions, and what result do you expect?
options: Br₂ with UV light, giving about 99% of the tertiary bromide
Cl₂ with UV light, then swap the chlorine for bromine
Br₂ in a dark flask, giving the tertiary bromide by polar substitution
NBS with UV light, which is the only way to reach a tertiary position
radical-halogenation.why: Bromine is the selective halogen: 1600 to 1 for tertiary over primary per hydrogen, which beats the nine-to-one head start the primary hydrogens have. Light is not optional — without it there is no initiation and no chain. NBS is for allylic positions, where the point is keeping the bromine concentration low, not reaching a tertiary carbon.

radical-halogenation.q: What makes a chain reaction efficient?
radical-halogenation.why: Initiation is the slow, expensive step and only has to happen once per chain. That is the whole trick.

radical-halogenation.q: Why does radical chemistry reappear in mass spectrometry?
options: The molecular ion is a radical cation
Bromine is used in the ionization source
radical-halogenation.why: The molecular ion fragments to leave the most stable radical it can, which is the same stability order you learned here.

radical-halogenation.q: A carbon radical holds its unpaired electron in which orbital?
options: A pi antibonding orbital on carbon
radical-halogenation.why: That planarity is exactly why a new stereocenter formed this way comes out racemic.

radical-halogenation.q: Radical bromination of butane at C2 creates a new stereocenter. What is the stereochemical outcome, and why?
options: A single enantiomer, set by the face the bromine approaches from
A single enantiomer, since the chain reaction is stereospecific
No stereocenter forms at all, since radicals cannot produce one
A racemic mixture, since the planar radical is open on both faces
radical-halogenation.why: The carbon radical is essentially planar, with its unpaired electron in a p orbital sticking out of both faces equally. Bromine arrives on one face or the other with equal ease, so the two enantiomers form in equal amounts. That is a structural fact about the intermediate — no change of solvent or temperature makes a plain radical halogenation enantioselective.

chirality.q: 2-Chloropropane is drawn with Cl on a wedge, H on a hash, and a methyl group on each side. Is it chiral?
options: Chiral: a wedge and a hash make any carbon handed
Chiral: chlorine outranks both of the methyl groups
Achiral: the two methyls reflect onto each other
Achiral: the chlorine cancels the two methyl groups
chirality.why: The vertical plane through Cl, C and H exchanges the two substituents on either side of it. Those are both methyl groups, so the reflection gives back the same molecule and the plane is genuine — 2-chloropropane is achiral. Swap one methyl for an ethyl, making 2-chlorobutane, and the same reflection sends methyl onto ethyl, which is a different molecule; that compound is chiral.

chirality.q: A student finds a mirror plane in one drawing and calls the compound achiral. What still has to be checked?
options: That the drawing uses wedges, not hashes
That the plane hits at least one stereocenter
That the groups it exchanges are identical throughout
That the molecule has an even carbon count
chirality.why: A plane is only a plane of symmetry if reflecting in it returns the same molecule, so every pair of groups it exchanges has to be identical — compared as whole groups, not just first atoms. A plane that swaps a methyl for an ethyl is a feature of the drawing, not of the molecule. Note that the reverse mistake is also common: failing to find a plane in one drawn conformation settles nothing, because a plane present in any accessible conformation makes the compound achiral.

chirality.q: Which of these is generally considered a chiral object in everyday life?
chirality.why: A shoe is a classic macroscopic chiral object — its mirror image (the other foot’s shoe) is not superimposable on the original.

chirality.q: A chiral molecule and its mirror image are related as:
chirality.why: The defining test for chirality is whether a molecule's mirror image can be rotated and translated to exactly overlap the original. If not, the molecule is chiral.

chirality.q: A molecule can be chiral even if it has no tetrahedral stereocenter at all.
chirality.why: Chirality is a property of the whole molecule's symmetry, not just of individual carbons. Substituted allenes and certain biphenyls are chiral through axial or restricted-rotation chirality without a classic stereocenter.

chirality.q: Which of the following molecules is achiral?
chirality.why: Dichloromethane's central carbon carries two identical chlorine atoms and two identical hydrogens, giving it an internal mirror plane, so it is achiral.

chirality.q: Every molecule that contains a carbon bonded to four different groups is necessarily chiral overall.
chirality.why: If a molecule has two or more such stereocenters arranged symmetrically, their effects can cancel, producing an achiral meso compound even though individual centers have four different substituents.

chirality.q: What physical phenomenon is used experimentally to detect that a sample is chiral (and not racemic)?
chirality.why: Chiral compounds (in non-racemic form) rotate the plane of polarized light passing through them; this optical activity is measured with a polarimeter.

chirality.q: Which amino acid, unlike the other 19 common amino acids, is achiral?
chirality.why: Glycine's alpha carbon bears two identical hydrogen atoms in addition to the amino and carboxyl groups, so it fails the four-different-groups test and is achiral.

chirality.q: A chiral stereocenter and a chiral molecule are exactly the same thing.
chirality.why: A stereocenter is a single atom whose substituents can be arranged two ways; chirality is a property of the entire molecule's overall symmetry, which can differ from what any one center suggests (as in meso compounds).

chirality.q: The two enantiomers of limonene smell different (orange versus pine) mainly because:
options: They have different boiling points that change volatility
chirality.why: Biological receptors are themselves chiral, so they often bind the two enantiomers of a chiral molecule differently, which is why mirror-image compounds can have different biological or sensory effects despite having identical formulas.

chirality.q: The thalidomide case is often used to illustrate chirality in pharmacology because:
options: One enantiomer was therapeutic, the other teratogenic
The racemic mixture was more potent than either pure enantiomer
chirality.why: Thalidomide's two enantiomers have very different biological activities, showing why distinguishing and controlling chirality matters in drug development, not just in academic classification.

chirality.q: cis-1,2-Dimethylcyclohexane flips between two chairs, neither with a mirror plane. What follows?
options: It is chiral, since no conformation has a plane
Nothing yet — chirality is judged over all conformations
It is chiral, and the chairs separate when cold
It has no stereocenters, so the question lapses
chirality.why: The two chairs are mirror images of each other and interconvert about a hundred thousand times a second, so the molecule spends half its life as each and cannot be resolved. Flattened out it does have an internal mirror plane between C1 and C2: the compound is meso, and achiral. A plane found in any accessible conformation settles the question; the absence of one in a single drawn conformation does not.

chirality.q: Counting stereocenters is always a completely reliable way to predict whether a specific molecule is chiral.
chirality.why: Stereocenter counting is a useful shortcut, but meso compounds show that a molecule with multiple stereocenters can still be achiral overall, so the mirror-image superimposability test is the truly reliable method.

chirality.q: Is 3-methylhexane a chiral molecule?
options: Yes, C3 has four different groups
Yes, because it contains a methyl branch
No, C3 carries two identical ethyl groups
No, because it is a straight-chain alkane
chirality.why: Count outward from C3 in both directions: one way is C2-C1, an ethyl group; the other is C4-C5-C6, a propyl group. With a methyl and a hydrogen as well, that is four different groups, so C3 is a stereocenter and the molecule is chiral. The chains only look symmetric until you count them.

chirality.q: Pure enantiomers of a chiral compound always have identical melting points, boiling points, and densities.
chirality.why: Enantiomers differ only in how they interact with other chiral influences, such as polarized light or chiral reagents; their standard bulk physical properties in an achiral environment are identical.

chirality.q: A biphenyl carrying four bulky ortho substituents can be chiral with no sp³ stereocenter anywhere. That chirality comes from:
chirality.why: When bulky ortho substituents prevent free rotation about the biaryl bond, the molecule is locked into a twisted, non-planar shape whose mirror image cannot be superimposed, producing chirality without a traditional stereocenter.

chirality.q: A chiral molecule must contain at least one carbon atom.
chirality.why: Chirality is a geometric property of overall molecular shape; it can also arise at nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur centers, or from axial chirality in carbon-free frameworks, so carbon is not strictly required.

chirality.q: Which compound below is chiral?
chirality.why: CHFClBr has a single carbon bonded to four completely different atoms (H, F, Cl, Br) and no internal symmetry to cancel the effect, making it chiral.

chirality.q: If you rotate a chiral molecule's drawn structure 180 degrees in the plane of the paper, does it become its enantiomer?
options: Yes, rotation always generates the enantiomer
Only if it has an even number of stereocenters
chirality.why: Simple rotation of a molecule (or its drawing) in space never changes its configuration or identity; only reflecting it (or swapping substituents) converts it into its mirror image.

chirality.q: A solution containing exactly equal amounts of both enantiomers of a chiral compound will rotate plane-polarized light.
chirality.why: In a racemic (50:50) mixture, the rotation caused by one enantiomer is exactly canceled by the equal and opposite rotation from the other, so the net optical rotation observed is zero.

chirality.q: Why is meso-tartaric acid achiral despite having two stereocenters, each bonded to four different groups?
options: It has no stereocenters at all
It is not a real compound
Its internal mirror plane makes it superimposable
Its two stereocenters have identical R configurations
chirality.why: Meso-tartaric acid's two stereocenters have opposite configurations that create an internal mirror plane, so the molecule as a whole coincides with its mirror image even though each center individually has four different substituents.

chirality.q: A chiral molecule can never have a center of symmetry (a point through which every atom has an identical, inverted counterpart).
chirality.why: A center of symmetry is an improper symmetry element; any molecule possessing one is automatically superimposable on its mirror image and therefore achiral, so a truly chiral molecule cannot have one.

chirality.q: Is 3-bromo-1-butene (CH₂=CH–CHBr–CH₃) chiral?
options: No — the double bond rules it out
No — C3 has two identical hydrogens
Yes — C3 carries H, Br, CH₃ and vinyl
Yes, but in its cis form alone
chirality.why: C3 carries four distinct groups (H, Br, CH3, and -CH=CH2), satisfying the stereocenter criterion, and there is no internal symmetry to cancel it, so the molecule is chiral.

chirality.q: Which statement correctly relates stereocenters and chirality in general?
options: A stereocenter suggests chirality; check the symmetry
A chiral molecule must have exactly one stereocenter
Chirality is unrelated to the number of stereocenters
Any molecule with an even number of stereocenters is achiral
chirality.why: Stereocenters are a strong clue toward chirality, but because of possible internal symmetry (as in meso compounds), the only fully reliable check is comparing the whole molecule to its mirror image.

chirality.q: The pairing of a left hand with a right hand is the standard everyday analogy for chirality, because the two are mirror images that cannot be superimposed.
chirality.why: Left and right hands look alike but cannot be perfectly overlaid on one another no matter how they are rotated, which is exactly the geometric relationship that defines chiral molecules and their enantiomers.

chirality.q: Why are the natural amino acids other than glycine chiral?
options: They all contain a nitrogen atom
They join up into peptide bonds
Their alpha carbon has four different groups
chirality.why: The alpha carbon of a standard amino acid is attached to a hydrogen, an amino group, a carboxyl group, and a unique side chain, four different substituents that make it a stereocenter and the molecule chiral.

chirality.q: Penta-2,3-diene, CH₃–CH=C=CH–CH₃, has no sp³ stereocenter. Why is it chiral?
options: Its methyl groups repel into a twist
Its central carbon has four different groups
Its cumulated double bonds hold the ends perpendicular
chirality.why: The central carbon of an allene is sp hybridized and its two π systems are at right angles, so the methyl and hydrogen on one end lie in a plane perpendicular to the methyl and hydrogen on the other. That arrangement is handed: no rotation superimposes it on its reflection. Restricted rotation is a distractor here — no alkene rotates about its double bond, and most alkenes are perfectly achiral.

chirality.q: Only molecules containing at least one sp3 carbon can be chiral.
chirality.why: Chirality is a property of the shape of the whole molecule, and a twist can supply it without any tetrahedral carbon. BINOL is the cleanest counterexample: every carbon in it is aromatic and sp², yet bulky groups beside the bond joining its two rings lock them at an angle, and the twisted shape is not superimposable on its mirror image. Substituted allenes make the same point.

chirality.q: Bromochlorofluoromethane (CHFClBr) and its mirror image:
options: Are identical and can be superimposed
Are enantiomers that cannot be superimposed
chirality.why: The single carbon in CHFClBr carries four different atoms with no internal symmetry, so the molecule and its mirror image are non-superimposable enantiomers, confirming the molecule is chiral.

stereocenters.q: A carbon stereocenter has:
options: A double bond to each neighbor
stereocenters.why: A stereocenter (typically a carbon) must have four different groups attached for swapping two to create a distinct stereoisomer.

stereocenters.q: How many stereoisomers can arise from a molecule with n independent stereocenters (maximum, ignoring symmetry)?
stereocenters.why: Each stereocenter independently can be R or S, giving up to 2ⁿ possible stereoisomers.

stereocenters.q: Can a nitrogen atom ever be a stereocenter?
options: No, nitrogen can never be a stereocenter
Only if it has five bonds
stereocenters.why: Nitrogen can be a stereocenter in specific cases (e.g., locked in a ring, or quaternary ammonium with 4 different substituents) where pyramidal inversion is prevented or irrelevant.

stereocenters.q: In 2-bromobutane, which carbon is the stereocenter?
stereocenters.why: C2 is bonded to Br, H, a methyl group, and an ethyl group, four different substituents, making it the stereocenter; the other carbons each have at least two identical substituents (such as extra hydrogens).

stereocenters.q: In 3-methylcyclohexan-1-ol, C1 carries OH, H and two ring bonds. Why is it a stereocenter?
options: Any ring carbon with an OH is one
The two ring paths reach the methyl at different counts
The OH and the methyl are different groups
A six-ring fixes its substituent positions
stereocenters.why: A ring carbon puts two of its four bonds into the ring, and those two bonds are different groups only if the ring differs in the two directions. Walk from C1 one way and the methyl-bearing carbon arrives after two carbons (C2, C3); walk the other way and it arrives after four (C6, C5, C4, C3). Different, so C1 is a stereocenter. Run the same walk on 4-methylcyclohexan-1-ol and both directions give three, so that C1 is not one.

stereocenters.q: How many stereocenters does 2,3-dibromobutane contain?
stereocenters.why: Both C2 and C3 are each bonded to Br, H, a methyl group, and a chain leading to the other substituted carbon, all different, so each qualifies independently as a stereocenter.

stereocenters.q: A tetrahedral carbon stereocenter, as typically defined in an introductory course, must be sp3 hybridized.
stereocenters.why: A classic tetrahedral stereocenter has four single bonds arranged tetrahedrally around an sp3 carbon; sp2 and sp carbons do not have the tetrahedral geometry needed for this type of stereocenter.

stereocenters.q: Which carbon below is NOT a stereocenter?
stereocenters.why: The carbon in CH2Cl2 bears two identical chlorine atoms and two identical hydrogens, so it fails the four-different-groups test, unlike the other examples listed.

stereocenters.q: In 3-methylpentane, is C3 a stereocenter?
options: Yes, because it has a methyl branch
Yes, because it is in the middle of the chain
No, both chains from C3 are ethyl
No, because C3 has no hydrogen attached
stereocenters.why: Tracing outward from C3 in both directions gives an ethyl group on each side, so two of C3's four substituents are identical; this classic trick shows that branching alone does not guarantee a stereocenter.

stereocenters.q: A quaternary carbon (bonded to four other carbon-containing groups, no hydrogens) can never be a stereocenter.
stereocenters.why: What matters is whether the four substituents are different from each other, not whether they are carbon groups or include hydrogen; a quaternary carbon bonded to four different carbon chains is a valid stereocenter.

stereocenters.q: Why do most trisubstituted amines show no optical activity, although N with three different groups and a lone pair looks like a stereocenter?
options: The lone pair blocks any stereochemistry
Amines are too weakly polar to rotate light
Rapid pyramidal inversion interconverts the two
stereocenters.why: Amines undergo fast umbrella-like pyramidal inversion at room temperature, rapidly racemizing any configuration at nitrogen, so the two mirror-image forms interconvert too quickly to be isolated or to show net optical activity.

stereocenters.q: A quaternary ammonium salt (R1R2R3R4N+) with four different groups can be isolated as stable, separable enantiomers.
stereocenters.why: Because nitrogen in a quaternary ammonium ion has no lone pair and cannot undergo pyramidal inversion, its four-different-group configuration is locked in place, unlike in a neutral trisubstituted amine.

stereocenters.q: A compound contains three stereocenters. Which statement about its stereoisomers is correct?
options: Exactly eight exist, in every compound of that kind
Exactly three exist, one for each stereocenter present
Sixteen exist, two for every pair of stereocenters
At most eight exist, and internal symmetry can make it fewer
stereocenters.why: 2ⁿ is a ceiling, not a count: each center can take either configuration, giving 2³ = 8 arrangements at most. Internal symmetry can make two of those arrangements the same substance — that is what a meso compound is — so the real number can be smaller. Tartaric acid is the standard case: two stereocenters, 2² = 4 predicted, three actual.

stereocenters.q: 2,3-dibromobutane has 2 stereocenters. How many total distinct stereoisomers actually exist for this specific compound?
stereocenters.why: Two stereocenters predict 2² = 4, but the two halves of 2,3-dibromobutane are identical, so the (2R,3S) and (2S,3R) arrangements are one and the same achiral substance — the meso form, which gets a section of its own shortly. What is left is an enantiomeric pair plus that one meso compound: three.

stereocenters.q: Which carbon in alanine (2-aminopropanoic acid) is the stereocenter?
stereocenters.why: The alpha carbon carries four distinct groups: a hydrogen, an amino group, a carboxylic acid group, and a methyl group, satisfying the requirement for a stereocenter.

stereocenters.q: Every carbon that is part of a ring (such as cyclohexane) is automatically excluded from being a stereocenter.
stereocenters.why: Ring carbons can absolutely be stereocenters; for example, in 1,2-dimethylcyclohexane, C1 and C2 are each bonded to four different groups once the two distinct ring paths are taken into account.

stereocenters.q: In 1,2-dimethylcyclohexane, which carbons are the stereocenters?
stereocenters.why: C1 and C2 each bear a methyl group, a hydrogen, and two different paths around the ring (one shorter, one longer, to reach the other substituted carbon), making each of them a stereocenter.

stereocenters.q: Sulfoxides (R-S(=O)-R') with two different R groups can act as stereocenters at sulfur because:
options: The lone pair acts as a fourth group
Sulfur has eight valence electrons always
Oxygen cannot double bond to sulfur
stereocenters.why: In a sulfoxide, sulfur's lone pair behaves like a fourth substituent, and unlike nitrogen in amines, the pyramidal inversion at sulfur in a sulfoxide is slow enough at room temperature that the two configurations can be isolated as separate stereoisomers.

stereocenters.q: A molecule must contain at least one stereocenter in order to be chiral.
stereocenters.why: Axial chirality, found in certain allenes and restricted biphenyls, shows that a molecule can be chiral without containing any classic tetrahedral stereocenter.

stereocenters.q: What is the fastest general strategy for spotting a stereocenter by eye in a skeletal structure?
options: Find an sp3 carbon and compare its branches
Count the total number of carbons in the molecule
stereocenters.why: Terminal or symmetric carbons are rarely stereocenters; the reliable method is to identify a tetrahedral (four single-bonded) carbon and compare its four attached groups by tracing outward until a difference (or confirmed sameness) is found.

stereocenters.q: In 4-methylheptane, is C4 a stereocenter?
options: Yes, because it has a methyl branch attached
Yes, because it is the central carbon of the chain
No, because both chains extending from C4 are identical propyl groups
No, because C4 is bonded to only three groups
stereocenters.why: C4 is flanked by a propyl group on each side of the main chain, making two of its four substituents identical, so despite the methyl branch it is not a stereocenter.

stereocenters.q: Scanning a skeletal structure for stereocenters, which carbons can be struck out before comparing any branches?
options: Every carbon that is bonded to an oxygen atom
Every CH₃, every chain CH₂, and every carbon in a double bond
Every carbon that sits inside a ring system
Every carbon at either end of the main chain
stereocenters.why: A CH₃ carries three identical hydrogens and a chain CH₂ carries two, so each already has a repeat and is out; a doubly bonded carbon has three groups rather than four and is not tetrahedral. One pass usually clears most of the molecule and leaves a handful of carbons worth a branch-by-branch comparison. Ring carbons survive the pass — they need the walk-both-ways test.

stereocenters.q: A molecule containing exactly one stereocenter and no other stereochemical features is necessarily chiral.
stereocenters.why: With only a single stereocenter there is no possibility of internal symmetry canceling its effect (that requires at least two stereocenters arranged symmetrically), so one isolated stereocenter always makes the molecule chiral.

stereocenters.q: Which statement about counting stereocenters in a molecule with several of them is most accurate?
options: The count gives an upper bound (2^n), not the total
The count always equals the number of observable stereoisomers
The count is irrelevant to the number of stereoisomers
Stereocenters can only be counted in rings
stereocenters.why: The formula 2^n for n stereocenters gives the maximum possible number of stereoisomers; internal molecular symmetry, as seen in meso compounds, can reduce the actual distinct count below that maximum.

stereocenters.q: In 3-bromo-2-butanol, how many stereocenters are present?
stereocenters.why: Both C2 (bonded to OH, H, CH3, and the rest of the chain) and C3 (bonded to Br, H, CH3, and the rest of the chain) have four different substituents, giving two independent stereocenters.

stereocenters.q: A carbon bonded to H, Cl, Br, and a vinyl group (-CH=CH2) qualifies as a stereocenter.
stereocenters.why: All four substituents, hydrogen, chlorine, bromine, and the vinyl group, are distinct from one another, so this carbon meets the requirement of four different groups and is a stereocenter.

stereocenters.q: Which of the following best explains why the carbon bearing the hydroxyl group in a simple secondary alcohol like 2-pentanol is typically a stereocenter?
options: All alcohols have stereocenters at the OH carbon
It bears OH, H, and two different chains
The OH group is always the largest substituent
stereocenters.why: In an unsymmetrical secondary alcohol, the carbon bearing OH is also bonded to a hydrogen and two alkyl chains of different length or branching, giving four distinct substituents and thus a stereocenter; this is not automatic for every alcohol, such as symmetric ones like 3-pentanol's C3.

stereocenters.q: Can a bridgehead or otherwise strained ring carbon still act as an ordinary tetrahedral stereocenter?
options: No, a ring carbon is never a stereocenter
Yes, provided all four of its substituents differ
Yes, but in six-membered rings alone
No, only carbons outside rings qualify
stereocenters.why: The same four-different-groups rule applies inside rings; a ring carbon with two distinguishable ring paths, a substituent, and a hydrogen can absolutely be a stereocenter, as shown in disubstituted cyclohexanes.

stereocenters.q: For a molecule whose only possible source of chirality is a tetrahedral stereocenter, the minimum number of stereocenters needed before it can have an enantiomer is:
stereocenters.why: One tetrahedral stereocenter has two possible arrangements, and those two are non-superimposable mirror images, so a single stereocenter is enough. The stem rules out the other routes on purpose: a molecule with no stereocenter at all can still be chiral through a twist, as an allene or a hindered biaryl is, so the answer would be zero if those were on the table.

stereocenters.q: A carbon whose four groups include two constitutional isomers of each other, such as n-propyl and isopropyl, still counts as a stereocenter.
stereocenters.why: Constitutional isomers are not identical groups; as long as no two of the four substituents are exactly the same, the carbon satisfies the four-different-groups requirement and is a valid stereocenter.

enantiomers.q: A sample of a chiral compound shows [α] = +21°. The pure (+) enantiomer is +30°. What is the enantiomeric excess?
enantiomers.why: ee = ([α]observed / [α]pure) × 100 = 21/30 = 70%. Read that as 70% of the sample being pure (+) and the remaining 30% being racemic, which works out to 85% (+) and 15% (−). The arithmetic works because rotation is additive: every molecule contributes the same amount regardless of what it is mixed with.

enantiomers.q: Enantiomers have identical physical properties except for their interaction with:
options: Plane-polarized light (optical activity) and chiral environments
enantiomers.why: Enantiomers rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions and behave differently only in chiral environments (e.g., with enzymes).

enantiomers.q: A racemic mixture contains enantiomers in what ratio?
enantiomers.why: A racemic mixture is an equal (50:50) mixture of both enantiomers, which shows no net optical rotation.

enantiomers.q: A sample is 92% (R) and 8% (S). What is its enantiomeric excess?
enantiomers.why: Enantiomeric excess is the excess of the major enantiomer over the minor: 92 − 8 = 84%. The 8% of (R) that pairs off against the 8% of (S) is racemic and contributes nothing to the rotation, leaving 84% of the sample behaving as a single pure enantiomer. A sample quoted at 84% ee therefore rotates light to 84% of the pure value.

enantiomers.q: (R)-2-butanol and (S)-2-butanol will have the same boiling point when each is tested as a pure, separate liquid.
enantiomers.why: Enantiomers have identical physical properties, such as boiling point, melting point, and density, in an achiral environment; they differ only in chiral interactions, such as with polarized light or other chiral molecules.

enantiomers.q: Why can two enantiomers of a drug act very differently in the body?
options: Enzymes and receptors are themselves chiral
One enantiomer has a different formula
The body converts one into a constitutional isomer
enantiomers.why: Biological receptors and enzymes are chiral structures, so they can bind the two mirror-image forms of a drug with very different affinities or effects, even though the enantiomers are chemically identical outside a chiral environment.

enantiomers.q: If a solution of a single pure enantiomer rotates polarized light +25 degrees, what rotation would you expect from an equal concentration of its pure enantiomer?
enantiomers.why: Enantiomers rotate plane-polarized light by equal magnitudes but in opposite directions, so the mirror-image enantiomer under the same conditions rotates light by -25 degrees.

enantiomers.q: A sample with an observed specific rotation of 0 degrees could be explained by which scenario?
options: A racemic mixture, or an achiral compound
A single enantiomer dissolved in a chiral solvent
enantiomers.why: Zero net rotation occurs either when opposite rotations from equal amounts of both enantiomers cancel out (a racemic mixture) or when the compound itself is achiral and has no rotation to begin with.

enantiomers.q: Converting one pure enantiomer into a 50:50 racemic mixture, without changing any other chemistry, will change which observable property?
enantiomers.why: Optical rotation drops to zero upon racemization, and in some compounds the racemic mixture also crystallizes differently than the pure enantiomer (sometimes called a racemic compound), giving it a different melting point from the pure enantiomer.

enantiomers.q: Reacting a single enantiomer of a chiral starting material with an achiral reagent, at a site well away from the stereocenter and with no chiral influence anywhere in the flask, will generally produce:
options: Only the opposite enantiomer of product
A racemic mixture of both enantiomers of product
enantiomers.why: Nothing in the flask can tell the two faces or the two mirror images apart, and no bond at the stereocenter is touched, so the configuration there is carried through untouched and the product is a single enantiomer. The stem has to say ‘away from the stereocenter’ for that to hold: an achiral reagent acting AT the stereocenter can invert it, as SN2 does, or destroy it and hand back a racemate, as SN1 does.

enantiomers.q: Two separate flasks each contain a pure enantiomer of the same chiral compound. Which technique could, in principle, distinguish which flask is which?
options: Measuring optical rotation with a polarimeter
enantiomers.why: Since enantiomers share identical achiral physical properties like boiling point, melting point, and density, only a chiral-sensitive measurement such as optical rotation can tell the two pure enantiomer samples apart.

enantiomers.q: A 1:1 mixture of two enantiomers is called a racemic mixture and is often denoted with the prefix:
enantiomers.why: A racemic mixture, containing equal parts of both enantiomers, is conventionally labeled with the prefix rac- or the symbol (±), reflecting that it shows no net optical rotation.

enantiomers.q: Enantiomers always differ in every one of their NMR and IR spectra taken in an ordinary (achiral) solvent.
enantiomers.why: In a standard achiral NMR or IR solvent, enantiomers give identical spectra because these techniques do not distinguish mirror-image forms; a chiral shift reagent or chiral environment is needed to tell enantiomers apart by NMR.

enantiomers.q: Which of the following is the enantiomer of (R)-2-chlorobutane?
enantiomers.why: The enantiomer of a molecule with a single stereocenter is obtained by inverting the configuration at that stereocenter, converting R to S while keeping the same constitution, giving (S)-2-chlorobutane.

enantiomers.q: For a molecule with only one stereocenter, how many enantiomers (excluding the molecule itself) does it have?
enantiomers.why: A single stereocenter has exactly two possible spatial arrangements, R and S; these two forms are mirror images of one another, so there is exactly one enantiomer for any given single-stereocenter compound.

enantiomers.q: Enzymes in the body are able to distinguish between enantiomers of a substrate because enzymes themselves are built from chiral amino acids.
enantiomers.why: Because enzyme active sites are chiral three-dimensional pockets built largely from chiral L-amino acids, they typically bind one enantiomer of a substrate much more effectively than its mirror image.

enantiomers.q: An optically pure chiral catalyst acts on an achiral starting material. What becomes possible that an achiral catalyst could not do?
options: The product comes out racemic regardless
The product can form as a single enantiomer
The starting material turns into a diastereomer
enantiomers.why: A chiral catalyst can favor formation of one transition state over its mirror image, leading to an enantioselective synthesis that produces one enantiomer in excess, something an achiral catalyst cannot do from achiral starting materials.

enantiomers.q: Which statement about (+) and (-) labels for enantiomers is correct?
options: (+) always corresponds to the R configuration
The sign shows observed rotation, not R or S
enantiomers.why: The (+) and (-) signs describe the experimentally measured direction of rotation of polarized light, which must be determined by measurement and is not something that can be predicted directly from the R or S configurational label alone.

enantiomers.q: A racemic mixture and a single pure enantiomer of the same compound have identical melting points in every case.
enantiomers.why: While this is often approximately true, some racemic mixtures form a distinct crystal packing (a racemic compound) with a melting point that differs, sometimes substantially, from that of the pure enantiomer.

enantiomers.q: Two enantiomers meet the same achiral reagent under identical conditions. Their reaction rates are:
options: Different, one enantiomer being more reactive
Identical, as the reagent cannot tell them apart
enantiomers.why: An achiral reagent reacting with two enantiomers experiences mirror-image transition states that are equal in energy, so the reaction rates with each enantiomer are identical unless a chiral influence is introduced.

enantiomers.q: Separating a racemic mixture into its two pure enantiomers (resolution) typically requires:
options: Interaction with a chiral resolving agent or chiral stationary phase
Simple recrystallization from a common solvent
enantiomers.why: Because enantiomers share identical boiling points, melting points, and solubilities in ordinary achiral solvents, standard separation techniques fail; a chiral resolving agent or chromatography using a chiral stationary phase is needed to separate them.

enantiomers.q: A solution at 0.20 g/mL is measured in a 1.0 dm tube and shows an observed rotation of +5.2°. What is the specific rotation?
enantiomers.why: [α] = α / (l × c) = 5.2 / (1.0 × 0.20) = +26°. Both divisions matter: doubling the tube length or doubling the concentration doubles the observed rotation, because the beam meets twice as many molecules on its way through. Dividing them out is what turns a reading off an instrument into a constant of the substance.

enantiomers.q: Label the relationship: (2R,3R)-2,3-dichlorobutane and (2S,3S)-2,3-dichlorobutane are:
enantiomers.why: Inverting the configuration at every stereocenter converts a molecule into its full mirror image; since both stereocenters are flipped here (R to S at both), these two structures are enantiomers of each other.

enantiomers.q: Enantiomeric excess (ee) of a sample is best described as:
options: The total percent yield of a reaction
The melting point difference between two enantiomers
The excess of major enantiomer over minor
The number of stereocenters in the molecule
enantiomers.why: Enantiomeric excess quantifies how far a sample is from racemic by reporting the percentage by which the major enantiomer exceeds the minor one; 100 percent ee means a single pure enantiomer, while 0 percent ee means fully racemic.

enantiomers.q: Reacting a racemic chiral compound with a single pure enantiomer of a chiral resolving agent is useful for separating enantiomers because it produces:
options: Two enantiomers that are now easier to distinguish by smell
A pair of separable diastereomeric salts
enantiomers.why: Combining each of the two original enantiomers with the same chiral resolving agent produces two diastereomeric adducts, which (unlike the original enantiomers) have different melting points and solubilities and so can be separated by standard techniques; this is the classic method of resolving a racemic mixture.

enantiomers.q: Why does an ordinary GC column fail to separate a racemate when a chiral GC column succeeds?
options: An achiral phase cannot distinguish the two; a chiral one can
Ordinary columns are simply too short for the job
The enantiomers differ in molecular weight
A chiral column heats each enantiomer differently
enantiomers.why: An ordinary achiral stationary phase cannot distinguish the two mirror-image shapes, so both enantiomers travel through at the same rate; a chiral stationary phase forms diastereomeric-like interactions of different strengths with each enantiomer, giving them different retention times.

enantiomers.q: Pure enantiomers of the same compound have identical refractive indices and solubilities in ordinary achiral solvents.
enantiomers.why: Refractive index and solubility in an achiral solvent are both achiral physical properties, so like melting point and boiling point they are identical for a pair of pure enantiomers, differing only in chiral interactions.

enantiomers.q: A racemic sample and an enantiomerically pure sample of the same chiral compound give identical proton NMR spectra when run in an ordinary, non-chiral solvent.
enantiomers.why: Standard NMR in an achiral solvent cannot distinguish between enantiomers, so a racemic mixture and a pure single enantiomer of the same compound give indistinguishable spectra unless a chiral shift reagent or chiral solvent is added.

enantiomers.q: The amino acids that make up natural proteins are overwhelmingly found in which configuration?
enantiomers.why: Biology strongly favors a single enantiomeric series; nearly all amino acids incorporated into natural proteins are of the L configuration, reflecting the chiral machinery (itself built from L-amino acids) that synthesizes and uses them.

enantiomers.q: A sample reported to have 60 percent enantiomeric excess (ee) of the (R) enantiomer corresponds to a composition of approximately 80 percent (R) and 20 percent (S).
enantiomers.why: Enantiomeric excess is calculated as the percent major enantiomer minus the percent minor enantiomer; since the two percentages must sum to 100, an ee of 60 percent corresponds to 80 percent major and 20 percent minor (80 minus 20 equals 60).

diastereomers.q: Diastereomers are stereoisomers that:
options: Are mirror images of each other
diastereomers.why: Diastereomers differ in configuration at some, but not all, stereocenters, so they are not mirror images.

diastereomers.q: Unlike enantiomers, diastereomers generally have:
diastereomers.why: Diastereomers are genuinely different compounds with different shapes, so their physical properties differ, unlike enantiomers.

diastereomers.q: Cis and trans isomers of a disubstituted cycloalkane are an example of:
diastereomers.why: Cis/trans ring isomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images of each other — classic diastereomers.

diastereomers.q: Which pair below is a pair of diastereomers even though neither molecule contains a stereocenter?
diastereomers.why: Count the stereocenters in either 2-butene and you get zero, yet the two compounds are distinct stereoisomers and neither is the mirror image of the other — so they are diastereomers. That is why the definition is written as ‘stereoisomers that are not mirror images’ rather than as a stereocenter count: a C=C is a stereogenic unit in its own right. The alcohols differ in connectivity, and two chairs are conformations of one compound.

diastereomers.q: Diastereomers generally have identical boiling points, melting points, and densities, just like enantiomers do.
diastereomers.why: Unlike enantiomers, diastereomers are genuinely different compounds in terms of shape and polarity in an achiral sense, so they typically have distinct physical properties such as melting point, boiling point, and solubility.

diastereomers.q: For (2R,3R)-2,3-dibromobutane and (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane, the relationship is:
diastereomers.why: Only one of the two stereocenters (C3) has its configuration flipped while the other (C2) stays the same, so these are stereoisomers but not full mirror images, making them diastereomers.

diastereomers.q: Cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane and trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane are related as:
diastereomers.why: Cis and trans forms of a disubstituted ring differ in the spatial arrangement at the ring stereocenters but are not mirror images of each other, so they fit the definition of diastereomers.

diastereomers.q: A molecule with three independent stereocenters can have diastereomers as well as an enantiomer.
diastereomers.why: With three stereocenters there are up to eight stereoisomers total; one of them is the full mirror image (the enantiomer), and the remaining six are diastereomers that differ in configuration at only one or two of the three centers.

diastereomers.q: Why can diastereomers be separated by distillation or recrystallization when enantiomers usually cannot?
options: Enantiomers cannot be purified at all
diastereomers.why: Because diastereomers differ in shape and interactions in ways that change melting point, boiling point, and solubility, standard separations can exploit those differences, unlike with enantiomers, which share those properties.

diastereomers.q: Two diastereomers of the same compound will always rotate plane-polarized light by exactly equal and opposite amounts.
diastereomers.why: That equal-and-opposite relationship is specific to enantiomers; diastereomers are different compounds, so their specific rotations are generally unrelated in magnitude or sign and must be measured independently.

diastereomers.q: Epimers are a kind of diastereomer, defined as isomers differing in configuration at:
diastereomers.why: Epimers are a subset of diastereomers that differ in configuration at exactly one of several stereocenters while all other stereocenters remain the same, making them easy to compare directly.

diastereomers.q: D-glucose and D-galactose, which differ in configuration at only one of their several stereocenters, are an example of:
diastereomers.why: Since glucose and galactose differ at only one stereocenter (C4) out of several, while sharing the same configuration everywhere else, they are epimers, a specific case of diastereomers.

diastereomers.q: A pair of diastereomers can consist of one chiral molecule and one achiral molecule.
diastereomers.why: meso-Tartaric acid, (2R,3S), and (2R,3R)-tartaric acid are stereoisomers that are not mirror images of each other, so they are diastereomers — and the meso one is achiral while the other is optically active. Being a mirror-image pair is what enantiomers require, and that does force both members to be chiral; diastereomers are defined by what they are not, so nothing constrains them to match in chirality, melting point or any other property.

diastereomers.q: Which pair of compounds is NOT a diastereomeric pair?
diastereomers.why: (2R,3R)- and (2S,3S)-tartaric acid have every stereocenter inverted relative to each other, making them full mirror images, or enantiomers, rather than diastereomers.

diastereomers.q: If a molecule has two stereocenters and exists as three observable stereoisomers instead of four, this is most likely because:
options: The molecule only has one stereocenter, not two
Diastereomers cannot exist for that molecule
Two of the four are one meso compound
diastereomers.why: When two stereocenters are symmetric with respect to each other (as in 2,3-dibromobutane), the R,S and S,R combinations become the same meso compound, reducing four possible stereoisomers down to three distinct ones: two enantiomers plus one meso diastereomer.

diastereomers.q: Two diastereomers can differ enough in reactivity that one reacts faster than the other with the same reagent.
diastereomers.why: Because diastereomers have genuinely different three-dimensional shapes and steric environments (unlike enantiomers in an achiral setting), they can and often do react at different rates with the same achiral reagent.

diastereomers.q: What separates diastereomers from constitutional isomers?
options: Diastereomers differ in connectivity; constitutional isomers do not
Diastereomers share connectivity and differ in space; constitutional isomers differ in connectivity
There is no real difference between the two categories
Constitutional isomers share a formula with unrelated diastereomers
diastereomers.why: Both share a molecular formula, and that is where the resemblance stops. Constitutional isomers are built differently — the atoms are joined up in a different order, as in butan-1-ol against butan-2-ol. Diastereomers have exactly the same connectivity and differ only in how that skeleton is arranged in space, and they are not mirror images of each other.

diastereomers.q: For a compound with two independent stereocenters and no internal symmetry, which statement about its four stereoisomers is correct?
options: Each one has three enantiomers among the other three
All four turn out to be the same compound
Each one has a single enantiomer and two diastereomers
diastereomers.why: Take (2R,3R). Inverting every center gives (2S,3S), its one enantiomer. The other two, (2R,3S) and (2S,3R), each have one center inverted and one not, so neither is a mirror image — they are its two diastereomers. Every stereoisomer of a two-center compound sits in that same pattern, which is what makes the six pairings break down into two enantiomeric and four diastereomeric relationships.

diastereomers.q: Geometric cis/trans isomers of alkenes (like cis-2-butene and trans-2-butene) are classified in modern terminology as a type of:
diastereomers.why: Cis and trans alkene isomers have the same connectivity but different spatial arrangement around the double bond, and they are not mirror images of one another, so they fall under the broader category of diastereomers.

diastereomers.q: Diastereomers, unlike enantiomers, can in principle be distinguished using standard NMR spectroscopy in an ordinary achiral solvent.
diastereomers.why: Because diastereomers are chemically distinct compounds with different local environments around their atoms, they generally give different NMR chemical shifts and coupling patterns even in a standard achiral solvent, unlike enantiomers which appear identical.

diastereomers.q: Flipping one of two stereocenters gives a diastereomer and flipping both gives the enantiomer. What does flipping neither give?
diastereomers.why: Flipping no stereocenters at all leaves the configuration completely unchanged, so you simply reproduce the original compound rather than generating any new stereoisomer.

diastereomers.q: Why control which diastereomer forms in a synthesis, when diastereomers can usually be separated?
options: Their formulas differ from each other
Only one of them is ever stable
They can differ in activity and stability
diastereomers.why: Since diastereomers are genuinely different compounds with potentially very different properties and activities, chemists often need diastereoselective reactions to favor the desired diastereomer rather than forming an unwanted (though separable) mixture.

diastereomers.q: A molecule with two stereocenters has four possible stereoisomers. How many total diastereomeric (non-mirror-image) relationships exist among those four, counting each pair once?
diastereomers.why: With 2 pairs of enantiomers (2 relationships) among the 4 stereoisomers, the remaining pairings across the two pairs are diastereomeric — there are 4 such cross-pairs out of the 6 total pairs possible among 4 stereoisomers.

diastereomers.q: If compound A and compound B have the same molecular formula, the same connectivity, but are not mirror images and not identical, they must be:
diastereomers.why: Same connectivity plus not mirror images plus not identical is exactly the definition of diastereomers — stereoisomers that are not enantiomers.

diastereomers.q: Threose and erythrose (four-carbon aldotetroses differing in relative stereochemistry at their two stereocenters) are related to each other as:
diastereomers.why: They share the same connectivity but differ in configuration at one of two stereocenters (not all of them), making them diastereomers rather than enantiomers.

diastereomers.q: Two diastereomers can have different dipole moments.
diastereomers.why: Because diastereomers have genuinely different 3D shapes, their bond vectors add up differently, so their dipole moments (and other physical properties) can differ.

diastereomers.q: In a reaction that creates a new stereocenter next to an existing one, producing a mixture of two diastereomeric products in unequal amounts, this outcome is called:
diastereomers.why: When a reaction favors formation of one diastereomer over another, that preference is called diastereoselectivity.

diastereomers.q: Anti addition of Br₂ to trans-2-butene gives meso-2,3-dibromobutane. What does the same reaction give with cis-2-butene?
options: The meso compound again, since the mechanism is unchanged
The (2R,3R) and (2S,3S) pair, in equal amounts
diastereomers.why: The mechanism is the same and the stereochemistry of the addition is the same — anti, through a bromonium ion — but the alkene geometry decides which face each methyl ends up on, so switching cis for trans switches the answer. Anti addition to the cis alkene gives the chiral pair as a racemate; anti addition to the trans alkene gives meso. Both flasks read zero on a polarimeter, for completely different reasons.

diastereomers.q: Which of these pairs is a diastereomeric pair rather than an enantiomeric pair?
options: A molecule and its exact superimposable copy
Two samples of the same pure enantiomer
diastereomers.why: Differing at only one of the two stereocenters (not both) means they are not mirror images of each other — that relationship is diastereomeric.

diastereomers.q: An ordinary achiral reagent can, in principle, react with two diastereomers at different rates.
diastereomers.why: Since diastereomers are different compounds with different shapes, even simple achiral reagents can react with them at different rates, unlike enantiomers which need a chiral environment to be distinguished.

meso.q: A meso compound contains stereocenters but is overall:
options: Achiral, due to an internal plane of symmetry
meso.why: A meso compound has stereocenters, but an internal mirror plane makes the whole molecule superimposable on its mirror image — achiral, optically inactive.

meso.q: Meso compounds commonly arise in molecules with:
meso.why: A classic meso case is a molecule with two stereocenters bearing the same substituents arranged symmetrically (e.g., meso-tartaric acid).

meso.q: Does a meso compound rotate plane-polarized light?
meso.why: Because a meso compound is achiral (despite having stereocenters), it does not rotate plane-polarized light.

meso.q: 2,3-Dibromobutane is meso as (2R,3S). Is (2R,3S)-2-bromo-3-chlorobutane meso too?
options: Yes — opposite descriptors is the meso pattern
No — one half ends in Br, the other in Cl
No — both halogens must share a carbon
meso.why: Opposite descriptors are evidence of meso only after the two halves have been checked for being identical. In 2,3-dibromobutane both halves are CH₃–CHBr–, so the reflection maps one onto the other. In 2-bromo-3-chlorobutane one half ends in bromine and the other in chlorine, and no reflection can send Br onto Cl. That compound is a perfectly ordinary chiral molecule with four stereoisomers and no meso form.

meso.q: A meso compound is always identical to a racemic mixture in terms of how it behaves with polarized light.
meso.why: A meso compound is a single, defined achiral substance that shows zero rotation on its own because of internal symmetry, whereas a racemic mixture is a 50:50 blend of two different chiral enantiomers that together also show zero net rotation; they are conceptually different even though both give zero rotation.

meso.q: Which classic example is commonly used to illustrate a meso compound?
meso.why: Meso-tartaric acid, one of the three possible stereoisomers of tartaric acid, has two stereocenters of opposite configuration related by an internal mirror plane, making it the textbook example of a meso compound.

meso.q: For tartaric acid, which three stereoisomers exist, and which one is the meso form?
options: Only (R,R) and (S,S), with no meso form
meso.why: Tartaric acid's two stereocenters give (R,R) and (S,S) as a pair of enantiomers, while the (R,S) (equivalent to S,R by the molecule's internal symmetry) combination is the single meso diastereomer.

meso.q: Anti addition of Br₂ to which alkene gives meso-2,3-dibromobutane as a single achiral product?
meso.why: Bromine adds anti, through a bromonium ion opened from the far face, and the geometry of the alkene then decides the relative configuration of the two new stereocenters. The trans alkene delivers the (R,S) arrangement, which is the meso compound. The cis alkene, run the same way, gives the chiral (2R,3R)/(2S,3S) pair as a racemate. The other two alkenes give only one new stereocenter, or none.

meso.q: A flask reads zero on a polarimeter. What decides whether it holds a meso compound or a racemate?
options: Whether the compound has an even stereocenter count
Whether the flask holds one compound or two
Whether its melting point is the highest
meso.why: Both readings are zero and both stay zero however carefully you measure, so the polarimeter cannot settle it. A meso compound is one pure achiral substance with one melting point and no enantiomer to be separated from. A racemate is two chiral compounds in a 50:50 mixture, which a chiral resolving agent or a chiral column could in principle pull apart. One compound or two is the whole question.

meso.q: 2,3-dibromobutane can exist as which set of stereoisomers?
options: An (R,R)/(S,S) enantiomer pair plus one meso (R,S) form
meso.why: The two symmetric stereocenters in 2,3-dibromobutane give a chiral (R,R)/(S,S) enantiomeric pair and a separate achiral meso (R,S) form, totaling three stereoisomers instead of the four that unrelated stereocenters would give.

meso.q: A meso compound is a diastereomer of the chiral stereoisomers that share its same constitution.
meso.why: The meso form and the chiral enantiomeric pair of the same constitution are stereoisomers that are not mirror images of one another, so by definition the meso compound is a diastereomer relative to each of the chiral forms.

meso.q: Why are (2R,3S)- and (2S,3R)-2,3-dibromobutane one compound rather than two?
options: A 180° turn superimposes one on the other
R and S labels carry no real meaning
The molecule has no stereocenters at all
meso.why: Due to the molecule's internal symmetry, simply rotating the (2R,3S) structure in space reproduces the (2S,3R) labeling of the same physical molecule, confirming that they are not two different compounds but one single meso compound.

meso.q: Two stereocenters carry entirely different sets of substituents. Can that compound have a meso form?
options: Yes, in every case where both are stereocenters
Yes, but in six-membered rings alone
No — meso needs a symmetric substitution pattern
No — meso needs at least three stereocenters
meso.why: A meso compound requires an internal mirror relationship between parts of the molecule, which is only possible when the relevant stereocenters sit in a symmetric arrangement; if the two stereocenters have completely different substituent sets, no such internal symmetry can form.

meso.q: In cyclic disubstituted compounds, cis-1,2-dibromocyclohexane (with a mirror plane through the ring) is an example of:
meso.why: The cis isomer of 1,2-dibromocyclohexane has a plane of symmetry passing through the molecule that relates its two stereocenters, making it achiral overall even though each ring carbon individually qualifies as a stereocenter, so it is meso.

meso.q: For the same 1,2-dibromocyclohexane system, is the trans isomer also meso?
options: Yes, trans is always meso like cis
No, the trans isomer has no stereocenters
Yes, but only in its boat conformation
No, trans is a chiral enantiomer pair
meso.why: Unlike the cis isomer, the trans arrangement of substituents breaks the internal mirror symmetry, so trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane exists as a genuinely chiral pair of enantiomers rather than a single meso compound.

meso.q: A meso compound's melting point should be compared against which other stereoisomers of the same constitution?
options: The chiral (R,R)/(S,S) pair, which it differs from
The chiral pair, whose values it matches exactly
Nothing — its properties cannot be measured
Its own value doubled, by convention
meso.why: Because the meso form is a diastereomer, not an enantiomer, of the chiral (R,R)/(S,S) pair, it is a genuinely different compound and commonly shows a distinct melting point and other physical properties from that chiral pair.

meso.q: Meso compounds are optically inactive for the same underlying structural reason that any other achiral molecule is optically inactive.
meso.why: Regardless of whether the achirality comes from having no stereocenters at all or from an internal mirror symmetry relating multiple stereocenters (as in a meso compound), the underlying reason for zero optical rotation is the same: the molecule is superimposable on its own mirror image.

meso.q: Identifying a meso compound from a structure is most reliably done by:
options: Counting the total number of atoms in the molecule
Checking for an internal mirror plane
Assuming any molecule with two stereocenters is automatically meso
meso.why: The definitive test is to look for an internal symmetry element, most commonly a mirror plane, that maps one half of the molecule (including its stereocenters) onto the other; simply having two stereocenters is not enough, since asymmetric stereocenters give no meso form.

meso.q: How many stereoisomers in total does tartaric acid have, counting the meso form?
meso.why: Tartaric acid's two stereocenters would normally allow up to four stereoisomers, but the symmetric substitution pattern collapses the R,S and S,R combinations into one meso form, leaving three total stereoisomers: two enantiomers and one meso diastereomer.

meso.q: A meso compound can be separated from its corresponding chiral enantiomeric pair using ordinary techniques such as recrystallization or chromatography on a normal (non-chiral) column.
meso.why: Since the meso form and the chiral (R,R)/(S,S) pair are diastereomers of each other with different physical properties, they can be separated by standard, non-chiral separation techniques, unlike a true pair of enantiomers.

meso.q: Which drawn arrangement of 2,3-dibromobutane is the meso form?
options: Br on a wedge to the left at the top and to the right at the bottom
Br on a wedge at the top center and in the plane at the bottom
Br on a hash at both centers, with both methyl groups on wedges
Br on a wedge to the left at both centers, H hashed to the right at both
meso.why: Draw the chain vertically and look for a horizontal mirror. With Br on a wedge to the left at both centers and H hashed to the right at both, reflecting the top half through a line between the two carbons lands Br on Br, H on H and methyl on methyl — the molecule contains its own mirror image and is achiral. Turn the lower center over so that its bromine points to the right, and the descriptors match instead of opposing — that drawing is the chiral (R,R) or (S,S) form.

meso.q: A meso compound must, by definition, contain an even number of stereocenters.
meso.why: The count is about symmetry, not parity. Three stereocenters can give a meso form when the middle one lies on the symmetry element and the outer two carry opposite configurations — ribitol and xylitol are the standard sugar-alcohol examples. What a meso compound needs is an internal improper symmetry element, and nothing about that requires the number of stereocenters to be even.

meso.q: A meso compound's specific rotation, when measured with a polarimeter, is expected to be:
meso.why: Being achiral, a meso compound does not rotate plane-polarized light at all — its specific rotation is 0.

meso.q: Meso compounds can only occur in molecules with exactly two stereocenters and never more.
meso.why: Meso forms can occur in molecules with more than two stereocenters as long as the overall structure has an internal mirror plane or similar symmetry relating the configurations.

meso.q: Why is a meso compound not the same thing as a racemic mixture?
options: It has no stereocenters, unlike a racemate
It is one pure, internally symmetric substance
