e2.why: Because E2 is concerted and doesn't generate a free ionic intermediate, it doesn't depend as strongly on a solvent's ability to stabilize charge the way the ionization step of SN1/E1 does.

e2.q: Why does a secondary substrate reacting with a small, strong base/nucleophile like NaOH often give a mixture of SN2 and E2 products?
options: NaOH is both a strong nucleophile and a strong base
NaOH cannot act as a nucleophile under any conditions
Secondary substrates can never undergo SN2
E2 never competes with SN2 on secondary substrates
e2.why: Hydroxide is simultaneously a good nucleophile and a good base, so on a substrate that is accessible enough for backside attack, both substitution and elimination pathways remain viable and compete.

e2.q: How does leaving group quality affect E2 rate, compared to its effect on SN2?
options: Leaving group quality has no effect on E2 rate, unlike SN2
Better leaving groups (e.g., I- > Br- > Cl- > F-) speed up E2, just as they do SN2
Worse leaving groups speed up E2 while better ones speed up SN2
Leaving group quality only matters for E1, not E2
e2.why: Since the leaving group departs in the same single step as proton removal, a more stable, easier-to-lose leaving group lowers the activation energy for E2 just as it does for SN2.

e2.q: In a disubstituted cyclohexane where the only beta-hydrogen on one side happens to be equatorial (not anti-periplanar to an axial leaving group), what happens to E2 elimination toward that side?
options: It proceeds normally regardless of the hydrogen's orientation
E2 switches automatically to E1 in that situation
It cannot; elimination must go the other way
The leaving group becomes equatorial instead to compensate
e2.why: Without a hydrogen positioned anti-periplanar to the leaving group on that side, the required transition-state geometry simply cannot be reached, so that elimination pathway is blocked.

e2.q: Menthyl chloride has only one beta-hydrogen that is trans-diaxial (anti-periplanar) to its chlorine. Why does its E2 reaction often give the less substituted (anti-Zaitsev) alkene as the major product?
options: Menthyl chloride has no accessible beta-hydrogens at all
Less substituted alkenes are always favored in E2, regardless of geometry
The chlorine in menthyl chloride is a poor leaving group
Only that hydrogen is anti-periplanar to the chlorine
e2.why: E2's strict geometric requirement can override simple product-stability preferences; if the only anti-periplanar hydrogen happens to give the less stable alkene, that's still the product that forms.

e2.q: The strict anti-periplanar requirement of E2 means that the stereochemistry of a specific diastereomer of starting material can determine which alkene stereoisomer (E or Z) actually forms.
e2.why: Because only certain conformations place a given hydrogen anti-periplanar to the leaving group, the starting material's three-dimensional arrangement directly dictates which hydrogen is removed and therefore the resulting double bond geometry.

e2.q: Why are deuterium kinetic isotope effects observed when comparing C-H versus C-D cleavage in E2, but not typically in SN2?
options: The beta C-H breaks in E2's rate-determining step
Deuterium always reacts faster than hydrogen in every mechanism
SN2 never involves any hydrogen atoms
E2 does not actually involve breaking any C-H bond
e2.why: A kinetic isotope effect appears specifically when the bond to the isotope is broken in the rate-determining step; since E2's only step breaks the beta C-H bond, while SN2's step does not touch that bond at all, only E2 shows this effect.

e2.q: You need 2-methylbut-1-ene, not 2-methylbut-2-ene, from 2-bromo-2-methylbutane in one step. Which base?
e2.why: The target is the less substituted alkene, which is the Hofmann product, and the way to get it is a base too bulky to reach the crowded internal hydrogen. tert-Butoxide fits: with this substrate it gives about 73% of the terminal alkene, where small ethoxide gives about 70% of the internal one. Iodide is a good nucleophile and a weak base, so it substitutes rather than eliminating; warm water gives unimolecular chemistry and, through the cation, the Zaitsev alkene again.

e2.q: Why can E2 occur at primary carbons even though SN1 and E1 essentially cannot?
options: Primary carbons are always more electrophilic than secondary or tertiary carbons
E2 actually proceeds through a primary carbocation intermediate
E2 is concerted and requires no carbocation intermediate
Primary substrates have no beta-hydrogens, which makes E2 easier
e2.why: Since no cationic intermediate ever forms in E2, the usual instability of a primary carbocation is simply irrelevant to whether E2 can proceed.

e2.q: A cyclohexyl bromide's most stable chair has the bromine equatorial. What must happen before E2?
options: The base has to be made bulkier
The ring must flip so the bromine becomes axial
The bromide must first ionize to a carbocation
Nothing — equatorial leaving groups eliminate normally
e2.why: On a chair, the only pairs of neighboring substituents that are genuinely anti-periplanar are trans-diaxial ones. An equatorial leaving group is roughly 60° from every hydrogen on both neighboring carbons, so no continuous orbital overlap is available and the concerted step cannot run. The ring has to flip first, which puts the bromine axial and every other substituent on the ring into its opposite position — and if those substituents are large, the cost of that flip shows up directly as a slower reaction. Menthyl chloride is the classic case.

e2.q: Comparing a tosylate (OTs) leaving group to a chloride on the same substrate with the same base, how does E2 rate typically compare?
options: The tosylate reacts faster, being the better leaving group
The chloride reacts faster, since chlorine is smaller
Both react at identical rates, since leaving group identity never affects E2
Neither leaving group allows E2 to occur
e2.why: Because the leaving group departs in the same concerted step as proton removal, a more stable, weaker-base leaving group like tosylate lowers the activation energy for elimination just as it does for substitution.

e2.q: Switching the base from weakly basic acetate to the very strongly basic amide ion (NH2-) can push an otherwise unhindered secondary substrate's reaction from predominantly SN2 toward predominantly E2. Why?
options: Amide ion cannot act as a nucleophile at all
Acetate is actually a stronger base than amide ion
Stronger bases always slow down every reaction
e2.why: As basicity increases sharply, a reagent's tendency to grab a proton (driving elimination) increasingly outcompetes its tendency to attack the carbon directly (driving substitution), even without added steric bulk.

substrate-effects.q: A strong, bulky base (like tert-butoxide) with a secondary substrate tends to favor:
substrate-effects.why: Bulky strong bases have trouble doing backside attack (poor SN2) but easily deprotonate, favoring E2.

substrate-effects.q: Polar protic solvents (like water or alcohols) favor which mechanism type by stabilizing cationic intermediates?
substrate-effects.why: Polar protic solvents solvate (stabilize) carbocations and leaving groups well, favoring the ionization step in SN1/E1.

substrate-effects.q: A primary substrate with a strong, non-bulky nucleophile/base (like NaOCH₃ in a small amount) and good backside access typically favors:
substrate-effects.why: Primary carbons have minimal steric hindrance for backside attack and cannot stabilize a carbocation well, so SN2 dominates with a decent nucleophile.

substrate-effects.q: Methyl and primary substrates, when paired with a non-bulky nucleophile, react almost exclusively via which mechanism?
substrate-effects.why: With essentially no steric hindrance at the carbon and no ability to form a stable carbocation, backside attack (SN2) dominates.

substrate-effects.q: A tertiary substrate with a weak nucleophile/base in a polar protic solvent typically reacts mainly via which mechanism(s)?
substrate-effects.why: Tertiary carbons can form stable carbocations, polar protic solvent stabilizes that ionization, and a weak base/nucleophile can't force a bimolecular pathway, so unimolecular substitution and elimination dominate.

substrate-effects.q: 2-Bromobutane meets NaN₃ in acetone, and separately in water. What changes?
options: Nothing — azide is a strong nucleophile in both
Acetone gives clean inverted SN2; water gives a mixture
Water gives clean SN2; acetone gives elimination
Both give mainly but-2-ene, since azide is a strong base
substrate-effects.why: Only the solvent moved, and for a secondary substrate that is enough to change the answer. In acetone, a polar aprotic solvent, azide is unsolvated and attacks fast: clean SN2, giving 2-azidobutane with inversion at C2. In water, azide is hydrogen-bonded and blunted while the solvent itself is strongly ionizing, so the substrate's own slow ionization starts to compete — the product becomes a mixture of inverted and racemized azide plus some butan-2-ol and a little alkene. Azide is a weak base either way, so elimination is never the main event.

substrate-effects.q: Primary substrates essentially cannot undergo SN1 or E1 because the primary carbocation is too unstable to form.
substrate-effects.why: With minimal alkyl substitution to stabilize the positive charge, a primary cation's energy is too high to form at a useful rate under normal conditions.

substrate-effects.q: Which single mechanism is essentially unavailable to a tertiary substrate, regardless of solvent, nucleophile strength, or temperature?
substrate-effects.why: SN2's requirement for a clear backside approach is a geometric barrier that no change in reagent or solvent can overcome at a tertiary carbon.

substrate-effects.q: Secondary substrates are often described as the mechanistic borderline case. Why?
options: They cannot undergo any substitution or elimination reactions
They only ever react via SN1
All four mechanisms are possible, depending on conditions
They are always less reactive than primary substrates
substrate-effects.why: Secondary carbons are sterically open enough for some backside attack yet can also form a moderately stable carbocation, so the outcome hinges heavily on the specific reagents and solvent chosen.

substrate-effects.q: Polar aprotic solvents generally favor which family of mechanisms?
options: The unimolecular pathways, SN1 and E1
The bimolecular pathways, SN2 and E2
substrate-effects.why: Polar aprotic solvents dissolve ionic reagents without caging the nucleophile/base through hydrogen bonding, keeping it highly reactive for a bimolecular attack.

substrate-effects.q: 1-Bromobutane is treated with potassium tert-butoxide. Elimination beats substitution here, even though the reacting carbon is primary and wide open.
substrate-effects.why: tert-Butoxide is a strong base carrying three methyl groups around the reacting oxygen. It is too fat to sit on the backside of C1 and push bromide out, but the beta hydrogens stick out on the outside of the chain where it can still reach one, so the E2 path is the cheap one and but-1-ene is the major product. Swap in ethoxide, which is just as basic but small, and the same substrate gives mostly butyl ethyl ether instead. Sterics on the BASE decide this one, not sterics on the carbon.

substrate-effects.q: Which single factor generally has the largest influence on whether SN2 or SN1/E1 is even feasible at all for a given substrate?
options: The degree of alkyl substitution at the reacting carbon
Solvent polarity, taken on its own
Reaction temperature, taken on its own
The molecular weight of the leaving group
substrate-effects.why: Substrate substitution pattern determines both whether backside attack is geometrically possible and whether a stable carbocation can form, which are the two gateway requirements for these mechanisms.

substrate-effects.q: 1-bromobutane (primary) is treated with NaSH (a strong, small nucleophile) in DMSO (polar aprotic). Which mechanism dominates?
substrate-effects.why: A primary substrate with an open backside path, a strong unhindered nucleophile, and a polar aprotic solvent that doesn't shield the nucleophile is the textbook setup for SN2.

substrate-effects.q: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (tertiary) is stirred in water (a weak nucleophile) at room temperature. Which mechanism(s) dominate?
substrate-effects.why: A tertiary substrate in an ionizing polar protic solvent with only a weak nucleophile present is set up to ionize on its own, giving substitution and elimination from the resulting carbocation.

substrate-effects.q: Cyclohexyl bromide (secondary) is treated with NaOEt (a moderately bulky, strong base) in ethanol. Which mechanism is the expected major pathway?
substrate-effects.why: A strong base on a secondary substrate tends to favor elimination, especially with a base that is reasonably hindered, though some competing substitution is still possible.

substrate-effects.q: Cyclohexyl bromide (secondary) is treated with NaI (a strong nucleophile that is a comparatively weak base) in acetone. Which mechanism dominates?
substrate-effects.why: A strong, minimally basic nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent favors attacking the carbon directly rather than removing a proton, pushing the reaction toward substitution.

substrate-effects.q: A secondary substrate reacting with a strong nucleophile that is a weak base, like NaN3, in a polar aprotic solvent gives predominantly substitution (SN2) rather than elimination.
substrate-effects.why: Because azide is a much better nucleophile than base, and the solvent keeps it highly reactive, the reaction favors attacking the carbon over removing a proton.

substrate-effects.q: Why does increasing temperature generally shift product distribution toward elimination products (E1 or E2) over substitution, for a given substrate and reagent combination?
options: Heat always destroys the substrate before it can react
Elimination has a more favorable activation entropy
Substitution products are never thermodynamically stable
Elimination never depends on temperature at all
substrate-effects.why: Forming two separate, more freely moving product pieces (the alkene and, e.g., water) from one substrate is entropically favorable, and that advantage becomes more significant as temperature rises.

substrate-effects.q: A tertiary substrate is treated with a strong, bulky base like potassium tert-butoxide in a polar aprotic solvent. What is the expected major outcome?
options: SN2, since bulky bases are good nucleophiles
SN1, since bulky bases promote ionization
E2, giving mainly the Hofmann alkene
No reaction, since the base cannot reach
substrate-effects.why: SN2 is blocked by the tertiary carbon's sterics, so a strong base reaching an available beta-hydrogen drives E2, and its bulk biases the outcome toward the less hindered, less substituted alkene.

substrate-effects.q: Methyl iodide is treated with a strong, bulky base like potassium tert-butoxide. What is the expected outcome?
options: E2 elimination, as with a tertiary substrate
SN2 substitution, since there is no beta carbon
SN1, since strong bases promote ionization
substrate-effects.why: Elimination requires a beta-hydrogen on an adjacent carbon, and methyl carbons have no adjacent carbon whatsoever, so substitution is the only mechanistic option available regardless of base bulk.

substrate-effects.q: Even with a very strong, bulky base, a primary substrate bearing beta-hydrogens can sometimes give significant E2 product if steric hindrance near the leaving group (not just the base) also gets in the way of substitution.
substrate-effects.why: Steric crowding doesn't have to come from the reacting carbon alone; a hindered neighboring group plus a bulky base together can tip the balance toward elimination even at a formally primary carbon.

substrate-effects.q: Neopentyl bromide, (CH₃)₃C–CH₂Br, meets NaOEt in warm ethanol. What happens?
options: E2 at the neighboring carbon, giving an alkene
Rapid SN1, since the neighbor is quaternary
Very slow SN2; elimination is not available at all
A methyl shift, then elimination to a branched alkene
substrate-effects.why: Count the beta hydrogens before proposing any elimination. Neopentyl has exactly one beta carbon and it is quaternary — three methyls and no hydrogen — so E2 is not slow here, it is impossible. The carbon bearing bromine is primary, so it will not ionize either, which rules out SN1, E1 and any rearrangement. That leaves SN2, which is allowed but throttled by the same quaternary neighbor blocking the backside: about 10⁵ times slower than ethyl bromide. Neopentyl is famous for being unreactive precisely because its one available pathway is crippled and its obvious alternative does not exist.

substrate-effects.q: A secondary substrate is placed in pure water (a highly ionizing polar protic solvent) along with a moderately strong nucleophile such as bromide ion. Why might SN1/E1 still dominate despite the decent nucleophile present?
options: Bromide ion cannot act as a nucleophile in water under any conditions
Ionization is rate-determining and protic solvent slows attack
SN1/E1 always dominates over SN2/E2 for any secondary substrate
Water prevents all substitution reactions from occurring
substrate-effects.why: Ionizing power and nucleophile/base reactivity are somewhat independent levers; a solvent that strongly favors ionization can tip the balance toward unimolecular pathways even when a competent bimolecular reagent is technically present, partly because that same solvent also dampens the nucleophile's effective reactivity.

substrate-effects.q: Raising the concentration of a strong nucleophile/base for a given substrate can shift the overall mechanism from largely unimolecular toward bimolecular, because increasing [Nu or base] increases the rate of SN2/E2 while the unimolecular (substrate-only) rate stays the same.
substrate-effects.why: Since the bimolecular rate laws depend directly on reagent concentration while the unimolecular ones do not, pushing up reagent concentration makes the bimolecular pathway increasingly competitive, even on a substrate that might otherwise favor ionization.

substrate-effects.q: A tertiary substrate sits in a nonpolar, non-nucleophilic, non-basic solvent (such as an inert hydrocarbon) with no added nucleophile or base. What happens, and why?
options: SN2 proceeds, since tertiary carbons favor substitution
SN1 and E1 proceed, since nonpolar solvents favor ionization
Essentially nothing happens, for want of both a solvent and a reagent
E2 proceeds rapidly even with no base present
substrate-effects.why: Both families of mechanism have a hard requirement that this solvent and reagent combination fails to meet: no ionizing power for SN1/E1, and no reactive species at all for SN2/E2.

substrate-effects.q: You want butan-2-yl ethyl ether from 2-bromobutane, with as little alkene as possible. Which conditions?
substrate-effects.why: The substrate is secondary, so all four mechanisms are on the table and the reagent decides. Ethoxide is a strong base as well as a strong nucleophile, so adding it — in any solvent, and especially with heat — buys you mostly but-2-ene. What you want is a weak nucleophile that is an even weaker base, which is what neutral ethanol is: it cannot force a bimolecular step, the substrate ionizes slowly instead, and ethanol traps the cation to give the ether. The price is some racemization and a little E1 alkene, but it is the cleanest route to this ether from this substrate.

substrate-effects.q: Why does substrate structure often override solvent and nucleophile choice when it comes to whether SN2 is even possible, rather than just how fast it goes?
options: Sterics at a tertiary carbon block backside attack geometrically
Solvent polarity always matters more than substrate structure for SN2 feasibility
Nucleophile strength can always compensate for any amount of steric hindrance
Tertiary substrates can undergo SN2 if the solvent is sufficiently polar
substrate-effects.why: Some barriers are about rate (how fast something happens) while others are about feasibility (whether it can happen at all); the tertiary SN2 backside-attack problem is of the second, more absolute kind.

substrate-effects.q: A primary substrate with available beta-hydrogens reacts with a weak, non-bulky, non-basic nucleophile such as I- in acetone. Why does SN2 dominate with essentially no elimination?
options: Primary substrates cannot undergo elimination under any circumstances
Iodide is a good nucleophile but a very weak base
Acetone actively prevents elimination from occurring
Iodide cannot act as a nucleophile in acetone
substrate-effects.why: Elimination requires the reagent to act as a base, and a species can be an excellent nucleophile while still being a poor base, which is exactly the combination that shuts down the elimination pathway here.

substrate-effects.q: A secondary alkyl halide's solvent is switched from polar aprotic (acetone) to polar protic (ethanol), while the same moderately strong nucleophile/base is used throughout. How does this shift the overall mechanistic balance?
options: It has no effect on the mechanistic balance at all
It shifts the balance toward more SN2/E2 character, since protic solvents always favor bimolecular pathways
Toward SN1/E1, as the protic solvent slows the nucleophile and stabilizes the cation
It shifts the balance toward SN2 only, with no change to elimination
substrate-effects.why: Protic solvents work against bimolecular pathways by caging the nucleophile/base through hydrogen bonding, and simultaneously work in favor of unimolecular pathways by stabilizing developing charge, so both effects push the balance the same direction.

substrate-effects.q: Of the four mechanisms, E2 is comparatively unique in that it can occur efficiently across primary, secondary, and tertiary substrates given a sufficiently strong base, making substrate structure the least restrictive variable for E2 relative to the other three mechanisms.
substrate-effects.why: SN2 is blocked at tertiary carbons and SN1/E1 are essentially blocked at primary carbons, but E2 needs neither backside access at the reacting carbon nor carbocation stability, so it tolerates the widest range of substrate types.

alkene-structure.q: But-2-ene is drawn with its two methyl groups on the same side of the C=C. That isomer is called:
alkene-structure.why: Same side means cis. Each alkene carbon here carries one methyl and one hydrogen, so the higher-priority group on each is the methyl, and the two winners are on the same side — Z. The two labels agree in this case, which is exactly why cis/trans survives for simple alkenes. They are separate compounds, not conformers, because the pi bond cannot rotate.

alkene-structure.q: 2-bromo-2-butene, CH3-C(Br)=CH-CH3, is drawn with its two methyl groups on opposite sides. What is the correct E/Z label?
options: E, because the methyls are trans
Z, because Br and the C4 methyl are on the same side
Neither label applies to this alkene
alkene-structure.why: Rank each carbon separately. On C2 the choice is Br against CH3, and bromine (Z=35) wins. On C3 it is CH3 against H, and the methyl wins. Those two winners — the Br and the C4 methyl — sit on the same side, so the alkene is Z. The skeleton looks trans because the methyls are opposed, which is the point: cis/trans reports the carbon chain and E/Z reports the priorities.

alkene-structure.q: Why can’t the two carbons of a C=C double bond freely rotate relative to each other?
options: The pi bond’s parallel p-orbital overlap would break upon rotation
Rotation around double bonds is actually free
alkene-structure.why: Rotating one carbon relative to the other would misalign the parallel p orbitals forming the pi bond, breaking that overlap — this restricted rotation is what gives rise to cis/trans alkene isomers.

alkene-structure.q: What is the hybridization of each carbon in a simple C=C double bond?
alkene-structure.why: Each alkene carbon forms three sigma bonds (to two substituents and the other alkene carbon) plus one pi bond from an unhybridized p orbital, which requires sp2 hybridization with 120° bond angles.

alkene-structure.q: What is the general molecular formula for an acyclic (non-cyclic) alkene with one double bond and n carbons?
alkene-structure.why: Each pi bond or ring removes two hydrogens relative to the saturated alkane formula CnH2n+2, so one double bond gives CnH2n.

alkene-structure.q: Alkenes have the general molecular formula CnH2n+2, the same as alkanes.
alkene-structure.why: CnH2n+2 is the alkane (fully saturated) formula. Alkenes have one fewer degree of saturation, so they follow CnH2n.

alkene-structure.q: In ethylene (H2C=CH2), the C=C bond is made up of:
options: one sigma bond and one pi bond
alkene-structure.why: A double bond always consists of one sigma bond (head-on overlap) and one pi bond (side-by-side overlap of p orbitals); you cannot have two sigma bonds between the same two atoms.

alkene-structure.q: A carbon-carbon double bond is shorter than a carbon-carbon single bond between the same two types of carbons.
alkene-structure.why: The additional pi bond in a double bond pulls the two carbons closer together, shortening the bond compared to a single (sigma-only) bond.

alkene-structure.q: How many sigma bonds are present in ethylene, H2C=CH2 (including the C-C sigma bond)?
alkene-structure.why: Ethylene has one C-C sigma bond and four C-H sigma bonds (5 total), plus one pi bond that is not counted as a sigma bond.

alkene-structure.q: A compound has the molecular formula C4H7Br. How many degrees of unsaturation does it have?
alkene-structure.why: A halogen caps a chain the way a hydrogen does, so it is counted with the hydrogens: DoU = (2x4 + 2 - 7 - 1)/2 = (10 - 8)/2 = 1. One ring or one pi bond fits — bromocyclobutane and 4-bromobut-1-ene are both C4H7Br.

alkene-structure.q: A compound with the molecular formula C5H10 and no rings has a degree of unsaturation of:
alkene-structure.why: Degree of unsaturation = (2(5)+2-10)/2 = (12-10)/2 = 1, consistent with one double bond and no ring.

alkene-structure.q: Which suffix in IUPAC nomenclature indicates the presence of a carbon-carbon double bond?
alkene-structure.why: The suffix -ene specifically designates a double bond in the parent chain, as in propene or 2-butene.

alkene-structure.q: According to general alkene stability trends, which alkene is typically the most stable?
alkene-structure.why: More substituted alkenes are stabilized by additional alkyl groups donating electron density (hyperconjugation) into the pi system, so tetrasubstituted alkenes are typically the most stable.

alkene-structure.q: Cis/trans labels break down for 2-bromobut-2-ene, CH3-C(Br)=CH-CH3, and E/Z is required instead. What is it about this alkene that forces the switch?
options: One double-bond carbon carries two different non-hydrogen groups
The alkene sits at the middle of the chain rather than the end
Bromine is heavier than any of the carbons in the molecule
The molecule has no plane of symmetry through the double bond
alkene-structure.why: Cis/trans works while each alkene carbon carries one hydrogen and one other group: 'same side' then has an obvious referent. C2 here carries a bromine AND a methyl, so 'the methyls are opposite' and 'the bromine and the C4 methyl are on the same side' describe the same molecule and disagree. CIP priority settles it: Br beats CH3 on C2, CH3 beats H on C3, and the two winners are on the same side, so it is Z.

alkene-structure.q: What is the degree of unsaturation of a compound with molecular formula C5H11N?
alkene-structure.why: Nitrogen is added to the numerator, not subtracted: DoU = (2x5 + 2 + 1 - 11)/2 = (13 - 11)/2 = 1. The check is to write the saturated amine first, C5H13N, and notice the compound is two hydrogens short — two missing hydrogens is one ring or one pi bond. Piperidine is the familiar example.

alkene-structure.q: A compound with a degree of unsaturation of 2 could contain one triple bond instead of two double bonds or a ring plus a double bond.
alkene-structure.why: A triple bond itself counts as two degrees of unsaturation (two pi bonds), so DoU=2 is consistent with one triple bond, two double bonds, two rings, or one ring plus one double bond.

alkene-structure.q: For CIP priority at an alkene carbon bearing both a chlorine atom and a methyl group, which substituent receives higher priority?
options: it depends on the rest of the molecule only
alkene-structure.why: CIP priority is assigned first by atomic number at the point of attachment; chlorine (Z=17) outranks a carbon-based methyl group (Z=6) regardless of what else is in the molecule.

alkene-structure.q: Geometric (cis/trans) isomerism is possible for an alkene only when:
options: each double-bond carbon bears two different substituents
there are at least three carbons total
alkene-structure.why: If either alkene carbon has two identical substituents, there is no distinct 'other side' to compare, so no cis/trans isomerism exists; each carbon needs two different groups.

alkene-structure.q: The pi bond of an alkene forms from the side-by-side overlap of:
options: an s orbital and a p orbital
two unhybridized p orbitals perpendicular to the sp2 plane
alkene-structure.why: Each sp2 carbon retains one unhybridized p orbital oriented perpendicular to the plane of the three sp2 orbitals; side-by-side overlap of these two p orbitals creates the pi bond.

alkene-structure.q: Alkenes are generally more chemically reactive than alkanes because the pi electrons are held less tightly and are more exposed than sigma electrons.
alkene-structure.why: Pi electrons sit above and below the molecular plane, farther from the nuclei and more accessible to electrophiles, making the C=C pi bond a reactive site compared to the strong, low-energy C-C and C-H sigma bonds in alkanes.

alkene-structure.q: Why is every ordinary cycloalkene, such as cyclohexene, cis rather than trans?
options: Trans double bonds are higher in energy in any molecule
A ring smaller than about eight carbons cannot span the double bond the long way
Ring carbons are sp3 and cannot be part of a double bond
Cyclic alkenes have no stereochemistry to report
alkene-structure.why: In a cycloalkene the ring itself is one substituent on each alkene carbon, and it has to reach from one to the other. On the same side that is a short span; on the opposite side the chain must loop around and twist the pi system. Below roughly eight carbons there is not enough chain, so trans-cyclohexene has never been isolated and trans-cyclooctene is the smallest one that can be bottled.

alkene-structure.q: Why is trans-2-butene more stable (lower in energy) than cis-2-butene?
options: the cis methyls crowd each other
cis has a longer bond length
trans has more degrees of unsaturation
alkene-structure.why: In the cis isomer, the two methyl groups point to the same side of the double bond and crowd each other, raising the molecule's energy; in trans they point to opposite sides, minimizing steric clash.

alkene-structure.q: What is the degree of unsaturation of a monoterpene with molecular formula C10H16?
alkene-structure.why: DoU = (2×10+2-16)/2 = 3, consistent with, for example, one ring and two double bonds, a common pattern in monoterpenes.

alkene-structure.q: At one alkene carbon the two groups are a vinyl group (-CH=CH2) and an isopropyl group (-CH(CH3)2). Which has the higher CIP priority?
options: Isopropyl, because it holds more carbon atoms overall
They tie, so the alkene cannot be labeled E or Z
Vinyl, because its CH2 carries a duplicated carbon
The one drawn nearer the top of the page
alkene-structure.why: Both attach through carbon, and both present the set (C, C, H) at that first atom — the vinyl only because a doubly bonded carbon is counted twice as a duplicate. The tie breaks one sphere further out: the vinyl's real CH2 carries (C, H, H) while each isopropyl methyl carries (H, H, H), and carbon beats hydrogen at the first point of difference. Duplicate atoms are phantoms with no substituents of their own, so they never win a tie-break.

alkene-structure.q: A double bond positioned at the bridgehead carbon of a small bicyclic ring system is typically extremely unstable or impossible to form because:
options: bridgehead carbons cannot bond to hydrogen
the ring prevents a planar sp2 carbon
pi bonds cannot exist in rings
alkene-structure.why: An sp2 alkene carbon needs its three attached groups and itself to lie in one plane; in small fused or bridged ring systems the bridgehead geometry can't twist into that planar arrangement without severe strain (this limitation is summarized by Bredt's rule).

alkene-structure.q: Why can a small ring like cyclohexene easily be cis but trans-cyclohexene is essentially impossible to isolate?
options: the ring is too small for trans
alkene-structure.why: Placing the ring's two connecting chains on opposite faces of the double bond (trans) in a small ring requires bond angles far from ideal, introducing enormous strain; only larger rings (roughly 8+ membered) can accommodate a stable trans-cycloalkene.

alkene-structure.q: Bredt's rule rules out a double bond at the bridgehead of a small bicyclic system. Which of these is the reliable form of the rule?
options: No bicyclic compound can contain a double bond anywhere
Bridgehead alkenes become isolable once the bicyclic skeleton has eight or more carbons
Bridgehead carbons cannot bond to hydrogen at all
Bridgehead alkenes are fine as long as the ring is aromatic
alkene-structure.why: An alkene carbon needs its three neighbors coplanar with it, and a bridgehead is held by three separate chains pulling in different directions. Below eight carbons the geometry is impossible — bicyclo[2.2.1]hept-1-ene cannot be made — while bicyclo[3.3.1]non-1-ene, with a longer bridge to give the room, is a real if reactive compound. The rule bites in elimination: a Zaitsev product that would be a bridgehead alkene simply does not form.

alkene-structure.q: In an alkene, the two double-bond carbons and the four atoms directly attached to them all lie approximately in a single plane.
alkene-structure.why: Because each alkene carbon is sp2 hybridized, its three sigma-bonded groups (including the other alkene carbon) are arranged trigonally in one plane, making the whole six-atom C=C unit planar.

alkene-structure.q: A smaller magnitude (less exothermic) heat of hydrogenation for an alkene indicates that alkene is:
options: less stable, higher in energy to begin with
more stable, lower in energy to begin with
alkene-structure.why: Hydrogenation converts all alkene isomers to the same alkane product, so the isomer that starts out lower in energy (more stable) releases less heat upon hydrogenation.

alkene-structure.q: 1-pentene releases 30.1 kcal/mol on hydrogenation, cis-2-pentene 28.6 and trans-2-pentene 27.6. All give pentane. What follows?
options: 1-pentene is the most stable of the three
The three are equally stable because the product is shared
Only the cis and trans pair can be compared this way
alkene-structure.why: All three end at the same alkane, so the heat released measures how far above that shared floor each one started. Releasing less heat means starting lower, i.e. more stable. The two effects visible here are the ones the chapter names: the disubstituted pentenes beat the monosubstituted one by alkyl donation into the pi system, and trans beats cis because the two substituents are not crowded on one side.

addition-reactions.q: In an addition reaction across a C=C double bond, the pi bond is:
options: Broken, and two new sigma bonds form
addition-reactions.why: Addition reactions break the reactive pi bond and add two new groups, one to each former alkene carbon.

addition-reactions.q: Which step typically starts an electrophilic addition to an alkene?
options: A halide ion adds to the alkene first
A proton is removed from the alkene
addition-reactions.why: Alkenes are electron-rich at the pi bond and act as nucleophiles toward an incoming electrophile, forming a carbocation (or similar) intermediate.

addition-reactions.q: Which of these is a classic electrophile added across an alkene in a halogenation (addition) reaction?
addition-reactions.why: Br₂ is polarized by the approaching alkene and forms a bromonium ion intermediate, a classic electrophilic addition across the double bond.

addition-reactions.q: In a general addition reaction, what happens to the alkene's degree of unsaturation?
addition-reactions.why: Addition reactions convert the pi bond into two new sigma bonds to the added atoms, removing one degree of unsaturation from the starting alkene.

addition-reactions.q: Addition reactions to alkenes increase the molecule's degree of unsaturation.
addition-reactions.why: Addition reactions consume the pi bond, converting an alkene (or alkyne) into a more saturated product, which decreases the degree of unsaturation, not increases it.

addition-reactions.q: What is the major product of adding HBr to 2-methyl-2-butene, (CH3)2C=CHCH3?
addition-reactions.why: The proton goes to the carbon that already carries more hydrogens — here the CH of the double bond — because that leaves the positive charge on the other carbon, which already bears two methyl groups. That tertiary cation is the more stable of the two on offer, and bromide captures it there, giving 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.

addition-reactions.q: What is the product of adding Br2 across ethylene (H2C=CH2)?
addition-reactions.why: Br2 adds across the double bond, putting one bromine on each former alkene carbon, giving the vicinal dihalide 1,2-dibromoethane.

addition-reactions.q: Acid-catalyzed hydration of an alkene adds an H atom and an OH group across the former double bond.
addition-reactions.why: Hydration is the addition of water (formally H and OH) across the pi bond, converting the alkene into an alcohol.

addition-reactions.q: Addition of Br2 or Cl2 to an alkene is an example of what general reaction category?
addition-reactions.why: The electron-rich pi bond of the alkene attacks the electrophilic halogen, and both halogen atoms end up added to the former double-bond carbons, making this an electrophilic addition.

addition-reactions.q: The gradual disappearance of the orange-brown color when Br2 is added to an unknown compound is commonly used as a qualitative test for the presence of:
options: a halogen already in the molecule
a carbon-carbon pi bond (alkene or alkyne)
addition-reactions.why: Colored Br2 is consumed as it adds across a reactive pi bond, turning colorless; alkanes lack this reactive pi bond and don't decolorize Br2 without light or heat.

addition-reactions.q: 2-methylpropene, (CH3)2C=CH2, is treated with Br2 in water. What is the major product?
addition-reactions.why: Bromine bridges the two carbons first. Water, in vast excess, then opens that bridge at the carbon carrying more positive character — the one with the two methyls — so the OH lands there and the bromine is left on the CH2 end. The product is 1-bromo-2-methylpropan-2-ol, with the two new groups anti to each other.

addition-reactions.q: Addition of a hydrogen halide (HX) across an alkene's double bond produces:
addition-reactions.why: HX adds H to one carbon and the halogen X to the other, converting the alkene directly into an alkyl halide.

addition-reactions.q: The electrophilic addition of Br2 to an alkene proceeds through which key intermediate?
addition-reactions.why: The alkene's pi electrons attack one bromine of Br2, displacing bromide and forming a three-membered ring bromonium ion in which bromine bridges both former alkene carbons, before bromide attacks from the opposite face.

addition-reactions.q: cis-2-butene is treated with Br2. What is the product?
addition-reactions.why: Bromine bridges one face, so bromide has to open the ring from the other — anti addition. Work the two new centers out for the cis alkene and they come out matched, (2R,3R); attacking the other carbon of the same bridged ion gives (2S,3S) at exactly the same rate. The product is therefore a racemate of two chiral molecules, not a meso compound.

addition-reactions.q: Oxymercuration-demercuration gives the Markovnikov alcohol without the carbocation rearrangements sometimes seen in acid-catalyzed hydration because the mechanism proceeds through:
options: direct SN2 attack by water on the alkene carbon
addition-reactions.why: Mercury bridges both alkene carbons in a cyclic mercurinium ion; the positive character is delocalized rather than concentrated on one carbon, so water attacks the more substituted carbon (Markovnikov) without a true carbocation able to rearrange.

addition-reactions.q: Addition of Br2 to an alkene gives anti (opposite-face) stereochemistry because the bridged bromonium ion is attacked by bromide from the face opposite the bromonium ring.
addition-reactions.why: Since the first bromine already blocks one face as part of the bromonium ion, the incoming bromide ion must attack from the backside, giving net anti addition of the two bromines.

addition-reactions.q: Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene over a metal surface delivers the two hydrogen atoms with what stereochemistry?
addition-reactions.why: Both the alkene and H2 adsorb onto the same flat metal surface, so both hydrogen atoms are transferred to the same face of the double bond, giving syn addition.

addition-reactions.q: trans-2-butene is treated with Br2. What is the product?
options: an equal mixture of syn and anti adducts
addition-reactions.why: The mechanism does not change — anti addition through the bromonium ion — but the starting geometry does, and that flips the answer. From the trans alkene the two new centers end up opposite, (2R,3S), and that molecule has an internal mirror plane, so it is meso and achiral. Same reagent, different alkene, different stereochemical outcome: that is what stereospecific means.

addition-reactions.q: 1-methylcyclohexene is treated with Br2 in water. Where do the OH and the Br end up?
options: OH on the carbon bearing the methyl, Br on the other, trans to it
Br on the carbon bearing the methyl, OH on the other, trans to it
OH and Br on the same carbon
OH on the carbon bearing the methyl, Br on the other, cis to it
addition-reactions.why: Two separate decisions. Charge decides which carbon: the bridged ion leans toward the more substituted carbon, so water attacks there and the OH lands on the carbon with the methyl. The blocked face decides which side: the ring still has to open from the far side, so the OH and the remaining Br finish anti. The product is 2-bromo-1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol.

addition-reactions.q: The acid-catalyzed addition of water across an alkene's double bond is called:
addition-reactions.why: Acid catalysis protonates the alkene to form a carbocation, which water then attacks, adding H and OH across the former double bond in a process called acid-catalyzed hydration.

addition-reactions.q: Which reagent adds H and Br across a double bond with Markovnikov selectivity via a carbocation intermediate?
addition-reactions.why: Without peroxides, HBr adds through a polar (ionic) mechanism: the alkene is protonated to form the more stable carbocation, which is then captured by bromide, giving the Markovnikov product.

addition-reactions.q: An alkene plus a reagent gives one diastereomer cleanly. What does that rule out?
options: Addition across the pi bond at all
addition-reactions.why: A free carbocation is flat, and the nucleophile can reach either face of it, so a single clean diastereomer is the one thing that mechanism cannot deliver. Clean anti points to a bridged ion that seals one face; clean syn points to a concerted step that delivers both groups together. When a question tells you the stereochemical outcome, it has told you what the intermediate was.

addition-reactions.q: You need 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol from 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene, with no rearranged by-product. Which conditions?
options: BH3 in THF, then H2O2 and NaOH
addition-reactions.why: Markovnikov puts the OH on C2, but the cation at C2 sits next to a quaternary carbon and would shift a methyl to become tertiary, so aqueous acid gives a rearranged alcohol. Oxymercuration reaches the same Markovnikov position through a bridged mercurinium ion, which never releases an open cation and so cannot rearrange. Hydroboration would give the anti-Markovnikov alcohol instead.

addition-reactions.q: In halohydrin formation from an unsymmetrical alkene, the OH ends up on the less substituted carbon.
addition-reactions.why: It is the other way round. The bridged halonium ion is unsymmetrical: the bond to the more substituted carbon is longer and weaker, so that carbon carries more positive character and is the one water attacks. The halogen is simply left holding the other carbon. Sterics would have sent water to the less hindered end, and charge overrules them.

addition-reactions.q: What is the correct order of key mechanistic steps in the ionic (non-radical) addition of HX to an alkene?
options: nucleophile attacks first, then protonation occurs
halide ion attacks the alkene directly in one step with no intermediate
protonation first gives a carbocation, then halide attacks
the alkene is first oxidized, then protonated
addition-reactions.why: In the standard two-step mechanism, the pi bond acts as a nucleophile toward the acidic H of HX, forming the more stable carbocation in the rate-determining first step, after which halide ion rapidly captures that carbocation.

addition-reactions.q: In the ionic addition of HX to an alkene, what determines the rate-determining step?
options: the final product stability has no bearing on rate at all
halide attack on the carbocation is always rate-determining
the reaction has no discernible rate-determining step
addition-reactions.why: Generating the carbocation requires breaking the pi bond and is the higher-activation-energy step; the subsequent capture of that carbocation by halide ion is fast, so the first step controls the overall rate.

addition-reactions.q: Acid-catalyzed hydration of an alkene can give rearranged (unexpected) products because the reaction proceeds through a carbocation intermediate that can undergo hydride or alkyl shifts.
addition-reactions.why: Because a genuine carbocation forms during acid-catalyzed hydration, it is free to rearrange to a more stable carbocation (via a 1,2-hydride or alkyl shift) before water attacks, sometimes giving a product with the OH in an unexpected position.

addition-reactions.q: Why does water open a bromonium ion at the more substituted carbon rather than the less hindered one?
options: That carbon is closer to the bromine atom
Water is too small for sterics to matter anywhere
That carbon carries more of the positive charge, so its transition state is lower
Bromine blocks the less substituted carbon completely
addition-reactions.why: The bridge is not the symmetrical triangle it is usually drawn as. The carbon better able to hold positive charge pulls the ion toward itself: its C-Br bond stretches and weakens, and it takes on real cationic character. Attacking a carbon that is already part way to being a cation is the lower barrier, so charge beats sterics here.

addition-reactions.q: How does the degree of alkyl substitution on an alkene generally affect its rate of electrophilic addition (e.g., with HX or Br2)?
options: more substituted alkenes react more slowly because they are more stable and less reactive
more substituted alkenes react faster, being more electron-rich
substitution has no effect on the rate of addition
only terminal alkenes undergo electrophilic addition at a useful rate
addition-reactions.why: Additional alkyl groups donate electron density into the pi system (making it a better nucleophile toward electrophiles) and stabilize the developing positive charge in the transition state, so more substituted alkenes typically react faster in electrophilic additions.

addition-reactions.q: HCl adds to 3-methyl-1-butene and the chlorine ends up on a carbon that was not part of the double bond. Why?
options: The reaction ran through a free carbocation that rearranged
Chloride attacked the alkene directly in one step
The reaction switched to a radical chain partway through
Markovnikov's rule does not apply to branched alkenes
addition-reactions.why: Protonation at C1 leaves a secondary cation at C2 with a tertiary C-H next door. A hydride migrates with its bonding pair, moving the charge to C3, and chloride captures it there — giving 2-chloro-2-methylbutane. Rearrangement is only possible if a genuine free cation existed, which is why it never shows up in concerted additions such as hydroboration.

markovnikov.q: In the Markovnikov addition of HBr to an alkene, the new hydrogen ends up on the carbon that is:
options: Always at the end of the chain
markovnikov.why: Protonating the less substituted carbon is what leaves the positive charge on the more substituted one, and that is the more stable cation. So the hydrogen goes to the carbon with more hydrogens already, and the bromide that arrives afterwards goes to the other one. Naming which species you mean matters: the H and the nucleophile end up on opposite carbons.

markovnikov.q: 1-butene is treated with HBr, once with peroxides and once without. What are the two major products?
markovnikov.why: Without an initiator the reaction is ionic: the proton adds first, the secondary cation forms at C2, and bromide lands there — 2-bromobutane. With peroxides a bromine radical adds first, and it adds to C1 so as to leave the more stable secondary radical at C2; that radical then picks up a hydrogen. Br therefore finishes at C1 — 1-bromobutane. Same reagents, different first-arriving species.

markovnikov.q: Markovnikov’s rule is best explained mechanistically by:
options: Formation of the more stable carbocation
Steric hindrance of the nucleophile alone
markovnikov.why: In ionic (non-radical) addition, the proton adds to give whichever carbon leads to the more stable carbocation — i.e., the more substituted one — and the nucleophile then attacks that cation.

markovnikov.q: Markovnikov's rule states that when HX adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the hydrogen atom adds preferentially to the carbon that:
options: already has the fewest hydrogens attached
already has the most hydrogens attached
markovnikov.why: Markovnikov's original empirical rule: the H of HX ends up on the carbon that already bears more hydrogens, while X ends up on the more substituted carbon.

markovnikov.q: Hydroboration-oxidation of 1-methylcyclohexene puts the OH on the carbon that already bears the methyl group.
markovnikov.why: Boron goes to the less substituted, less hindered carbon — C2 — and the OH replaces it there on oxidation, so the product is 2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol, not the 1-methyl isomer. The Markovnikov alcohol with OH on the methyl-bearing carbon is what aqueous acid or oxymercuration would give instead.

markovnikov.q: What is the major product when HCl adds to propene (CH3-CH=CH2)?
markovnikov.why: Protonation occurs at the terminal CH2 carbon to generate the more stable secondary carbocation, which chloride then captures, giving 2-chloropropane as the Markovnikov product.

markovnikov.q: Anti-Markovnikov addition of HBr to an alkene is observed specifically under which condition?
options: with excess HBr and no catalyst
markovnikov.why: Peroxides generate bromine radicals that initiate a radical chain addition mechanism, which adds Br first and gives the opposite (anti-Markovnikov) regiochemistry compared to the normal ionic pathway.

markovnikov.q: When HBr adds to propene in the presence of peroxides, the major product is 1-bromopropane rather than 2-bromopropane.
markovnikov.why: Under radical (peroxide) conditions, bromine adds first to the terminal carbon to generate the more stable secondary radical, placing Br at the end of the chain — the anti-Markovnikov product, 1-bromopropane.

markovnikov.q: Acid-catalyzed (Markovnikov) hydration of 2-methylpropene (isobutylene) gives which alcohol as the major product?
markovnikov.why: Protonation generates the more stable tertiary carbocation at the central carbon, which water then attacks, giving tert-butanol as the Markovnikov product.

markovnikov.q: In determining the Markovnikov product, which carbocation is more stable and therefore favored as the reaction intermediate?
markovnikov.why: Carbocation stability increases with substitution (methyl less than primary less than secondary less than tertiary) due to hyperconjugation and inductive donation from neighboring alkyl groups, so the reaction favors forming the more substituted, more stable carbocation.

markovnikov.q: In hydroboration, the boron and the hydrogen add to the same face of the double bond.
markovnikov.why: Boron and hydrogen are joined to the two alkene carbons in one four-membered arrangement at the moment of reaction, so neither can arrive from the far side. That closed ring is where syn addition comes from — it is a geometric consequence of the transition state rather than a preference. Oxidation then swaps boron for OH without disturbing it.

markovnikov.q: Which conditions convert 1-methylcyclohexene into 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol?
options: BH3 in THF, then H2O2 and NaOH
markovnikov.why: The target has the OH on the more substituted carbon, so you want the Markovnikov route: aqueous acid protonates C2, the tertiary cation forms at C1, and water attacks there. Hydroboration would give the anti-Markovnikov alcohol at C2 instead, peroxide HBr would install a bromide, and Br2 in water would give a bromohydrin.

markovnikov.q: What is the major product of HBr addition (no peroxides) to 1-methylcyclohexene?
options: Br ends up on C2, away from the methyl group
Br ends up on C1, bearing the methyl group
Br adds to both carbons equally
No reaction occurs because the alkene is in a ring
markovnikov.why: Protonation of the ring double bond occurs at C2 to place the positive charge on C1 (already bearing a methyl group), forming the more stable tertiary carbocation; bromide then attacks C1, so Br and the methyl end up on the same carbon.

markovnikov.q: What is the major product of HI addition to 2-methyl-2-butene, (CH3)2C=CHCH3?
markovnikov.why: Protonating the less substituted alkene carbon generates the more stable tertiary carbocation at the other carbon; iodide then attacks that tertiary center, giving 2-iodo-2-methylbutane as the Markovnikov product.

markovnikov.q: Which conditions convert 1-methylcyclohexene into trans-2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol?
options: BH3 in THF, then H2O2 and NaOH
markovnikov.why: Two things have to be right at once. The OH must end up on C2, which rules out both Markovnikov hydrations, and hydroboration puts boron there because it is the less hindered carbon. And the relative stereochemistry must be defined, which the syn addition supplies: the new H on C1 and the new OH on C2 arrive on the same face, which pushes the existing methyl to the other face.

markovnikov.q: For a terminal alkene CH2=CHR reacting with HX under normal ionic conditions, the halogen X ends up mainly on:
options: neither carbon; X leaves as HX unreacted
the internal carbon bearing R (the more substituted carbon)
markovnikov.why: Protonation at the terminal CH2 carbon generates the more stable carbocation at the internal, more substituted carbon, which halide then attacks, placing X on that more substituted carbon.

markovnikov.q: How does the regiochemistry of hydroboration-oxidation compare to Markovnikov's rule?
options: anti-Markovnikov: OH on the less substituted carbon
it gives a random mixture with no preference
it works on alkynes only, never on alkenes
markovnikov.why: Hydroboration adds B and H across the alkene in one four-center transition state, so no free cation forms. The transition state is still polarized: the partial positive charge develops on the more substituted carbon, which is where it is best supported, and that puts boron on the less substituted one. Sterics push the bulky boron the same way, so both arguments point at the same carbon. Oxidation then replaces C-B with C-OH in place, leaving OH on the less substituted carbon.

markovnikov.q: Oxymercuration-demercuration of an alkene installs the new OH group following which regiochemical pattern?
options: anti-Markovnikov orientation (OH on the less substituted carbon)
Markovnikov orientation (OH on the more substituted carbon)
OH always ends up on a terminal carbon regardless of substitution
no defined pattern; products are random
markovnikov.why: Water attacks the more substituted carbon of the bridged mercurinium ion, where positive character is greater, giving the same overall Markovnikov regiochemistry as acid-catalyzed hydration, but without carbocation rearrangement.

markovnikov.q: In the anti-Markovnikov radical addition of HBr, a bromine radical (not a hydrogen atom) is the species that adds first, attaching to the terminal carbon.
markovnikov.why: The radical chain begins when a bromine radical adds to the less hindered terminal carbon, generating the more stable internal (secondary or tertiary) carbon radical, which then abstracts H from HBr — this order is why Br ends up terminal.

markovnikov.q: What intermediate determines the regiochemistry of anti-Markovnikov radical addition of HBr?
markovnikov.why: Radical addition proceeds by bromine radical adding to generate the most stable carbon radical (paralleling how ionic mechanisms favor the most stable carbocation), which dictates where Br ultimately attaches.

markovnikov.q: Both propagation steps are downhill for HBr. Which step is uphill for HCl, stalling its chain?
options: The chlorine atom adding to the pi bond
The carbon radical taking H from H-Cl
The peroxide splitting into two radicals
markovnikov.why: Chlorine adds to the alkene very readily — a C-Cl bond at about 84 kcal/mol comfortably repays the 65 kcal/mol pi bond, roughly -19. The failure is the second step: pulling a hydrogen off H-Cl costs about 103 kcal/mol and returns a C-H worth about 98, so it is about +5 and uphill, and the chain stalls. HI fails at the opposite end, on the addition step.

markovnikov.q: Addition of HCl to 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene, (CH3)3C-CH=CH2, can give a rearranged product in addition to the expected one because:
options: the secondary carbocation shifts a methyl to become tertiary
HCl never reacts with this alkene
the methyl groups block all possible addition
the secondary carbocation is already the most stable possible intermediate here
markovnikov.why: Protonation gives a secondary carbocation adjacent to a carbon bearing three methyl groups; a methyl group can shift over (1,2-shift) to generate a more stable tertiary carbocation, leading to a rearranged chloride product alongside the 'simple' Markovnikov product.

markovnikov.q: Which conditions give 3,3-dimethylbutan-1-ol from 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene?
options: BH3 in THF, then H2O2 and NaOH
markovnikov.why: The OH has to land on the terminal carbon, which is the anti-Markovnikov position, so hydroboration is the only route on the list that reaches it. There is a second reason it is the right answer here: a cation at C2 would sit beside a quaternary carbon and shift a methyl to become tertiary, and hydroboration never makes a cation at all, so nothing can rearrange.

markovnikov.q: Hydroboration-oxidation can give a rearranged alcohol when a more stable carbocation is one shift away.
markovnikov.why: Rearrangement needs a discrete carbocation to migrate into, and hydroboration never produces one: boron and hydrogen add in a single concerted step. That is what makes the reaction valuable twice over — it reaches the anti-Markovnikov alcohol, and it reaches any alcohol from a substrate whose cation would have shifted.

markovnikov.q: In peroxide-mediated (anti-Markovnikov) HBr addition, what species initiates the radical chain?
options: a bromide anion formed by simple ionization of HBr
a proton (H+) generated from the peroxide
a bromine radical from peroxide plus HBr
a carbocation formed directly from the peroxide
markovnikov.why: Peroxides undergo weak O-O bond homolysis to generate alkoxy radicals, which abstract a hydrogen atom from HBr to generate a bromine radical; this bromine radical is what adds to the alkene to begin the chain.

markovnikov.q: Markovnikov's original rule (H goes to the carbon with more H's already) becomes ambiguous or insufficient in which situation, revealing why the carbocation-stability explanation is actually needed?
options: never; the simple rule always works perfectly for every alkene
only for symmetrical alkenes, which have no regiochemistry question at all
only when no acid catalyst is present
for complex alkenes, counting H's doesn't identify the stabler cation
markovnikov.why: The simple 'more H's' heuristic can fail to clearly distinguish outcomes for more complex or highly substituted alkenes; the mechanistic version — protonate to form the more stable carbocation — is the general and reliable explanation underlying the empirical rule.

markovnikov.q: Why is anti-Markovnikov addition essentially unique to HBr among the hydrogen halides (HF, HCl, HBr, HI), rather than occurring readily with HCl or HI too?
options: the radical chain steps are selective for Br but not Cl or I
HCl and HI simply don't exist as reagents
HCl and HI are too unreactive to add to alkenes by any mechanism
anti-Markovnikov addition actually works equally well for all four halides
markovnikov.why: A chain needs both propagation steps to be roughly downhill, and for HBr they are: Br adding to the pi bond is about -5 kcal/mol and taking H from H-Br about -11. The two failures sit at opposite ends of the cycle. HCl stalls at the hydrogen abstraction, since H-Cl is worth 103 kcal/mol against the roughly 98 of the C-H being made, about +5 uphill. HI stalls at the addition, since a C-I bond returns only about 56 kcal/mol against the 65 of the pi bond broken, about +9 uphill.

markovnikov.q: Anti-Markovnikov regiochemistry from a radical mechanism is a special case associated with HBr addition; it does not apply to ordinary acid-catalyzed hydration or to halogenation (Br2/Cl2 addition) reactions under typical conditions.
markovnikov.why: Hydration and halogenation (Br2/Cl2 addition) proceed through cationic or bridged-ion intermediates that follow normal Markovnikov-type (most stable intermediate) selectivity; the radical chain pathway that flips the regiochemistry is essentially unique to peroxide-mediated HBr addition.

markovnikov.q: Comparing HBr addition to 2-methyl-1-butene with and without peroxides, what regiochemical difference is expected?
options: no difference; both conditions give the identical major product
without peroxides, Br goes to C2; with peroxides, to C1
without peroxides, Br ends up on C1; with peroxides, Br ends up on C2
peroxides prevent the reaction from occurring at all
markovnikov.why: The ionic pathway is governed by carbocation stability, favoring Br at the more substituted carbon (C2); the radical pathway is governed by radical stability formed by Br adding first to the terminal carbon (C1), flipping the regiochemistry.

markovnikov.q: Hydroboration-oxidation of 1-methylcyclohexene is a syn addition, yet the product is trans-2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol. Why is that not a contradiction?
options: The word syn describes the two groups added — the H and the OH, which are cis
Oxidation with H2O2 inverts the carbon that held the boron
The ring flips after the addition and reverses the relationship
Syn and trans mean the same thing on a six-membered ring
markovnikov.why: Syn is a statement about the two new groups only. The hydrogen lands on C1 and the OH on C2, both from the same face, so those two are cis to each other. The methyl on C1 was already there, and since the new hydrogen took the front face of C1 the methyl is pushed to the back — which leaves it trans to the OH. Oxidation keeps both position and configuration.

alkynes.q: A terminal alkyne’s C–H is unusually acidic (pKa ~25) because:
options: There is no acidity difference from alkanes
alkynes.why: sp hybrid orbitals have 50% s-character (vs. 25% for sp³), holding the lone pair closer to the nucleus and stabilizing the conjugate base — more s-character, more acidic.

alkynes.q: How many pi bonds are in a carbon-carbon triple bond?
alkynes.why: A triple bond is 1 sigma bond plus 2 pi bonds.

alkynes.q: Compared to an alkene, an alkyne undergoing addition of 2 equivalents of HX can ultimately give what kind of product?
options: Only a single addition is ever possible
A geminal dihalide (both halogens on the same carbon) after two additions
alkynes.why: The first HX addition (following Markovnikov) gives a vinyl halide; a second addition of HX to that alkene gives a geminal dihalide, both halogens on the same, more substituted carbon.

alkynes.q: What is the hybridization of each carbon in a carbon-carbon triple bond?
alkynes.why: Each alkyne carbon forms two sigma bonds (linear, 180°) using sp hybrid orbitals, leaving two unhybridized p orbitals to form the two pi bonds of the triple bond.

alkynes.q: Propyne is treated with NaNH2, then with bromoethane. What is the product?
alkynes.why: Amide removes the terminal C-H (pKa 25) to give the acetylide CH3-C=C(-). That carbanion is an excellent SN2 nucleophile, and bromoethane is primary, so it displaces bromide and forms a new carbon-carbon bond. Three carbons plus two carbons, joined at the old terminal position, gives pent-2-yne.

alkynes.q: Alkynes are generally somewhat less reactive than alkenes toward many electrophilic addition reactions because the sp carbons hold their pi electrons more tightly.
alkynes.why: Alkyne pi electrons are held closer to the carbon nuclei due to the higher s-character (more electronegative character) of sp carbons, making the alkyne pi bond somewhat less available to electrophiles compared to the more loosely held pi electrons of an alkene.

alkynes.q: What is the general molecular formula for an acyclic alkyne with one triple bond and n carbons?
alkynes.why: A triple bond counts as two degrees of unsaturation, removing four hydrogens relative to the saturated alkane (CnH2n+2), giving CnH2n-2.

alkynes.q: A terminal alkyne is defined by having the triple bond:
options: in the middle of a long carbon chain
at the end of the chain, with one triple-bond carbon bonded directly to a hydrogen
alkynes.why: In a terminal alkyne, such as HC≡C-CH3 (propyne), one sp carbon of the triple bond is bonded to a hydrogen atom rather than to another carbon, placing the triple bond at the very end of the chain.

alkynes.q: In an internal alkyne, both triple-bond carbons are bonded to other carbons rather than to hydrogen.
alkynes.why: An internal alkyne, like 2-butyne (CH3-C≡C-CH3), has the triple bond flanked on both sides by carbon substituents, distinguishing it from a terminal alkyne, which has a triple-bond C-H.

alkynes.q: Addition of exactly 1 equivalent of Br2 to an internal alkyne gives what kind of product?
options: a saturated alkane with four bromines
a tetrahalide with no unsaturation remaining
a dihaloalkene, with one degree of unsaturation still remaining
alkynes.why: Just as with alkenes, Br2 adds across one of the two pi bonds of the triple bond first, converting the alkyne into a dihalogenated alkene; a second equivalent of Br2 would be needed to fully saturate it into a tetrahalide.

alkynes.q: Which IUPAC suffix indicates a carbon-carbon triple bond?
alkynes.why: The suffix -yne is used specifically to denote a triple bond in the parent chain, as in ethyne (acetylene) or 2-butyne.

alkynes.q: A vicinal dibromide is heated with sodium amide to make a terminal alkyne. How many equivalents of NaNH2 are needed?
options: none — amide is not basic enough
alkynes.why: Two eliminations remove two molecules of HBr, one to reach the vinyl halide and one to reach the alkyne, which accounts for two equivalents. The third is consumed immediately by the product itself: a terminal alkyne C-H at pKa 25 is deprotonated by any amide still in the flask, so the acetylide is what you actually have until water is added at the end.

alkynes.q: Which sequence converts acetylene, HC=CH, into cis-hex-3-ene?
options: NaNH2 then CH3CH2Br, twice over, then H2 with Lindlar catalyst
NaNH2 then CH3CH2Br, twice over, then Na in liquid NH3
NaNH2 then (CH3)3CBr, twice over, then H2 with Lindlar catalyst
H2 with Lindlar catalyst, then NaNH2 and CH3CH2Br twice
alkynes.why: Build the skeleton first, then set the geometry. Two rounds of deprotonate-and-alkylate with a primary halide put an ethyl group on each end of the triple bond, giving hex-3-yne. Lindlar delivers both hydrogens from one catalyst surface, so the alkene comes out cis; sodium in ammonia would have given the trans isomer, and a tertiary halide would have given E2 instead of alkylation.

alkynes.q: Given the approximate pKa values: alkane C-H ~50, alkene C-H ~44, alkyne C-H ~25, water ~15.7, which of these four is the most acidic?
alkynes.why: A lower pKa means a stronger acid; water at pKa ~15.7 is far more acidic than even a terminal alkyne C-H (pKa ~25), even though the alkyne C-H is unusually acidic compared to other hydrocarbon C-H bonds.

alkynes.q: Which of the following bases is commonly strong enough to fully deprotonate a terminal alkyne C-H?
alkynes.why: Since the conjugate acid of amide ion, ammonia (pKa ~38), is a much weaker acid than a terminal alkyne (pKa ~25), sodium amide is a strong enough base to completely deprotonate terminal alkynes to form acetylide ions; hydroxide (conjugate acid water, pKa ~15.7) is not strong enough.

alkynes.q: The acetylide ion formed by deprotonating a terminal alkyne is a good nucleophile that can be used in SN2 reactions with primary alkyl halides to form a new carbon-carbon bond.
alkynes.why: Acetylide ions are strong, relatively unhindered carbanion-like nucleophiles that readily displace halide from primary (unhindered) alkyl halides via SN2, a classic method for extending carbon chains and building larger alkynes.

alkynes.q: Acid/Hg2+-catalyzed (Markovnikov) hydration of a terminal alkyne proceeds through an unstable enol intermediate that then converts into what final functional group?
alkynes.why: Markovnikov addition of water places OH on the more substituted alkyne carbon, generating an enol, which rapidly tautomerizes (favoring the more stable keto form) into a ketone.

alkynes.q: Anti-Markovnikov hydration of a terminal alkyne via hydroboration-oxidation ultimately yields what functional group?
alkynes.why: Boron adds to the less substituted terminal carbon; oxidation replaces boron with OH there, giving an enol with OH on the terminal carbon, which tautomerizes to an aldehyde rather than a ketone.

alkynes.q: Treating an alkyne with excess H2 and a Pt (or Pd/Ni) catalyst results in complete reduction to the corresponding alkane.
alkynes.why: With an unrestricted (non-poisoned) metal catalyst and excess H2, both pi bonds of the triple bond are hydrogenated in sequence, first to the alkene and then fully to the alkane.

alkynes.q: But-1-yne is treated with two equivalents of HBr, no peroxides. What is the product?
alkynes.why: The first addition is Markovnikov and puts the bromine on the internal carbon, giving 2-bromobut-1-ene. The second addition is Markovnikov on that alkene, and the bromine already present stabilizes the cation beside it by donating a lone pair, so the second bromine lands on the same carbon. The product is the geminal dihalide, 2,2-dibromobutane.

alkynes.q: An acetylide anion is treated with 2-bromopropane instead of a primary halide. What happens?
options: SN2 proceeds normally, just more slowly
E2 dominates: propene forms and the alkyne is recovered
The acetylide attacks the bromine atom instead
Nothing at all — acetylides are not nucleophilic
alkynes.why: An acetylide is a strong base as well as a strong nucleophile, and a secondary substrate is hindered enough at the back side that elimination wins. The alkyne is protonated back to its neutral form and the halide becomes an alkene, so the intended carbon-carbon bond is never made. Acetylide alkylation is reliable on methyl and primary halides only.

alkynes.q: Mechanistically, why does Lindlar's catalyst stop at the cis-alkene stage rather than continuing on to the fully saturated alkane?
options: the cis-alkene is simply the only possible product from any hydrogenation of a triple bond
the poisoned catalyst adds H2 to the alkyne but is far less active toward the alkene
Lindlar's catalyst only works on terminal alkynes
the reaction is run with insufficient H2 gas to go any further
alkynes.why: Lead and quinoline additives reduce the catalytic activity of Pd just enough that it can still deliver H2 syn across a triple bond but is much less effective at further adsorbing and reducing the resulting alkene, letting the reaction be stopped cleanly at the cis-alkene stage.

alkynes.q: Mechanistically, at which point in the Na/NH3 reduction of an internal alkyne is the trans geometry of the product decided?
options: At the vinyl radical, which inverts fast and sits mostly trans, and is then locked by the vinyl anion
At the first electron transfer, since the radical anion is already locked trans
At the final protonation by ammonia, which always delivers H to the far face
After the alkene forms, by base-catalyzed isomerization of an initial cis product
alkynes.why: The sequence is electron, proton, electron, proton. The first electron and proton give a vinyl RADICAL, which inverts rapidly at the carbon bearing the odd electron and therefore equilibrates to the less crowded trans-like geometry. The second electron makes that a vinyl ANION, which is configurationally stable on the timescale of the reaction, so the geometry it inherits survives the final protonation. Catalytic hydrogenation has no such step: both hydrogens arrive on one face from the metal surface, which is why Lindlar gives cis.

alkynes.q: Acid-catalyzed hydration of an unsymmetrical internal alkyne can give a mixture of two different ketones, because water can add with its oxygen ending up on either of the two different triple-bond carbons.
alkynes.why: Unless the internal alkyne is symmetrical, Markovnikov addition of water is not perfectly selective for one carbon over the other when both are similarly substituted, so both possible enol/ketone regiochemistries can form, giving a mixture of ketone products.

alkynes.q: When a terminal alkyne reacts with 2 equivalents of HBr (no peroxides), Markovnikov addition occurs in both steps. What is the final product?
options: a 1,2-dibromide with one Br on each of the original terminal alkyne carbons
a vicinal dihalide alkene still containing a double bond
an alkane with no halogens at all
a geminal dihalide, with both bromine atoms ending up on the same (internal, more substituted) carbon
alkynes.why: The first HBr addition follows Markovnikov's rule, putting Br on the more substituted carbon to form a bromoalkene; the second HBr addition again follows Markovnikov's rule on that bromoalkene, placing the second Br on the very same carbon, yielding a geminal dihalide.

alkynes.q: You need hexan-2-one from hex-1-yne. Which conditions?
alkynes.why: Mercury-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov: the mercurinium bridge is opened by water at the more substituted carbon, so the oxygen lands on C2 and the enol tautomerizes to the methyl ketone. The bulky borane would have delivered the oxygen to the terminal carbon instead, giving hexanal, and neither reduction installs an oxygen at all.

alkynes.q: Terminal alkynes, but not internal alkynes, give an aldehyde product from hydroboration-oxidation, because boron selectively adds to the less hindered, terminal carbon of the triple bond.
alkynes.why: Only a terminal alkyne has a CH-bearing end carbon available for boron's steric preference to place OH there after oxidation, generating a terminal enol that tautomerizes to an aldehyde; internal alkynes lack a terminal position and instead give ketones.

alkynes.q: Ranking carbon-carbon bond lengths and relative bond strengths from a single bond to a triple bond, which statement is correct?
options: triple bonds are the longest and weakest of the three
triple bonds are the shortest and strongest
all three bond types have essentially identical length and strength
double bonds are shorter than triple bonds
alkynes.why: More shared electron pairs (three bonding pairs in a triple bond) pull the bonded atoms closer together and require more energy to break, and the increased s-character of sp orbitals further shortens the sigma bond, making triple bonds the shortest and strongest, followed by double, then single bonds.

alkynes.q: Why does a carbon-carbon triple bond contain two mutually perpendicular pi bonds rather than one larger pi bond?
options: because triple bonds actually only have one pi bond, just like double bonds
because the two pi bonds merge into a single circular orbital around the bond axis
each sp carbon has two perpendicular p orbitals that overlap separately
because nitrogen atoms are required to form the second pi bond
alkynes.why: sp hybridization uses only one s and one p orbital, leaving two p orbitals unhybridized and oriented perpendicular to each other; each of these forms its own independent pi bond with the matching p orbital on the other sp carbon, giving two distinct, perpendicular pi bonds plus the one sigma bond.

alkynes.q: Treating a symmetrical internal alkyne, such as 2-butyne (CH3-C≡C-CH3), with H2O/H2SO4/HgSO4 gives what outcome, and why?
options: a mixture of two different ketones, because the molecule isn't symmetrical enough to favor one over the other
no reaction at all, because symmetrical alkynes cannot undergo hydration
an alcohol with no carbonyl group formed
a single ketone (2-butanone), since symmetry makes either addition give the same product
alkynes.why: Because both triple-bond carbons of 2-butyne carry identical methyl substituents, it doesn't matter which carbon water's oxygen ends up on — both regiochemical outcomes converge on the same single ketone product (2-butanone), avoiding the mixture problem seen with unsymmetrical internal alkynes.

conjugated-systems.q: Which of these C₆H₁₀ chains has its two double bonds conjugated?
conjugated-systems.why: Read the chain for a run of sp2 carbons with the bonds alternating. Hexa-1,3-diene has double, single, double across C1 to C4, so its p orbitals overlap continuously. The 1,5- and 1,4-dienes each have sp3 carbons breaking the run, and the 1,2-diene is cumulated: its central sp carbon holds the two pi systems at right angles.

conjugated-systems.q: How many pi electrons are in conjugation in hepta-1,3,6-triene, CH₂=CH–CH=CH–CH₂–CH=CH₂?
options: Six, from all three double bonds
conjugated-systems.why: C1=C2 and C3=C4 form one unbroken run of sp2 carbons, so those two pi bonds — four electrons — are conjugated with each other. C5 is sp3 and stops the chain there, leaving C6=C7 on its own as an ordinary terminal alkene. The molecule contains a conjugated diene and an isolated alkene, and only the first four electrons count.

conjugated-systems.q: Which of these dienes can never react from an s-cis conformation?
options: A diene held across a ring fusion
