conjugated-systems.why: s-cis and s-trans interconvert by rotation about the central single bond, which is free in any open chain — so both butadiene and isoprene reach s-cis whenever they need to. Cyclopentadiene is already locked there by its ring. A diene whose two double bonds are in different rings of a fused system has its ends held on opposite sides of that bond, and no rotation is available to bring them round.

conjugated-systems.q: Rank buta-1,3-diene, penta-1,4-diene and propa-1,2-diene from most to least stable.
conjugated-systems.why: Conjugated beats isolated beats cumulated. Buta-1,3-diene collects about 15 kJ/mol of delocalization energy for having its p orbitals in one continuous run. Penta-1,4-diene collects none, because an sp3 carbon separates its double bonds. Propa-1,2-diene collects none either and pays besides, since its sp center holds the two pi systems perpendicular to each other.

conjugated-systems.q: A cumulated diene is the least stable of the three arrangements. Why?
options: All three arrangements sit at essentially one energy
Its two pi systems are perpendicular and cannot share
Its bond angles are badly distorted from what they want
Its p orbitals repel each other along the chain
conjugated-systems.why: An allene is not strained: its sp central carbon wants 180 degrees and gets it, and the two sp2 ends want 120 degrees and get that. What it cannot do is delocalize. The two pi systems meet at the same carbon but lie at right angles, so neither one stabilizes the other, and the molecule pays for two pi bonds while collecting nothing back.

conjugated-systems.q: Hydrogenating cyclohexene releases 120 kJ/mol; cyclohexa-1,3-diene releases 232 kJ/mol. What is the diene's delocalization energy?
conjugated-systems.why: Build a reference with the same number of pi bonds as the compound you are testing: two independent C=C should release 2 × 120 = 240 kJ/mol. The diene releases only 232 reaching the same saturated ring, so it began 240 − 232 = 8 kJ/mol lower down. Subtracting one cyclohexene instead measures the second double bond rather than the conjugation.

conjugated-systems.q: Why does a conjugated diene release LESS heat on hydrogenation than two isolated double bonds?
options: Part of the heat is absorbed by the catalyst
It began lower in energy than they did
It has one fewer pi bond to hydrogenate
Its saturated product sits higher in energy
conjugated-systems.why: Both runs finish at the same kind of product, a saturated alkane, and both break the same number of pi bonds. If one gives out less energy on the way to an equally stable destination, the only place that difference can have come from is a lower starting point. That is exactly what delocalization energy means.

conjugated-systems.q: How long is the C2-C3 bond of buta-1,3-diene?
conjugated-systems.why: Shorter than an ordinary C-C single bond at 1.54 A, because the pi system is delocalized and the bond has partial double-bond character.

conjugated-systems.q: What does the s in s-cis stand for?
conjugated-systems.why: It describes the conformation about the SINGLE bond joining the two double bonds, not a double-bond geometry.

conjugated-systems.q: Can s-cis and s-trans interconvert at room temperature?
options: Only with an acid catalyst present
conjugated-systems.why: They are conformations about a single bond, so rotation is free. cis and trans across a double bond cannot interconvert without breaking the pi bond.

conjugated-systems.q: Which conformation of an open-chain conjugated diene is more stable, and by roughly how much?
options: They sit at the same energy
conjugated-systems.why: s-trans wins because s-cis brings the inward-pointing hydrogen on C1 and the one on C4 close enough to crowd each other. The penalty is around 12 kJ/mol — nearly the size of the whole delocalization energy, so it is not a rounding error. It is still small enough that rotation keeps refilling the s-cis population at room temperature.

conjugated-systems.q: Which conformation does the Diels-Alder reaction require?
conjugated-systems.why: The two ends of the diene must reach the two ends of the dienophile at once, which only s-cis allows.

conjugated-systems.q: Why is a diene locked s-trans unreactive in a Diels-Alder?
options: It is not a conjugated system at all
It is stabilized too much to react
Its two ends cannot reach the dienophile at the same time
It is far too electron-poor to react with anything
conjugated-systems.why: The requirement is geometric. Both new bonds form at once, so C1 and C4 of the diene have to point the same way to meet the two ends of the dienophile together. A ring that holds them on opposite sides of the central bond makes that impossible, and no amount of electron-donating substitution changes it.

conjugated-systems.q: Where does the positive charge sit in an allylic cation?
conjugated-systems.why: Draw both resonance forms: the charge appears at the termini and never in the middle.

conjugated-systems.q: Why are allylic and benzylic cations unusually stable?
options: They are sterically protected from attack
Their charge is delocalized by conjugation
conjugated-systems.why: An empty p orbital next to a pi system conjugates with it, which is the same delocalization you draw as resonance.

conjugated-systems.q: Which of these can conjugate with an adjacent pi bond?
options: Only another pi bond can do this
A lone pair, empty p orbital or radical
conjugated-systems.why: Conjugation needs a p orbital that can align, and all of these provide one.

conjugated-systems.q: Methyl vinyl ether, CH₂=CH–OCH₃, is conjugated with only one double bond. What conjugates with the pi bond?
options: The methyl group's three C–H bonds
Nothing — one double bond cannot conjugate
An oxygen lone pair sitting in a p orbital
conjugated-systems.why: Conjugation needs a row of parallel p orbitals, not a row of double bonds. One of oxygen's two lone pairs occupies a p orbital lined up with the alkene's, so it overlaps and the electron density spreads onto the alkene carbons. The same picture explains enamines and amides, and it is why an enol ether's terminal carbon is unusually nucleophilic.

conjugated-systems.q: Which cation does the neighboring pi bond stabilize: CH₂=CH–CH₂⁺ or CH₂=CH⁺?
options: Both equally, since each carries a double bond
Neither — a pi bond cannot stabilize a positive charge
The allylic one, whose empty orbital lies parallel to the pi bond
The vinylic one, whose charge sits closer to the pi bond
conjugated-systems.why: Alignment decides it, not proximity. In CH₂=CH–CH₂⁺ the empty p orbital on the CH₂ is parallel to the pi system next to it, so the two overlap and the charge spreads over both end carbons. In CH₂=CH⁺ the empty orbital is an sp2 orbital lying in the molecular plane, perpendicular to the pi bond, so there is no overlap to be had — which is why vinylic cations are among the worst intermediates in organic chemistry.

conjugated-systems.q: Why can the two pi systems of an allene not conjugate?
conjugated-systems.why: Conjugation needs p orbitals aligned closely enough to overlap. At right angles they cannot.

conjugated-systems.q: Penta-1,4-diene is isolated rather than conjugated. How many sp3 carbons does it take to break a conjugated run?
options: It depends on the chain length
conjugated-systems.why: An sp3 carbon has no p orbital to contribute, so the row of parallel p orbitals simply stops there. Penta-1,4-diene has exactly one such carbon, C3, and that is already fatal: each alkene behaves as though the other were not in the molecule. Reading the rule as 'two or more' is the commonest way to mis-classify this compound.

conjugated-systems.q: Which hybridization do the carbons of a conjugated diene have?
conjugated-systems.why: Every carbon in the conjugated run is sp2, which is what lets the p orbitals line up.

conjugated-systems.q: How many pi molecular orbitals does buta-1,3-diene have, and which one is its HOMO?
options: Four orbitals, with ψ₃ the HOMO
Eight orbitals, with ψ₄ the HOMO
Four orbitals, with ψ₂ the HOMO
Two orbitals, with ψ₁ the HOMO
conjugated-systems.why: Overlapping n parallel p orbitals produces n molecular orbitals, so four p orbitals give ψ₁ to ψ₄. Each carbon contributes one electron, so the four pi electrons fill the lowest two. ψ₂ is therefore the highest occupied orbital and ψ₃ the lowest empty one — the pair that decides how the molecule reacts and what wavelength it absorbs.

conjugated-systems.q: Which carbons of buta-1,3-diene carry the largest share of its HOMO?
options: The two in the middle of the chain
All four carbons share it evenly
The two at the ends of the system
conjugated-systems.why: In ψ₂ the coefficients are biggest at C1 and C4 and smallest at C2 and C3, with the phase flipping once in the middle. That is the orbital statement of the same thing the resonance forms say, and it is why a conjugated system reacts at its termini — bromide capture in the next section, and both new bonds of a Diels-Alder.

conjugated-systems.q: Why is cyclopentadiene unusually reactive as a diene?
conjugated-systems.why: It never has to pay the rotation penalty, and it dimerizes on standing as a result.

conjugated-systems.q: Conjugation is best described as what, in orbital terms?
conjugated-systems.why: It is the orbital picture of the same delocalization you draw with resonance structures.

conjugated-systems.q: How does an allylic radical compare to an ordinary alkyl radical?
conjugated-systems.why: Its half-filled p orbital conjugates with the adjacent pi bond, spreading the unpaired electron.

conjugated-systems.q: Which is NOT evidence for delocalization in buta-1,3-diene?
conjugated-systems.why: The formula is the same as for an isolated diene. The other three all report on the electrons.

conjugated-systems.q: What happens to reactivity along a conjugated system?
conjugated-systems.why: The termini carry the charge, the odd electron, or the largest orbital coefficients.

conjugated-systems.q: Why is conjugation relevant to allylic bromination?
options: It blocks the position from attack
conjugated-systems.why: Abstracting an allylic hydrogen leaves a resonance-delocalized radical, which makes that abstraction much easier.

conjugated-systems.q: Buta-1,3-diene sits mostly s-trans, and reaching s-cis costs about 12 kJ/mol. Why does the Diels-Alder still work on it?
options: Rotation is fast, so the s-cis pool is refilled as it reacts
The dienophile forces the diene into s-trans instead
A 12 kJ/mol penalty is too small to shift an equilibrium
Butadiene is locked s-cis in the first place
conjugated-systems.why: s-cis is a minor conformer, not an absent one. Rotation about the central single bond happens far faster than the cycloaddition, so every molecule consumed from the s-cis pool is replaced at once and the reaction drains the whole sample through that conformation. A diene held s-trans by a ring has no rotation available, which is why that case is fatal and this one is only slow.

diene-addition.q: Adding one equivalent of HBr to buta-1,3-diene gives how many products?
diene-addition.why: The intermediate is an allylic cation with two reactive ends, so bromide has two places to attack.

diene-addition.q: What kind of intermediate forms when HBr protonates buta-1,3-diene?
diene-addition.why: Protonating C1 puts the charge next to the remaining double bond, so it delocalizes.

diene-addition.q: In the 1,2-addition product from buta-1,3-diene, where is the double bond?
diene-addition.why: 3-bromobut-1-ene keeps a terminal CH2= group.

diene-addition.q: Buta-1,3-diene plus one equivalent of Br₂, run warm. What is the major product?
diene-addition.why: Br₂ opens on the diene the same way HBr does: a bromonium ion forms at one end and collapses to an allylic cation, leaving bromide with two carbons to choose between. Warm conditions let the first-formed product ionize again, so the mixture drains into the one with the more substituted alkene — 1,4-dibromobut-2-ene. Cold, you would isolate 3,4-dibromobut-1-ene instead.

diene-addition.q: What is the 1,2-addition product of HBr and buta-1,3-diene?
diene-addition.why: Bromide captures C2, the carbon carrying most of the positive charge.

diene-addition.q: What is the 1,4-addition product of HBr and buta-1,3-diene?
diene-addition.why: Bromide captures C4, at the far end of the delocalized system.

diene-addition.q: At about -80 C, which product dominates?
diene-addition.why: Roughly 80:20 in favor of 1,2. Cold and irreversible means the rates decide.

diene-addition.q: HBr adds to 2-methylpenta-1,3-diene, CH₂=C(CH₃)–CH=CH–CH₃, at −80 °C. Major product?
diene-addition.why: Choose the end to protonate first. Adding H to C1 puts the charge on C2, which is tertiary; adding it to C5's end puts the charge on C3, which is only secondary. So protonate C1. Cold means kinetic control, so bromide takes the carbon carrying most of the charge — the tertiary C2 — and the alkene stays between C3 and C4. Warm the same flask and you get 4-bromo-2-methylpent-2-ene, whose alkene is trisubstituted.

diene-addition.q: Why does bromide attack C2 faster than C4?
options: More positive charge sits on C2
C4 is not electrophilic at all here
diene-addition.why: The resonance form with charge on C2 is secondary and the other is primary, so the better form puts more charge on C2.

diene-addition.q: Why is the 1,4-product more stable?
diene-addition.why: Alkene stability rises with substitution, and the 1,4-product's double bond is internal and disubstituted.

diene-addition.q: What does 1,4-addition also get called?
diene-addition.why: You will meet the same name in enolate chemistry, for the same reason.

diene-addition.q: In the term 1,4-addition, what do the numbers refer to?
options: The number of new bonds formed
diene-addition.why: They describe where the two new groups landed relative to the starting diene, not the product's own numbering.

diene-addition.q: Warming the pure 1,2-product with a trace of HBr gives a 15:85 mixture. What does that prove?
diene-addition.why: Bromide can leave again and regenerate the allylic cation, so the system re-equilibrates.

diene-addition.q: Which sequence describes HBr adding to buta-1,3-diene?
options: HBr splits into radicals, which add to the diene in turn
Protonate a terminus, then bromide captures an end of the cation
Bromide attacks a terminus, then the proton adds at the far end
Both the proton and the bromide arrive in one concerted step
diene-addition.why: The π system is the nucleophile in the room, so it reaches for the proton first; that is what generates the allylic cation. Only then does bromide, which has been a spectator, arrive at one of the two charged ends. Nothing about this is concerted, and the radical route needs peroxides deliberately added.

diene-addition.q: Which resonance form of that cation is the major contributor?
diene-addition.why: A secondary carbocation is more stable than a primary one, so it describes more of the real intermediate.

diene-addition.q: Protonating 2-methylbuta-1,3-diene at C1 gives which cation?
diene-addition.why: The charge lands on C2, which bears two methyls and the chain.

diene-addition.q: What is the 1,2-product from HBr and 2-methylbuta-1,3-diene?
diene-addition.why: Bromide captures the tertiary carbon, leaving the terminal alkene intact.

diene-addition.q: What is the 1,4-product from HBr and 2-methylbuta-1,3-diene?
diene-addition.why: Bromide captures the far end, and the alkene moves inward to become trisubstituted.

diene-addition.q: Why is penta-1,3-diene a poor example for comparing 1,2 and 1,4 products?
options: It does not react with HBr at all
diene-addition.why: With a methyl at each end of the allylic cation, capturing at either end gives the same compound.

diene-addition.q: Which carbon of the allylic cation never carries positive charge?
diene-addition.why: Neither resonance form places charge on the middle carbon of the three-carbon system.

diene-addition.q: Is the double bond moving in 1,4-addition a rearrangement?
options: No, it is the other resonance form being captured
No, and the double bond does not actually move
diene-addition.why: Nothing shifts. The intermediate was already delocalized, and capture at the far end simply fixes the other form.

diene-addition.q: What is the first step of HBr addition to a conjugated diene?
options: The proton adds to a terminal carbon
diene-addition.why: The pi system is nucleophilic and takes the proton, which generates the allylic cation.

diene-addition.q: Why is protonation at a terminal carbon preferred?
diene-addition.why: Protonating an inner carbon would give a cation that cannot delocalize into the remaining double bond.

diene-addition.q: What would you change to favor the kinetic product?
diene-addition.why: Cold conditions prevent the products from reverting, so the first-formed ratio is frozen in.

diene-addition.q: A diene plus an electrophile gives two products, but the capture step cannot reverse at any temperature. What does heating change?
options: Nothing about the ratio — the faster product, faster
It shifts the mixture toward the more stable product
It stops the reaction from happening at all
It switches the reaction to a radical mechanism
diene-addition.why: Thermodynamic control is bought with reversibility, not with temperature. Heat is only useful because it lets a product ionize back to the intermediate and try again; if that path is closed, nothing that has formed can be unformed and the ratio stays wherever the two rates put it.

diene-addition.q: 3-bromobut-1-ene is solvolyzed in warm ethanol. Besides the expected ether, what else forms?
options: Only the alkene, from elimination of HBr
Nothing else; an allylic halide gives a single product
The ether with the OEt and the double bond both moved along
A rearranged carbon skeleton, from a methyl shift
diene-addition.why: Ionizing that C–Br bond regenerates exactly the allylic cation the HBr addition went through, and ethanol can return to either end of it. Capture at the far end gives 1-ethoxybut-2-ene alongside 3-ethoxybut-1-ene. Chemists call it allylic rearrangement; it is the substitution-side view of the same delocalized intermediate.

diene-addition.q: Both products from buta-1,3-diene and HBr have which formula?
diene-addition.why: One HBr adds across the system, so both are isomers of the same formula.

diene-addition.q: Which statement about the two products is correct?
options: They are different compounds with the same formula
diene-addition.why: They are constitutional isomers, differing in where the Br and the double bond sit.

diene-addition.q: What makes an intermediate capable of giving two products?
diene-addition.why: A localized cation has one electrophilic carbon; a delocalized one has two.

diene-addition.q: Where does conjugate addition reappear later in the course?
diene-addition.why: A nucleophile adding to the far end of a conjugated enone is the same idea with a different intermediate.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: What is the kinetic product?
options: The one with the most new bonds
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Lower transition state, smaller activation energy. It need not be the most stable product available.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: What is the thermodynamic product?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Lower in energy once formed. It need not be the one that forms fastest.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: What must be true for thermodynamic control to operate?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: The system can only settle into the most stable product if it is able to leave the others.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: What conditions favor kinetic control?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Low temperature stops anything climbing back out, so the first-formed ratio is frozen in.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: Two products, one intermediate. A's barrier is 10 kJ/mol lower than B's and neither can revert. What ratio at room temperature?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Rate depends exponentially on the barrier, so small-looking gaps are not small. At room temperature about 6 kJ/mol is already a factor of ten, and 10 kJ/mol is around fifty. Because nothing can revert, that rate ratio is frozen in as the product ratio — which is what kinetic control means.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: Kinetics is about which of these?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: How high the hill is on the way out. Thermodynamics is how deep the valley is when you land.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: You are handed a reaction-coordinate diagram with one intermediate and two routes down. How do you find the thermodynamic product?
options: Take whichever route is drawn on the left
Take whichever route is drawn shorter
Look for the deeper of the two wells
Look for the lower of the two hilltops
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Thermodynamics is about where you land, not how hard the climb was. The depth of a well is the stability of the product that sits in it, so the deeper well holds the thermodynamic product. The lower hilltop answers a different question — which product forms faster — and on an interesting diagram the two answers point at different routes.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: Does the route with the lower barrier always lead to the more stable product?
options: Yes, in every reaction without exception
Only when the reaction is fully reversible
Only for reactions that add across a pi bond
No; the interesting cases are the disagreements
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: They coincide often enough, and when they do there is nothing to discuss. The vocabulary exists for the cases where the lower hill and the deeper valley point in opposite directions — HBr plus a diene being the standard example — because then the conditions, not the substrate, choose the product.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: What does raising the temperature actually change?
options: Which of the products is intrinsically more stable
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Stability and rates are properties of the system. Temperature decides whether the system is allowed to find out.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: A stated temperature of -78 C usually signals what?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: An unusually low temperature is there to stop the reaction reversing, which freezes in the faster-formed product.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: A bulky base at −78 °C pulls a proton from a ketone that has two different carbons next to its C=O. Which product?
options: The one from the more accessible proton, frozen in by the cold
The more substituted one, the more stable of the two
Both in roughly equal amounts, since the base is blunt
Neither one, because the cold shuts the reaction down
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: A bulky base reaches the least hindered proton fastest, so that product forms first; at −78 °C nothing has the energy to shuffle the proton around afterwards, so the first-formed ratio is the final one. In Enolate Chemistry this product has a name — the kinetic enolate — but the reasoning is the one from this section.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: The same ketone is treated with a small base under warm, equilibrating conditions. Which product now dominates?
options: An even mixture of the two
The more substituted, more stable one
The one from the more accessible proton
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Equilibrating conditions mean the proton can come off and go back on repeatedly, so the mixture is free to re-sort itself and drains into whichever product is lower in energy — here the more substituted one. Nothing about which formed faster survives that process.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: An –SO₃H group can be put on a benzene ring to block a position and taken off later. What makes that possible?
options: The reaction runs through a radical chain
The bond from sulfur to the ring is very weak
The group never fully attaches to the ring
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Hot dilute acid drives the sulfonation backwards and the group leaves, which is a rare privilege among substitutions on a ring. That reversibility is exactly the condition for thermodynamic control, and it is what makes –SO₃H usable as a temporary blocking group in synthesis.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: Under ordinary E2 conditions the Zaitsev alkene is the major product. Is that thermodynamic control?
options: No; the Zaitsev alkene is the less stable of the two
No; an E2 cannot reverse, so the alkenes never re-sort
Yes; the more substituted alkene is also the more stable
Yes; an E2 equilibrates its products at any temperature
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Thermodynamic control requires a way back, and an E2 has none: once an alkene has formed it stays. Under ordinary conditions the Zaitsev alkene happens to be both the faster-formed and the more stable one, so there is no contest to referee. Calling it the thermodynamic product invites the idea that it needs equilibration, and it does not.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: A bulky base gives the less substituted Hofmann alkene. Why?
options: The Hofmann alkene is the more stable of the two
The mixture equilibrates toward the smaller alkene
A bulky base reverses the alkene stability order
Sterics raise the barrier to the Zaitsev transition state
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: The bulky base cannot reach the interior proton comfortably, so the transition state leading to the more substituted alkene is pushed up and the other route becomes the faster one. Nothing about the alkenes themselves has changed — the Zaitsev product is still the more stable, it is simply no longer the quicker.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: Product A forms faster; product B is more stable. Cold and irreversible, what do you get?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Rates decide, and B's extra stability is irrelevant because nothing will ever visit it.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: A reaction gives 80:20 of P to Q at −40 °C and 10:90 at 60 °C. What does that tell you?
options: A different mechanism takes over at 60 °C
Q forms faster while P is the more stable
The products can interconvert, and Q is the more stable
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: A ratio that changes with temperature from the same starting materials means the mixture is being re-sorted, which needs a route back to the common intermediate. Cold, the rates decided and P won, so P is the kinetic product. Warm, the stabilities decided and Q won, so Q sits in the deeper well.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: B is more stable than A, but the step forming it cannot reverse. Does heating the reaction help?
options: Yes, though it takes prolonged heating
Yes, and more B appears the longer you heat
Only if a catalyst is added as well
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Heat is useful only because it lets a product climb back out and try again. Close that route and B's extra stability never gets a chance to matter, because nothing that has formed can be unformed. All the extra heat buys you is more of the faster product, sooner.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: In the diene case, which route has the lower barrier?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Bromide attacks C2, which carries more positive charge, so that route is faster.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: At room temperature, one product is favored about 100 to 1 at equilibrium. Roughly how much more stable is it?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Equilibrium ratios depend exponentially on the free-energy difference, so a factor of a hundred needs surprisingly little: around 12 kJ/mol at room temperature, which is about the size of one weak hydrogen bond. It is the same steepness that makes a 10 kJ/mol barrier difference worth a factor of fifty in rate.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: Why does warming the diene mixture invert the ratio?
options: Bromide can leave again and re-equilibrate
The charge distribution in the cation shifts
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Nothing about the mechanism or the intermediate changes. What changes is what the products can do afterwards.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: The more crowded endo Diels-Alder adduct forms faster than the less crowded exo one. What does that show about the word 'kinetic'?
options: It means the more stable of the available options
It means the step in question is reversible
It means faster, and says nothing about crowding
It means the less hindered of the available options
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Kinetic is a statement about a barrier and only about a barrier. Sterics are usually what makes one barrier lower, which is why 'kinetic' and 'less hindered' so often travel together — but here a favorable orbital interaction outweighs the crowding, and the more congested arrangement is still the quicker one.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: A product mixture does not change however long you heat it. What can you conclude?
options: Either it is already at equilibrium, or nothing can reverse
The reaction must be under thermodynamic control
The reaction must be under kinetic control
The two products are really one compound
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: An unchanging mixture is consistent with two opposite situations, and the observation alone cannot separate them: the system may have finished equilibrating and be sitting in the deepest well, or it may be frozen because no product can get back to the intermediate. To tell them apart, start from pure one product and see whether the mixture reappears.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: A reaction is run at high temperature but its first step cannot reverse. Which control applies?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Reversibility, not temperature, is the actual requirement. Heat without a way back changes nothing.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: Which question should you ask first when predicting the major product?
options: Which of the two products is more stable overall
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: That question determines which of the two comparisons you should even be making.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: What does the double dagger in ΔG‡ mark?
options: That the step in question is reversible
That the reaction gives off heat overall
That the quantity belongs to a transition state
That the value is measured in kilojoules
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: ΔG is the free-energy change between two real species, and it tells you where an equilibrium sits. ΔG‡ is the climb from the starting point to the transition state at the top of the hill, and it tells you how fast. The dagger is the notation's way of saying that the thing at the other end is not something you could isolate.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: Two products form from a common intermediate. What does that make possible?
options: Only one possible outcome, whatever the conditions
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: A branch point is what lets conditions select between outcomes.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: Which is NOT a case of kinetic versus thermodynamic control?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Each of the others is a genuine branch point where one route is faster and another gives the more stable product, and where conditions pick between them. SN2 stereochemistry is not a competition at all: backside attack is the only geometry the reaction has, so inversion is forced by the mechanism rather than selected by the conditions.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: If a reaction gives one product cold and another warm, what can you infer?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Reversibility is what lets the warm run reach a different answer from the same intermediate.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: What does it mean that a product is trapped under kinetic control?
options: It cannot revert to starting material
It cannot be purified by ordinary means
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Once formed it stays, so the product ratio simply records which route was faster.

diels-alder.q: The Diels-Alder is classified as which kind of reaction?
diels-alder.why: Four pi electrons from the diene and two from the dienophile.

diels-alder.q: Buta-1,3-diene reacts with dimethyl fumarate, whose esters are trans across the C=C. What comes out?
options: A cyclohexane with the esters trans to each other
A cyclohexene with the esters trans on adjacent carbons
A cyclohexene with the esters cis on adjacent carbons
Equal amounts of the cis and trans ring products
diels-alder.why: Both new bonds form on one face of the dienophile in a single step, so nothing is ever free to rotate and the starting geometry survives intact. Trans across the alkene becomes trans on the ring — on neighboring carbons, one up and one down. Run it with dimethyl maleate, the cis isomer, and you get the cis product just as cleanly.

diels-alder.q: How many new sigma bonds form?
diels-alder.why: Three pi bonds go in; two sigma bonds and one pi bond come out, which is why the reaction is downhill.

diels-alder.q: Is there an intermediate in a Diels-Alder reaction?
diels-alder.why: Every bond breaks and forms in one step through a single cyclic transition state.

diels-alder.q: Why does the Diels-Alder never give rearranged products?
options: The reaction conditions are always mild
There is no carbocation to rearrange
diels-alder.why: With no intermediate there is nothing to shift, nothing to lose stereochemistry and nothing whose stability to compare.

diels-alder.q: Which conformation must the diene adopt?
diels-alder.why: Both ends of the diene must reach both ends of the dienophile at once.

diels-alder.q: What is the commonest reason a Diels-Alder fails?
diels-alder.why: It is a geometric requirement, and no amount of electronic tuning fixes it.

diels-alder.q: Why is cyclopentadiene exceptionally reactive?
diels-alder.why: It pays no rotation penalty, and dimerizes on standing as a result.

diels-alder.q: How is cyclopentadiene stored and prepared for use?
options: As the dimer, cracked by distillation
Frozen and stored in liquid nitrogen
diels-alder.why: It dimerizes at room temperature via a Diels-Alder, and the retro reaction on heating gives it back.

diels-alder.q: What makes a good dienophile?
diels-alder.why: They lower its LUMO, bringing it closer to the diene's HOMO.

diels-alder.q: What makes a good diene?
diels-alder.why: They raise its HOMO, narrowing the gap to the dienophile's LUMO.

diels-alder.q: Rank these dienophiles with cyclopentadiene, fastest first.
options: All three react at about the same rate
diels-alder.why: Count the groups pulling the LUMO down. Maleic anhydride has two carbonyls flanking its C=C; methyl acrylate has one ester; ethene has nothing at all and needs forcing conditions. The narrower the gap to the diene's HOMO, the faster the pair reacts, so the order follows the electron-withdrawing power directly.

diels-alder.q: Isoprene reacts with methyl acrylate. Which regioisomer dominates?
options: The 'para' one, the two substituents 1,4 across the ring
The 'ortho' one, the two substituents on adjacent carbons
The 'meta' one, the two substituents 1,3 across the ring
An even mixture, since the orientation is uncontrolled
diels-alder.why: Polarize each partner. Isoprene's methyl sits on C2, which puts the nucleophilic end of the diene at C1; the ester on the dienophile puts the electrophilic end on the CH₂ that does not carry it. Bond those two, and the methyl and the ester finish 1,4 apart. A 2-substituted diene always gives this 'para' relationship; the 1,3 arrangement is not on the menu at all.

diels-alder.q: Why does ethene react only under forcing conditions?
options: It is simply too stable to react at all
diels-alder.why: Nothing lowers its LUMO, so the orbital gap to the diene stays wide.

diels-alder.q: Two substituents cis on the dienophile end up how in the product?
diels-alder.why: Both bonds form on the same face in one step, so nothing can rotate and the relationship is preserved.

diels-alder.q: You want dimethyl cyclohex-4-ene-1,2-dicarboxylate with its esters cis. Which pair makes it?
diels-alder.why: Cut the target at its retro-Diels-Alder disconnection: step one carbon out from each end of the ring double bond and break the two bonds leading away, which leaves buta-1,3-diene and a two-carbon piece carrying both esters. Since the reaction preserves the dienophile's geometry, cis esters in the product demand cis esters in the dienophile — dimethyl maleate. Fumarate would give the trans ring product, and cyclopentadiene would give a bicyclic one.

diels-alder.q: What does stereospecific mean here?
options: Only one stereoisomer of the dienophile can react
The starting geometry determines the product geometry
diels-alder.why: Stereospecific means the answer is read off the starting material rather than guessed: change the geometry going in and you get a predictably different geometry coming out. Both new bonds form on one face of each partner — suprafacial, in the formal vocabulary — so nothing gets a chance to scramble.

diels-alder.q: Which product is favored when the dienophile bears a substituent?
diels-alder.why: The endo transition state benefits from a secondary orbital interaction, making it faster.

diels-alder.q: Cyclopentadiene and maleic anhydride give a bicyclic adduct. Where does the anhydride sit in the major product?
options: Split evenly between the two possible sides
On the same side as the two-carbon C=C bridge
On the same side as the one-carbon CH₂ bridge
diels-alder.why: That arrangement is the endo one, and it comes from the stack in which the anhydride is tucked under the diene as the bond forms. It is the more crowded of the two approaches and still the faster, because the anhydride's pi system touches the diene's in the transition state. Note that endo is the kinetic answer here: the exo adduct is usually the more stable of the two.

diels-alder.q: The endo product is which kind of product?
diels-alder.why: It forms faster, which is a useful corrective to reading kinetic as less hindered.

diels-alder.q: What is a retro-Diels-Alder?
options: The reverse reaction, splitting the ring
A Lewis-acid catalyzed version of it
diels-alder.why: Heating a suitable cyclohexene sends it back to a diene and a dienophile.

diels-alder.q: Why is the retro-Diels-Alder useful in synthesis planning?
options: It removes stereocenters from the target
diels-alder.why: Mentally cutting a six-membered ring at that disconnection is one of the most productive moves in retrosynthesis.

diels-alder.q: What makes a reaction pericyclic?
options: Two separate molecules combine to make a ring
It is driven by light rather than by heat
It runs through a cyclic carbocation intermediate
Every bond breaks and forms together, round a closed loop
diels-alder.why: The defining feature is the single step with no intermediate and the electrons travelling in a closed circuit, not the shape of the product. Cycloadditions such as the Diels-Alder are one family; electrocyclic ring closures and sigmatropic shifts like the Cope and Claisen rearrangements are the others. Plenty of ring-forming reactions are not pericyclic at all.

diels-alder.q: (E)-Penta-1,3-diene reacts with propenal. Where do the methyl and the aldehyde end up?
options: In whichever positions chance puts them
On adjacent ring carbons — the 'ortho' product
diels-alder.why: The methyl sits on a terminal carbon of the diene, which makes this a 1-substituted diene, and those give the 'ortho' relationship. Check it by polarizing: the donor end puts the diene's nucleophilic carbon at the far terminus, that carbon bonds to the dienophile's CH₂, and the methyl-bearing end is therefore left bonded to the carbon carrying the CHO — next-door neighbors on the new ring.

diels-alder.q: Can an alkyne serve as a dienophile?
diels-alder.why: An alkyne brings two pi electrons to the ring just as an alkene does, and its second pi bond is untouched by the reaction. So the product keeps that bond alongside the new one between the diene's old C2 and C3, and what you isolate is a cyclohexa-1,4-diene rather than a cyclohexene.

diels-alder.q: Where does the new double bond sit in the product?
options: Between the diene's former C2 and C3
diels-alder.why: The two terminal carbons form the new sigma bonds, and the central bond becomes the alkene.

diels-alder.q: Why is the reaction thermodynamically favorable?
diels-alder.why: Sigma bonds are stronger, so trading two pi bonds for two sigma bonds releases energy.

diels-alder.q: What does concerted mean?
options: All bonds break and form in one step
diels-alder.why: One transition state, no intermediate, and every consequence of that follows.

diels-alder.q: A Lewis acid such as AlCl₃ speeds up a Diels-Alder. How?
options: It generates a carbocation the diene can attack
It raises the effective temperature of the mixture
It binds the dienophile's carbonyl and lowers its LUMO
It helps the diene rotate into its s-cis conformation
diels-alder.why: Coordinating to the carbonyl oxygen drains electron density out of the C=C next to it, dropping the dienophile's LUMO closer to the diene's HOMO. Rates can rise by orders of magnitude and the endo preference usually sharpens. It is a genuine catalyst and not a requirement — the reaction is downhill on bond energies alone.

diels-alder.q: Which diene cannot do a Diels-Alder at all?
options: One locked s-trans in a ring
diels-alder.why: It can never reach the conformation where both ends point the same way.

uv-vis.q: What transition does UV-Vis spectroscopy probe in an organic molecule?
uv-vis.why: A pi to pi-star transition, promoting an electron across the frontier orbital gap.

uv-vis.q: A bigger HOMO-LUMO gap means absorption at which wavelength?
uv-vis.why: A bigger gap needs a higher energy photon, and higher energy means shorter wavelength.

uv-vis.q: A smaller HOMO-LUMO gap means absorption at which wavelength?
uv-vis.why: Less energy is needed, and lower energy light has a longer wavelength.

uv-vis.q: What happens to the HOMO-LUMO gap as conjugation extends?
uv-vis.why: More p orbitals give more molecular orbitals over a similar range, so the highest occupied rises and the lowest empty falls.

uv-vis.q: Which absorbs at the longer wavelength: hexa-1,3,5-triene or hexa-1,4-diene?
options: The triene, with three C=C in one conjugated run
The 1,4-diene, which has more sp3 carbons
Both the same, since they are isomers
Neither, within reach of a routine instrument
uv-vis.why: Count what is actually conjugated, not what is present. Hexa-1,3,5-triene has three double bonds in one unbroken run, so it has the most molecular orbitals packed into the same energy range and the narrowest HOMO-LUMO gap — 258 nm. Hexa-1,4-diene has an sp3 carbon between its two double bonds, so it behaves as two lone alkenes and absorbs below 200 nm, out of reach.

uv-vis.q: One band sits at 217 nm with ε ≈ 21,000; another at 280 nm with ε ≈ 20. What are you looking at?
options: An impurity rather than a real second band
A conjugated diene, and a carbonyl's lone pair
Two conjugated systems of different lengths
Two lone pairs on different heteroatoms
uv-vis.why: The wavelength tells you the gap; the ε tells you how allowed the jump is. A π to π* transition in a conjugated system runs to ε in the tens of thousands. A lone pair on a carbonyl oxygen points sideways relative to the π* it has to reach, so the n to π* band is nearly forbidden — ε of ten to a hundred — even though it sits at a long wavelength. A long λ with a tiny ε is the signature of a lone pair.

uv-vis.q: In A = εcl, what units must ε carry?
options: It has no units, like A
uv-vis.why: Derive it rather than memorizing it. A is a bare number, c is in mol per litre and l is in centimetres, so ε has to supply exactly what cancels those two: litres per mole per centimetre. Writing 'ε = 21,000' without units is shorthand for 21,000 L·mol⁻¹·cm⁻¹.

uv-vis.q: A 1.00 cm cell gives A = 0.63 for a diene with ε = 21,000. What is the concentration?
uv-vis.why: Rearrange first: c = A / εl = 0.63 / (21,000 × 1.00) = 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹. Check the units as you go — L·mol⁻¹·cm⁻¹ times cm leaves L·mol⁻¹, and dividing a unitless absorbance by that gives mol·L⁻¹. Thirty micromolar is a few milligrams in a litre, which is what a large ε buys you.

uv-vis.q: A formula fits either a conjugated triene or a compound with three isolated C=C. The sample absorbs at 258 nm. Which is it?
options: Neither structure fits a band there
The one with isolated double bonds
uv-vis.why: Isolated double bonds do not pool their orbitals, so each behaves as a lone alkene absorbing below 200 nm where a routine instrument cannot look. A band at 258 nm needs a single run of three conjugated C=C. This is the one structural question UV-Vis answers sharply: how long the conjugation is, though not where in the molecule it sits.

uv-vis.q: What is a chromophore?
options: Any compound that looks colored to the eye
A solvent chosen to be transparent
The group of atoms responsible for the absorption
uv-vis.why: In organic UV-Vis it is nearly always the conjugated π system, and sometimes a lone pair beside one. A group that is not itself a chromophore but shifts the band of a neighboring one — an OR or an NR₂ — is called an auxochrome, and that is how a dye's color is tuned without lengthening the chain.

uv-vis.q: Why does beta-carotene look orange?
options: You see the light it does not absorb
It emits orange light after absorbing
uv-vis.why: It removes blue light around 450 nm, and what reaches your eye is the complementary color.

uv-vis.q: Why are most organic compounds colorless?
options: They are transparent in the solid state
uv-vis.why: Without a long conjugated system the gap is too wide, so absorption stays in the ultraviolet.

uv-vis.q: What is the Beer-Lambert law?
uv-vis.why: Absorbance equals molar absorptivity times concentration times path length.

uv-vis.q: In A = ecl, what does e represent?
uv-vis.why: A constant for that compound at that wavelength, measuring how strongly it absorbs.

uv-vis.q: In A = ecl, what does l represent?
uv-vis.why: Conventionally 1 cm for a standard cuvette.

uv-vis.q: Why is UV-Vis quantitative?
options: It counts the molecules present directly
uv-vis.why: The Beer-Lambert relationship makes it the standard way to follow a concentration while a reaction runs.

uv-vis.q: Typical molar absorptivity for a conjugated system is roughly what?
uv-vis.why: Conjugated systems absorb strongly, which is part of why the technique is sensitive.

uv-vis.q: Two isomers: one absorbs at 227 nm, one below 200 nm. Which is conjugated?
uv-vis.why: Conjugation narrows the gap, so the conjugated isomer absorbs at the longer wavelength.

uv-vis.q: What does a UV-Vis spectrum NOT tell you?
options: How concentrated it is, given ε
uv-vis.why: It reports on conjugation, and on amount once ε is known — but nothing about position or connectivity. Pair it with NMR for that.

uv-vis.q: Roughly where does the visible region begin?
uv-vis.why: Below about 400 nm is ultraviolet, so a compound absorbing past that point can appear colored.

uv-vis.q: Why does an isolated alkene appear invisible to a routine UV-Vis instrument?
options: It does not absorb at all
It absorbs below the accessible range
It absorbs only in the infrared region
uv-vis.why: A single C=C absorbs below about 200 nm, which ordinary instruments do not reach comfortably.

uv-vis.q: A diene picks up two alkyl substituents and one extra conjugated double bond. Roughly how far does λₘₐₓ move?
options: It does not move at all
uv-vis.why: The Woodward-Fieser increments make this arithmetic: each alkyl group or ring residue is worth about +5 nm and each extra conjugated C=C about +30, so 5 + 5 + 30 is roughly +40. Notice the size of the two terms — lengthening the conjugation dominates, and substituents only nudge, which is why UV-Vis counts double bonds well and identifies substituents badly.

uv-vis.q: Which technique best reports the extent of conjugation?
uv-vis.why: Each technique answers a different question, and this is the one UV-Vis answers sharply.

uv-vis.q: Which technique names functional groups?
uv-vis.why: IR reports on bond vibrations, which are characteristic of particular groups.

uv-vis.q: Why does UV-Vis sit in the conjugation chapter?
options: It is the oldest of the techniques
uv-vis.why: It turns the chapter's central claim into a number you can read off an instrument.

uv-vis.q: What is absorbance?
uv-vis.why: Read off the instrument, and proportional to concentration by Beer-Lambert.

uv-vis.q: Extending conjugation by one double bond does what to lambda-max?
uv-vis.why: Each additional conjugated double bond narrows the gap further and pushes absorption to longer wavelength.

uv-vis.q: What kind of orbital is the LUMO of a conjugated alkene?
options: A sigma antibonding orbital, far higher in energy
A non-bonding orbital holding a lone pair
A vacant 3s orbital on one of the carbons
A π* antibonding orbital — the far end of the π to π* jump
uv-vis.why: Combining the p orbitals of a conjugated system gives a set of π orbitals; the bottom half are bonding and filled, the top half antibonding and empty. The lowest empty one is the π* that an absorbed photon promotes an electron into. Naming it matters because the other common band in organic UV-Vis ends in the same π* but starts from a lone pair instead, and that one is weak.

uv-vis.q: Retinal, the visual pigment, works because of what?
uv-vis.why: Extended conjugation brings its absorption into the visible, which is what makes vision possible.

uv-vis.q: Can UV-Vis distinguish two conjugated isomers of the same length?
options: Often poorly, since it reports conjugation not position
Only if the compounds are colored
uv-vis.why: It answers one question sharply and says little about connectivity, so NMR does the placing.

alcohol-reactions.q: Why can’t OH⁻ typically leave directly from an alcohol in a substitution reaction?
options: OH⁻ is too strong a base
alcohol-reactions.why: Hydroxide is a strong base (poor leaving group); alcohols are typically first protonated (or converted to a better leaving group like a tosylate) before substitution/elimination.

alcohol-reactions.q: Protonating an alcohol with strong acid converts –OH into:
alcohol-reactions.why: Protonation turns the leaving group into neutral H₂O, which is a much weaker base (and thus a far better leaving group) than OH⁻.

alcohol-reactions.q: Which reagent is commonly used to convert an alcohol into a good leaving group (a tosylate) without disturbing its stereochemistry?
options: Tosyl chloride (TsCl) with a mild base
alcohol-reactions.why: TsCl converts the OH into OTs, a weak-base, excellent leaving group, via a mechanism that doesn’t touch the stereocenter’s configuration (unlike acid-catalyzed substitution, which can invert or racemize it).

alcohol-reactions.q: Which mechanism does tert-butanol follow when it reacts with concentrated HCl to form tert-butyl chloride?
alcohol-reactions.why: Tertiary carbocations are stable enough to form, so the reaction proceeds through ionization (loss of water) followed by chloride capture, a classic SN1 pathway.

alcohol-reactions.q: Primary alcohols react with HBr via an SN1 mechanism because primary carbocations form easily.
alcohol-reactions.why: Primary carbocations are far too unstable to form, so a primary alcohol reacts with HX by SN2 instead: the acid protonates the oxygen, and bromide attacks the carbon from the back while neutral water - the actual leaving group - departs.

alcohol-reactions.q: Which reagent converts a primary alcohol to the corresponding alkyl chloride with the least risk of carbocation rearrangement?
alcohol-reactions.why: SOCl2 reacts through a chlorosulfite intermediate without generating a free carbocation, avoiding the hydride or alkyl shifts that can occur in purely acid-catalyzed routes.

alcohol-reactions.q: Which reagent converts butan-2-ol into 2-bromobutane with no risk of a skeletal rearrangement?
options: PBr3 in ether at room temperature
NaBr in acetone, heated to reflux
alcohol-reactions.why: PBr3 converts the OH into an ester of phosphorus that bromide then displaces in one backside step, so no carbocation is ever formed and nothing can shift. The HBr and H2SO4/NaBr routes both work by protonating the OH, which at a secondary carbon means ionization to a cation - and a cation is free to rearrange. NaBr alone does nothing at all, because hydroxide cannot leave.

alcohol-reactions.q: 3,3-Dimethylbutan-2-ol is treated with concentrated HBr. What is the major product?
alcohol-reactions.why: Protonation and loss of water give a secondary cation at C2. Its neighbor C3 is quaternary, so it has no hydrogen to send across - but it can send a whole methyl group with its bonding pair, and that 1,2-methyl shift converts the secondary cation into a tertiary one. Bromide captures that rearranged cation, so the bromine sits on a carbon that never carried the hydroxyl.

alcohol-reactions.q: A molecule contains an acid-sensitive group elsewhere, and you need to dehydrate its secondary alcohol without rearrangement. The best choice is:
options: Dilute aqueous HCl at room temperature
Solid KOH, heated with the alcohol
alcohol-reactions.why: POCl3 converts the OH into a dichlorophosphate ester under basic conditions, and pyridine then removes an anti-periplanar beta hydrogen in a single concerted E2 step. No acid is used and no carbocation is formed, so nothing else in the molecule is exposed and the skeleton cannot shift. Hot H2SO4 does the same dehydration but through a cation, and hydroxide is far too poor a leaving group for base alone to eliminate it.

alcohol-reactions.q: Converting a chiral secondary alcohol to its tosylate leaves the configuration at that carbon unchanged.
alcohol-reactions.why: Tosylation happens at sulfur: the alcohol oxygen attacks the S of TsCl and chloride leaves, so the C-O bond is never broken. Nothing at carbon moves, and the stereocenter is handed on intact. Any inversion you see later belongs to the substitution step that displaces the tosylate, not to the tosylation.

alcohol-reactions.q: Acid-catalyzed dehydration of 2-butanol gives mainly:
alcohol-reactions.why: Zaitsev's rule favors the more stable, more substituted alkene; in the E1 mechanism the carbocation loses a proton preferentially toward the more substituted side, forming the more stable double bond.

alcohol-reactions.q: Put the steps of acid-catalyzed (E1) dehydration of an alcohol in the correct order.
options: Loss of a proton, protonation of OH, loss of water
Protonation, loss of water, then loss of a proton
Loss of water, loss of a proton, protonation of OH
Protonation of OH, loss of a proton, loss of water
alcohol-reactions.why: The OH must first be protonated to become a good leaving group (water), which then departs to generate a carbocation; a base finally removes a beta-proton to form the alkene.

alcohol-reactions.q: Dehydration rates for alcohols under acid catalysis follow the order 3 degrees > 2 degrees > 1 degree primarily because:
options: Primary alcohols have stronger O-H bonds
More substituted carbocations are more stable and form faster
Steric hindrance speeds up primary alcohol dehydration
alcohol-reactions.why: The rate-limiting step is carbocation formation; hyperconjugation and inductive electron donation from additional alkyl groups stabilize more substituted carbocations, lowering the activation energy for their formation.

alcohol-reactions.q: Acid-catalyzed dehydration of a secondary alcohol can give a rearranged alkene product that would not be predicted from simply removing a proton adjacent to the original carbinol carbon.
alcohol-reactions.why: Because the mechanism passes through a carbocation intermediate, a hydride or alkyl shift can occur before the proton is lost, shifting the position of the resulting double bond or even the carbon skeleton.

alcohol-reactions.q: Adding sodium metal to ethanol produces:
options: No reaction; alcohols do not react with Na
alcohol-reactions.why: Alcohols are weak acids; the reactive Na metal reduces the O-H proton, releasing H2 gas and leaving behind the sodium alkoxide salt.

alcohol-reactions.q: In a Williamson ether synthesis starting from an alcohol, the first step is usually to:
options: Oxidize the alcohol to a ketone
alcohol-reactions.why: The alkoxide, not the neutral alcohol, is the nucleophile needed to perform SN2 displacement on the alkyl halide partner, so a strong, non-nucleophilic base like NaH is used first to form it.

alcohol-reactions.q: (S)-Butan-2-ol is treated with TsCl/pyridine and the product is then treated with NaCN. The configuration at C2 in the nitrile is:
options: Retained, since tosylation does not touch the C-O bond
Inverted, from the single SN2 step that displaces the tosylate
Racemic, because the tosylate ionizes before cyanide arrives
Undefined, since C2 is no longer a stereocenter
alcohol-reactions.why: Count the steps that break the C-O bond at C2: exactly one. Tosylation happens at sulfur and leaves the stereocenter alone, then cyanide displaces the tosylate by backside attack. One inversion means the product is inverted, not racemic - a tosylate is a good enough leaving group that a secondary carbon has no reason to ionize with a strong nucleophile present.

alcohol-reactions.q: 3,3-Dimethylbutan-2-ol is heated with concentrated H2SO4. The major alkene is:
alcohol-reactions.why: Work in the order the mechanism runs: protonate, lose water to a secondary cation, then check for a shift before applying Zaitsev. A methyl migrates from the quaternary neighbor to give a tertiary cation, and losing a beta hydrogen from that rearranged skeleton gives the tetrasubstituted alkene. Applying Zaitsev to the original skeleton instead gives a confident wrong answer.

alcohol-reactions.q: A secondary alcohol is converted to its tosylate and the tosylate is then heated with sodium ethoxide, a strong base. The main product is:
options: An alkene, from E2 elimination of the tosylate
An ether, from SN2 attack by ethoxide
The starting alcohol, regenerated by hydrolysis
No reaction, since tosylates are unreactive toward bases
alcohol-reactions.why: Once the OH is a tosylate, that carbon behaves like a secondary alkyl halide, so the SN2-versus-E2 competition from Substitution and Elimination applies unchanged. Ethoxide is a strong base as well as a nucleophile, and at a secondary carbon a strong base takes a beta hydrogen faster than it attacks the crowded carbon, so elimination dominates.

alcohol-reactions.q: Apart from methanol, simple alcohols are slightly weaker acids than water.
alcohol-reactions.why: Alkyl groups donate electron density to the alkoxide oxygen and crowd it out of good solvation, so ethanol (pKa 16) and tert-butanol (pKa 18) are both weaker acids than water (15.7). Methanol is the exception that makes the wording matter: at pKa 15.5 it is slightly more acidic than water, because it carries the least alkyl bulk of all.

alcohol-reactions.q: Compared to methanol, tert-butanol is:
options: Less acidic (higher pKa), owing to alkyl donation
More acidic (lower pKa), because of steric relief on ionization
Equally acidic; alkyl substitution does not affect alcohol pKa
More acidic because tertiary carbons stabilize negative charge better
alcohol-reactions.why: The added alkyl groups push electron density onto the already-negative alkoxide oxygen, destabilizing the anion (and hindering its solvation), which raises the pKa relative to methanol.

alcohol-reactions.q: Adding a Grignard reagent (R-MgBr) to an alcohol results in:
options: Nucleophilic addition to give a new, larger alcohol
Simple acid-base protonation that destroys the Grignard reagent
An SN2 substitution that gives an ether
No reaction, since Grignards do not react with alcohols
alcohol-reactions.why: The O-H of an alcohol is acidic enough to protonate the strongly basic, carbanion-like Grignard reagent, quenching it as an alkane before it can perform any useful addition chemistry.

alcohol-reactions.q: The role of the chlorosulfite intermediate R-O-SOCl formed from an alcohol and SOCl2 is to:
options: Oxidize the carbinol carbon before substitution occurs
Protonate the hydroxyl so that water can leave
Convert the OH into a group that leaves as SO2 and chloride
Trap any carbocation formed during the reaction
alcohol-reactions.why: The alcohol oxygen attacks sulfur, which parks a leaving group on the oxygen rather than on carbon. That group departs as sulfur dioxide and chloride, two stable and weakly basic pieces, so chloride can finish the job with an ordinary backside displacement. Nothing is oxidized and no positive charge is ever built on carbon, which is why the product is cleanly inverted and never rearranged.

alcohol-reactions.q: Heating an alcohol with sodium cyanide displaces the hydroxide and gives a nitrile directly.
alcohol-reactions.why: Hydroxide is the conjugate base of water, pKa 15.7, which makes it a strong base and one of the worst leaving groups in the course. Cyanide cannot displace it however hot the flask gets. The OH has to be activated first - as a tosylate, or by protonation - and then cyanide will do the SN2.

alcohol-reactions.q: Which of these is the strongest acid?
alcohol-reactions.why: Acidity falls as alkyl groups are added around the oxygen: methanol 15.5, water 15.7, ethanol 16, tert-butanol 18. Those alkyl groups donate electron density into an already negative alkoxide and, more importantly in solution, wrap it in bulk that keeps solvent molecules from stabilizing the charge. Methanol carries the least bulk, so its alkoxide is the best solvated and methanol is the strongest acid of the four.

alcohol-reactions.q: Primary alcohols dehydrate only under forcing conditions, and when they do the mechanism is described as E2-like rather than E1. The reason is that:
options: Primary C-O bonds are much stronger than secondary ones
A primary carbocation is too unstable to form
Primary alcohols cannot be protonated by sulfuric acid
Primary alcohols have no beta hydrogen to lose
alcohol-reactions.why: E1 requires the leaving group to depart before anything else happens, which means paying the full price of the carbocation. A primary cation is stabilized by almost nothing, so that route is closed. The elimination instead happens in one concerted step, with the base removing the beta hydrogen as water leaves, which never puts a full positive charge on carbon - and it is why primary alcohols need higher temperatures than secondary or tertiary ones.

alcohol-reactions.q: The reaction of a secondary alcohol with PBr3 proceeds through:
options: An SN1 mechanism with a free carbocation, racemizing the product
An SN2-like mechanism with backside attack by bromide, inverting configuration
Simple proton transfer with no bond-breaking at carbon
alcohol-reactions.why: PBr3 first converts the OH into a good leaving group, and bromide then displaces it in a single concerted backside attack, giving clean inversion rather than the racemization seen with carbocation intermediates.

alcohol-reactions.q: Treating a chiral secondary alcohol with PBr3 gives the alkyl bromide with inverted stereochemistry at that carbon.
alcohol-reactions.why: Because PBr3 operates through a concerted SN2-type displacement without a free carbocation, bromide must attack from the side opposite the leaving group, inverting the configuration.

alcohol-reactions.q: Treating that same chiral secondary alcohol with concentrated HBr alone (simple acid-catalyzed substitution) tends to give a racemized, or partially racemized, product.
alcohol-reactions.why: Protonation of the OH followed by loss of water generates a planar carbocation that can be attacked by bromide from either face, scrambling the stereochemistry relative to the clean inversion seen with PBr3.

alcohol-reactions.q: Among methanol, isopropanol, and tert-butanol, which dehydrates fastest when heated with strong acid?
options: They all dehydrate at the same rate
alcohol-reactions.why: Acid-catalyzed dehydration proceeds through a carbocation intermediate; tert-butanol forms the most stable (tertiary) carbocation most readily, so it reacts fastest, while methanol has no adjacent carbon to form a double bond with at all.

ether-chemistry.q: Why are ethers generally unreactive under basic conditions?
options: There is no good leaving group
The C–O bond is too strong to ever break
Ethers react only with other ethers
ether-chemistry.why: Like alcohols, ethers need protonation (acidic conditions) to turn the alkoxide oxygen into a viable leaving group (neutral alcohol) before cleavage.

ether-chemistry.q: Strong acid cleavage of an ether with HI runs by which mechanism at a tertiary carbon?
ether-chemistry.why: A tertiary carbon ionizes readily once the oxygen is protonated, so the alcohol leaves on its own and iodide captures the resulting carbocation - SN1. A primary or methyl carbon cannot support a cation, so there iodide attacks directly, SN2. A secondary carbon sits between the two and does some of each.

ether-chemistry.q: Why are ethers often used as solvents for reactions involving strong nucleophiles/bases (like Grignard reagents)?
options: They are highly reactive and participate directly
They are unreactive yet coordinate cations
Ethers decompose readily under these conditions
ether-chemistry.why: Ethers lack an acidic proton and don’t have a good leaving group under neutral/basic conditions, so they tolerate strongly basic/nucleophilic reagents while still solvating them through the oxygen’s lone pairs.

ether-chemistry.q: Why do ethers generally have lower boiling points than alcohols of similar molecular weight?
options: Ethers are always smaller molecules than alcohols
Ethers have stronger London dispersion forces
Ether molecules cannot hydrogen-bond to each other, unlike alcohols
ether-chemistry.why: Alcohols can hydrogen-bond to one another through their O-H groups, which raises their boiling points substantially; ethers lack an O-H bond, so they only experience weaker dipole-dipole and dispersion forces between molecules.

ether-chemistry.q: Ethers can act as hydrogen bond acceptors (through their oxygen lone pairs) but not as hydrogen bond donors.
ether-chemistry.why: An ether oxygen has lone pairs that can accept a hydrogen bond from an O-H or N-H elsewhere, but since ethers have no O-H or N-H of their own, they cannot donate a hydrogen bond.

ether-chemistry.q: Methyl propyl ether is heated with one equivalent of concentrated HI. The products are:
options: Equal amounts of both alkyl iodides
No reaction; ethers are inert to HI
ether-chemistry.why: Protonation makes the oxygen a viable leaving group, but neither carbon here can carry a positive charge, so the cleavage has to be an SN2 - and an SN2 goes where the approach is clearest, the methyl. That gives methyl iodide and propan-1-ol. Only with excess HI and more heating does the propanol go on to become propyl iodide.

ether-chemistry.q: Treating tert-butyl methyl ether with one equivalent of HI gives:
options: A mixture of tert-butyl and methyl iodide in equal amounts
No reaction, since tertiary ethers resist acidic cleavage
ether-chemistry.why: The tertiary carbon ionizes to a stable carbocation once the oxygen is protonated, so cleavage happens there and iodide captures the cation: tert-butyl iodide and methanol. Note that the most hindered carbon is attacked precisely because no backside attack is involved. With excess HI the methanol would go on to give methyl iodide as well.

ether-chemistry.q: An unsymmetrical ether with one primary alkyl group and one tertiary alkyl group is treated with HBr. The major products are expected to be:
options: The primary bromide and the tertiary alcohol
Both carbons are substituted with equal probability
The tertiary bromide and the primary alcohol
Neither C-O bond breaks under these conditions
ether-chemistry.why: The tertiary carbon can ionize to a stable carbocation far more easily than the primary carbon can undergo a slow SN2 displacement, so cleavage occurs preferentially at the tertiary center, releasing the primary alcohol intact.

ether-chemistry.q: Ethyl isopropyl ether is heated with one equivalent of HI, giving ethyl iodide and propan-2-ol. The reason the iodide ends up on the ethyl group is that:
options: The secondary carbon forms a cation too readily for iodide to reach it
Neither carbon supports a cation well, so the SN2 goes to the less hindered one
Secondary C-O bonds are stronger than primary C-O bonds
Iodide is too large to approach a secondary carbon at all
ether-chemistry.why: Ask which mechanism is running before asking which carbon reacts. A secondary cation is not stable enough to form readily under these conditions, so the cleavage is an SN2, and an SN2 is decided by sterics: iodide attacks the primary ethyl carbon. Had one carbon been tertiary, the answer would have flipped, because that carbon would ionize without help.

ether-chemistry.q: Why is the Williamson ether synthesis generally a poor method for making an ether from a tertiary alkyl halide?
options: Tertiary alkyl halides are never soluble in the reaction solvent
Alkoxides cannot act as nucleophiles toward tertiary carbons
Tertiary halides spontaneously hydrolyze before the alkoxide can react
The strongly basic alkoxide promotes E2 elimination instead of SN2 substitution on the tertiary halide
ether-chemistry.why: A bulky, basic alkoxide approaching a hindered tertiary carbon strongly favors removing a beta-hydrogen (E2) over performing a backside SN2 attack, so elimination products dominate instead of the desired ether.

ether-chemistry.q: To cleanly synthesize an unsymmetrical ether via the Williamson method, you should generally:
options: Use the alkoxide from the more hindered alcohol paired with the less hindered (often primary) alkyl halide
Use the alkoxide from the less hindered alcohol paired with a tertiary alkyl halide
It never matters which partner is the alkoxide versus the halide
Always use two different tertiary components for best yield
ether-chemistry.why: Because the alkyl halide is the electrophile undergoing SN2 attack, choosing one that is primary (or otherwise unhindered) avoids competing elimination, regardless of how bulky the alkoxide nucleophile itself is.

ether-chemistry.q: Crown ethers such as 18-crown-6 are useful in organic synthesis mainly because they:
options: React covalently with alkyl halides to form new ethers
Bind metal cations and solubilize their salts
ether-chemistry.why: The ring of oxygen atoms in a crown ether can wrap around a metal cation of the right size, effectively dissolving otherwise poorly soluble ionic salts in nonpolar solvents.

ether-chemistry.q: 18-Crown-6 binds K+ more selectively than it binds Na+ because its cavity size is a better match for the potassium ion.
ether-chemistry.why: Crown ethers show size selectivity, and the numbers to compare are diameters: 18-crown-6 has a cavity about 2.7 Angstroms across and K+ is 2.66 Angstroms, so the ion fills the hole and contacts all six oxygen lone pairs at once. Na+ is only 1.9 Angstroms across, so it sits in a cavity too large for it, touches fewer oxygens at a time and binds far more weakly.

ether-chemistry.q: Dissolving KF with 18-crown-6 in a nonpolar organic solvent makes fluoride a much more effective nucleophile because:
options: The crown ether reduces the overall negative charge on fluoride
Crown ethers convert fluoride into a stronger base but weaker nucleophile
The crown ether sequesters the potassium cation, leaving a more 'naked,' poorly ion-paired fluoride anion
The crown ether reacts with fluoride to form a more reactive complex
ether-chemistry.why: Normally F- is tightly ion-paired with its counter-cation and poorly solvated in nonpolar media, dampening its reactivity; encapsulating K+ inside the crown ether frees the anion to act as a much more potent, less hindered nucleophile.

ether-chemistry.q: You need tert-butyl methyl ether by a Williamson synthesis. Which pairing works?
ether-chemistry.why: The halide is the electrophile in an SN2, so it has to be the unhindered partner - here, iodomethane. Pairing methoxide with a tertiary halide instead gives elimination: the alkoxide is a strong base, and at a tertiary carbon it removes a beta hydrogen rather than attacking. Put the bulk on the alkoxide and the simplicity on the halide.

ether-chemistry.q: Tetrahydrofuran (THF) is a commonly used ether solvent mainly because it:
options: Is a strong acid that activates electrophiles
Reacts readily with Grignard reagents to improve yields
Coordinates metal centers while staying unreactive
ether-chemistry.why: THF's oxygen lone pairs coordinate to metal cations (helping stabilize organometallic reagents in solution) while its ring is chemically unreactive toward most nucleophiles and bases, making it a versatile, widely used solvent.

ether-chemistry.q: Old bottles of diethyl ether that have been stored for a long time can become dangerous to distill because they slowly form explosive peroxides through reaction with atmospheric oxygen.
ether-chemistry.why: Autoxidation at the carbon next to the ether oxygen slowly generates peroxide and hydroperoxide species that can concentrate and detonate, especially when the ether is evaporated or distilled, which is why old ether stocks are handled with caution.

ether-chemistry.q: Why does peroxide formation (autoxidation) occur preferentially at the carbon directly attached to the ether oxygen?
options: The adjacent oxygen stabilizes the resulting radical
That carbon has the most hydrogens available statistically
The oxygen atom itself is directly oxidized first
Ether oxygens catalyze peroxide formation only at the far end of the chain
ether-chemistry.why: Removing a hydrogen from the carbon next to the ether oxygen gives a radical that is stabilized by overlap with a lone pair on oxygen, making that particular C-H bond especially susceptible to slow radical autoxidation by atmospheric O2.

ether-chemistry.q: Which method installs an ether group at a tertiary carbon?
options: A Williamson synthesis using a tertiary alkyl halide
Heating a tertiary alcohol with a primary alcohol
Treating a tertiary alkyl halide with an alcohol and base
ether-chemistry.why: Every route through an SN2 fails at a tertiary carbon, because the alkoxide is a strong base and eliminates instead. Alkoxymercuration avoids SN2 entirely: mercury bridges the alkene, the alcohol opens that bridge at the carbon better able to carry positive charge (Markovnikov), and NaBH4 then replaces the mercury with hydrogen. No free cation is involved, so nothing rearranges either.

ether-chemistry.q: Heating diethyl ether with a large excess of concentrated HI eventually gives, as the final organic products:
options: One equivalent of ethyl iodide and one of ethanol
Diethyl ether is unreactive toward HI even in excess
ether-chemistry.why: With excess strong acid and heat, both C-O bonds of the symmetrical ether are eventually cleaved by iodide via SN2, first releasing ethanol (which itself then reacts further with HI) and ultimately converting both ethyl groups into ethyl iodide.

ether-chemistry.q: Protonation of an ether's oxygen atom by a strong acid forms:
ether-chemistry.why: Adding a proton to the ether oxygen gives it three bonds plus a formal positive charge, a species called an oxonium ion, which makes the adjacent C-O bonds much easier to break.

ether-chemistry.q: Simple ethers have no O-H bond, so they cannot be oxidized at carbon by PCC- or Jones-type reagents the way alcohols are.
ether-chemistry.why: Chromium oxidation of an alcohol works by forming a chromate ester at the O-H and then removing a hydrogen from the carbinol carbon; with no O-H, an ether offers no way in, so these reagents leave it alone. That is a statement about deliberate oxidation at carbon, not about the slow radical autoxidation at the alpha C-H that forms peroxides in a bottle left open to air.

ether-chemistry.q: Grignard reagents generally fail to form well, or are ineffective, when prepared in purely hydrocarbon solvents like hexane mainly because:
options: No ether lone pairs coordinate the magnesium
Hydrocarbons react violently with magnesium metal
Hydrocarbon solvents are too polar for Grignard chemistry
Grignard reagents require an acidic solvent to initiate
ether-chemistry.why: Ether solvents donate electron density from their oxygen lone pairs to the electrophilic magnesium center, which helps stabilize and solubilize the highly reactive organomagnesium species; nonpolar hydrocarbons cannot offer this coordination.

ether-chemistry.q: Methoxide is treated with 2-bromo-2-methylpropane in the hope of making tert-butyl methyl ether. The main organic product is:
options: tert-Butyl methyl ether, in good yield
ether-chemistry.why: An alkoxide is a strong base as well as a good nucleophile, and a tertiary carbon offers it no backside to attack. So it takes a beta hydrogen instead and eliminates, giving 2-methylpropene plus methanol. This is the standard exam trap in Williamson planning: the two disconnections of an unsymmetrical ether are not interchangeable.

ether-chemistry.q: Tetrahydrofuran (THF) is best classified as a:
ether-chemistry.why: THF is a five-membered ring containing one oxygen atom and four carbons, making it a saturated cyclic ether rather than an open-chain one.

ether-chemistry.q: IUPAC nomenclature typically names simple ethers as alkoxy-substituted alkanes, such as calling CH3-O-CH2CH3 'methoxyethane.'
ether-chemistry.why: Rather than using a standalone 'ether' suffix, the preferred IUPAC approach treats the shorter alkyl-oxygen unit as an alkoxy substituent on the longer parent chain, giving names like methoxyethane for ethyl methyl ether.

ether-chemistry.q: Ethers are generally poor nucleophiles themselves in most reactions, but their oxygen lone pairs make them good Lewis bases, able to form a stable complex with a Lewis acid such as BF3.
options: False, ethers cannot interact with Lewis acids at all
False, only alcohols can coordinate to Lewis acids
True, but only aromatic ethers can do this
True, an ether-BF3 complex (an 'etherate') is a well-known, stable adduct
ether-chemistry.why: The ether oxygen's lone pair can donate into the empty orbital of a Lewis acid like BF3, forming a stable donor-acceptor (Lewis acid-base) adduct, such as the BF3 etherate commonly used as a mild Lewis acid catalyst.

ether-chemistry.q: Small ethers like diethyl ether show modest but real solubility in water, higher than a comparably sized pure hydrocarbon would have.
ether-chemistry.why: Although ethers cannot donate hydrogen bonds, their oxygen lone pairs can accept hydrogen bonds from water molecules, giving small ethers noticeably greater water solubility than alkanes of similar size.

ether-chemistry.q: Ether cleavage reactions are typically carried out with HI or HBr rather than HCl mainly because:
options: Iodide and bromide are better nucleophiles
HCl cannot protonate an ether oxygen at all
HI and HBr are weaker acids, which favors cleavage
Chloride ions are too large to attack the ether carbon
ether-chemistry.why: After the ether oxygen is protonated, the halide ion must still act as the nucleophile (or cation-trapping species) that displaces the alcohol; iodide and bromide are considerably more nucleophilic than chloride, making the overall cleavage much faster and more practical.

ether-chemistry.q: Which sequence converts cyclohexene into cyclohexyl methyl ether?
ether-chemistry.why: Alkoxymercuration-demercuration adds methanol across the double bond with Markovnikov selectivity and no rearrangement, giving the ether directly. Alkoxide does not add to an isolated alkene; mCPBA then methanol gives a methoxy alcohol rather than a simple ether, because the epoxide leaves an OH behind; and HBr then methoxide is a Williamson on a secondary halide, which loses mostly to E2.

epoxides.q: Epoxides are much more reactive than regular ethers because:
