alcohol-oxidation.why: No carbinol C-H means nothing for the oxidation to take.

alcohol-oxidation.q: Hexane-1,6-diol is treated with excess Jones reagent. What comes out?
options: No reaction; diols are inert to Cr(VI)
alcohol-oxidation.why: There is nothing site-selective about these oxidants. Both ends are primary alcohols with two carbinol hydrogens, and the reagent is aqueous, so both climb two rungs to the acid.

carbonyl-reduction.q: What does a hydride reagent attack?
carbonyl-reduction.why: It is a nucleophile attacking the electrophilic carbon, which is the same general carbonyl addition you already know.

carbonyl-reduction.q: What does NaBH4 give from a ketone?
carbonyl-reduction.why: Hydride adds to the carbonyl carbon and the alkoxide is protonated on workup.

carbonyl-reduction.q: What does NaBH4 give from an ester?
carbonyl-reduction.why: NaBH4 is far too mild, which is exactly what makes it useful for reducing a ketone in a molecule containing an ester.

carbonyl-reduction.q: What does LiAlH4 give from an ester?
carbonyl-reduction.why: Two hydrides are delivered: the first gives an aldehyde, which is more electrophilic and is reduced immediately.

carbonyl-reduction.q: What does LiAlH4 give from an amide?
carbonyl-reduction.why: The nitrogen stays attached and the oxygen leaves entirely. This is the standard amide-to-amine route and the row most often missed.

carbonyl-reduction.q: What does LiAlH4 give from a nitrile?
carbonyl-reduction.why: Reduction of the C-N triple bond leaves a primary amine.

carbonyl-reduction.q: What do NaBH4 and LiAlH4 both give from an aldehyde?
carbonyl-reduction.why: Both reduce aldehydes and ketones, which is the row where the choice does not matter.

carbonyl-reduction.q: What does either hydride reagent do to an isolated alkene?
carbonyl-reduction.why: A hydride is a nucleophile and needs a polarized pi bond; C=C has no electrophilic end.

carbonyl-reduction.q: Why is LiAlH4 more reactive than NaBH4?
options: It is supplied at a much higher concentration
Al is less electronegative, so Al-H is more polarized
carbonyl-reduction.why: That single fact produces all the practical differences between them.

carbonyl-reduction.q: In what solvent can NaBH4 be used?
carbonyl-reduction.why: It reacts with protic solvents only slowly, which is a real convenience.

carbonyl-reduction.q: What solvent does LiAlH4 require?
carbonyl-reduction.why: It reacts violently with water, including atmospheric moisture, and needs a separate aqueous workup afterwards.

carbonyl-reduction.q: A molecule has a ketone and an ester. To reduce only the ketone, use what?
carbonyl-reduction.why: Deliberately choosing the weaker reagent is the commonest way this material appears in a synthesis question.

carbonyl-reduction.q: Why can you not normally stop an ester reduction at the aldehyde?
options: The aldehyde is more electrophilic than the ester
There is no aldehyde intermediate formed at any point
carbonyl-reduction.why: You cannot stop a reaction at an intermediate that is more reactive than the starting material.

carbonyl-reduction.q: Which reagent can stop an ester at the aldehyde?
carbonyl-reduction.why: A deliberately weakened reagent, used cold. Worth knowing it exists even if the details come later.

carbonyl-reduction.q: What happens to the alkoxide formed during a hydride reduction?
carbonyl-reduction.why: Which is why an aqueous workup is part of the procedure.

carbonyl-reduction.q: What does the Clemmensen reduction do?
options: Reduces C=O to CH2 under acid
Reduces C=O to a plain alcohol
carbonyl-reduction.why: Zn(Hg) and concentrated HCl. Use it when the molecule survives acid but not base.

carbonyl-reduction.q: What conditions does the Wolff-Kishner reduction use?
options: LiAlH4 in dry ether at 0 C
carbonyl-reduction.why: Strongly basic, and the partner to the Clemmensen for acid-sensitive molecules.

carbonyl-reduction.q: Why do Clemmensen and Wolff-Kishner exist as a pair?
carbonyl-reduction.why: Whichever your substrate tolerates, the other is available.

carbonyl-reduction.q: Which substrate does NOT give a CH2 group with Clemmensen or Wolff-Kishner?
carbonyl-reduction.why: Both reactions attack a C=O directly, so they are aldehyde-and-ketone reactions. An ester's carbonyl is deactivated by its own oxygen and has a leaving group to expel instead.

carbonyl-reduction.q: What does NaBH4 give from a carboxylic acid?
carbonyl-reduction.why: It is not strong enough. LiAlH4 does reduce acids, all the way to the primary alcohol.

carbonyl-reduction.q: Which reagent reduces a nitrile?
carbonyl-reduction.why: Giving a primary amine. Catalytic hydrogenation also reduces nitriles, but with a different catalyst and more forcing conditions than the 1 atm Pd/C case in the next section.

carbonyl-reduction.q: How many hydrides does reducing a ketone require?
carbonyl-reduction.why: The alkoxide formed has nothing to expel, so the reaction stops after one delivery.

carbonyl-reduction.q: What makes a hydride reduction the same mechanism as a Grignard addition?
options: Both are nucleophilic addition to the carbonyl carbon
carbonyl-reduction.why: If you can draw one, you can already draw the other, with H- standing in for the carbon nucleophile.

carbonyl-reduction.q: Which substrate does NaBH4 NOT reduce?
carbonyl-reduction.why: Amides need LiAlH4, and the product is an amine rather than an alcohol.

carbonyl-reduction.q: What is the product of reducing a ketone?
carbonyl-reduction.why: The carbonyl carbon already bore two carbon substituents, and gains an H and an OH.

carbonyl-reduction.q: What is the product of reducing an aldehyde?
carbonyl-reduction.why: The carbonyl carbon bore one carbon substituent and one hydrogen.

carbonyl-reduction.q: Supply the reagent: CH3CH2CO2CH3 (methyl propanoate) into CH3CH2CH2OH (propan-1-ol).
options: LiAlH4 in dry THF, then aqueous workup
carbonyl-reduction.why: An ester needs two hydrides and only LiAlH4 delivers them. NaBH4 is too mild for an ester, hydrogenation leaves esters alone, and PCC is an oxidant - the wrong direction.

carbonyl-reduction.q: A molecule contains a ketone, an ester and a terminal alkene. You want the alkene reduced and nothing else. Which reagent?
options: H2 over PtO2 at high pressure
carbonyl-reduction.why: Hydride reagents are the complement of hydrogenation: they take carbonyls and leave C=C. At one atmosphere over Pd/C only the alkene reacts; the ketone needs higher pressure and a catalyst such as PtO2.

carbonyl-reduction.q: Which two reagents reduce a carboxylic acid?
carbonyl-reduction.why: NaBH4 does not react with a carboxylic acid at all.

carbonyl-reduction.q: Butan-2-one is reduced with NaBH4 in methanol, then worked up. What is the product?
options: Butane, by loss of the oxygen
carbonyl-reduction.why: The carbonyl carbon is flat and has two faces. Hydride arrives at each equally, so the two enantiomers form in equal amounts. An achiral substrate plus an achiral reagent cannot give one enantiomer.

hydrogenation.q: What is required for H2 to reduce an alkene?
hydrogenation.why: Hydrogen gas and an alkene together do nothing at room temperature; breaking the H-H bond needs a surface.

hydrogenation.q: Which catalysts are used for hydrogenation?
hydrogenation.why: All work by adsorbing both hydrogen and the alkene onto a metal surface.

hydrogenation.q: What is the stereochemistry of catalytic hydrogenation?
hydrogenation.why: Both hydrogens come from the surface the alkene is lying against, so they arrive on the same face.

hydrogenation.q: Hydrogenating 1,2-dimethylcyclohexene gives what?
hydrogenation.why: Syn addition to a ring shows up directly as the cis product.

hydrogenation.q: Which group is readily reduced by H2/Pd at 1 atm?
hydrogenation.why: Alkenes, alkynes, imines, nitro groups and azides are on the readily-reduced list.

hydrogenation.q: What does H2/Pd/C at 1 atm do to a benzene ring?
hydrogenation.why: Aromatic rings need high pressure and temperature, which is what makes the reaction useful on aromatic substrates.

hydrogenation.q: What does H2/Pd/C do to a nitro group?
hydrogenation.why: The standard route to an aromatic amine from a nitroarene, and a row often forgotten.

hydrogenation.q: What conditions reduce a ketone by hydrogenation?
hydrogenation.why: Under ordinary conditions over Pd/C a ketone survives.

hydrogenation.q: What does an alkyne give over ordinary Pd/C?
hydrogenation.why: It is reduced past the alkene straight through to the alkane.

hydrogenation.q: What does the Lindlar catalyst give from an alkyne?
hydrogenation.why: Deliberately poisoned palladium that stops at the alkene, and it is still a syn surface addition.

hydrogenation.q: What is the Lindlar catalyst?
hydrogenation.why: The poisoning is what makes it stop at the alkene rather than continuing.

hydrogenation.q: What does Na in liquid NH3 give from an alkyne?
hydrogenation.why: Sodium adds an electron, ammonia protonates, a second electron gives a vinyl anion, and that anion is configurationally stable with its two R groups apart.

hydrogenation.q: Why does Na/NH3 give the trans alkene?
options: The radical anion adopts the less hindered form
The vinyl anion formed after the second electron transfer is configurationally stable and sits with its R groups apart
It is a surface reaction on the metal, like Lindlar
Ammonia coordinates one face and blocks it
hydrogenation.why: The sequence is electron, proton, electron, proton. The vinyl radical in the middle flips between its two bent shapes far too fast for its preference to matter; the vinyl anion after the second electron does not, and it sits trans. No surface is involved here.

hydrogenation.q: You need the trans alkene from an internal alkyne. Which conditions?
hydrogenation.why: Lindlar gives the cis alkene; plain Pd/C gives the alkane.

hydrogenation.q: Why is hydrogenation the complement of hydride reduction?
options: Both of them reduce ketones well
One reduces C=C and the other C=O
hydrogenation.why: A molecule with an alkene and a ketone can be reduced at either position by choosing the reagent.

hydrogenation.q: But-1-ene releases 127 kJ/mol on hydrogenation, cis-but-2-ene 120 and trans-but-2-ene 116. All three give butane. Which is most stable, and how do you know?
options: but-1-ene, because it releases the most energy
cis-but-2-ene, because its value is in the middle
trans-but-2-ene, because it releases the least energy and so started lowest
They are equally stable, since they give the same product
hydrogenation.why: Every bar ends at the same molecule, so a smaller heat out can only mean a starting material already lower in energy. That gives trans-disubstituted > cis-disubstituted > monosubstituted - measured, not asserted.

hydrogenation.q: (Z)-3,4-dimethyloct-3-ene is hydrogenated over Pd/C. What is the stereochemical outcome at the two former alkene carbons?
options: A single enantiomer, because the addition is syn
One diastereomer, formed as a racemic mixture
A mixture of all four stereoisomers
No stereocenters are formed at all
hydrogenation.why: Both carbons become stereocenters carrying different substituents. Syn addition fixes the relative configuration - one diastereomer - but not the absolute one, because the alkene can lie on the catalyst either face down. So it forms as a racemate.

hydrogenation.q: Why does the catalyst matter so much?
options: It lowers the barrier to splitting H-H
It shifts the position of the equilibrium
hydrogenation.why: The reaction is thermodynamically downhill already; the barrier is what stops it.

hydrogenation.q: Is catalytic hydrogenation thermodynamically favorable?
options: Only at high pressure and temperature
Yes, but slow without a catalyst
hydrogenation.why: Which is why a catalyst is enough to make it go.

hydrogenation.q: What does H2/Pd/C do to an ester?
hydrogenation.why: Esters, acids and amides are essentially untouched by catalytic hydrogenation.

hydrogenation.q: An imine treated with H2/Pd gives what?
hydrogenation.why: Imines are on the readily-reduced list, which makes this the basis of reductive amination (which you will meet in Amines).

hydrogenation.q: Which reagent reduces an alkene but not a ketone?
hydrogenation.why: Exactly the complement of NaBH4, which does the reverse.

hydrogenation.q: Which reagent reduces a ketone but not an alkene?
hydrogenation.why: Hydride reduction needs a polarized pi bond, which C=C does not provide.

hydrogenation.q: What does poisoned mean for the Lindlar catalyst?
hydrogenation.why: Quinoline and lead reduce its activity on purpose.

hydrogenation.q: Where do the two hydrogens come from in catalytic hydrogenation?
hydrogenation.why: Which is why they can only arrive on one face.

hydrogenation.q: Which of these does H2/Pd/C at 1 atm NOT reduce?
options: A nitro group on a ring
hydrogenation.why: Carboxylic acids, esters and amides are essentially untouched.

hydrogenation.q: An alkyne, a ketone and a benzene ring in one molecule, treated with H2/Pd/C at 1 atm. What reacts?
hydrogenation.why: And it is reduced all the way to the alkane unless a poisoned catalyst is used.

hydrogenation.q: Why is an alkyne useful as a synthetic intermediate?
options: It is unusually unreactive toward everything
hydrogenation.why: Lindlar for cis, dissolving metal for trans, from the same starting material.

hydrogenation.q: What does syn addition mean?
options: The groups add to opposite faces
Both groups add to the same face
hydrogenation.why: It is a direct consequence of both hydrogens being delivered by one surface.

hydrogenation.q: Raney nickel is used for what?
hydrogenation.why: One of the standard hydrogenation catalysts alongside Pd/C and Pt.

alkene-oxidation.q: What does mCPBA give from an alkene?
alkene-oxidation.why: A single oxygen delivered across the double bond in one concerted step.

alkene-oxidation.q: Is epoxidation with mCPBA stereospecific?
options: Only for cis alkenes, not trans ones
Yes, the alkene geometry is retained
alkene-oxidation.why: It is concerted, so a cis alkene gives the cis-substituted epoxide and trans gives trans.

alkene-oxidation.q: What does OsO4 give from an alkene?
alkene-oxidation.why: Both oxygens are delivered to the same face through a cyclic osmate ester.

alkene-oxidation.q: What is NMO used for alongside OsO4?
options: As the solvent for the reaction
As a co-oxidant to make OsO4 catalytic
alkene-oxidation.why: OsO4 is expensive and toxic, so it is regenerated in situ.

alkene-oxidation.q: What does mCPBA followed by aqueous acid give?
alkene-oxidation.why: Water attacks the protonated epoxide from the face opposite the C-O bond being broken.

alkene-oxidation.q: Why does epoxide opening give the anti diol?
alkene-oxidation.why: Backside attack puts the second oxygen on the opposite face from the first.

alkene-oxidation.q: Which reagent pair gives opposite diol stereochemistry?
alkene-oxidation.why: One delivers both oxygens to one face, the other goes via an epoxide and opens it from the other side.

alkene-oxidation.q: What does O3 followed by Me2S do?
alkene-oxidation.why: The reductive workup stops at the aldehydes and ketones.

alkene-oxidation.q: What does O3 followed by H2O2 give from a carbon that bore a hydrogen?
alkene-oxidation.why: The oxidative workup takes the aldehyde fragment one rung further.

alkene-oxidation.q: What does an oxidative ozonolysis workup do to a ketone fragment?
alkene-oxidation.why: A ketone has no hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon to lose.

alkene-oxidation.q: A carbon of the alkene bearing two substituents becomes what on ozonolysis?
alkene-oxidation.why: Two substituents means no hydrogen on that carbon, so it can only be a ketone.

alkene-oxidation.q: A carbon of the alkene bearing one hydrogen becomes what with reductive workup?
alkene-oxidation.why: With oxidative workup that aldehyde would go on to a carboxylic acid.

alkene-oxidation.q: What does cold dilute basic KMnO4 give from an alkene?
alkene-oxidation.why: The same outcome as OsO4, more cheaply and less cleanly.

alkene-oxidation.q: What does hot concentrated KMnO4 give from an alkene?
alkene-oxidation.why: The conditions, not the reagent, decide which of the two rows applies.

alkene-oxidation.q: Why does KMnO4 appear twice in the summary table?
options: It is used with two different solvents
The conditions change the outcome completely
alkene-oxidation.why: A question specifying KMnO4 without conditions is incomplete.

alkene-oxidation.q: cis-But-2-ene is treated with OsO4 then NaHSO3. What is the product?
options: a 50:50 mixture of the meso and racemic diols
alkene-oxidation.why: Syn delivery onto a cis alkene puts the two OH groups on the same face of a molecule with an internal mirror plane, so the two stereocenters cancel: meso and achiral. The same reagent on trans-but-2-ene gives the racemic pair instead.

alkene-oxidation.q: An alkene gives propanal and propanone on ozonolysis. What was it?
alkene-oxidation.why: Rejoin at the carbonyl carbons: CH3CH2-CH=C(CH3)2, which is C6H12.

alkene-oxidation.q: One fragment is an aldehyde and one a ketone. What does that say about the alkene?
alkene-oxidation.why: One carbon bore a hydrogen and the other did not.

alkene-oxidation.q: Ozonolysis of a symmetric internal alkene gives what?
options: A single ketone and one acid
alkene-oxidation.why: The two fragments are identical, so you observe one compound at twice the molar amount.

alkene-oxidation.q: Ozonolysis of a cyclic alkene gives what?
alkene-oxidation.why: The two ends stay connected through the rest of the ring.

alkene-oxidation.q: You need the anti diol from a cis alkene. What do you do?
alkene-oxidation.why: Going via the epoxide changes the stereochemical outcome; no conditions convert a syn diol into an anti one.

alkene-oxidation.q: Why can OsO4 never give the anti diol?
options: It delivers both oxygens to one face
It only ever works on ring systems
alkene-oxidation.why: The cyclic osmate ester forces both new C-O bonds onto the same side.

alkene-oxidation.q: What is the full name of mCPBA?
alkene-oxidation.why: A peroxyacid, which is what delivers the single oxygen atom.

alkene-oxidation.q: Why are epoxides reactive?
alkene-oxidation.why: Which is what makes the ring-opening step of the anti-diol route possible.

alkene-oxidation.q: What does a peroxyacid transfer to an alkene?
alkene-oxidation.why: In one concerted step through a cyclic transition state.

alkene-oxidation.q: Which reagent leaves the alkene carbons still bonded to each other?
alkene-oxidation.why: Dihydroxylation adds across the double bond; ozonolysis cuts through it.

alkene-oxidation.q: Why does the workup, rather than the ozone, decide whether you get an aldehyde or an acid?
options: Because the ozone is consumed before any carbonyl forms
Because the aldehyde is volatile and escapes
Because the workup changes where the C=C is cut
Because the ozone step stops at an ozonide, which is not a carbonyl compound yet
alkene-oxidation.why: Ozone adds to give a molozonide, which rearranges to an ozonide in which the two former alkene carbons are still bridged by oxygens. Nothing is a carbonyl compound until that ozonide is broken open, and the reagent that breaks it sets the level.

alkene-oxidation.q: Which two methods give the same diol stereochemistry?
alkene-oxidation.why: Both deliver both oxygens to the same face, giving the syn diol.

alkene-oxidation.q: A question gives KMnO4 with no conditions stated. What is the problem?
options: It only works on alkynes, not alkenes
alkene-oxidation.why: Cold and dilute gives a diol; hot and concentrated cleaves.

alkene-oxidation.q: Oct-1-ene is treated with O3, then H2O2. What products are isolated?
options: Heptanoic acid alone - the terminal CH2 ends up as CO2 and is lost
alkene-oxidation.why: Cleavage gives a seven-carbon fragment with a hydrogen on its carbonyl carbon, taken on to heptanoic acid, and a one-carbon =CH2 fragment, which ends up as CO2 and bubbles away. With Me2S you would isolate heptanal and formaldehyde.

carboxylic-acids.q: Carboxylic acids are much more acidic than alcohols mainly because their conjugate base (carboxylate) is stabilized by:
carboxylic-acids.why: The carboxylate anion spreads its negative charge equally over two equivalent oxygens via resonance, which is far more stabilizing than an alkoxide’s localized charge.

carboxylic-acids.q: Typical pKa range for carboxylic acids is around:
carboxylic-acids.why: Most simple carboxylic acids have pKa values around 4–5, far more acidic than alcohols (pKa ~16–18).

carboxylic-acids.q: Why is a carboxylate anion’s negative charge considered fully delocalized rather than sitting on one specific oxygen?
options: Only one oxygen can ever hold charge
Carboxylate ions don’t actually have resonance
The two C–O bonds and the negative charge are equivalent by resonance/symmetry
The molecule constantly flips between two different isolable structures
carboxylic-acids.why: The two resonance structures of a carboxylate are equivalent, so the true structure is a symmetric hybrid with the charge (and bond order) shared equally between both oxygens, confirmed by equal C–O bond lengths.

carboxylic-acids.q: 3-Phenylpropanoic acid is treated with SOCl2, then with excess methanol. What is the final product?
options: An equilibrium mixture of the acid and its methyl ester
carboxylic-acids.why: Step 1: SOCl2 replaces the OH with Cl, giving 3-phenylpropanoyl chloride plus SO2 and HCl, both of which leave as gases. Step 2: methanol attacks that acyl chloride, the tetrahedral intermediate collapses by expelling chloride, and a proton is lost, giving the methyl ester. Because chloride leaves and never comes back, this route is irreversible - unlike Fischer esterification of the acid itself, which would leave the acid and its ester in equilibrium instead.

carboxylic-acids.q: You need to convert 1-bromobutane into pentanoic acid. Which sequence works?
carboxylic-acids.why: Count carbons first: 1-bromobutane has four and pentanoic acid has five, so the route has to ADD one. Cyanide is the one-carbon nucleophile: SN2 on the primary bromide gives pentanenitrile, five carbons. Hot aqueous acid then hydrolyzes that nitrile through the amide to pentanoic acid, with no oxidant needed because a nitrile carbon and an acid carbon sit on the same oxidation rung. The other three routes all keep four carbons.

carboxylic-acids.q: A carboxylic acid can act as both a hydrogen bond donor and a hydrogen bond acceptor.
carboxylic-acids.why: The O-H proton donates a hydrogen bond while the carbonyl oxygen (and the hydroxyl oxygen) can accept one, which is why carboxylic acids dimerize strongly.

carboxylic-acids.q: What is the simplest (one-carbon) carboxylic acid called?
carboxylic-acids.why: Formic acid, HCOOH, is the one-carbon carboxylic acid found in ant stings and formic acid solutions.

carboxylic-acids.q: Carboxylic acids are generally weaker acids than strong mineral acids such as HCl.
carboxylic-acids.why: Most carboxylic acids have pKa around 4-5, meaning they are only partially ionized in water, unlike strong mineral acids which ionize essentially completely.

carboxylic-acids.q: Rank these in order of INCREASING acidity: acetic acid, chloroacetic acid, trichloroacetic acid.
options: Trichloroacetic acid < chloroacetic acid < acetic acid
Chloroacetic acid < acetic acid < trichloroacetic acid
Acetic acid < chloroacetic acid < trichloroacetic acid
carboxylic-acids.why: Each added electronegative chlorine withdraws electron density inductively, further stabilizing the negative charge on the conjugate base, so acidity increases with each additional chlorine.

carboxylic-acids.q: Moving a chlorine substituent farther away from the carboxyl carbon along the chain (e.g. from the alpha to the beta or gamma position) generally has what effect on acidity?
options: It increases acidity, since the inductive effect strengthens with distance
It has no effect at any distance
It converts the compound into a base
It decreases acidity, since the inductive effect weakens with distance
carboxylic-acids.why: Inductive electron withdrawal is transmitted through sigma bonds and falls off quickly with distance, so a halogen closer to the carboxyl group stabilizes the conjugate base more than one farther away.

carboxylic-acids.q: Para-nitrobenzoic acid is more acidic than benzoic acid.
carboxylic-acids.why: The nitro group is a strong electron-withdrawing group that stabilizes the negative charge on the carboxylate through both induction and resonance, increasing acidity relative to unsubstituted benzoic acid.

carboxylic-acids.q: In nonpolar solvents or the gas phase, carboxylic acid molecules tend to exist as:
options: Separate monomers with no intermolecular attraction
carboxylic-acids.why: Two carboxylic acid molecules can hydrogen bond to each other reciprocally (each O-H donating to the other's carbonyl oxygen), forming a stable cyclic dimer, especially pronounced without a polar solvent to compete for hydrogen bonding.

carboxylic-acids.q: As the length of the hydrocarbon chain in a carboxylic acid increases, its solubility in water:
options: Decreases, as the nonpolar chain dominates
Stays exactly the same regardless of chain length
carboxylic-acids.why: Water solubility depends on the balance between the polar, hydrogen-bonding carboxyl group and the nonpolar alkyl chain; as the chain grows, the hydrophobic character increasingly dominates and solubility drops.

carboxylic-acids.q: A carboxylic acid has a higher boiling point than an alcohol of similar molecular weight mainly because carboxylic acids can form stronger, doubled hydrogen-bonded dimers.
carboxylic-acids.why: Each carboxylic acid molecule can both donate and accept two hydrogen bonds in a dimer, giving a stronger net intermolecular attraction than a single alcohol O-H can provide.

carboxylic-acids.q: When a carboxylic acid is treated with aqueous NaHCO3, what is typically observed?
options: Formation of a precipitate with no gas
Bubbling as CO2 gas is released
The acid is reduced to an alcohol
carboxylic-acids.why: Carboxylic acids (pKa about 4-5) are acidic enough to protonate bicarbonate (pKa of carbonic acid about 6.4), releasing CO2 gas; this bubbling test is used to distinguish carboxylic acids from weaker acids like phenols.

carboxylic-acids.q: Phenol also releases visible CO2 bubbles when treated with aqueous NaHCO3.
carboxylic-acids.why: Phenol (pKa about 10) is not acidic enough to protonate bicarbonate significantly, so it does not produce a noticeable bubbling reaction, unlike carboxylic acids; this difference is a classic diagnostic test.

carboxylic-acids.q: Heating a beta-keto carboxylic acid (RCOCH2COOH, the ketone on the carbon beta to the carboxyl) typically causes:
carboxylic-acids.why: The carboxyl O-H can reach the ketone oxygen through a six-membered cyclic transition state. As that proton transfers, the C-C bond to the carboxyl breaks and CO2 leaves, giving an enol that tautomerizes to the ketone. Nothing else in the molecule has to move, which is why gentle warming is enough - and why the carbonyl has to be exactly at the beta position for the ring to be the right size.

carboxylic-acids.q: Bubbling CO2 gas through a Grignard reagent (RMgX) followed by aqueous acid workup produces:
carboxylic-acids.why: The Grignard carbanion adds to the electrophilic carbon of CO2 to give a magnesium carboxylate, which is protonated on acidic workup to give the carboxylic acid; this is a classic way to build a carboxylic acid while adding one carbon.

carboxylic-acids.q: Which oxidizing condition converts a primary alcohol all the way to a carboxylic acid, in contrast to a milder oxidant that stops at the aldehyde?
carboxylic-acids.why: Strong oxidants like hot KMnO4 or Jones reagent fully oxidize a primary alcohol through the aldehyde stage to the carboxylic acid, whereas PCC is a mild oxidant that stops cleanly at the aldehyde.

carboxylic-acids.q: Which reagent is commonly used to convert a carboxylic acid directly into an acyl chloride?
carboxylic-acids.why: SOCl2 (or PCl3/PCl5) reacts with the carboxylic acid's OH group, converting it into a much better leaving group and producing the reactive acyl chloride along with SO2 and HCl gas.

carboxylic-acids.q: LiAlH4 reduces a carboxylic acid all the way to what product?
carboxylic-acids.why: LiAlH4 is a strong enough hydride donor to reduce carboxylic acids completely past the aldehyde stage to the primary alcohol; it does not stop partway.

carboxylic-acids.q: NaBH4 is an effective, commonly used reagent for reducing carboxylic acids to primary alcohols.
carboxylic-acids.why: NaBH4 is too mild a hydride source to reduce the relatively unreactive carboxylic acid carbonyl efficiently; LiAlH4 (a stronger hydride donor) is needed for that reduction.

carboxylic-acids.q: Rank by increasing pKa (weakest acid last): (i) 2-chlorobutanoic acid, (ii) 4-chlorobutanoic acid, (iii) butanoic acid.
carboxylic-acids.why: Induction travels through sigma bonds and dies off fast with distance. The chlorine on C2 is next door to the carboxyl and stabilizes the carboxylate strongly: 2-chlorobutanoic acid is pKa 2.86. Move the same chlorine to C4 and it is two bonds further away and barely helps: 4-chlorobutanoic acid is 4.52, against butanoic acid's 4.82. So acidity falls, and pKa rises, in the order given.

carboxylic-acids.q: The carbon of the carboxyl group in a carboxylic acid is best described as:
carboxylic-acids.why: The carboxyl carbon is doubly bonded to one oxygen and singly bonded to the other oxygen and to the R group, giving three sigma bonds plus one pi bond -- the sp2, trigonal planar geometry typical of carbonyl carbons.

carboxylic-acids.q: Trifluoroacetic acid (CF3COOH) has a pKa that is:
options: Much lower, due to fluorine induction
Undefined, since fluorine makes it a base
carboxylic-acids.why: The three highly electronegative fluorines withdraw electron density inductively, strongly stabilizing the conjugate base and dropping the pKa to 0.23, far more acidic than acetic acid's pKa of about 4.76.

carboxylic-acids.q: For a dicarboxylic acid like malonic acid, why is the second ionization constant (Ka2, removing the second proton) much smaller than the first (Ka1)?
options: The second proton is chemically identical and should ionize equally, this is experimental error
Malonic acid has no second ionizable proton
The second ionization is always stronger than the first for all diacids
Removing a proton from an already anionic carboxylate is electrostatically unfavorable
carboxylic-acids.why: Once the first carboxyl group loses its proton to become negatively charged, pulling a second positive proton away from the nearby second carboxyl group is both electrostatically harder and the inductive withdrawal helping acidity is reduced, so Ka2 is substantially smaller than Ka1.

carboxylic-acids.q: Neat acetic acid absorbs near 1710 cm-1; heavily diluted, near 1760. What changed?
options: The dimers came apart into free monomers
The acid was deprotonated by the solvent
The OH donates more strongly into the C=O
The carbonyl carbon rehybridized to sp3
carboxylic-acids.why: Dilution changes nothing inside the molecule; it changes what the molecule is touching. Neat or concentrated, carboxylic acids sit as hydrogen-bonded dimers, and the hydrogen bond to the carbonyl oxygen pulls density out of the C=O, weakening it and dropping the stretch to about 1710. Dilute far enough in a nonpolar solvent and the dimers break up, and the free monomer absorbs near 1760 - above an ester's 1735, not below it. That matters whenever you use IR to rank acyl derivatives: the familiar 1710 is a dimerization artifact, not a measure of how hard the OH donates into the carbonyl.

carboxylic-acids.q: A dicarboxylic acid generally has two distinct pKa values rather than one value applying to both -COOH groups equally.
carboxylic-acids.why: Removing the first proton changes the electronic environment (the molecule becomes anionic), so the second -COOH ionizes with a different, typically higher, pKa than the first.

carboxylic-acids.q: Warmed to 80 °C: CH3COCH2COOH and CH3COCH2CH2COOH. Which one loses CO2?
options: Both, since any ketone activates a carboxyl
Neither, without a metal catalyst present
Only the first: the ring closed is six-membered
Only the second: its ring is less strained
carboxylic-acids.why: This is a geometry question wearing a functional-group disguise. Losing CO2 here is not a general property of keto acids: the carboxyl O-H has to reach across to the ketone oxygen through a cyclic transition state, and only as that proton transfers does the C-C bond to the carboxyl break and CO2 leave. Count the ring for the beta-keto acid CH3COCH2COOH - ketone O, ketone C, alpha carbon, carboxyl C, carboxyl O, and the moving H. Six atoms, the size that closes with no strain, which is why gentle warming is enough. Put one more carbon between the two groups, as in the gamma-keto acid, and the same proton transfer would have to close a seven-membered ring; it does not happen at 80 °C. Note also what comes out first: the enol, which then tautomerizes to acetone.

carboxylic-acids.q: Treating a carboxylic acid with aqueous NaOH produces:
options: A carboxylate salt and water, via a simple acid-base neutralization
No reaction, since carboxylic acids do not react with hydroxide
carboxylic-acids.why: Carboxylic acids are acidic enough to be fully deprotonated by a strong base like NaOH, giving the sodium carboxylate salt and water in a straightforward neutralization.

esters-amides.q: Which is generally more reactive toward hydrolysis: esters or amides?
options: Esters, because alkoxide leaves more readily
Amides, because nitrogen is a poor leaving group
esters-amides.why: Amide resonance delocalizes nitrogen’s lone pair strongly into the carbonyl, making amides far less electrophilic and far more hydrolytically stable than esters.

esters-amides.q: The carbonyl stretch in IR for amides appears at a lower wavenumber than esters mainly because:
esters-amides.why: Nitrogen’s lone pair donates into the carbonyl more than an ester oxygen does, giving the amide C=O more single-bond character and a lower, weaker stretching frequency.

esters-amides.q: Which has the higher boiling point for a given molecular weight, an ester or a primary amide?
esters-amides.why: Amides with N–H bonds can hydrogen-bond extensively (donor and acceptor), giving them notably higher melting/boiling points than comparable esters, which lack an O–H/N–H donor.

esters-amides.q: In Fischer esterification, a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol under acid catalysis (such as H2SO4) to form:
esters-amides.why: Fischer esterification is the acid-catalyzed condensation of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol, releasing water and forming an ester; it is an equilibrium reaction.

esters-amides.q: Why is an amide usually NOT made by simply mixing a carboxylic acid directly with an amine at room temperature?
options: The amine deprotonates the acid, giving an unreactive salt
Amines cannot act as nucleophiles under any conditions
Carboxylic acids have no carbonyl carbon to attack
This reaction always works perfectly and is the standard method
esters-amides.why: Because the amine is a base and the carboxylic acid is an acid, a simple acid-base proton transfer forming the carboxylate salt happens faster than nucleophilic attack on the carbonyl; forming the amide usually requires heating to drive off water or first converting the acid to a more reactive derivative (such as an acyl chloride).

esters-amides.q: Methyl propanoate is heated with excess ethanol and a drop of H2SO4. What is the major organic product?
esters-amides.why: This is transesterification. Ethanol attacks the ester carbonyl under acid catalysis, giving a tetrahedral intermediate carrying both OMe and OEt. Methoxide and ethoxide are almost equally good leaving groups, so nothing electronic decides the outcome - the large excess of ethanol does, by mass action. Methanol is expelled and ethyl propanoate is left. Note what does not happen: the acyl group never leaves the molecule, so the answer is still a propanoate.

esters-amides.q: In the ester name 'ethyl acetate,' which parts come from the alcohol and which from the acid?
options: 'Ethyl' comes from the acid; 'acetate' comes from the alcohol
'Ethyl' comes from the alcohol (ethanol); 'acetate' comes from the acid (acetic acid)
Both words come from the alcohol
Both words come from the acid
esters-amides.why: Ester names follow the pattern 'alkyl acid-oate,' where the alkyl group names the alcohol-derived R group and the '-oate' part names the acid-derived acyl portion.

esters-amides.q: Amides contain a C-N bond with significant restricted rotation due to resonance.
esters-amides.why: Delocalization of the nitrogen lone pair into the carbonyl pi system gives the C-N bond partial double-bond character, making it shorter and stronger than a typical single bond, and restricting rotation around it much like a true double bond.

esters-amides.q: Transesterification is the process by which:
options: An ester is converted into a carboxylic acid
An amide is converted into an ester directly
An ester's alkoxy group is exchanged
A ketone is converted into an ester
esters-amides.why: In transesterification, a new alcohol attacks the ester's carbonyl carbon and displaces the original alkoxide leaving group, swapping one ester for another (commonly used, for example, in making biodiesel from vegetable oil).

esters-amides.q: Saponification refers to:
options: Reduction of an ester with LiAlH4
Formation of an amide from an ester
esters-amides.why: Saponification is the hydroxide-mediated hydrolysis of esters, classically triglycerides, yielding glycerol and fatty acid carboxylate salts, which are soaps; this reaction is effectively irreversible.

esters-amides.q: Fischer esterification is a reversible equilibrium reaction.
esters-amides.why: Because Fischer esterification is acid-catalyzed and both the forward (esterification) and reverse (acid-catalyzed hydrolysis) reactions are accessible, the reaction reaches equilibrium and excess alcohol or removal of water is often used to push the equilibrium toward the ester.

esters-amides.q: Treating an ester with excess LiAlH4 gives:
esters-amides.why: LiAlH4 reduces the ester carbonyl all the way to a primary alcohol while releasing the original alkoxy group as its own (separate) alcohol, so two different alcohols are produced overall.

esters-amides.q: Treating an amide with LiAlH4 typically gives what type of product, in contrast to the alcohol product from an ester?
esters-amides.why: Reduction of an amide's C=O by LiAlH4 proceeds with loss of the oxygen (rather than the nitrogen), converting the carbonyl carbon into a CH2 group attached to nitrogen and giving an amine, unlike ester reduction which gives alcohols.

esters-amides.q: A beta-lactam is a better acylating agent than an ordinary amide because its four-membered ring twists the nitrogen lone pair out of alignment with the C=O.
esters-amides.why: An ordinary amide is unreactive because the nitrogen lone pair lies in the carbonyl's plane and donates into the pi system, feeding electron density to the carbonyl carbon and tying the nitrogen in place. A four-membered ring cannot hold that arrangement: roughly 90 degree bond angles pyramidalize the nitrogen and twist its lone pair out of alignment with the C=O, so most of that donation is switched off. What is left is a carbonyl carrying an amide's leaving group without an amide's protection - electrophilic enough that a serine hydroxyl in a bacterial enzyme attacks it and is acylated, which is how penicillin works. Note what has not changed: nitrogen's electronegativity is the same and the carbonyl carbon is still sp2. What was lost is the orbital overlap.

esters-amides.q: Why is an amide nitrogen's lone pair much less available to act as a base compared to a simple amine nitrogen?
options: Amide nitrogen has no lone pair at all
Amide nitrogen is positively charged in the ground state
Its lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl
There is no difference between amide and amine basicity
esters-amides.why: Resonance donation of the nitrogen lone pair toward the carbonyl oxygen gives the amide significant C=N double bond character and delocalizes the electron density, so the nitrogen is a much weaker base than an ordinary amine nitrogen.

esters-amides.q: Which ranking of nitrogen basicity is correct?
options: An amide is more basic than a simple alkylamine
Amides and amines have identical basicity
Basicity cannot be compared between these groups
A simple alkylamine is more basic than an amide
esters-amides.why: Because the amide nitrogen's lone pair is tied up in resonance with the carbonyl, it is a much poorer proton acceptor (weaker base) than the lone pair on a simple, non-delocalized amine nitrogen.

esters-amides.q: A tertiary amide (with no N-H) cannot act as a hydrogen bond donor, even though it can still accept hydrogen bonds through its carbonyl oxygen.
esters-amides.why: Without any N-H or O-H bond, a tertiary amide has no hydrogen to donate, but its carbonyl oxygen (made more electron-rich by nitrogen resonance donation) remains an excellent hydrogen bond acceptor.

esters-amides.q: A tertiary amide like N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) still has a notably high boiling point even though it cannot donate hydrogen bonds, mainly because of:
options: Its very large dipole moment from the polarized, resonance-stabilized carbonyl
Strong N-H hydrogen bonding between molecules
esters-amides.why: Even without an N-H donor, the amide carbonyl is highly polarized by nitrogen lone pair donation, giving tertiary amides large dipole-dipole attractions and correspondingly high boiling points relative to their size.

esters-amides.q: A polyester such as PET (used in plastic bottles) is built from repeating units connected by:
options: Amide linkages between a diacid and a diamine
Ester linkages formed between a diacid and a diol
esters-amides.why: Polyesters are condensation polymers in which a dicarboxylic acid (or its derivative) repeatedly reacts with a diol, forming many ester linkages along the polymer backbone.

esters-amides.q: Nylon is a classic example of which type of polymer?
esters-amides.why: Nylon is made by repeatedly forming amide bonds between a dicarboxylic acid (or its derivative) and a diamine, making it a polyamide.

esters-amides.q: The peptide bond that links amino acids together in proteins is chemically an example of:
esters-amides.why: A peptide bond forms when the carboxyl group of one amino acid condenses with the amino group of another, producing the same C(=O)-N bond found in any amide.

esters-amides.q: Which two-step sequence converts butanoic acid into N,N-dimethylbutanamide?
esters-amides.why: Mixing the acid with the amine directly does only one thing: an acid-base reaction, giving a dimethylammonium butanoate salt with a protonated nucleophile and a negatively charged electrophile. So the acid has to be activated first. SOCl2 replaces the OH with Cl, putting the acyl group at the top of the ladder, and dimethylamine then acylates it easily. Excess amine (or added pyridine) is needed because each acylation releases one HCl, which protonates a second equivalent of amine.

esters-amides.q: Adding excess Grignard reagent to an ester ultimately gives:
options: The starting ester is recovered unchanged
esters-amides.why: The first equivalent of Grignard reagent displaces the alkoxide to give a ketone, which is even more reactive than the ester and is immediately attacked by a second equivalent of Grignard reagent, giving (after workup) a tertiary alcohol.

esters-amides.q: Esters can hydrogen bond to water as both a donor and an acceptor.
esters-amides.why: Esters have no O-H or N-H bond, so they cannot donate a hydrogen bond; they can only accept hydrogen bonds through their carbonyl (and ether-like) oxygens.

esters-amides.q: A lactone is best described as:
options: A cyclic ether with no carbonyl
esters-amides.why: A lactone forms when a hydroxyl group and a carboxyl group within the same molecule condense intramolecularly, producing a ring containing an ester linkage.

esters-amides.q: A lactam is best described as:
esters-amides.why: A lactam is the nitrogen analog of a lactone: an intramolecular condensation between an amine and a carboxyl group within the same molecule forms a ring containing an amide linkage.

esters-amides.q: What is the common name for the base-promoted hydrolysis reaction used to convert fats/esters into carboxylate soaps?
esters-amides.why: Saponification specifically refers to the hydroxide-driven hydrolysis of esters (classically fats and oils) into glycerol and carboxylate salts (soap).

esters-amides.q: Why do esters generally have lower boiling points than carboxylic acids of similar molecular weight?
options: Esters are always heavier than carboxylic acids
Esters have no O-H to form dimers
esters-amides.why: Without an O-H to donate, ester molecules can only engage in weaker dipole-dipole interactions with each other, while carboxylic acids form doubly hydrogen-bonded dimers, giving acids a notably higher boiling point for comparable size.

esters-amides.q: Resonance delocalization in an amide puts partial positive charge on NITROGEN and extra electron density on the carbonyl oxygen, and it leaves the carbonyl carbon less electron-poor than a ketone's.
esters-amides.why: The second contributor is O(-)-C=N(+): the nitrogen lone pair has moved toward oxygen, so nitrogen carries partial positive charge and oxygen partial negative. Carbon gains, not loses, electron density relative to a ketone - which is exactly why an amide is the least electrophilic derivative, and why its C=O stretch drops to about 1650 cm-1.

esters-amides.q: An ester's carbonyl carbon is bonded to two different oxygens: one by a double bond, and one (the alkoxy oxygen) by a single bond.
esters-amides.why: The ester functional group, -C(=O)-O-R, has a carbonyl oxygen double bonded to carbon and a separate ether-like oxygen singly bonded to carbon and to the R group.

acyl-substitution.q: Nucleophilic acyl substitution differs from nucleophilic addition (at aldehydes/ketones) because:
acyl-substitution.why: Acyl substitution goes through a tetrahedral intermediate (addition step) that then expels a leaving group, regenerating the carbonyl — net substitution rather than simple addition.

acyl-substitution.q: Generally, which is the better leaving group in acyl substitution: chloride (from an acyl chloride) or amide nitrogen (from an amide)?
acyl-substitution.why: Chloride is a much weaker base than an amine/amide nitrogen, making acyl chlorides far more reactive electrophiles than amides in acyl substitution.

acyl-substitution.q: Acetic anhydride is treated with one equivalent of ethanol. What comes out?
acyl-substitution.why: Ethanol attacks one of the two carbonyls. The tetrahedral intermediate collapses by expelling the other half of the molecule as acetate, which then picks up a proton. So one acyl group becomes the ester and the other leaves as the acid: ethyl acetate plus acetic acid. Half the anhydride is spent as a leaving group, which is the atom-economy cost of acylating this way.

acyl-substitution.q: The overall mechanism by which nucleophiles replace the leaving group on a carboxylic acid derivative's carbonyl carbon is called:
acyl-substitution.why: Nucleophilic acyl substitution proceeds by the nucleophile first adding to the carbonyl carbon, then a leaving group being eliminated to restore the carbonyl, an addition-elimination sequence distinct from simple substitution at sp3 carbon.

acyl-substitution.q: What is the correct first step when a nucleophile reacts with an acyl chloride, ester, or amide?
options: The nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate
The leaving group departs first, forming a carbocation
Two nucleophiles attack simultaneously in one step
acyl-substitution.why: Nucleophilic acyl substitution begins with nucleophilic addition to the sp2 carbonyl carbon, producing a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate, before any leaving group departs.

acyl-substitution.q: Benzoic acid is esterified with ¹⁸O-methanol under acid. Where does the label end up?
options: In the water that is formed
In the ester, on its O-CH3 oxygen
In the ester, on its carbonyl oxygen
Split evenly between ester and water
acyl-substitution.why: Trace the oxygen atom by atom. Methanol attacks the protonated acid using its own oxygen, so that oxygen forms the new C–O bond and is never asked to leave again; what departs as water is one of the two OH oxygens that came from the carboxylic acid, after acid protonates it. The label therefore stays in the ester, on the single-bonded oxygen still carrying its methyl group — the C–¹⁸O–CH₃ bond was never broken at any point. That is the experiment that settles where the ester bond is made and broken: at the acyl carbon, not at the alkyl carbon. Had the label come out in the water, esterification would have to be an SN2 at methyl, and it is not. Run the reverse reaction in H₂¹⁸O and the same bookkeeping puts the label in the carboxylic acid.

acyl-substitution.q: Which order correctly ranks these four carboxylic acid derivatives from MOST to LEAST reactive toward nucleophilic acyl substitution?
acyl-substitution.why: Reactivity tracks how good each group's substituent is as a leaving group and how poorly it donates electron density into the carbonyl by resonance; chloride is the best leaving group and poorest resonance donor, while nitrogen in an amide is the worst leaving group and best resonance donor, giving this overall order.

acyl-substitution.q: In general, a weaker base makes a better leaving group in nucleophilic acyl substitution.
acyl-substitution.why: Weaker bases are more stable as free anions (or neutral species) and are less prone to holding onto a bonding pair of electrons, which is exactly why chloride (a very weak base) leaves far more readily than an amide nitrogen (effectively a strong base, as NH2-/RNH-) leaves.

acyl-substitution.q: Which single reagent converts propanoyl chloride into propanoic anhydride?
acyl-substitution.why: An anhydride needs a carboxylate as the nucleophile, not the neutral acid. Propanoic acid has its lone pairs tied up in the O-H and in resonance and is a poor nucleophile; deprotonating it gives propanoate, which attacks the acyl chloride readily, expels chloride and gives the anhydride. Propan-1-ol would give an ester instead, and water would give the acid.

acyl-substitution.q: Why is an acyl chloride the MOST reactive of the common acyl derivatives toward nucleophilic acyl substitution?
options: Chlorine makes the carbonyl carbon less electrophilic than any other group
Acyl chlorides have no leaving group at all
Chlorine strongly donates electron density by resonance, activating the ring
Chlorine donates poorly by resonance and chloride leaves easily
acyl-substitution.why: Chlorine's lone pairs are in a larger, poorly overlapping orbital, so they donate little electron density into the carbonyl by resonance, leaving the carbon highly electrophilic; additionally chloride ion, being a very weak base, departs easily once the tetrahedral intermediate forms.

acyl-substitution.q: A carboxylate ion (RCOO-) is generally a better leaving group than chloride ion in acyl substitution reactions.
acyl-substitution.why: Carboxylate is a moderately basic, resonance-stabilized anion, but chloride is an even weaker base and therefore a better leaving group, which is part of why acyl chlorides outrank anhydrides in reactivity.

acyl-substitution.q: What is the product when an acyl chloride reacts with water?
options: No reaction occurs because water is not nucleophilic enough
acyl-substitution.why: Water acts as the nucleophile, attacking the highly electrophilic acyl chloride carbonyl; after the tetrahedral intermediate collapses and chloride leaves, loss of a proton gives the carboxylic acid and HCl.

acyl-substitution.q: What is the product when an acyl chloride reacts with excess alcohol?
acyl-substitution.why: The alcohol's oxygen attacks the acyl chloride carbonyl; after chloride departs and a proton is lost (often assisted by a base or excess alcohol), the product is an ester plus HCl.

acyl-substitution.q: When an anhydride reacts with two equivalents of amine, the typical outcome is:
options: Two separate amide products with no other byproducts
The anhydride is unreactive toward amines
One amide plus an ammonium carboxylate salt
acyl-substitution.why: One equivalent of amine attacks a carbonyl and expels carboxylate, giving the amide. That carboxylate picks up a proton, and the carboxylic acid it becomes is a far stronger acid (pKa about 5) than the ammonium ion of the amine (pKa about 10) - so the second equivalent of amine is simply protonated. Net: one amide plus one ammonium carboxylate salt.

acyl-substitution.q: When an anhydride reacts with an alcohol, the products are one ester plus one carboxylic acid.
acyl-substitution.why: The alcohol attacks one of the anhydride's two carbonyl carbons; the other acyl-oxygen half departs as a carboxylate (which is then protonated), so the overall products are an ester and a carboxylic acid.

acyl-substitution.q: Put these in the correct order for saponification of ethyl acetate: (i) ethoxide deprotonates acetic acid, (ii) hydroxide attacks the carbonyl carbon, (iii) the tetrahedral intermediate expels ethoxide.
acyl-substitution.why: Addition always comes first: hydroxide attacks and the pi electrons go up onto oxygen (ii). The alkoxide then pushes back down and expels the better leaving group, ethoxide (iii). Only now does a carboxylic acid exist, and the ethoxide just released - a much stronger base than carboxylate - takes its proton (i). That final step is irreversible and is what drives the whole reaction; it cannot come earlier because there is nothing acidic to deprotonate until step iii is done.

acyl-substitution.q: Amides can easily be converted directly into esters simply by treating them with an alcohol under normal laboratory conditions.
acyl-substitution.why: This would require nitrogen (a strongly basic, poor leaving group) to depart, which is extremely unfavorable; amides are the least reactive acyl derivative and are not readily converted into more reactive derivatives like esters by simple nucleophilic substitution.

acyl-substitution.q: In acid-catalyzed ester hydrolysis, why is the carbonyl oxygen protonated as an early step?
options: Protonation makes the carbonyl carbon significantly more electrophilic, allowing a weak nucleophile like water to attack effectively
Protonation destroys the carbonyl group entirely
Protonation makes the oxygen a better nucleophile instead of the carbon a better electrophile
Protonation has no effect on the reaction
acyl-substitution.why: Protonating the carbonyl oxygen pulls electron density away from the carbon through the resulting resonance-stabilized cation, making the carbon much more attractive to a comparatively weak nucleophile such as water, which otherwise would react too slowly.

acyl-substitution.q: Compared to acid-catalyzed Fischer esterification, why does making an ester via an acyl chloride plus alcohol proceed faster and without needing an acid catalyst?
options: Acyl chlorides have no carbonyl group
Chloride is a far better leaving group than hydroxide
Alcohols cannot react with acyl chlorides
Fischer esterification does not involve a carbonyl carbon
acyl-substitution.why: In Fischer esterification, the leaving group would have to be hydroxide (a poor leaving group), so acid catalysis is needed to make departure possible and the reaction is a slow equilibrium; with an acyl chloride, chloride is already an excellent leaving group, so the reaction proceeds quickly without a catalyst and is essentially irreversible.

acyl-substitution.q: For nucleophiles reacting with a given acyl derivative under comparable conditions, which general ranking of nucleophilicity toward the carbonyl carbon is typically observed?
options: Water is always the strongest nucleophile
Alcohols are always stronger nucleophiles than amines
Amines are usually more nucleophilic than alcohols, which are usually more nucleophilic than water
All nucleophiles react at exactly the same rate
acyl-substitution.why: Nitrogen is less electronegative and holds its lone pair less tightly than oxygen, making amines generally better nucleophiles than comparably substituted alcohols, which in turn are typically better nucleophiles than water.

acyl-substitution.q: When excess Grignard reagent is added to an ester, the mechanism proceeds through which intermediate before reaching the final tertiary alcohol product?
options: The starting ester is never converted into an intermediate
A ketone, formed after the first equivalent of Grignard reagent displaces the alkoxide leaving group
acyl-substitution.why: The first Grignard equivalent adds to the ester carbonyl and the tetrahedral intermediate collapses, expelling the alkoxide leaving group to give a ketone; because the ketone is even more electrophilic than the starting ester, a second equivalent of Grignard reagent immediately adds to it.

acyl-substitution.q: Grignard reagents reacting with esters under normal conditions stop cleanly at the ketone stage, without further reaction.
acyl-substitution.why: The ketone intermediate generated from the first addition is actually more reactive toward the Grignard reagent than the original ester was, so under normal conditions with excess Grignard reagent the reaction proceeds on to give a tertiary alcohol rather than stopping at the ketone.

acyl-substitution.q: The tetrahedral intermediate formed after a nucleophile adds to an acyl derivative's carbonyl carbon carries what kind of charge on the former carbonyl oxygen, before the leaving group departs?
options: A negative charge, as an alkoxide
The oxygen is lost at this stage
acyl-substitution.why: When the nucleophile's electron pair adds to the carbon, the carbon-oxygen pi bond breaks and its electrons move fully onto the oxygen, giving a negatively charged alkoxide oxygen in the tetrahedral intermediate.

acyl-substitution.q: What provides the main driving force for the tetrahedral intermediate to collapse and expel a leaving group, regenerating a carbonyl?
options: The intermediate is simply unstable with no particular driving force
Reformation of the strong, stable C=O pi bond is energetically favorable
Leaving groups are always expelled instantly with no energetic preference
The nucleophile repels the oxygen, forcing collapse
acyl-substitution.why: A pi bond to oxygen is strong and energetically favorable to reform; the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate is generally higher in energy than either the starting carbonyl compound or the product, so it collapses to restore the stable carbonyl as soon as a leaving group can depart.

acyl-substitution.q: Why does nucleophilic acyl substitution proceed by an addition-elimination pathway rather than a concerted, SN2-like backside attack?
options: SN2 reactions only occur at nitrogen atoms
The sp2 carbon is planar, with no backside to attack
There is no mechanistic difference between the two pathways
acyl-substitution.why: Classic SN2 substitution occurs at an sp3 carbon with backside attack displacing a leaving group in one step; the carbonyl carbon in acyl substitution is sp2 and planar, so the nucleophile must add to one face to form a new sp3 tetrahedral intermediate before a leaving group can depart in a separate step.

acyl-substitution.q: The overall outcome of a nucleophilic acyl substitution reaction is that the carbonyl group is retained in the product, while the original leaving group is replaced by the incoming nucleophile.
acyl-substitution.why: Unlike nucleophilic addition (which destroys the carbonyl pi bond permanently), acyl substitution regenerates the carbonyl in the final product; only the group attached via the leaving position has been swapped out.

acyl-substitution.q: Acyl chlorides used as highly reactive starting materials in nucleophilic acyl substitution are themselves typically synthesized from carboxylic acids using which reagents?
options: H2 gas with a metal catalyst
acyl-substitution.why: Thionyl chloride or phosphorus chlorides convert the poor -OH leaving group of a carboxylic acid into the excellent -Cl leaving group, producing the highly reactive acyl chloride used in many subsequent nucleophilic acyl substitution reactions.

acyl-substitution.q: Why is base-promoted ester hydrolysis (saponification) essentially irreversible, while acid-catalyzed ester hydrolysis is a reversible equilibrium?
options: Saponification gives a carboxylate that will not re-form the ester
Saponification does not actually break any bonds
Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis produces a product with no leaving group potential
Both mechanisms are identical and equally reversible
acyl-substitution.why: Once hydroxide attacks and the carboxylate anion is formed, its negative charge (stabilized by resonance) makes it far too unreactive an electrophile to be attacked again by the departed alkoxide, effectively trapping the reaction as products; acid-catalyzed hydrolysis, by contrast, gives a neutral carboxylic acid that remains in equilibrium with the ester under the same conditions.

acyl-substitution.q: Anhydrides are generally more reactive toward nucleophilic acyl substitution than esters.
acyl-substitution.why: A carboxylate leaving group (departing from an anhydride) is a better leaving group than an alkoxide (departing from an ester), and the second carbonyl group in an anhydride also inductively withdraws electron density, both of which make anhydrides more reactive than esters.

acyl-substitution.q: Why does a carboxylic acid itself react only slowly and poorly with nucleophiles like amines directly at its carbonyl, even though it technically has a carbonyl carbon that could undergo nucleophilic acyl substitution?
options: Carboxylic acids have no carbonyl carbon
-OH is a poor leaving group, and the acidic proton is transferred first
Carboxylic acids are completely unreactive toward all nucleophiles under all conditions
Carboxylic acids react fastest of all acyl derivatives with nucleophiles
acyl-substitution.why: Hydroxide is a poor leaving group, so direct substitution at a carboxylic acid's carbonyl is slow; additionally, with basic nucleophiles such as amines, simple acid-base proton transfer (forming a salt) usually outcompetes attack on the carbonyl, which is why carboxylic acids are often first converted to a more reactive derivative (like an acyl chloride) before substitution.

alpha-hydrogens.q: Alpha hydrogens (on the carbon next to a carbonyl) are unusually acidic because the resulting carbanion is stabilized by:
alpha-hydrogens.why: Removing an alpha H gives a carbanion that resonance-delocalizes onto the carbonyl oxygen, forming a stabilized enolate — this is why alpha H’s (pKa ~20) are far more acidic than typical C–H bonds (pKa ~50).

alpha-hydrogens.q: An enolate has its negative charge delocalized primarily between which two atoms?
options: The alpha carbon and the carbonyl oxygen
The carbonyl carbon and a distant hydrogen
alpha-hydrogens.why: The enolate is the whole anion, not one of its drawings. Its two resonance contributors put the negative charge either on the alpha carbon, the carbanion form, or on the carbonyl oxygen, which is the major contributor because oxygen holds a charge far better. So the charge is shared between the alpha carbon and the carbonyl oxygen - and it is the alpha carbon, the minor contributor, that does the attacking.

alpha-hydrogens.q: A 1,3-diketone’s central CH₂ has alpha hydrogens that are far more acidic (pKa ~9-11) than a simple ketone’s alpha H (pKa ~20) because:
options: Diketones have no resonance at all
The resulting anion is stabilized by resonance into TWO carbonyls instead of one
The central carbon has extra protons
alpha-hydrogens.why: Deprotonating the central CH₂ gives an anion that can delocalize into either flanking carbonyl, doubling the resonance stabilization compared to a mono-ketone’s enolate.

alpha-hydrogens.q: Which hydrogen is referred to as an 'alpha hydrogen' relative to a carbonyl group?
options: A hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon itself
A hydrogen on the carbonyl oxygen
A hydrogen two carbons away from the carbonyl
A hydrogen on the carbon directly bonded to the carbonyl carbon
alpha-hydrogens.why: The carbon directly attached to the carbonyl carbon is called the alpha carbon, so hydrogens on it are alpha hydrogens. The carbonyl carbon itself has no H in ketones and usually one in aldehydes, but that H is not called 'alpha.'

alpha-hydrogens.q: A simple ketone's alpha C-H bond has a pKa of roughly 20, which is far more acidic than a typical alkane C-H (pKa around 50).
alpha-hydrogens.why: Alpha hydrogens are unusually acidic compared to ordinary C-H bonds because the resulting carbanion can be stabilized by resonance delocalization into the adjacent carbonyl, something an alkyl carbanion cannot do.

alpha-hydrogens.q: Which base is the classic choice for cleanly and essentially completely deprotonating a ketone's alpha carbon to generate its enolate?
alpha-hydrogens.why: LDA is a strong, bulky, non-nucleophilic base that removes alpha protons quickly and cleanly without attacking the carbonyl carbon itself, driving deprotonation essentially to completion at low temperature.

alpha-hydrogens.q: An enol is best described as which of the following?
options: A salt formed by deprotonating any alcohol
The tautomer with a C=C bearing an -OH group
The conjugate base of a ketone
A carbonyl compound with an extra oxygen atom added
alpha-hydrogens.why: Keto-enol tautomers differ only in the position of a proton and a double bond: the keto form has C=O and a C-H at the alpha carbon, while the enol form has C=C-OH. They are neutral isomers, not charged species.

alpha-hydrogens.q: An enolate anion is the resonance-stabilized species formed by removing a proton from the carbonyl oxygen itself, not from the alpha carbon.
alpha-hydrogens.why: An enolate is formed by removing an alpha C-H, not an O-H; a simple ketone or ester typically has no O-H to remove in the first place. The resulting negative charge is then delocalized onto oxygen by resonance.

alpha-hydrogens.q: Benzaldehyde (PhCHO) cannot form a simple enolate at the position where its carbonyl is attached to the ring because:
options: Aromatic rings are always more acidic than alkyl groups
The alpha carbon is an aromatic carbon with no H
Benzaldehyde's carbonyl oxygen is not electronegative
alpha-hydrogens.why: The 'alpha carbon' on the aryl side of PhCHO is part of the aromatic ring; removing a ring C-H there would destroy aromaticity and is not the kind of alpha-deprotonation relevant to enolate chemistry, so PhCHO's only true alpha hydrogens would have to come from an alkyl substituent, which it lacks.

alpha-hydrogens.q: A much stronger base is required to deprotonate an alpha carbon than to deprotonate the O-H of an alcohol because:
options: Alpha hydrogens are not acidic at all
Alcohols have no lone pairs on oxygen
Carbonyl groups repel all bases electronically
Alpha C-H (pKa ~20) is less acidic than O-H
alpha-hydrogens.why: Even though both deprotonations are stabilized somewhat by electronegative oxygen, the alcohol O-H is still considerably more acidic, so only a weak-to-moderate base is needed there, while alpha C-H deprotonation needs a much stronger base such as an amide base.

alpha-hydrogens.q: Between the two major resonance structures of an enolate, which one is generally considered the larger contributor to the true structure?
options: The structure with the negative charge on the oxygen
The structure with the negative charge on the alpha carbon
Both contribute exactly equally with no difference
Neither is valid; enolates have only one Lewis structure
alpha-hydrogens.why: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so it stabilizes negative charge better, making the oxygen-centered resonance form the greater contributor even though many enolate reactions proceed through the carbon end as the nucleophile.

alpha-hydrogens.q: Rank these from most acidic to least acidic: (A) an alpha C-H of acetone (pKa about 20), (B) an alpha C-H of ethyl acetoacetate (pKa about 11), (C) a vinylic C-H on an unactivated alkene (pKa about 44).
alpha-hydrogens.why: Ethyl acetoacetate's central CH2 sits between a ketone and an ester carbonyl, giving it two stabilizing resonance pathways and a much lower pKa than acetone's single-carbonyl-stabilized alpha H, while a vinylic C-H has essentially no special stabilization and is among the least acidic C-H bonds listed.

alpha-hydrogens.q: Diethyl malonate's alpha CH2 (flanked by two ester carbonyls) has a pKa of about 13, which is noticeably higher (less acidic) than a 1,3-diketone's central CH2 (pKa about 9-11) despite both having two flanking carbonyls. Why?
options: Malonate esters have three acidic protons instead of two
Esters are aromatic and therefore less acidic
The ester oxygen donates into the carbonyl, weakening stabilization
Malonate's carbonyls are further away from the CH2 than a diketone's carbonyls
alpha-hydrogens.why: In an ester, resonance donation from the alkoxy oxygen competes with the carbonyl's ability to stabilize an adjacent negative charge, making ester groups somewhat less effective than ketone carbonyls at lowering alpha C-H pKa, which is why malonates (two esters) are less acidic than 1,3-diketones (two ketones).

alpha-hydrogens.q: A nitrile group (C≡N) adjacent to a CH2, as in a beta-ketonitrile, can also help stabilize an alpha carbanion by resonance delocalization into the nitrile, similar to how a carbonyl does.
alpha-hydrogens.why: Nitriles, like carbonyls, have a pi system into which a negative charge on the adjacent carbon can be delocalized, so alpha hydrogens next to a nitrile are likewise more acidic than ordinary alkane C-H bonds, though typically less so than those next to a ketone.

alpha-hydrogens.q: Why does an ester's alpha C-H (pKa about 25) tend to be less acidic than a ketone's alpha C-H (pKa about 20), even though both groups contain a carbonyl?
options: Esters contain no carbonyl group at all
The ester oxygen donates density into the carbonyl
Ketones always have more alpha hydrogens than esters
The ester oxygen is less electronegative than a ketone oxygen
alpha-hydrogens.why: The same resonance donation from the ester's -OR oxygen that makes ester carbonyls less electrophilic toward nucleophiles also makes them somewhat less effective at stabilizing an adjacent carbanion than a ketone carbonyl is.

alpha-hydrogens.q: A carboxylic acid's own O-H proton is far more acidic (pKa about 4-5) than its alpha C-H (pKa about 25-30), so under mild base, deprotonation occurs at the O-H, not the alpha carbon.
alpha-hydrogens.why: Carboxylic acids have two acidic sites, but the O-H is dramatically more acidic because its conjugate base (carboxylate) is stabilized by two equivalent resonance structures with the negative charge shared between both oxygens; a much stronger base is needed to reach the alpha carbon, and the carboxylate must usually be protected or already formed first.

alpha-hydrogens.q: In 2-methylcyclohexanone, how many distinct alpha carbons bear alpha hydrogens available for enolate formation?
options: Only one, because the methyl group removes all alpha hydrogens from that side
Three, including the methyl group's own hydrogens
Two: C2 (already bearing a methyl group) and C6 (unsubstituted), on either side of the carbonyl
None, because substitution at C2 blocks enolization entirely
alpha-hydrogens.why: The carbonyl of cyclohexanone is flanked by two different alpha carbons, C2 and C6. Putting a methyl on C2 still leaves one alpha hydrogen there, and C6 still has two, so enolization can happen on either side. Watch what that does to C2: it is a stereocenter in the ketone, and forming the enolate on that side flattens the carbon and destroys the stereocenter, which is why alpha stereocenters racemize under base.

alpha-hydrogens.q: Why is a nitro group (-NO2) an especially strong activator of an adjacent alpha C-H's acidity, often outperforming even two ketone carbonyls?
options: Nitro groups have no effect on adjacent C-H acidity
Nitro groups only work through induction, never through resonance
Nitro groups make the carbon basic instead of acidic
Nitro resonance stabilizes negative charge extremely well
alpha-hydrogens.why: Like a carbonyl, the nitro group has resonance forms that can accept and stabilize a developing negative charge on the adjacent carbon, making nitroalkane alpha hydrogens strongly acidic despite nitro not being a classic carbonyl-type carbon.

alpha-hydrogens.q: A compound with alpha hydrogens flanked by a ketone on one side and a nitrile on the other would be expected to have alpha C-H acidity roughly comparable to a simple monoketone's alpha C-H, since a nitrile provides essentially no stabilization at all.
alpha-hydrogens.why: A nitrile does provide meaningful resonance stabilization of an adjacent carbanion (just generally less than a carbonyl), so a beta-ketonitrile's alpha C-H is typically considerably more acidic than a simple ketone's (often in the pKa 9-13 range), not merely equal to it.

alpha-hydrogens.q: Why can triethylamine (a weak, non-bulky amine base, pKa of conjugate acid about 10-11) only partially and reversibly deprotonate a simple ketone's alpha carbon (pKa about 20), while it can essentially fully deprotonate a 1,3-diketone (pKa about 9-11)?
options: Its conjugate acid pKa exceeds the diketone's but not the ketone's
Triethylamine physically cannot reach the diketone's CH2 due to sterics
Simple ketones are not acidic at all, so no base can deprotonate them
1,3-diketones have no carbonyls, so ordinary acid-base rules do not apply
alpha-hydrogens.why: Acid-base equilibria favor the side with the weaker acid and weaker base; since a 1,3-diketone is more acidic than triethylammonium, its deprotonation is favorable, but a simple ketone is less acidic than triethylammonium, so that deprotonation is unfavorable and only a small equilibrium concentration of enolate forms.

alpha-hydrogens.q: Sodium hydroxide (pKa of water, conjugate acid, about 15.7) is commonly used to generate useful concentrations of a 1,3-diketone's enolate, but would be a poor choice to fully deprotonate a simple monoketone's alpha carbon. What does this reveal about matching bases to substrates?
options: Stronger bases always work equally well regardless of the substrate's pKa
A base's conjugate acid pKa should be at or above the substrate's
The identity of the base never matters, only its concentration
NaOH cannot deprotonate any carbon-bound hydrogen under any circumstances
alpha-hydrogens.why: Because a 1,3-diketone's pKa (~9-11) is well below water's pKa (~15.7), hydroxide readily and nearly completely deprotonates it; a monoketone's pKa (~20) is well above water's pKa, so hydroxide deprotonates it to only a tiny, unfavorable extent, illustrating why base strength must be matched to the acidity of the specific alpha hydrogens involved.

alpha-hydrogens.q: An alpha,beta-unsaturated ketone (an enone) can, under basic conditions, form an extended dienolate by losing a hydrogen from the gamma carbon rather than from a true alpha carbon, because that anion is also stabilized through the conjugated pi system.
alpha-hydrogens.why: Number the enone out from the carbonyl: C1 is the carbonyl carbon, C2 is alpha, C3 is beta and C4 is gamma. Taking the gamma hydrogen gives the extended dienolate, an anion delocalized along O-C1-C2-C3-C4 with its charge density on the oxygen, on C2 and on C4 - including the carbon that was just deprotonated. Deprotonating the alpha-prime carbon on the other side of the carbonyl gives the cross-conjugated dienolate instead, and the two names are not interchangeable.

alpha-hydrogens.q: Why is it generally true that an alpha carbon bonded to a quaternary (fully substituted) adjacent carbon can still have acidic alpha hydrogens, but a carbon with zero hydrogens attached (fully substituted alpha carbon itself) cannot serve as a site of enolization?
options: Quaternary carbons are never adjacent to carbonyls
All alpha carbons always retain exactly two hydrogens regardless of substitution
A fully substituted carbonyl carbon cannot exist in organic chemistry
The alpha carbon must itself bear a removable hydrogen
alpha-hydrogens.why: Enolate formation requires removing an actual hydrogen from the alpha carbon; if that specific carbon has been substituted until it bears no hydrogens (as in a ketone with a fully branched alpha carbon), there is no alpha C-H to remove at that position, regardless of what is going on elsewhere in the molecule.

alpha-hydrogens.q: Between the alpha hydrogens of acetophenone (PhCOCH3, on the methyl side) and the alpha-like aromatic hydrogens of the phenyl ring, only the methyl hydrogens are considered classic 'alpha hydrogens' relevant to enolate chemistry.
alpha-hydrogens.why: Only the sp3 CH3 carbon attached to the carbonyl is the true alpha carbon capable of forming a resonance-stabilized enolate; the ring carbon on the other side of the carbonyl is aromatic and its hydrogens are not involved in this kind of carbonyl-stabilized deprotonation.

alpha-hydrogens.q: Consider 1,3-cyclohexanedione. Explain why its pKa (around 5-6) is even lower than that of an acyclic 1,3-diketone like 2,4-pentanedione (pKa around 9).
options: Its enolate and enol tautomer are unusually well stabilized in the ring
Ring compounds are always less acidic than chain compounds with the same functional groups
The ring prevents any resonance stabilization of the enolate
alpha-hydrogens.why: Cyclic 1,3-diketones such as 1,3-cyclohexanedione are known to be notably more acidic than their open-chain counterparts, partly because the enol tautomer is particularly stable and well-conjugated in the ring, pulling the equilibrium and making the corresponding proton unusually easy to remove.

alpha-hydrogens.q: If you compare the alpha hydrogens of a ketone to a secondary amide's alpha hydrogens, which is generally more acidic?
options: Amide alpha hydrogens are always more acidic than ketone alpha hydrogens
The ketone's, because the amide N donates into the carbonyl
They are essentially identical in acidity in all cases
Amides have no alpha hydrogens by definition
alpha-hydrogens.why: Nitrogen is a better pi-donor than oxygen, so amide resonance (donation of the nitrogen lone pair into the carbonyl) is even stronger than the ester case, making amide carbonyls notably less effective at stabilizing an adjacent alpha carbanion, which is why amide alpha C-H bonds are less acidic (pKa often above 30) than ketone alpha C-H bonds.

alpha-hydrogens.q: Which compound has no alpha hydrogens at all, and so can never form an enolate?
alpha-hydrogens.why: The one alpha carbon of 2,2-dimethylpropanal is the quaternary carbon, and it carries no hydrogen. The CHO hydrogen sits on the carbonyl carbon itself rather than next to it, so it is not an alpha hydrogen and it is not acidic. Each of the other three has a CH3 or a CH2 bonded straight to the carbonyl carbon.
