nucleophilic-aromatic.q: What happens to the ring after the halide leaves in SNAr?
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: Which is the thermodynamic payoff for the whole sequence.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: Which halide is worst for SNAr?
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: Iodine is the least electronegative of the four, so it activates the carbon least.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What is the benzylic position?
options: The carbon attached to the ring
The carbon two away from the ring
benzylic-reactivity.why: It is not part of the ring, and it behaves unlike any other sp3 carbon.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Why is a benzylic cation stabilized?
benzylic-reactivity.why: The charge spreads over the benzylic carbon plus both ortho and the para positions.

benzylic-reactivity.q: How many carbons share a benzylic charge?
benzylic-reactivity.why: The benzylic carbon plus the two ortho and one para ring positions.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Which other position uses the same argument?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Allylic delocalization spreads over three carbons; benzylic over four.

benzylic-reactivity.q: A benzylic halide is good at which mechanisms?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Rare, and it is why benzyl bromide is used as an alkylating agent everywhere.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Why is a primary benzylic halide good at SN1?
benzylic-reactivity.why: It sits roughly where a tertiary alkyl halide does.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Why is a benzylic halide also good at SN2?
options: The halide is a better leaving group
The ring stabilizes the transition state
benzylic-reactivity.why: And a benzylic carbon is usually unhindered, which helps as well.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Which reagent brominates the benzylic position?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Light means radicals, and the benzylic radical is by far the most stable.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Why is NBS used rather than Br2?
options: It is a stronger brominating agent
It is a radical initiator itself
It keeps the Br2 concentration low
benzylic-reactivity.why: Low Br2 suppresses the ionic addition that would attack any alkene present.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What other position does NBS brominate?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Same reagent, same mechanism, and a selectivity problem if a molecule has both.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What does hot KMnO4 do to toluene?
benzylic-reactivity.why: The side chain is cut back to one carbon and oxidized to the carboxyl.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What does hot KMnO4 do to propylbenzene?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Chain length makes no difference; everything past the benzylic carbon is cut away.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What does hot KMnO4 do to tert-butylbenzene?
benzylic-reactivity.why: There is no benzylic hydrogen, so the reaction cannot start.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What does the tert-butylbenzene result reveal?
options: The reaction starts at a benzylic C-H
benzylic-reactivity.why: The one exception that shows what the mechanism requires.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Does hot KMnO4 attack the benzene ring?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Aromatic stabilization keeps the ring inert to conditions that destroy alkenes.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Why does a radical abstract the benzylic hydrogen preferentially?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Stability of the radical formed is what selectivity tracks.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What should a benzoic acid suggest retrosynthetically?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Oxidation converts any alkyl chain to a carboxyl, so the chain identity is free.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Which alkylbenzene will not oxidize?
benzylic-reactivity.why: No benzylic hydrogen means no starting point.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What is benzyl bromide used for?
benzylic-reactivity.why: It appears in malonic ester and enamine chemistry for exactly this reason.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Is a benzylic anion stabilized?
options: Only if the ring is substituted
benzylic-reactivity.why: The same resonance that stabilizes the cation and the radical.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What comparison does benzylic stabilization most resemble?
benzylic-reactivity.why: One alkene replaced by a whole ring, so the charge spreads further.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Which intermediate is NOT stabilized at a benzylic position?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Cation, radical and anion are all delocalized by the same resonance.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What conditions does benzylic bromination need?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Ionic conditions would brominate the ring instead.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Why can an alkyl group be put on a ring and then oxidized?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Electrophilic substitution cannot deliver a carboxyl group directly.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What happens to the carbons beyond the benzylic one in KMnO4 oxidation?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Which is why chain length is irrelevant to the product.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Which product comes from isopropylbenzene and hot KMnO4?
benzylic-reactivity.why: One benzylic hydrogen is enough, and both methyls go with the rest of the chain.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Does Friedel-Crafts alkylation give a benzylic carbon?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Any carbon attached directly to the ring is benzylic by definition.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What limits selectivity if a molecule is both allylic and benzylic?
benzylic-reactivity.why: One reagent and one mechanism means it cannot tell them apart.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Why is the benzylic C-H weaker than an ordinary alkane C-H?
options: The radical it forms is stabilized
benzylic-reactivity.why: Bond strength tracks the stability of the fragments it gives.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Which position does an aromatic ring make reactive without being reactive itself?
benzylic-reactivity.why: The ring supplies the stabilization and stays intact.

phenols.q: What is a phenol?
options: An OH attached directly to a ring
An OH on a carbon next to a ring
phenols.why: An OH on a carbon next to the ring is a benzylic alcohol, which behaves quite differently.

phenols.q: What is phenol's approximate pKa?
phenols.why: Six orders of magnitude more acidic than ethanol.

phenols.q: What is ethanol's approximate pKa?
phenols.why: Its conjugate base has the charge on one oxygen with nowhere to go.

phenols.q: Why is phenol more acidic than ethanol?
phenols.why: Acidity is about the stability of the conjugate base, not the bond that breaks.

phenols.q: Where does the phenoxide charge go?
phenols.why: Which is also why only ortho and para substituents affect the acidity much.

phenols.q: Which base deprotonates a phenol?
phenols.why: Bicarbonate is not strong enough, which is what makes it useful as a discriminator.

phenols.q: Which base deprotonates a carboxylic acid but not a phenol?
phenols.why: Carbonic acid at pKa 6.4 sits between the two.

phenols.q: How do you separate a phenol from a carboxylic acid?
phenols.why: The acid leaves as its water-soluble salt and the phenol stays behind.

phenols.q: What is carbonic acid's pKa?
phenols.why: Between a phenol at 10 and a carboxylic acid at 4.8, which is the whole basis of the separation.

phenols.q: What is 4-nitrophenol's approximate pKa?
phenols.why: Nitro withdraws by resonance from para, taking the charge onto its own oxygens.

phenols.q: What is picric acid's approximate pKa?
phenols.why: 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, more acidic than most carboxylic acids.

phenols.q: Why is 4-nitrophenol more acidic than 3-nitrophenol?
options: Para is closer to the OH
phenols.why: From meta only induction is available, which is the smaller effect.

phenols.q: What kind of substituent makes a phenol more acidic?
phenols.why: Anything that stabilizes the phenoxide strengthens the acid.

phenols.q: Which positions matter most for a substituent's effect?
phenols.why: Only those can reach the negative charge by resonance.

phenols.q: Is OH an activator or deactivator on a ring?
phenols.why: The same lone pair that stabilizes the anion also donates into the ring.

phenols.q: Is OH ortho/para or meta directing?
phenols.why: Donation reaches the ortho and para positions, which is where the substitution goes.

phenols.q: What does phenol plus bromine water give?
phenols.why: No Lewis acid catalyst is needed, and all three activated positions react at once.

phenols.q: Why does phenol brominate without a catalyst?
phenols.why: A Lewis acid is needed only for rings that are not already electron-rich.

phenols.q: Can a phenol undergo SN2 at its C-O bond?
phenols.why: The backside is behind the ring, which rules the trajectory out entirely.

phenols.q: In a Williamson ether synthesis with a phenol, what is the nucleophile?
phenols.why: The aryl carbon can never be the electrophile in a substitution.

phenols.q: What does oxidizing a phenol give?
phenols.why: Not aromatic any more, which is why quinones are colored.

phenols.q: Why are quinones colored?
options: They are conjugated and not aromatic
phenols.why: A long conjugated system with a small HOMO-LUMO gap absorbs visible light.

phenols.q: Can a phenol be dehydrated like an alcohol?
phenols.why: Nothing that needs SN1 or SN2 at that carbon works.

phenols.q: How are phenols usually made?
phenols.why: Warm water on an aryl diazonium salt is the standard route.

phenols.q: What does a phenol plus an acyl chloride give?
phenols.why: Aspirin is one of these.

phenols.q: What is 2,4-dinitrophenol's approximate pKa?
phenols.why: Two nitro groups in resonance-capable positions, and now as acidic as a carboxylic acid.

phenols.q: Why is a methyl group on a phenol slightly deactivating toward acidity?
phenols.why: Donating electron density destabilizes the anion, which weakens the acid.

phenols.q: Which compound is least acidic?
phenols.why: An ordinary alcohol has no way to spread the charge at all.

phenols.q: Which is more acidic, phenol or acetic acid?
phenols.why: 4.8 against 10, because a carboxylate spreads charge over two equivalent oxygens.

phenols.q: Why does a carboxylate beat a phenoxide at stabilizing charge?
options: Charge sits on two electronegative oxygens
phenols.why: A phenoxide spreads charge onto carbons, which hold it less well than oxygen does.

birch-reduction.q: What does a Birch reduction produce from benzene?
birch-reduction.why: The unconjugated isomer, which is the less stable of the two dienes.

birch-reduction.q: What are the Birch conditions?
options: Na or Li in liquid NH3 with an alcohol
birch-reduction.why: A dissolving-metal reduction rather than a catalytic one.

birch-reduction.q: What does the deep blue color indicate?
birch-reduction.why: The reducing agent is a free electron in solution.

birch-reduction.q: What is the sequence of steps?
birch-reduction.why: Alternating, which is what makes the intermediates controllable.

birch-reduction.q: What is the first intermediate?
birch-reduction.why: One electron added to the ring.

birch-reduction.q: What does the alcohol do?
birch-reduction.why: The electrons come from the metal and the solvent is ammonia.

birch-reduction.q: Why is the 1,4-diene formed rather than the 1,3?
birch-reduction.why: Protonation happens where charge density is highest, not where stability is greatest.

birch-reduction.q: Which isomer is more stable?
birch-reduction.why: And it is not what forms, which is how you know stability is not deciding.

birch-reduction.q: With a donating group, where does the substituted carbon end up?
birch-reduction.why: A donor destabilizes charge on its own carbon, so the carbanion goes elsewhere.

birch-reduction.q: With a withdrawing group, where does the substituted carbon end up?
birch-reduction.why: A withdrawing group holds the charge on its own carbon, so that carbon is protonated.

birch-reduction.q: What does anisole give on Birch reduction?
birch-reduction.why: Methoxy is donating, so its carbon stays on a double bond.

birch-reduction.q: What does benzoic acid give on Birch reduction?
birch-reduction.why: Carboxyl is withdrawing, so its carbon ends up sp3.

birch-reduction.q: What single question answers both substituent rules?
options: Where is the carbanion most stable
birch-reduction.why: That carbon gets protonated and comes out saturated.

birch-reduction.q: Which reaction uses the same electron-then-proton pattern?
birch-reduction.why: Both are dissolving-metal reductions running on solvated electrons, and both give the opposite outcome from catalytic hydrogenation on the same substrate.

birch-reduction.q: What does catalytic hydrogenation give from benzene?
birch-reduction.why: It either leaves the ring alone or reduces it completely; there is no halfway.

birch-reduction.q: Why is the Birch useful?
birch-reduction.why: An unconjugated diene is a handle nothing else in the course provides.

birch-reduction.q: What does a Birch-derived enol ether give on mild acid hydrolysis?
birch-reduction.why: Which is the standard route into a substituted cyclohexenone from a flat ring.

birch-reduction.q: Which starting material gives an enol ether on Birch reduction?
birch-reduction.why: The methoxy stays on a double bond, and a C=C with an OR on it is an enol ether.

birch-reduction.q: Why can an unconjugated diene be functionalized selectively?
options: Its two double bonds are independent
birch-reduction.why: A conjugated diene reacts as one system, which makes single-site chemistry harder.

birch-reduction.q: What kind of control does the Birch operate under?
birch-reduction.why: The product that forms fastest, rather than the one that is most stable.

birch-reduction.q: Which metal is used besides sodium?
birch-reduction.why: Both dissolve in liquid ammonia to give solvated electrons.

birch-reduction.q: How many electrons are added in total?
birch-reduction.why: Two electrons and two protons, alternating.

birch-reduction.q: What is the solvent?
birch-reduction.why: It solvates the electrons, which is what makes the blue solution.

birch-reduction.q: Does a Birch reduction touch an isolated alkene?
birch-reduction.why: Which is the opposite selectivity from catalytic hydrogenation.

birch-reduction.q: Why does a withdrawing group put its carbon sp3?
birch-reduction.why: The carbanion sits where the substituent lets it, and that carbon gets the proton.

birch-reduction.q: What is a radical anion?
options: A species with an unpaired electron and a charge
birch-reduction.why: One electron added to a neutral molecule gives both at once.

birch-reduction.q: Which position is protonated second?
options: Where the carbanion's charge is highest
birch-reduction.why: Which is what sets the 1,4 relationship in the product.

birch-reduction.q: What does toluene give on Birch reduction?
birch-reduction.why: Methyl is a weak donor, and direction rather than strength decides the outcome.

birch-reduction.q: Why does the Birch not over-reduce to cyclohexane?
options: The diene is not aromatic and resists further electron addition
birch-reduction.why: Adding an electron to an isolated alkene is far harder than to an aromatic ring.

birch-reduction.q: What makes a dissolving-metal reduction different from hydrogenation?
options: It adds electrons, not surface hydrogens
birch-reduction.why: Which is why it can stop where a surface reaction cannot.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What is the formula of an aryl diazonium ion?
diazonium-chemistry.why: And it leaves as N2 gas, which is what makes it so useful.

diazonium-chemistry.q: How is a diazonium salt made?
diazonium-chemistry.why: Cold, because the salt decomposes above about 5 degrees.

diazonium-chemistry.q: At what temperature is diazotization run?
diazonium-chemistry.why: Warmer and the salt loses nitrogen before you can use it.

diazonium-chemistry.q: Why is N2+ such a good leaving group?
options: It leaves as stable N2 gas
diazonium-chemistry.why: A gas that escapes the solution and cannot come back.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What are the three steps to reach a diazonium salt from benzene?
diazonium-chemistry.why: The first two are reactions the course already covered.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What reduces a nitro group to an amine?
diazonium-chemistry.why: Or H2 with a catalyst, which does the same job.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What does CuCl do to a diazonium salt?
diazonium-chemistry.why: A Sandmeyer reaction.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What does CuCN do to a diazonium salt?
diazonium-chemistry.why: A group electrophilic substitution cannot install at all.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What does KI do to a diazonium salt?
diazonium-chemistry.why: No copper salt is needed for the iodide.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What does HBF4 then heat give?
diazonium-chemistry.why: The Schiemann reaction, and effectively the only route to an aryl fluoride.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What does warm water give?
options: The aryl alcohol on the side chain
diazonium-chemistry.why: The standard way phenols are made, since no substitution works at that C-O bond.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What does H3PO2 give?
diazonium-chemistry.why: Which is the most useful row on the menu once you see what it is for.

diazonium-chemistry.q: Which groups can diazonium chemistry install that EAS cannot?
diazonium-chemistry.why: Four groups no electrophilic substitution reaches.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What is the point of replacing N2+ with H?
options: The amine directed a previous step and is no longer needed
diazonium-chemistry.why: A substituent installed to control a step and then deleted.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What does NH2 do as a substituent on a ring?
diazonium-chemistry.why: Which is why it is worth installing purely to direct.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What is the aromatic analogue of a protecting group here?
options: An amine installed to direct, then removed
diazonium-chemistry.why: Same idea as the second carbonyl of a malonic ester synthesis.

diazonium-chemistry.q: Which other group is used reversibly to block a position?
diazonium-chemistry.why: Sulfonation is reversible, so the group can be removed afterwards.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What is azo coupling?
options: A diazonium salt attacking an activated ring
diazonium-chemistry.why: The diazonium acts as a weak electrophile here rather than as a substrate.

diazonium-chemistry.q: Which rings will couple with a diazonium salt?
diazonium-chemistry.why: The diazonium is too weak an electrophile for anything less activated.

diazonium-chemistry.q: Where does azo coupling occur?
diazonium-chemistry.why: Ortho/para directors send it there, and para is less hindered.

diazonium-chemistry.q: Why are azo compounds colored?
options: A long conjugated system absorbs visible light
diazonium-chemistry.why: Two rings joined by a conjugated N=N bridge gives a small HOMO-LUMO gap.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What industry did azo chemistry create?
diazonium-chemistry.why: Methyl orange is one of these compounds.

diazonium-chemistry.q: Why can 1,3,5-tribromobenzene not be made by direct bromination?
diazonium-chemistry.why: Each bromine sends the next one ortho or para, so 1,3,5 is unreachable.

diazonium-chemistry.q: How is 1,3,5-tribromobenzene made?
diazonium-chemistry.why: The amine directs all three bromines, then H3PO2 deletes it.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What does aniline plus bromine water give?
diazonium-chemistry.why: Strongly activated, so all three positions react without a catalyst.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What intermediate forms when a diazonium salt loses N2?
diazonium-chemistry.why: Badly unstable, which is why it grabs whatever nucleophile is present at once. In warm water that nucleophile is water, and the product is the phenol.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What is the Sandmeyer reaction specifically?
diazonium-chemistry.why: CuCl, CuBr and CuCN are the three standard cases.

diazonium-chemistry.q: Which reaction sequence lets you place a group meta when it would go ortho/para?
diazonium-chemistry.why: Directing effects cannot be argued with, so you change what is doing the directing.

diazonium-chemistry.q: Can an aryl halide be converted to a phenol directly?
diazonium-chemistry.why: An unactivated aryl halide does neither SN1 nor SN2.

diazonium-chemistry.q: Why is diazonium chemistry described as a hub?
options: It is used in every synthesis
diazonium-chemistry.why: A single ring position becomes a socket almost anything can be plugged into.

polymer-basics.q: What is a monomer?
options: The small unit a polymer is built from
The repeating piece inside the chain
polymer-basics.why: The repeating piece inside the chain is the repeat unit, which may differ from the monomer.

polymer-basics.q: What is the degree of polymerization?
polymer-basics.why: For step-growth it is 1/(1-p), where p is the fraction of groups reacted.

polymer-basics.q: How many reactive sites does a chain-forming monomer need?
polymer-basics.why: One stops after a single bond; three or more gives a network.

polymer-basics.q: What does a monomer with three reactive sites give?
polymer-basics.why: Which is what makes a thermoset, and why it cannot be melted.

polymer-basics.q: What does a monomer with one reactive site give?
polymer-basics.why: It makes one bond and is finished.

polymer-basics.q: What is lost in an addition polymerization?
polymer-basics.why: The pi bond simply opens, so the repeat unit matches the monomer.

polymer-basics.q: What is lost in a condensation polymerization?
polymer-basics.why: Which is what the word condensation means.

polymer-basics.q: How do you tell addition from condensation quickly?
polymer-basics.why: A lighter repeat unit means something was expelled; matching formulas mean nothing was, so for an alkene monomer, addition.

polymer-basics.q: Which monomer class gives addition polymers?
polymer-basics.why: The double bond supplies both reactive ends.

polymer-basics.q: Which reaction builds a condensation polymer?
polymer-basics.why: Esterification or amide formation, run repeatedly.

polymer-basics.q: What is a thermoplastic?
polymer-basics.why: Heating lets the chains slide, so it can be melted and remolded.

polymer-basics.q: What is a thermoset?
polymer-basics.why: Heating destroys it rather than softening it, because melting would mean breaking bonds.

polymer-basics.q: Which can be melted and remolded?
polymer-basics.why: A network has nothing to loosen.

polymer-basics.q: What is the repeat unit of polyethylene?
polymer-basics.why: Break the pi bond of ethylene and bracket what is left.

polymer-basics.q: Why does chain length raise melting point?
options: Longer chains have more contact and entangle
polymer-basics.why: More surface in contact means more total intermolecular attraction.

polymer-basics.q: What does branching do to packing?
polymer-basics.why: Which is the whole difference between LDPE and HDPE.

polymer-basics.q: What do cross-links do?
polymer-basics.why: A few make rubber elastic; many make a rigid thermoset.

polymer-basics.q: What does regularity along a chain allow?
polymer-basics.why: Chains that match can lie against each other.

polymer-basics.q: Which grows faster in an addition polymerization?
polymer-basics.why: One active end adds monomer very fast, so long chains exist from the start.

polymer-basics.q: How do chains grow in a step-growth polymerization?
options: Only monomer adds to a chain
polymer-basics.why: Which is why nothing is long until conversion is very high.

polymer-basics.q: What is the degree of polymerization at 99% conversion in a step-growth?
polymer-basics.why: 1/(1-0.99), and 99% sounds finished while giving a marginal material.

polymer-basics.q: What is the degree of polymerization at 90% conversion?
polymer-basics.why: An oil rather than a plastic.

polymer-basics.q: Why does step-growth need exact stoichiometry?
polymer-basics.why: Two like groups cannot react with each other, so growth stops.

polymer-basics.q: Why does a monofunctional impurity matter so much?
polymer-basics.why: A small mole fraction of it wrecks the molecular weight.

polymer-basics.q: Which polymer class is polyethylene?
polymer-basics.why: From an alkene, with nothing lost.

polymer-basics.q: Which polymer class is nylon?
polymer-basics.why: A diacid and a diamine, losing water at each amide.

polymer-basics.q: What is a repeat unit?
polymer-basics.why: It equals the monomer only for addition polymers.

polymer-basics.q: Why is no new reaction needed for this chapter?
polymer-basics.why: Alkene addition and acyl substitution, run on a monomer with two ends.

polymer-basics.q: What does glycerol's three OH groups predict?
polymer-basics.why: Three sites lets each monomer join three others.

polymer-basics.q: Which question predicts the material before any mechanism?
polymer-basics.why: One, two or three or more gives three different outcomes.

addition-polymers.q: What are the three stages of radical polymerization?
addition-polymers.why: The same three as radical halogenation.
It breaks homolytically to give two radicals.

options: The radical adds to the next alkene
addition-polymers.why: Generating a new radical at the end of a longer chain, thousands of times.
Either combining or disproportionating.
So propagation runs a long way before two radicals find each other.

addition-polymers.q: Which end of CH2=CHX does the growing radical attack?
addition-polymers.why: That leaves the radical on the substituted, more stable carbon.
It follows from taking the more stable radical every time.

addition-polymers.q: Which rule does head-to-tail regiochemistry resemble?
addition-polymers.why: Both come from asking which intermediate is more stable.
Foam cups and packaging.

addition-polymers.q: What polymer comes from vinyl chloride?
addition-polymers.why: Pipe, flooring and insulation.
Teflon, and there is no head-to-tail question because both carbons are identical.

addition-polymers.q: What polymer comes from methyl methacrylate?
addition-polymers.why: Plexiglas, and it is transparent because it is amorphous.

options: How substituents are arranged along the chain
addition-polymers.why: Each substituted backbone carbon has a fixed orientation, and tacticity names the pattern they make.
Packs well, so the material is crystalline and strong.
Regular, so it packs well too.
Cannot pack, so the material is amorphous and soft.

addition-polymers.q: What tacticity does radical polymerization give?
options: It alternates strictly along the chain
addition-polymers.why: A planar radical has no strong preference about which face the next monomer arrives on.
It holds the chain on a metal center so every addition happens the same way.
Nothing packs, so there is no strength.

addition-polymers.q: How does branching happen in radical polymerization?
addition-polymers.why: The chain then continues from that point, leaving a branch.
High-pressure radical polymerization does this constantly.
A Ziegler-Natta catalyst suppresses the backbiting that makes branches.
Branched, badly packed and flexible.
Linear, well packed and rigid.

addition-polymers.q: Do LDPE and HDPE have the same formula?
addition-polymers.why: Same monomer, same repeat unit, different architecture.

addition-polymers.q: How do you draw an addition polymer from its monomer?
addition-polymers.why: Then write a bond leaving each side of the bracket.

options: Radical polymerization places the phenyls at random
Phenyl groups are too bulky to pack
Its chains are too short to form crystals
addition-polymers.why: Syndiotactic polystyrene has the same phenyl group and is crystalline, melting near 270 C, so bulk is not the cause. Atacticity is.

addition-polymers.q: What kind of polymerization suits an alkene with donating groups?
addition-polymers.why: The growing cation has to be stabilized.

addition-polymers.q: What kind of polymerization suits an alkene with withdrawing groups?
addition-polymers.why: The mirror image of the cationic case.

addition-polymers.q: What does a Ziegler-Natta catalyst control?
addition-polymers.why: Holding the chain at a defined metal site does both at once.

condensation-polymers.q: What does a diacid plus a diol give?
condensation-polymers.why: Losing water at each ester bond.

condensation-polymers.q: What does a diacid plus a diamine give?
condensation-polymers.why: Losing water at each amide bond.

condensation-polymers.q: What is PET made from?
condensation-polymers.why: The drinks bottle and the polyester shirt.

condensation-polymers.q: What is nylon 6,6 made from?
condensation-polymers.why: First number the diamine's carbons, second the diacid's: hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid.

condensation-polymers.q: What do the numbers in nylon 6,6 count?
condensation-polymers.why: Six in the diacid and six in the diamine, readable straight from the name.

condensation-polymers.q: What is Kevlar made from?
condensation-polymers.why: Both aromatic and both para-substituted, which is what makes the chains straight.

condensation-polymers.q: Why is Kevlar so strong?
condensation-polymers.why: Three factors compounding, none of them exotic.

condensation-polymers.q: Which resists hydrolysis better?
options: It depends on the chain length
condensation-polymers.why: Amides are the least reactive acyl derivative, which carries over to the material.

condensation-polymers.q: Why is PET chemically recyclable?
options: Its ester bonds can be hydrolyzed back to monomers
condensation-polymers.why: The property that makes it less durable is what makes it recoverable.

condensation-polymers.q: What comparison does a polyamide invite?
condensation-polymers.why: Same amide, same planarity, same interchain hydrogen bonding.

condensation-polymers.q: Nylon is strong for the same reason as which biological structure?
condensation-polymers.why: Backbone hydrogen bonds between neighboring chains.

condensation-polymers.q: What is a polyurethane made from?
condensation-polymers.why: The alcohol adds across the N=C=O group.

condensation-polymers.q: What is unusual about polyurethane formation?
condensation-polymers.why: Which is why the class is properly called step-growth rather than condensation.

condensation-polymers.q: Why is the class called step-growth rather than condensation?
options: It grows in steps of ten
It is a newer name only
condensation-polymers.why: Polyurethane is the exception that forces the broader name.

condensation-polymers.q: What linkage does a polycarbonate have?
condensation-polymers.why: Two oxygens on one carbonyl.

condensation-polymers.q: What is polycarbonate used for?
condensation-polymers.why: Transparent and extremely impact-resistant.

condensation-polymers.q: What is the formula for degree of polymerization in step-growth?
condensation-polymers.why: Which is why the last tenth of a percent is where the material appears.

condensation-polymers.q: At 99.9% conversion, what is the degree of polymerization?
condensation-polymers.why: And 99% gives only 100, which is barely a plastic.

condensation-polymers.q: Why must the water be removed continuously?
options: To drive the equilibrium to completion
To prevent hydrolysis of the monomer
condensation-polymers.why: Every step is an equilibrium, and the reaction has to be driven the whole way.

condensation-polymers.q: What happens with a 2% excess of one monomer?
condensation-polymers.why: Two like groups cannot react with each other, so growth halts.

condensation-polymers.q: Which polymer is made from lactic acid?
condensation-polymers.why: One monomer carrying both an OH and a COOH.

condensation-polymers.q: Why can lactic acid polymerize with itself?
options: It has both an OH and a COOH
condensation-polymers.why: Two reactive sites is the only requirement, and they need not be the same kind.

condensation-polymers.q: What bond does PET's backbone contain?
condensation-polymers.why: Which is the handle that hydrolysis can select.

condensation-polymers.q: Why does para substitution matter in Kevlar?
options: It makes the ring more reactive
condensation-polymers.why: A straight chain lets neighbors touch along their whole length.

condensation-polymers.q: How many reactive groups does each condensation monomer need?
condensation-polymers.why: The same rule as every chain polymer.

condensation-polymers.q: What kind of reaction forms each join?
condensation-polymers.why: Esterification or amide formation, and nothing else.

condensation-polymers.q: Why does polyester fabric lose strength in hot alkali faster than nylon?
options: Esters hydrolyze more readily than amides
condensation-polymers.why: The acyl reactivity ladder applied to a material. It is not a blanket ranking: nylon is the one attacked by acid, chlorine and sunlight.

condensation-polymers.q: What does 90% conversion give in a step-growth?
condensation-polymers.why: Which is why these reactions are run to a completeness that looks excessive.

condensation-polymers.q: Is Kevlar a thermoset?
condensation-polymers.why: No cross-links, so not a network. It has no melt either, decomposing near 500 C and spun from solution.

condensation-polymers.q: What are the two monomers of a polyester, read backwards?
condensation-polymers.why: Cut the acyl C-O bond, leaving the oxygen on the alcohol side, and check each fragment has two reactive sites.

polymer-properties.q: What are crystalline regions in a polymer?
polymer-properties.why: Almost every real polymer has both crystalline and amorphous regions.

polymer-properties.q: What does higher crystallinity do to density?
polymer-properties.why: Packed chains occupy less space.

polymer-properties.q: Why is a highly crystalline polymer opaque?
options: Crystalline and amorphous regions scatter light
polymer-properties.why: Their refractive indices differ, so light scatters at every boundary.

polymer-properties.q: Which polymers are used for windows?
polymer-properties.why: No crystalline regions means nothing to scatter light.

polymer-properties.q: What is Tg?
polymer-properties.why: Essentially every polymer has one; only semicrystalline ones also have a Tm.

polymer-properties.q: What is Tm?
polymer-properties.why: A fully amorphous polymer has no Tm at all.

polymer-properties.q: Which transition does every polymer have?
polymer-properties.why: Because every polymer has amorphous regions.

polymer-properties.q: Why does rubber shatter in liquid nitrogen?
polymer-properties.why: Below Tg the chains are frozen and cannot deform.

polymer-properties.q: Why is rubber elastic at room temperature?
polymer-properties.why: Its amorphous chains are mobile, and the cross-links pull them back.

polymer-properties.q: What is vulcanization?
polymer-properties.why: Short S-S bridges form between the chains.

polymer-properties.q: What does a few percent of cross-links give?
polymer-properties.why: Chains can stretch apart and are pulled back, which is a tire.

polymer-properties.q: What does heavy cross-linking give?
polymer-properties.why: Nothing can move at all.

polymer-properties.q: What is rubber with no cross-links like?
polymer-properties.why: Chains slide past each other permanently.

polymer-properties.q: Why is rubber elasticity an entropy effect?
polymer-properties.why: Releasing it lets entropy pull the chains back into a coil.

polymer-properties.q: What happens to a stretched rubber band when heated?
polymer-properties.why: The entropic restoring force scales with temperature, unlike almost every other material.

polymer-properties.q: Why does a rubber band warm when stretched?
polymer-properties.why: The standard demonstration that the elasticity is entropic.

polymer-properties.q: What holds a thermoplastic together?
polymer-properties.why: Which heat can overcome, so the chains slide and it can be remolded.

polymer-properties.q: What holds a thermoset together?
polymer-properties.why: One network, so melting would mean breaking bonds.

polymer-properties.q: Which is recyclable by melting?
polymer-properties.why: A network has nothing to loosen.

polymer-properties.q: Give an example of a thermoset.
polymer-properties.why: Bakelite and vulcanized rubber are others.

polymer-properties.q: What do bulky side groups do?
polymer-properties.why: They raise Tg and slow crystallization. In polystyrene the random placement is what actually prevents packing.

polymer-properties.q: What do interchain hydrogen bonds do?
polymer-properties.why: Nylon and Kevlar both depend on them.

polymer-properties.q: Which argument from the biomolecules chapter does packing repeat?
polymer-properties.why: Straight chains stack and melt high; kinked or branched ones do not.

polymer-properties.q: What does more crystallinity do to transparency?
polymer-properties.why: Scattering at the boundaries between regions is what causes the cloudiness.

polymer-properties.q: Which has a sharp melting point?
polymer-properties.why: Amorphous material softens over a range instead.

polymer-properties.q: What does a long flexible spacer do to Tg?
polymer-properties.why: More mobility in the chain means less energy needed to unfreeze it.

polymer-properties.q: Why is HDPE rigid?
options: It has a higher formula weight
polymer-properties.why: The same repeat unit as LDPE, arranged differently.

polymer-properties.q: What does stretching do to a polymer's chains?
polymer-properties.why: Which is also how fibers are drawn to increase strength.

polymer-properties.q: Which property does crystallinity NOT increase?
polymer-properties.why: It reduces transparency, because ordered regions scatter light.

polymer-properties.q: How many transition temperatures can a polymer have?
polymer-properties.why: Tg for the amorphous regions and Tm for the crystalline ones.

polymer-design.q: A polymer backbone contains only carbons. What was the monomer?
polymer-design.why: Put the double bond back into the repeat unit.

polymer-design.q: A polymer backbone contains esters. What were the monomers?
polymer-design.why: Cut the acyl C-O bond of each ester: OH to the acid side, H to the alcohol side.

polymer-design.q: A polymer backbone contains amides. What were the monomers?
polymer-design.why: Cut every amide C-N bond.

polymer-design.q: A disconnection gives a fragment with one reactive group. What does that mean?
options: You cut in the wrong place
polymer-design.why: Every chain-forming monomer must have two, which is what let it join on both sides.

polymer-design.q: How do you check a polyester disconnection by atom count?
options: Monomers minus repeat unit should be two waters
polymer-design.why: One water per ester bond, and a diacid-plus-diol repeat unit has two. PET: 166 + 62 - 192 = 36.

polymer-design.q: Which feature gives high strength?
polymer-design.why: Rigid, straight chains that align along their whole length.

polymer-design.q: Which feature gives hydrolytic resistance?
polymer-design.why: Amides are the least reactive acyl derivative.

polymer-design.q: Which feature gives flexibility?
polymer-design.why: Both lower Tg and prevent packing.

polymer-design.q: Which feature gives transparency?
polymer-design.why: Crystalline regions scatter light at every boundary.

polymer-design.q: Which feature gives a shape that cannot be melted?
polymer-design.why: Three reactive sites gives a network.

polymer-design.q: Which feature gives degradability?
polymer-design.why: They hydrolyze, and enzymes can reach them.

polymer-design.q: Why do durability and persistence go together?
options: Both come from an unreactive backbone
polymer-design.why: The honest version of the plastics problem rather than a failure of chemistry.

polymer-design.q: What is mechanical recycling?
polymer-design.why: Thermoplastics only, and each cycle shortens the chains a little.

polymer-design.q: What is chemical recycling?
polymer-design.why: It needs a backbone bond that can be cleaved selectively.

polymer-design.q: Which plastic is most chemically recyclable?
polymer-design.why: Its ester bonds are a handle hydrolysis can select.

polymer-design.q: Why is polyethylene not chemically recyclable?
polymer-design.why: No bond hydrolysis can pick out from any other. Cracking it back to feedstock works, but that is pyrolysis, not selective cleavage.

polymer-design.q: Why can a thermoset not be recycled either way?
polymer-design.why: The hardest case at end of life.

polymer-design.q: What does PLA hydrolyze back to?
polymer-design.why: An ordinary metabolite, which is what makes it compostable.

polymer-design.q: What is the qualifier on PLA's biodegradability?
polymer-design.why: Biodegradable is a claim about conditions as much as about structure.

polymer-design.q: What decides whether a polymer can be chemically recycled?
polymer-design.why: One functional group is the whole difference.

polymer-design.q: What does each mechanical recycling cycle do?
polymer-design.why: Which is why mechanically recycled material degrades with reuse.

polymer-design.q: Which backbone is a handle for hydrolysis?
polymer-design.why: An amide is one too, though a more resistant one.

polymer-design.q: When was a polymer's end of life decided?
polymer-design.why: The backbone functional group is fixed by the monomer.

polymer-design.q: Which polymer can be both recycled and composted?
polymer-design.why: A polyester that hydrolyzes to a metabolite.

polymer-design.q: Why is a polyolefin so persistent?
polymer-design.why: The properties that make it cheap and inert make it permanent.

polymer-design.q: What must every fragment of a correct disconnection have?
polymer-design.why: That is the self-check that catches an error without knowing the compound.

polymer-design.q: Which property argues against crystallinity?
polymer-design.why: The other three all improve with crystallinity.

polymer-design.q: What does an amorphous rigid polymer get its rigidity from?
polymer-design.why: PMMA through bulky side groups; polycarbonate through rigid bisphenol A units in the backbone.

polymer-design.q: Which monomer would you add to make a thermoset?
polymer-design.why: A third reactive site lets chains tie to each other.

polymer-design.q: What is the honest summary of the plastics problem?
polymer-design.why: You cannot have an inert, durable material that also disappears.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: Adding water across a C=O gives what kind of product?
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: Two OH groups end up on the one former carbonyl carbon.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: A gem-diol is more commonly called a:
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: The common name records where it came from, not its structure.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: Which carbonyl is the least hydrated at equilibrium?
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: Only about 0.1%, since two methyls both crowd and feed the carbon.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: Acetaldehyde's percent hydrate is closest to:
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: One methyl instead of two puts it halfway between formaldehyde and acetone.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: Which hydrate is stable enough to isolate?
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: Its equilibrium sits essentially all the way over.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: Why is chloral almost completely hydrated?
options: The chlorines donate electron density to carbon
The chlorines strengthen the C=O bond
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: Three of them pulling makes the carbonyl carbon badly electron poor.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: What happens to the carbonyl carbon during hydration?
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: A flat carbon turns tetrahedral, and the substituents that sat 120 degrees apart are squeezed to about 109 — which is why crowding decides where the equilibrium sits.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: Hydration squeezes the substituent angles from about 120 degrees to:
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: Tetrahedral geometry, and groups that were comfortable at 120 no longer are.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: Why do two methyls disfavor the hydrate more than two hydrogens?
options: They block the oxygen lone pairs
They crowd the new sp3 carbon
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: Hydrogens have almost nothing to give up when the angle closes.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: Alkyl groups affect a carbonyl by:
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: That donation stabilizes the starting material, so it has less reason to react.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: Toward nucleophiles, the reactivity order is:
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: Sterics and electronics point the same way, and the hydration table measures it.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: Which two factors set the hydration equilibrium?
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: The same pair sets every carbonyl reactivity order in the chapter.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: Cyanohydrin formation is run with HCN plus a catalytic amount of cyanide. What goes wrong if only NaCN is used, with no HCN present?
options: Cyanide is too weak a nucleophile to attack the carbonyl
The alkoxide has no proton source, so the addition reverses
Cyanide attacks the carbonyl oxygen instead of the carbon
The carbonyl is protonated first and cannot be attacked
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: Two species are doing two jobs. Cyanide attacks the carbonyl carbon and leaves an alkoxide, and something has to hand that alkoxide a proton or it simply expels cyanide again and the equilibrium never closes. HCN is the proton source, and giving it up regenerates cyanide for the next turn, which is what makes the cyanide catalytic. HCN alone fails for the opposite reason: with its carbon holding a hydrogen instead of a lone pair, it is a poor nucleophile.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: Which is hydrated to a greater extent at equilibrium: acetophenone (PhCOCH3) or 2,2,2-trifluoroacetophenone (PhCOCF3)?
options: Acetophenone, because a methyl group is smaller than CF3
They are hydrated equally, since both are aryl ketones
The trifluoro compound, because three fluorines pull density from the carbonyl
Neither hydrates at all, because conjugation with the ring forbids it
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: Three effects are in play and two of them are identical across the pair: both are ketones and both are conjugated with the same ring, so those cancel. What differs is the second substituent. A methyl donates weakly; a CF3 withdraws strongly through three C-F bonds, leaving the carbonyl carbon markedly more electron-poor and the hydrate correspondingly more favorable. CF3 is also the bulkier group, so this is a case where electronics beats sterics — the same reasoning that makes hexafluoroacetone essentially fully hydrated.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: Cyanide adds to a carbonyl to give:
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: Attack at carbon, then protonation of the alkoxide.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: A cyanohydrin carbon carries which two groups?
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: One came from the old carbonyl oxygen, the other from cyanide.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: What makes cyanohydrin formation worth doing synthetically?
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: Hydration and bisulfite addition build no new carbon skeleton.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: Starting from butan-2-one, which sequence gives 2-hydroxy-2-methylbutanoic acid?
options: HCN with catalytic cyanide, then aqueous acid and heat
HCN with catalytic cyanide, then LiAlH4 and workup
Aqueous bisulfite, then aqueous acid and heat
Water and acid, then LiAlH4 and workup
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: Count the carbons in the target: one more than the ketone, and the new carbon is a carboxyl group sitting next to the old carbonyl carbon, which now holds an OH. That is a cyanohydrin whose nitrile has been hydrolyzed. Reduction would instead give a CH2NH2 and therefore an amino alcohol; a bisulfite adduct adds no carbon at all and just gives the ketone back; and hydration adds no carbon either.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: Cyanohydrin formation is run near pH 8-10. Why that range?
options: Both CN- and HCN are present
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: CN- is the nucleophile that attacks the carbonyl, and HCN is the acid that protonates the alkoxide that results. Too acidic and almost everything is HCN, with too little cyanide to start; too basic and there is no HCN left to finish the job, and the alkoxide simply expels cyanide again.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: Hydrolyzing a cyanohydrin's nitrile gives:
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: The nitrile becomes the acid and the OH is already in place.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: Reducing a cyanohydrin with LiAlH4 gives:
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: The nitrile carbon becomes CH2NH2, one carbon away from the OH.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: Which step turns a cyanohydrin into an unsaturated nitrile?
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: Losing the OH and an adjacent hydrogen conjugates the nitrile.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: A cyanohydrin extends the carbon chain by how many carbons?
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: And that one carbon arrives with a functional group already on it.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: Carbon dioxide plus a Grignard reagent gives:
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: Another one-carbon extension, chosen for what it leaves behind.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: A nitrile plus a Grignard reagent gives:
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: Same one-carbon logic, different functional group at the end.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: Sodium bisulfite adds to a carbonyl to give:
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: Solid and water soluble, which is exactly what makes it handy.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: Why is the bisulfite adduct useful?
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: Filter off the solid, then regenerate the carbonyl.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: Which of these will not form a bisulfite adduct?
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: The same crowding that keeps hindered ketones from hydrating.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: The bisulfite adduct is reversed by:
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: Reversibility is the point, since you want the carbonyl back.

hydrates-cyanohydrins.q: A ketone bearing three fluorines on the next carbon would hydrate:
hydrates-cyanohydrins.why: Fluorine pulls like chlorine does in chloral.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: An aldehyde is readily oxidized to:
aldehyde-oxidation.why: It is the one carbonyl in the chapter still able to climb a rung.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: Which reagent would you actually put over the arrow to convert butanal into butanoic acid?
options: Jones reagent, CrO3 in aqueous acid
aldehyde-oxidation.why: The tests in this section are diagnostics rather than preparations, so the practical answers are KMnO4, Jones reagent and Ag2O. Jones is the workhorse: it is aqueous, so the aldehyde hydrates and the oxidation runs on to the acid. PCC is deliberately anhydrous and stops at the aldehyde, borohydride reduces rather than oxidizes, and Tollens’ would technically work but nobody burns stoichiometric silver to make an ordinary acid.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: Oxidation at a carbon means:
options: Trading a C-H for a C-O
Trading a C-O for a C-H
aldehyde-oxidation.why: The same hydrogen bookkeeping that ranked the alcohols.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: Which species is actually oxidized when an aldehyde becomes an acid?
aldehyde-oxidation.why: A bare carbonyl carbon has no hydroxyl for an oxidant to grip.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: A molecule contains an aldehyde and, elsewhere, an alkene and a secondary alcohol. Which reagent oxidizes the aldehyde and leaves the other two alone?
aldehyde-oxidation.why: Take the constraints one at a time. Hot permanganate cleaves the alkene, and Jones oxidizes the secondary alcohol to a ketone as well as taking the aldehyde up, so both are too indiscriminate. PCC is an alcohol oxidant that would also touch the secondary alcohol, and it is the wrong tool for the aldehyde in any case. Silver(I) is the mild option: it takes the aldehyde to the acid and ignores alkenes and alcohols, which is exactly why the expense is sometimes worth paying.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: Why does PCC stop at the aldehyde?
aldehyde-oxidation.why: Anhydrous dichloromethane keeps the second oxidation from ever starting.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: Jones reagent takes a primary alcohol to:
aldehyde-oxidation.why: Water in the flask keeps regenerating the hydrate.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: Tollens' reagent contains which metal ion?
aldehyde-oxidation.why: Held in solution by ammonia under basic conditions.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: The active species in Tollens' reagent is:
aldehyde-oxidation.why: The diammine complex keeps silver soluble in base.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: Under Tollens' conditions the aldehyde ends up as:
aldehyde-oxidation.why: The solution is basic, so the acid is deprotonated as it forms.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: A positive Tollens' test looks like:
aldehyde-oxidation.why: Metallic silver plating out on clean glass.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: In a Tollens' test the silver(I) is:
aldehyde-oxidation.why: The aldehyde is what gets oxidized, so silver has to go the other way.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: What makes Tollens' useful as a test?
options: It oxidizes alcohols and alkenes too
aldehyde-oxidation.why: A reagent that picks out one group and skips its neighbors.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: Tollens’ reagent oxidizes aldehydes cleanly. Why is it still the wrong choice for preparing a carboxylic acid?
options: It is too mild to oxidize an aldehyde on a preparative scale
It would also oxidize any alkene in the molecule
The properties that make it a good test make it a poor preparation
It gives the carboxylate rather than an isolable product
aldehyde-oxidation.why: A diagnostic reagent is built to be feeble and selective, so that a positive result means one specific thing — and feeble and selective is the opposite of what a preparation wants, where throughput and cost decide. Silver is consumed stoichiometrically, which settles the matter on its own. The basic conditions do give the carboxylate first, but that is undone by acidifying on workup, so it is not the real objection; and leaving alkenes alone is a virtue, not a fault.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: Fehling's solution holds Cu(II) with which ligand?
aldehyde-oxidation.why: Benedict's is the one built on citrate.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: Why does fructose give a positive Benedict's test?
options: Base isomerizes it to an aldose
Its ring cannot open at all
aldehyde-oxidation.why: Through an enediol, which is why a free anomeric carbon rather than an aldehyde is the real test.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: A positive Fehling's or Benedict's test shows:
aldehyde-oxidation.why: The red solid drops out of the blue solution that was there before.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: An unknown gives a silver mirror with Tollens’ reagent and no precipitate with Fehling’s solution. What is the best conclusion?
options: It is a ketone, since the two tests disagree
It is an aromatic aldehyde, which Fehling’s handles badly
It contains no aldehyde, since Fehling’s was negative
It is a non-reducing sugar such as sucrose
aldehyde-oxidation.why: A positive Tollens’ needs a carbon carrying both an oxygen and a hydrogen, so an aldehyde or something in equilibrium with one is present; a ketone and a non-reducing sugar are both ruled out by it. The negative Fehling’s then looks like a contradiction, and it is resolved by remembering that Fehling’s has a known blind spot: it is unreliable with aromatic aldehydes. Treating a negative result from a reagent with a known weakness as evidence of absence is the trap being set.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: Which reagent pair is more robust and used clinically?
aldehyde-oxidation.why: Citrate holds the copper better than tartrate does.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: Fehling's solution is unreliable with:
aldehyde-oxidation.why: Aliphatic aldehydes are the case it handles well.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: Why does glucose test positive although it is drawn as a ring?
aldehyde-oxidation.why: Opening exposes the aldehyde the ring drawing hides.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: How much open-chain aldehyde does glucose hold at equilibrium?
aldehyde-oxidation.why: Delivered continuously, and consumed as fast as it appears.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: A sugar is called reducing because of:
options: What it does to the metal
aldehyde-oxidation.why: The sugar is in fact the thing being oxidized.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: Why is sucrose not a reducing sugar?
aldehyde-oxidation.why: The glycosidic bond ties up both anomeric carbons, and a free one is what a positive test needs.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: Lactose and maltose test positive because each:
aldehyde-oxidation.why: One ring can still open and deliver an aldehyde.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: Aldehydes oxidize in air by:
aldehyde-oxidation.why: No added reagent is needed at all.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: Air oxidizes an aldehyde by a radical chain. Which hydrogen does the chain abstract, and why that one?
options: A hydrogen on the alpha carbon, which is the most acidic
A hydrogen on the alkyl chain, which is the most plentiful
The hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon, giving a stabilized acyl radical
The hydrogen of the hydrate’s O-H group
aldehyde-oxidation.why: Radical chains take whichever hydrogen leaves the most stable radical, and here that is the aldehyde C-H at roughly 88 kcal/mol — the weakest C-H in the molecule, because the acyl radical it leaves behind has its unpaired electron next to the carbonyl and delocalized onto it. Oxygen then adds to that acyl radical, and the resulting peroxy radical takes the same hydrogen from the next molecule, so the chain propagates. Acidity governs enolate chemistry, not radical abstraction, and a ketone has no such C-H at all.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: Convert butan-1-ol into butanoic acid, stopping at butanal on the way to check it. Which two reagents, in order?
options: Jones reagent, then PCC in dichloromethane
PCC in dichloromethane, then Jones reagent
aldehyde-oxidation.why: The first step has to stop one rung short, which means anhydrous conditions: with no water there is no hydrate, and with no hydrate the second oxidation has nothing with an O-H to attack. PCC does that. The second step wants the opposite — aqueous Cr(VI), so the aldehyde hydrates and is oxidized again — which is Jones. Running them in the other order finishes the job before the aldehyde can be isolated, borohydride reduces rather than oxidizes, and Tollens’ is far too weak to touch an alcohol.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: Oxidizing a ketone requires:
aldehyde-oxidation.why: There is no hydrogen on that carbon to take.

aldehyde-oxidation.q: The Baeyer-Villiger converts a ketone to:
aldehyde-oxidation.why: An oxygen is inserted into one of the C-C bonds.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: By-products of the SOCl2 route to an acid chloride?
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: Both leave as gases, so the equilibrium is pulled forward.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: Oxalyl chloride with catalytic DMF releases:
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: All three are gases, which is why workup is an evaporation.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: Propanoic acid is treated with SOCl2, then with one equivalent of aniline (PhNH2) and no other base. What is the yield problem?
options: Aniline is not nucleophilic enough to react at all
The acyl chloride hydrolyzes before the aniline reaches it
Half the aniline is protonated by the HCl released, capping the yield near 50%
Two acyl groups add to the same nitrogen
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: Each acylation releases one HCl. The most basic species in the flask is the amine, so it takes that proton and becomes an anilinium ion with no lone pair left to attack. One equivalent of amine therefore supplies only half an equivalent of nucleophile. The fix is a second equivalent of aniline, or one equivalent plus pyridine - basic enough to mop up HCl, too weakly nucleophilic to compete for the carbonyl.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: Which target CANNOT be reached from a carboxylic acid by SOCl2 followed by one nucleophile?
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: Acyl substitution swaps the leaving group and keeps the carbonyl: an alcohol gives the ester, an amine the amide, a carboxylate the anhydride. A secondary alcohol would need the carbonyl reduced AND one new carbon substituent added, which is not a substitution at all - it needs a hydride and an organometallic, and it is a different kind of step.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: Why are SOCl2 and oxalyl chloride preferred?
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: Gases escape as they form, driving the reaction to completion.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: Why is a carboxylic acid a poor acylating agent for amines?
options: It has no leaving group at all
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: Acid-base transfer wins, leaving an ammonium carboxylate dead end.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: Typical pKa of a carboxylic acid:
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: Acidic enough that any good nucleophile takes the proton instead.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: Which nucleophile converts an acid chloride to an ester?
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: An alcohol, and unlike Fischer esterification the step is irreversible.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: Which reagent turns an acid chloride into an anhydride?
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: The carboxylate, not the neutral acid, is the nucleophile.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: How many equivalents of amine are needed for amide formation?
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: Trace the protons. The first equivalent of amine attacks the acyl chloride, chloride leaves, and the nitrogen still carries a proton it must lose - so one HCl is released per acylation. The most basic thing in the flask is the amine itself, so that HCl protonates a second molecule of amine and switches it off as a nucleophile. Two equivalents therefore give one equivalent of amide; one equivalent gives you half.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: Why does amide formation consume extra amine?
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: An ammonium ion has no lone pair left to attack with.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: What replaces the sacrificial second equivalent of amine?
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: Basic enough to take up HCl without competing for the carbonyl.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: Pyridine attacks an acid chloride. Why does that not spoil the acylation?
options: The acylpyridinium passes the acyl on
HCl protonates it before it attacks
Its sp2 lone pair sits in the ring plane
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: Pyridine is a perfectly competent nucleophile toward an acid chloride: it attacks and gives an N-acylpyridinium ion. That is not a loss, because the acylpyridinium is itself a potent acylating agent — it hands the acyl group on to the amine, often faster than the direct route would. This is the whole basis of DMAP catalysis, where 4-dimethylaminopyridine speeds acylations up thousands of times by exactly this detour. And pyridine has no N–H, so unlike the amine it can never end up in the product. The sp² lone pair does explain pyridine's modest basicity (pKaH 5.2); it does not make pyridine a poor nucleophile.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: Leaving group expelled from an anhydride:
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: Trace the tetrahedral intermediate: the nucleophile has added, and the oxygen now pushes back down and has to expel one of the two acyl-oxygen groups. What leaves is the other half of the anhydride, as a carboxylate. That anion is resonance-stabilized over two oxygens, so it departs willingly - but its conjugate acid is pKa about 5 against HCl's -7, which is exactly why an anhydride sits one rung below an acid chloride.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: Correct reactivity order?
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: Tracks leaving-group ability: chloride beats carboxylate beats alkoxide.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: Standard acetylating agent:
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: Work down the ladder. Acetic acid needs activation before an amine or alcohol will acylate at all; ethyl acetate and acetonitrile are at or below the ester rung and far too sluggish. Acetic anhydride is the compromise: reactive enough to acylate an alcohol or an amine directly at room temperature, yet stable enough to weigh out in air, which an acetyl chloride is not.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: Acetic anhydride acetylates which group of salicylic acid?
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: That single acetylation converts salicylic acid into aspirin.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: By-product of the aspirin synthesis:
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: Half the anhydride leaves unused, which is the atom-economy cost.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: Main drawback of acylating with an anhydride:
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: One acyl group becomes product, the other becomes waste.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: Heating succinic acid gives:
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: Water is expelled intramolecularly to close a five-membered ring.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: Ring size formed when phthalic acid is heated:
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: Diacids that would need a larger ring do not cyclize this way.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: A cyclic anhydride plus an amine first gives:
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: The amine attacks one of the two carbonyls and the tetrahedral intermediate expels the other as a carboxylate - the ordinary anhydride reaction. The difference is that the carboxylate is tethered to the amide by the carbon chain, so it cannot wander off. What you isolate is an amic acid: an amide at one end, a carboxylic acid at the other, on one molecule. Heat that and it loses water and closes to the imide.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: An amic acid becomes an imide on treatment with:
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: A second intramolecular condensation closes the ring again.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: Which of these is an imide?
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: Two acyl groups share one nitrogen rather than one oxygen.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: An acid chloride with AlCl3 ionizes to:
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: That cation is the electrophile the aromatic ring attacks.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: Friedel-Crafts acylation forms which bond?
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: The only reaction here that builds the skeleton rather than decorating it.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: Benzoic acid to benzophenone: which reagent is used first?
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: The ring cannot be acylated until the acid is activated; AlCl3 comes second.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: SOCl2 converts alcohols into:
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: Same reagent, same idea, different substrate. An alcohol's OH is a terrible leaving group; SOCl2 converts it into a chlorosulfite, which is an excellent one, and chloride then displaces it to give the alkyl chloride. On a carboxylic acid the sulfur does exactly the same thing to the carboxyl OH. In both cases the by-products are SO2 and HCl, both gases, so the reaction is pulled to completion.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: What does SOCl2 do to an OH group?
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: A terrible leaving group is swapped for an excellent one.

acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.q: How does esterification via an acid chloride differ from Fischer?
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides.why: Compare the leaving groups. Fischer esterification has to expel water and can re-form the acid just as easily, so it settles at an equilibrium near 65% and must be driven with excess alcohol or by removing water. Acylation of an alcohol by an acid chloride expels chloride, which is far too weak a base to come back and attack the ester, so the reaction runs to completion and needs no acid catalyst.

nitriles.q: Oxidation level of the nitrile carbon:
nitriles.why: Three bonds to heteroatom, all of them to the same nitrogen.

nitriles.q: Which sits on the same oxidation rung as a nitrile?
nitriles.why: Also three carbon-heteroatom bonds, so interconversion needs no oxidant.

nitriles.q: Which sequence converts benzyl bromide, PhCH2Br, into 1-phenylpropan-2-one, PhCH2COCH3?
nitriles.why: Count first: seven carbons in, nine out, so two have to be added and the product is a ketone. Cyanide adds one by SN2 on the primary benzylic bromide, giving PhCH2CN. A methyl Grignard then adds once to the nitrile carbon - it cannot add twice, because the intermediate is an imine anion rather than a carbonyl - and aqueous workup hydrolyzes that imine to the ketone, which is where the second carbon came from. Route 1 gives an amine, route 3 an acid, and route 4 adds only one carbon.

nitriles.q: Converting a nitrile into an amide counts as:
nitriles.why: Count the bonds to heteroatoms on the carbon in question. A nitrile carbon has three, all to the same nitrogen; an amide carbon has three too - two to the carbonyl oxygen and one to nitrogen. Same count means same oxidation level, so adding water across the triple bond is a sideways move along the rung and needs no oxidant. Carry on under the same conditions and hydrolysis goes one step further to the acid, still on the same rung.

nitriles.q: RCH2X plus NaCN gives:
nitriles.why: Cyanide displaces halide and the chain gains one carbon.

nitriles.q: Mechanism of cyanide with a primary alkyl halide:
nitriles.why: Backside attack, which is why primary substrates are required.

nitriles.q: An unknown C4H7N shows a sharp medium IR band at 2247 cm-1 and no absorption between 1650 and 1800 cm-1. Which structure fits?
nitriles.why: Two of these can be thrown out on the formula alone: butanamide is C4H9NO and but-1-yne is C4H6 with no nitrogen at all. That leaves two genuine C4H7N isomers, and only the spectrum separates them. C4H7N has two degrees of unsaturation, and both a C-N triple bond and a C=C plus a C=N account for exactly two, so counting does not settle it. The 2247 band does. The 2500-2000 window is almost empty in an ordinary spectrum, and a sharp medium band there means a triple bond - a nitrile, since the alkyne is already gone. The imine CH2=CHCH2CH=NH has nothing to put at 2247 and would instead show a C=N stretch near 1670, which the stem explicitly rules out by reporting nothing between 1650 and 1800. So the answer is butanenitrile, and notice that the negative evidence - an empty region - did as much work as the peak that is there.

nitriles.q: Approximate pKa of HCN:
nitriles.why: Weakly basic conjugate base, so elimination is not promoted.

nitriles.q: 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane + NaCN in DMSO, heated. Major product?
nitriles.why: Start with what cannot happen: three alkyl groups shield the tertiary carbon, so there is no backside attack and no SN2, which takes the nitrile off the table however good a nucleophile cyanide is. DMSO then removes the other escape route — there is no water to solvolyze the halide, so no tertiary alcohol. That leaves elimination. Cyanide is a weak base (HCN pKa 9.2) and a poor one for E2, but with heat and nothing competing it is enough, and Zaitsev gives the more substituted alkene. Notice how much work the solvent is doing: run the same halide in hot aqueous ethanol and solvolysis takes over and you get mostly the alcohol — and still no nitrile. That is the standing limit on cyanide chain extension: primary substrates work, secondary are poor, tertiary give none of the nitrile at all.

nitriles.q: Dehydrating a primary amide gives:
nitriles.why: Dehydration removes H2O from RCONH2, and the carbon ends up with three bonds to nitrogen instead of two to oxygen and one to nitrogen - the same count either way. So it is a move along the rung, not a reduction, which is why SOCl2 or P2O5 does it and no reducing agent is involved. Run it the other way with water and heat and the nitrile hydrates back to the amide.

nitriles.q: Which reagents dehydrate a primary amide?
nitriles.why: Both strip water from the amide rather than changing oxidation level.

nitriles.q: A cyanohydrin comes from cyanide plus which of these?
nitriles.why: Addition to the carbonyl leaves an OH on the neighboring carbon.

nitriles.q: The Sandmeyer route to an aryl nitrile starts from:
nitriles.why: CuCN replaces the nitrogen that leaves as N2.

nitriles.q: Why can't EAS put a CN group on a benzene ring?
options: There is no electrophilic cyanide reagent
The CN group is too large
nitriles.why: So aryl nitriles come from a diazonium salt, or from dehydrating an aryl amide.

nitriles.q: RCN with aqueous H3O+ and heat gives:
nitriles.why: Through the amide, and no oxidant is needed because it is a move along the rung.

nitriles.q: Nitrile hydrolysis passes through:
nitriles.why: Water adds across the C-N triple bond to give first an imidic acid, which tautomerizes to the amide - and the amide is a real, isolable compound: stop at milder conditions and that is what you get. Push with more heat and more acid or base and the amide is hydrolyzed in turn to the carboxylic acid. Two acyl substitutions in series, both sideways moves on the same oxidation rung.

nitriles.q: Mild hydrolysis of a nitrile can be stopped at:
nitriles.why: Stopping early exploits the amide being an intermediate, not a side product.

nitriles.q: LiAlH4 then water converts RCN into:
nitriles.why: Two hydrides are delivered and the nitrogen stays attached.

nitriles.q: Butanenitrile with LiAlH4 gives:
nitriles.why: The nitrile carbon becomes the CH2, so no carbon is gained or lost.

nitriles.q: DIBAL-H, one equivalent at -78 C, converts RCN into:
nitriles.why: Workup hydrolyzes the intermediate rather than reducing it further.

nitriles.q: The species present before DIBAL-H workup is:
nitriles.why: It survives until water is added because nothing attacks it.

nitriles.q: Why does DIBAL-H stop after a single hydride?
nitriles.why: One hydride adds to the nitrile carbon and the product is a metalated imine anion. An anion is not an electrophile, so there is nothing left for a second hydride to attack, however long you wait or how much reagent you add - the aldehyde only appears when water hydrolyzes that anion on workup. Contrast LiAlH4, which is not stopped by anything: rationing it to one equivalent does not give an aldehyde, it gives a mixture. The reagent is crippled, not rationed.

nitriles.q: A Grignard on a nitrile, after workup, gives:
nitriles.why: The carbon-carbon bond forms before any carbonyl exists.

nitriles.q: Why does only one Grignard equivalent add to a nitrile?
nitriles.why: An imine salt is not an electrophile, so the reagent has nothing to attack.

nitriles.q: With an ester, what does the Grignard release mid-reaction?
nitriles.why: That ketone is more electrophilic than the ester, so attack repeats.

nitriles.q: The C-N triple bond stretch appears near:
nitriles.why: Sharp and medium, in a region almost nothing else occupies.

nitriles.q: Why is that nitrile stretch diagnostic?
nitriles.why: Between 2500 and 2000 there is little else to confuse it with.

nitriles.q: RX to RCN to RCOOH accomplishes:
nitriles.why: Follow the carbon. Cyanide does an SN2 on RX and the CN carbon is new, so RCN has one more carbon than RX. Hydrolysis then converts that same carbon into the COOH carbon without adding or losing any, since a nitrile and an acid sit on the same oxidation rung. Net result: one carbon longer, finishing as an acid. The Grignard-plus-CO2 route achieves the identical extension, and you pick between them on what else the substrate carries.

nitriles.q: The cyanide route is chosen over a Grignard when the substrate has:
nitriles.why: A Grignard would be destroyed by the acidic proton before reacting.

nitriles.q: The Grignard route to a chain-extended acid fails on substrates with:
nitriles.why: Any acidic proton quenches the organometallic reagent.

alpha-halogenation.q: Where does the halogen end up in alpha-halogenation?
alpha-halogenation.why: Both the enol and the enolate are nucleophilic at that carbon.

alpha-halogenation.q: Under acid, what is the slow step?
alpha-halogenation.why: Halogen is consumed only as fast as enol is made.

alpha-halogenation.q: Which conditions give clean monohalogenation?
alpha-halogenation.why: The halogen makes the carbonyl harder to protonate, so the second enol forms more slowly.

alpha-halogenation.q: Why does acid halogenation stop after one halogen?
options: The acid is consumed in the first step
The halogen makes the carbonyl less basic
The halogen blocks the alpha carbon sterically
The halogen makes the alpha H less acidic
alpha-halogenation.why: Enolization needs the oxygen protonated, and withdrawal makes that harder.

alpha-halogenation.q: Why does base halogenation run past one halogen?
options: The next alpha H is more acidic
alpha-halogenation.why: Halogen stabilizes the next enolate's charge, so each step speeds up the one after.

alpha-halogenation.q: Which species attacks Br2 under acidic conditions?
alpha-halogenation.why: Acid generates the neutral tautomer, not the anion.

alpha-halogenation.q: Which species attacks Br2 under basic conditions?
alpha-halogenation.why: Base removes an alpha proton outright.

alpha-halogenation.q: The haloform reaction needs which substrate?
options: An aldehyde with no alpha H
alpha-halogenation.why: Three identical hydrogens on one carbon are required.

alpha-halogenation.q: What reagents run the haloform reaction?
options: Iodine with no base at all
alpha-halogenation.why: Every methyl hydrogen must be replaced before cleavage happens.

alpha-halogenation.q: What leaves in the haloform cleavage step?
alpha-halogenation.why: Three halogens stabilize the departing carbanion.

alpha-halogenation.q: The cleavage step of the haloform reaction is:
options: An SN2 displacement at the alpha carbon
alpha-halogenation.why: Hydroxide adds and the tetrahedral intermediate collapses.

alpha-halogenation.q: What are the haloform products?
alpha-halogenation.why: Acidic workup then delivers the free acid.

alpha-halogenation.q: Acetone with excess I2 and NaOH gives which acid?
alpha-halogenation.why: Three carbons become two; the methyl leaves as CHI3.

alpha-halogenation.q: How does the haloform reaction change the carbon count?
alpha-halogenation.why: The methyl group departs as the haloform itself.

alpha-halogenation.q: Which compound gives a positive iodoform test?
alpha-halogenation.why: Alkaline hypoiodite oxidizes it to a methyl ketone first.

alpha-halogenation.q: Which alcohol gives a positive iodoform test?
alpha-halogenation.why: It is the primary alcohol that oxidizes to acetaldehyde.

alpha-halogenation.q: What fragment does a positive iodoform test report?
alpha-halogenation.why: It is not a test for ketones as such.

alpha-halogenation.q: Why will a carboxylic acid not halogenate directly?
alpha-halogenation.why: The hydroxyl oxygen already donates into the carbonyl.

alpha-halogenation.q: What are the Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reagents?
alpha-halogenation.why: Red phosphorus serves as well, making PBr3 in situ.

alpha-halogenation.q: What species does HVZ actually halogenate?
alpha-halogenation.why: That derivative enolizes where the acid will not.

alpha-halogenation.q: What is the HVZ product?
alpha-halogenation.why: Exchange with more starting acid releases it and carries the cycle on.

alpha-halogenation.q: HVZ followed by excess NH3 gives:
alpha-halogenation.why: Ammonia displaces the alpha bromide by SN2.

alpha-halogenation.q: HVZ followed by water gives:
alpha-halogenation.why: Same SN2 displacement, different nucleophile.

alpha-halogenation.q: Amino acids made by HVZ then ammonia are:
alpha-halogenation.why: Nothing in the sequence selects one face over the other.

alpha-halogenation.q: Why is an alpha-halo ketone a good alkylating agent?
options: That position is activated toward SN2
The halide there is a poor leaving group
alpha-halogenation.why: Sitting next to the carbonyl lowers the barrier to displacement.

alpha-halogenation.q: Treating an alpha-bromo ketone with base gives:
alpha-halogenation.why: Loss of HX reaches the same enone the aldol condensation does.

alpha-halogenation.q: 3,3-Dimethylbutan-2-one, CH3COC(CH3)3, is treated with excess I2 and NaOH, then acidified. What is isolated?
options: No reaction, since the substrate has no alpha hydrogen
The triiodo ketone, with no cleavage
alpha-halogenation.why: The only alpha carbon carrying hydrogens is the methyl attached straight to the carbonyl, so base iodinates it three times and hydroxide then adds to the carbonyl and expels the CI3 group. What is left is the acyl fragment, (CH3)3C-CO2H. Count the carbons: six in, five out, because the haloform reaction always costs one.
