alpha-halogenation.q: 2-Methylcyclohexanone is treated with one equivalent of Br2 in acetic acid. Where does the bromine end up?
options: On C2, the carbon that already carries the methyl
alpha-halogenation.why: Under acid the reaction runs through the enol, and the two enols are free to equilibrate, so the more stable of them - the more substituted one - is the one that reacts and it decides where the halogen lands. That is C2. It is the same more-substituted-is-more-stable logic used for thermodynamic enolates, arriving one section early.

alpha-halogenation.q: You need to convert butanoic acid into 2-aminobutanoic acid. Which sequence does it?
options: Br2 with a catalytic amount of PBr3, then excess NH3
Br2 with excess NaOH, then NH3
Br2 in acetic acid, then NH3
alpha-halogenation.why: A carboxylic acid has essentially no enol of its own, so direct halogenation fails in acid and in base alike. Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky makes the acyl bromide with PBr3 first; that enolizes, brominates at the alpha carbon, and exchanges back to give 2-bromobutanoic acid. Ammonia then displaces the bromide by SN2, in excess because the amino acid product is itself nucleophilic. The product is racemic.

alpha-halogenation.q: Which of these gives a NEGATIVE iodoform test?
alpha-halogenation.why: The test reports a CH3CO fragment, or a CH3CH(OH) fragment that alkaline hypoiodite oxidizes into one. 3-Pentanol is CH3CH2CH(OH)CH2CH3: its carbinol carbon carries two ethyl groups and no methyl, so oxidation gives 3-pentanone, which has no methyl on the carbonyl and can never form a CI3 to expel. The other three all carry the reported fragment.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: In 2-methylcyclohexanone, what is C6?
enolate-regiochemistry.why: C2 is the crowded side; C6 has nothing on it.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: How many ring hydrogens sit on C2 of 2-methylcyclohexanone?
enolate-regiochemistry.why: The methyl group occupies what would be the second one.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: Deprotonating C6 of 2-methylcyclohexanone gives:
enolate-regiochemistry.why: The less substituted C=C, which is the kinetic choice.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: Deprotonating C2 of 2-methylcyclohexanone gives a C=C that is:
enolate-regiochemistry.why: The methyl already sits on a carbon of the new double bond.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: Which base gives the kinetic enolate?
enolate-regiochemistry.why: Bulky, and strong enough to make deprotonation irreversible.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: Which conditions give the thermodynamic enolate?
options: LDA in THF at -78 degrees C
enolate-regiochemistry.why: Reversible deprotonation lets the mixture settle on the stable enolate.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: What makes LDA deprotonation irreversible?
options: Its poor solubility in cold THF
enolate-regiochemistry.why: Against a ketone's 20, deprotonation goes to completion.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: Why does LDA pick the less hindered alpha carbon?
enolate-regiochemistry.why: Two isopropyl groups do the discriminating; strength alone would not.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: Why is C6 deprotonated faster in 2-methylcyclohexanone?
options: Two open protons instead of one
The resulting anion is more stable
Its C=C is the more substituted
C6 is closer to the carbonyl
enolate-regiochemistry.why: Statistics and access both point the same way.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: Why add the ketone to the base, not the reverse?
enolate-regiochemistry.why: Leftover ketone shuttles protons and equilibrates the two enolates.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: What temperature is standard for the kinetic enolate?
enolate-regiochemistry.why: Cold enough that nothing equilibrates once it has formed.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: LDA at room temperature - does its own deprotonation reverse and hand the proton back to the base?
enolate-regiochemistry.why: LDA's deprotonation does not reverse at any temperature, so warmth alone cannot undo it - that is the point of the question. A separate route is still open at room temperature, though: the diisopropylamine LDA generated can shuttle protons between the two enolates, which erodes the regiochemistry over time. An irreversible base, and a route still open.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: What does thermodynamic control require here?
enolate-regiochemistry.why: Only a reversible first step lets the stable enolate accumulate.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: Which enolate accumulates under equilibrating conditions?
enolate-regiochemistry.why: It is the more stable one, and everything can revert to reach it.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: Which rule ranks the two enolates for stability?
enolate-regiochemistry.why: The same ranking that makes Zaitsev products favored.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: What lets the two enolates interconvert?
options: A proton donor left in the flask
enolate-regiochemistry.why: Leftover ketone or the amine the base generated will do it; NaH is irreversible and still thermodynamic.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: Where is the branch point in this control problem?
enolate-regiochemistry.why: Reversing it just moves a proton back onto the ketone.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: A ketone plus a secondary amine gives:
enolate-regiochemistry.why: A primary amine would stop at the imine instead.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: Where does an enamine put its double bond?
enolate-regiochemistry.why: The substituted alternative twists the nitrogen lone pair out of alignment.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: An enamine is nucleophilic at:
enolate-regiochemistry.why: The nitrogen lone pair pushes electron density out to that carbon.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: Why does an enamine stop after one alkylation?
options: Alkylation gives an iminium, not a nucleophile
It is less reactive than an enolate
The amine is consumed in the first step
The product precipitates out of solution
enolate-regiochemistry.why: No nucleophilic carbon is left and no base is present to restore one, so a second alkylation is impossible.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: What completes the Stork enamine sequence?
enolate-regiochemistry.why: Alkylate the enamine first, then unmask the carbonyl.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: Enolate alkylation proceeds by which mechanism?
enolate-regiochemistry.why: That is exactly what limits which halides are usable.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: Which halide alkylates a lithium enolate cleanly?
enolate-regiochemistry.why: Methyl and primary halides are the reliable ones.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: A tertiary halide with a lithium enolate gives:
enolate-regiochemistry.why: The enolate acts as a base rather than as a nucleophile.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: Secondary halides with lithium enolates give:
enolate-regiochemistry.why: Enough SN2 to tempt you, enough E2 to hurt the yield.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: 2-Methylcyclohexanone is added to one equivalent of LDA in THF at -78 C, and iodomethane is then added. What is the major product?
enolate-regiochemistry.why: LDA at -78 C with the ketone added to the base gives the kinetic enolate, formed at C6 - the open CH2 with two hydrogens. Nothing in the flask can equilibrate it, so C6 is still the nucleophilic carbon when CH3I arrives and the new methyl lands there. Under NaOEt in ethanol at room temperature the same two reagents give 2,2-dimethylcyclohexanone instead.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: 2-Methylcyclohexanone is treated with NaOEt in ethanol at room temperature, then with iodomethane. What is the major product?
options: No reaction, ethoxide being too weak a base
enolate-regiochemistry.why: Ethoxide's deprotonation reverses, so the two enolates interconvert and the population collects in the more stable one, the trisubstituted C1=C2 enolate. Alkylation therefore happens at C2, the carbon that already carries a methyl, giving the quaternary 2,2-dimethyl product. Ethoxide being too weak to deprotonate completely is not a problem here; it is the whole mechanism of thermodynamic control.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: A chemist forms the kinetic enolate of 2-methylcyclohexanone with LDA at -78 C, then lets the flask warm to room temperature for an hour before adding the electrophile. What has gone wrong?
options: The enolate has been protonated by the THF solvent
LDA reverses its own deprotonation on warming
Nothing: temperature stops mattering once the enolate has formed
The diisopropylamine in the flask shuttles protons, so the mixture drifts thermodynamic
enolate-regiochemistry.why: LDA's deprotonation never reverses, so that route really is shut. But forming the enolate also generated a full equivalent of diisopropylamine, which is a proton donor, and warming lets it carry a proton from one alpha carbon to the other. The cold in the recipe is there to stop the amine, not to stop the base.

enolate-regiochemistry.q: You want 2-benzyl-6-methylcyclohexanone from 2-methylcyclohexanone and benzyl bromide. Which conditions?
options: NaOEt in EtOH, warm; then PhCH2Br
NaH, warm, several hours; then PhCH2Br
LDA (1 eq), THF, -78 C, ketone added to the base; then PhCH2Br
LDA (1 eq), THF, 0 C, base added dropwise to the ketone; then PhCH2Br
enolate-regiochemistry.why: The benzyl group has to land on C6, the unsubstituted carbon, which means the kinetic enolate: LDA, one equivalent, -78 C, with the ketone added to the base. NaOEt and NaH are both equilibrating conditions that leave a route open between the two enolates, so they alkylate at C2. Adding LDA dropwise to the ketone instead gets the base right and the technique wrong: dripping LDA into a flask of ketone leaves un-deprotonated ketone in solution, and free ketone shuttles protons between the two enolates until the more substituted one wins. The halide is fine either way, since benzylic halides are excellent SN2 partners for an enolate.

amine-synthesis.q: Why does ammonia plus RX give mixtures?
options: Each new amine is more nucleophilic
Ammonia is a very poor nucleophile
Alkyl halides cannot undergo SN2 here
The nitrogen lone pair is delocalized
amine-synthesis.why: Each added alkyl group pushes electron density onto nitrogen, so the product outruns the ammonia still in the flask.

amine-synthesis.q: Direct alkylation of ammonia delivers what?
amine-synthesis.why: Relative rates decide it, so adding less halide does not help; only a big excess of ammonia biases it.

amine-synthesis.q: When is runaway alkylation actually welcome?
options: Making an amide from an acid chloride
amine-synthesis.why: There is nowhere further to alkylate, so one compound comes out.

amine-synthesis.q: You need pentan-1-amine, CH3(CH2)4NH2, and the only carbon source on the shelf is 1-bromobutane. Which sequence works?
options: Excess NH3, then distill the product
amine-synthesis.why: Count first. 1-Bromobutane has four carbons and the target has five, so the route must ADD one. Azide and Gabriel both hand back exactly the skeleton you put in, so both would give butylamine, one carbon short, and excess ammonia has the same problem plus a mixture. Cyanide brings the extra carbon: 1-bromobutane plus NaCN gives pentanenitrile, and LiAlH4 turns the nitrile carbon into the CH2 bearing nitrogen.

amine-synthesis.q: Why can phthalimide be alkylated only once?
amine-synthesis.why: The imide nitrogen's lone pair is also tied into both carbonyls.

amine-synthesis.q: Which step frees the amine in a Gabriel synthesis?
amine-synthesis.why: Hot aqueous acid or base does the same job less gently.

amine-synthesis.q: Gabriel synthesis gives which class of amine?
amine-synthesis.why: The nitrogen leaves the imide carrying just one alkyl group.

amine-synthesis.q: Which of these halides would give the best yield in the alkylation step of a Gabriel synthesis?
amine-synthesis.why: The step is an SN2, so tertiary halides give only alkene, a secondary one gives poor yields with elimination alongside, and bromobenzene is an aryl halide, which does not do SN2 at all.

amine-synthesis.q: Why does azide displacement avoid over-alkylation?
amine-synthesis.why: Nothing left after the displacement can attack more halide.

amine-synthesis.q: Which reagents reduce an alkyl azide to an amine?
amine-synthesis.why: Both leave the nitrogen attached to the same carbon it displaced onto.

amine-synthesis.q: Azide displacement gives which class of amine?
amine-synthesis.why: Only one alkyl group ever reaches that nitrogen.

amine-synthesis.q: Which single reagent converts butanamide, CH3CH2CH2CONH2, into butylamine?
amine-synthesis.why: LiAlH4 reduces the amide C=O all the way to CH2, so four carbons go in and four come out: butanamide gives butylamine. Br2/NaOH is the Hofmann rearrangement, which takes the same starting material to PROPYLamine by expelling the carbonyl carbon as CO2 - one substrate, one carbon's difference, decided entirely by the reagent.

amine-synthesis.q: 1-Bromopropane with NaCN, then LiAlH4, gives:
amine-synthesis.why: Three carbons in, four out, because cyanide supplies one.

amine-synthesis.q: How does reductive amination build the C–N bond?
amine-synthesis.why: No leaving group is displaced, so the product amine has nothing to attack.

amine-synthesis.q: Which hydride reagent suits reductive amination?
amine-synthesis.why: It survives the mildly acidic pH that imine formation wants.

amine-synthesis.q: Why is NaBH4 wrong for reductive amination?
amine-synthesis.why: The ketone is consumed before it has a chance to condense.

amine-synthesis.q: What pH does reductive amination need?
amine-synthesis.why: The attenuated hydride reagents were chosen to tolerate that range.

amine-synthesis.q: Which amines can reductive amination deliver?
amine-synthesis.why: One carbonyl and one amine in decides the product.

amine-synthesis.q: Why is acylation of an amine self-limiting?
amine-synthesis.why: Its lone pair is tied up in the carbonyl.

amine-synthesis.q: What does LiAlH4 do to an amide carbonyl?
amine-synthesis.why: No carbon is lost, so the skeleton is unchanged.

amine-synthesis.q: Cleanest general route to a secondary amine?
amine-synthesis.why: Every SN2 route on a nitrogen surrogate stops at primary.

amine-synthesis.q: RCOCl + R'NH2, then LiAlH4, gives:
amine-synthesis.why: The carbonyl becomes CH2 and both alkyl groups stay on nitrogen.

amine-synthesis.q: The Hofmann rearrangement changes carbon count how?
amine-synthesis.why: The old carbonyl carbon leaves as CO2.

amine-synthesis.q: Butanamide with Br2 and NaOH gives:
amine-synthesis.why: Four carbons in, three out.

amine-synthesis.q: In the Hofmann rearrangement, what migrates?
amine-synthesis.why: That migration is what builds the isocyanate.

amine-synthesis.q: Which intermediate do Hofmann and Curtius share?
amine-synthesis.why: Its hydrolysis is where the carbon is lost in both.

amine-synthesis.q: How is the Curtius rearrangement started?
amine-synthesis.why: It reaches the same isocyanate without bromine.

amine-synthesis.q: (R)-2-bromobutane is treated with NaN3, then with H2 over Pd. What is the product?
options: Butan-2-amine with the configuration inverted at that carbon
Butan-2-amine with the configuration retained throughout
A racemic mixture of the two butan-2-amines
But-1-ene, because azide is too basic to substitute
amine-synthesis.why: Azide displacement is an SN2: the nucleophile attacks the backside of the C-Br carbon and the configuration inverts. Reducing the azide to the amine never touches that carbon, so the inversion survives into the product. Note that the R/S letter may or may not flip with it - check the CIP priorities separately from the geometry. This control is a reason to pick azide over reductive amination, which builds the bond on a flat C=N and gives a racemic product.

amine-synthesis.q: First question when choosing an amine synthesis?
options: Is the halide primary or secondary?
amine-synthesis.why: That cuts most of the table before substitution level matters.

amine-synthesis.q: Why can Gabriel never give a tertiary amine?
amine-synthesis.why: The nitrogen leaves the imide with a single substituent.

hofmann-elimination.q: Why can an amine not undergo E2 directly?
options: R2N− is a poor leaving group
hofmann-elimination.why: Very strong bases make very poor leaving groups.

hofmann-elimination.q: What converts the amine into an E2 substrate?
hofmann-elimination.why: Nitrogen ends up quaternary and positively charged.

hofmann-elimination.q: What actually leaves in a Hofmann elimination?
hofmann-elimination.why: It carries no negative charge away, unlike R2N−.

hofmann-elimination.q: Why is a trialkylamine a good leaving group?
options: It leaves with the negative charge
It is a very strong base
hofmann-elimination.why: The nitrogen was positive before it left and uncharged after.

hofmann-elimination.q: Which conditions carry out the elimination step?
hofmann-elimination.why: Silver oxide and water together supply the hydroxide base.

hofmann-elimination.q: What does the silver do besides supplying base?
hofmann-elimination.why: That removes the competing nucleophile from solution.

hofmann-elimination.q: Hofmann elimination follows which mechanism?
hofmann-elimination.why: One step and anti-periplanar, on an unusual substrate.

hofmann-elimination.q: Which alkene does Hofmann elimination favor?
hofmann-elimination.why: That is the opposite of the Zaitsev preference.

hofmann-elimination.q: Why is the less substituted alkene favored?
options: The alkene formed is more stable
hofmann-elimination.why: Bulk on the substrate shields the crowded beta carbon.

hofmann-elimination.q: 2-Amino-2-methylbutane, (CH3)2C(NH2)CH2CH3, is exhaustively methylated and then heated with Ag2O and water. What is the major alkene?
hofmann-elimination.why: The nitrogen sits on C2, so the beta carbons are the two methyls on C2 and the CH2 of the ethyl group. Taking a hydrogen from a methyl gives 2-methylbut-1-ene, disubstituted; taking one from the CH2 gives 2-methylbut-2-ene, trisubstituted and more stable. Zaitsev would pick the trisubstituted one; Hofmann conditions do not, because the bulky trimethylammonium group shields the more substituted side.

hofmann-elimination.q: Which base gives the Hofmann product in ordinary E2?
hofmann-elimination.why: Its bulk reaches only the least hindered beta hydrogen.

hofmann-elimination.q: The transition state takes on what character?
hofmann-elimination.why: The C–H bond breaks well ahead of the C–N bond.

hofmann-elimination.q: Why are the beta hydrogens unusually acidic here?
hofmann-elimination.why: That is what shifts the transition state toward E1cb.

hofmann-elimination.q: Which beta carbon best carries partial negative charge?
options: The one with most alkyl groups
The one bearing the fewest hydrogens
The one with fewest alkyl groups
hofmann-elimination.why: Alkyl groups destabilize a carbanion.

hofmann-elimination.q: How many equivalents of CH3I does 2-aminobutane take?
hofmann-elimination.why: Each equivalent alkylates the lone pair in an SN2; the ammonium salt that results still has an N-H, which a base removes to hand back a neutral, more substituted amine that goes again. The count is the number of N-H hydrogens plus one, so a primary amine takes three.

hofmann-elimination.q: Exhaustive methylation of 2-aminobutane gives:
hofmann-elimination.why: The nitrogen stays on C2 and picks up three methyls.

hofmann-elimination.q: Which carbons are beta in sec-butyltrimethylammonium?
hofmann-elimination.why: The leaving group sits on C2.

hofmann-elimination.q: A trialkylamine is treated with H2O2 to give the amine oxide, then heated to 150 C. Compared with a Hofmann elimination, what is different?
options: The alkene formed is the more substituted one instead of the less
The elimination is syn-periplanar rather than anti, and needs no added base
The mechanism becomes E1, by way of a carbocation intermediate
Nitrogen leaves as an amide anion rather than as a neutral amine
hofmann-elimination.why: This is a Cope elimination. The amine oxide's own oxygen removes the beta hydrogen through a flat five-membered transition state, so the C-H and the C-N that break must be on the SAME side - syn-periplanar, the opposite geometric requirement to E2. No hydroxide or other base is needed. The regiochemistry, though, comes out the same as Hofmann: the less substituted alkene, for the same steric reason.

hofmann-elimination.q: Major product from sec-butyltrimethylammonium hydroxide?
hofmann-elimination.why: Monosubstituted, and the less stable of the two choices.

hofmann-elimination.q: Exhaustive methylation then Ag2O and heat converts PhCH2-CH(NH2)-CH3 mainly into PhCH=CH-CH3, not into PhCH2-CH=CH2. Why?
options: PhCH=CH-CH3 is in fact the less substituted of the two alkenes
The benzylic beta hydrogen is far more acidic, and the E1cb character of the transition state lets acidity outweigh sterics
Ag2O changes the mechanism to E1, so alkene stability decides the outcome
A benzene ring blocks elimination toward a methyl group entirely
hofmann-elimination.why: Hofmann regiochemistry usually comes from two effects that agree: the bulky leaving group makes the hindered side hard to reach, and the positive nitrogen acidifies the beta hydrogens so the C-H breaks ahead of the C-N. Here one beta position is benzylic, its hydrogen is much more acidic, and removing it gives a conjugated alkene - so the acidity effect wins and the more substituted product forms. The real rule is the most acidic ACCESSIBLE beta hydrogen.

hofmann-elimination.q: Besides the alkene, what else is formed?
hofmann-elimination.why: The neutral amine is the leaving group departing.

hofmann-elimination.q: Which of these is NOT a reason exhaustive methylation is required before the elimination can happen?
options: It turns the leaving group from an amide anion into a neutral amine
It makes the beta hydrogens more acidic
It makes the leaving group bulky, which sets the regiochemistry
It changes the nitrogen from sp3 to sp2 hybridized
hofmann-elimination.why: The nitrogen stays sp3 throughout - a quaternary ammonium nitrogen has four sigma bonds and is tetrahedral. The other three are genuine consequences of quaternization: what departs is now a neutral trialkylamine rather than R2N-, the positive charge acidifies the beta hydrogens and gives the transition state E1cb character, and the bulk of the N(CH3)3 group is what shields the more substituted beta carbon.

hofmann-elimination.q: An amine taking two equivalents of CH3I is:
hofmann-elimination.why: One methyl per N–H, plus one to quaternize.

hofmann-elimination.q: How much CH3I does a tertiary amine consume?
hofmann-elimination.why: It has no N–H, so only the quaternizing methyl is needed.

hofmann-elimination.q: Why does a cyclic amine need two rounds?
hofmann-elimination.why: The first elimination only opens the ring.

hofmann-elimination.q: A nitrogen freed only after two rounds was:
hofmann-elimination.why: One C–N bond survives the first elimination.

hofmann-elimination.q: Why is the classical method obsolete?
options: NMR does it on a milligram
hofmann-elimination.why: It answers the same question in minutes rather than weeks.

hofmann-elimination.q: What did the released alkenes reveal?
hofmann-elimination.why: The class of the nitrogen came from the methyl count instead.

hofmann-elimination.q: An unknown amine consumes one equivalent of CH3I on exhaustive methylation and releases its nitrogen after a single round of Ag2O and heat. What is it?
options: A tertiary amine, with the nitrogen not in a ring
A secondary amine, with the nitrogen in a ring
A primary amine, with the nitrogen not in a ring
A quaternary ammonium salt to begin with
hofmann-elimination.why: Two independent readings. One equivalent of CH3I means no N-H hydrogens at all, so the amine is tertiary. One round of elimination freeing the nitrogen means only one C-N bond held it to the fragment being degraded, so the nitrogen was not in a ring - a ring would take two rounds, because the first elimination only opens it.

hofmann-elimination.q: What does Hofmann elimination teach about Zaitsev?
options: It never applies to E2 reactions
It is a tendency, not a law
hofmann-elimination.why: Bulk on the leaving group alone can invert the regiochemistry.
